Tell him to wear a respirator at work
explanation:
Serial peak flows at home and at work
The diagnosis to rule out is occupational asthma, and the optimal way to do this is with serial peak flow measurements at home and at work. Ideally these should take place every 4 h (or at least four times over the course of the day), and include an extended period away from the possible precipitant if possible. In this case flour dust is a well-known precipitant of disease.

Reassurance
Reassurance is incorrect. This gentleman clearly has an undiagnosed respiratory problem that should be investigated.

stem: A 45-year-old man has a history of chronic cough and shortness of breath. Most recently he has begun to suffer from an annoying red/purple nodular rash affecting both shins. There is no past medical history of note apart from mild asthma, for which he has been prescribed a salbutamol inhaler by his GP, and he continues to smoke ten cigarettes per day. On examination his BP is 135/72 mmHg, pulse is 75/min and regular. There is mild wheeze on auscultation of the chest. He has a number of red/purple nodules affecting both shins. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 10.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 201 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 65 mm/1 st hour 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 103 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Corrected Calcium (Ca 2+) 2.82 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Chest X-Ray Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy Which of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Sarcoidosis
The presence of chest symptoms, erythema nodosum, hypercalcaemia and signs of systemic inflammation is highly suggestive of a diagnosis of sarcoidosis. Confirmation of the diagnosis is usually via trans-bronchial biopsy, demonstrating the presence of non-caseating granulomata. Prominent skin lesions or lymph nodes may provide an alternative source of tissue. Corticosteroids are the mainstay of therapy.

Asthma
Asthma is incorrect. The hypercalcaemia, rash (erythema nodosum) and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy are not in keeping with a diagnosis of asthma, they are in keeping with sarcoidosis.

Bronchial carcinoma
Bronchial carcinoma is incorrect. Bronchial carcinoma is a differential diagnosis here, but the presence of a rash suggestive of erythema nodosum is more suggestive of sarcoidosis.

COPD
COPD is incorrect. The hypercalcaemia, rash (erythema nodosum) and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy are not in keeping with a diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD); they are in keeping with sarcoidosis.

Primary hyperparathyroidism
Primary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. The patient is hypercalcaemic but there is clearly more going on here than hyperparathyroidism given the hilar lymphadenopathy, rash and chest symptoms.

stem: A 65-year-old woman has been diagnosed with lung cancer. Which of the following statements is true?
options: Hypercalcaemia associated with bone metastases is best treated with intravenous steroids
Hypercalcaemia can occur without bone metastasis
Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (HPOA) is commonly seen patients with small-cell
Inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) is commonly seen in patients with
Paraneoplastic syndromes occur more commonly with squamous-cell carcinomas
explanation:
Hypercalcaemia can occur without bone metastasis
Hypercalcaemia can occur as a paraneoplastic syndrome with squamous-cell carcinoma. This is caused by the production of a parathyroid hormone-related peptide by the tumour, which increases bone resorption, and renal tubular reabsorption of calcium.

Hypercalcaemia associated with bone metastases is best treated with intravenous steroids
Hypercalcaemia secondary to bone metastases is best treated with intravenous fluids and bisphosphonates. (Steroids are mainly used for treating hypercalcaemia associated with sarcoidosis).

Inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) is commonly seen in patients with
squamous-cell carcinoma SIADH is most common in patients with small-cell carcinoma.

stem: A 50-year-old woman patient presents with increasing dyspnoea. She is obese, smokes and takes oestrogens for menopausal symptoms. On examination you find clinical, electrocardial and radiological findings of a right- sided heart failure without signs of left ventricular failure. What is the most likely cause for the cor pulmonale?
explanation:
Recurrent small pulmonary embolisms
Pulmonary hypertension develops as the result of a critical reduction of cross-sectional area for blood flow. The relatively high flow through non-occluded vessels can cause secondary hypertensive changes in the resistive or precapillary vessels. Patients with mean pulmonary artery pressures over 30 mmHg have a 5-year survival rate of 30%, but this rate falls to 10% if the mean pulmonary artery pressure is over 50 mmHg. Most patients do not have an obvious history of venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism. Dyspnoea is present in virtually all, but in the early stages might occur only on exertion. Compensatory right ventricular hypertrophy develops, and there can be a period of months to years when symptoms remain stable, but ultimately right ventricular function deteriorates. Symptoms then include worsening dyspnoea, fatigue, presyncope, syncope (rarely), pleuritic pain, angina-like pain, abdominal swelling and peripheral oedema. Signs of respiratory and right ventricular failure develop, with cyanosis, grossly elevated jugular venous pulse, palpable right ventricular heave, right ventricular gallop, a loud P2 heart sound, hepatomegaly, ascites and peripheral oedema. Bruits can be heard over the pulmonary arteries.

stem: A 42-year-old man of Pakistani origin comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. He has recently returned from a 6-month visit to a rural area of the country. Prior to presentation he had developed over 6–8 weeks a chronic cough, night sweats and had lost 6 kg in weight. He was confirmed as having active tuberculosis, and is coming to the clinic for a 1-month appointment having started isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide. He feels better but has begun to develop some nausea over the past few days. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 119 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.3 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 181 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 122 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) 290 IU/l (25 at baseline) 5–30 IU/l Alkaline Phosphatase 92 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 10 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Stop all therapy
This patient’s ALT has crossed the threshold of 5× the upper limit of normal (ULN) and intervention for probable drug-induced liver injury is therefore required. Mild non-specific liver injury (ALT < 100) occurs in up to 20% of patients taking isoniazid therapy and most cases of hepatitis as a whole are seen within the first 2–3 months of starting treatment. In this case at 5× the ULN, it is sensible to at least temporarily withdraw all of the anti- tuberculous medications. They can then be progressively re-started, one medication at a time,guidelines usually recommend starting ethambutol first.

Continue treatment with increased monitoring
Continue treatment with increased monitoring is incorrect. Given the degree of hepatic dysfunction, and the fact that the cause of this patient's abnormal liver function tests (LFTs) isn't clear, continuing medication could risk significant liver damage.

Stop isoniazid
Stop isoniazid is incorrect. Given the degree of hepatic dysfunction, and the fact that the cause of this patient's abnormal LFTs isn't clear, continuing medication could risk significant liver damage.

Stop isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide
Stop isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide is incorrect. Ethambutol is a rare cause of hepatotoxicity, all 4 medications should therefore, be discontinued.

Stop rifampicin
Stop rifampicin is incorrect. Stopping rifampicin alone is inadequate given that both isoniazid and pyrazinamide are significant causes of hepatotoxicity.

stem: Which one of the following features is most characteristic of small-cell bronchial carcinoma?
options: A history of prior asbestos exposure
Cancer cell origin from small lymphocytes
Has a relatively better prognosis than other bronchial cancers
Surgery is often the only possible treatment
explanation:
Hyponatraemia
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) resulting in hyponatraemia occurs in approximately 15% of patients with small-cell lung cancer.

A history of prior asbestos exposure
A history of prior asbestos exposure is incorrect. Asbestos exposure increases the risk of lung cancer but is most associated with pleural malignancy (malignant mesothelioma).

Cancer cell origin from small lymphocytes
Cancer cell origin from small lymphocytes is incorrect. Small-cell lung cancer is of neuroendocrine cell origin.

Has a relatively better prognosis than other bronchial cancers
Has a relatively better prognosis than other bronchial cancers is incorrect. The prognosis is very poor and survival beyond two 2 years is exceptional.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has presented with a 3-month history of increasing shortness of breath. The clinical examination is unremarkable, the chest X-ray shows a diffuse reticulonodular appearance and there is hilar lymphadenopathy. A transbronchial biopsy shows widened alveolar septae and granulomas without necrosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sarcoidosis
Respiratory involvement has been described in more than 90% of patients with sarcoidosis. The lung involvement includes both the lymph nodes and the lung parenchyma. Non-caseating granulomas would be seen on biopsy and indicate a diagnosis of sarcoidosis. Scadding and Wurm independently described four stages of the chest X-ray appearances: Stage 1 – hilar adenopathy alone Stage 2 – adenopathy and parenchymal disease Stage 3 – parenchymal disease alone Stage 4 – fibrosis The interstitial disease usually has a diffuse reticulonodular appearance, but confluent patches of disease (alveolar sarcoidosis) have been described. Fibrotic changes due to sarcoidosis are usually present in the upper level lobe, with retraction. The staging system has proved useful in standardising reports of the pulmonary Tutor of

stem: A 51-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis comes to the Emergency Department for review with an exacerbation of her asthma. Current medication includes naproxen, methotrexate, Seretide 250 and salbutamol PRN. She has a cough productive of thick mucus plugs and has been unable to sleep for the past three nights because of coughing. Examination reveals a BP of 123/80 mmHg; pulse is 80/min and regular. Temperature is 37.8 °C. There is bilateral wheeze on auscultation of the chest and peak flow is reduced at 380 (510 expected). Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 122 g/l 115 - 155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.9 × 10 9/l 4 - 11 x 10 9/l Platelets 191 × 10 9/l 150 - 400 x 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 121 μmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Glucose 5.9 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.5 mmol/l* C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 49 mg/l 0 - 10 mg/l Chest X-Ray Clear lung fields Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Prednisolone
Prednisolone is correct. This woman in all likelihood has a viral exacerbation of her asthma. As such the most appropriate intervention is a course of oral steroids, with instruction to use ten puffs of her salbutamol via a spacer at home in lieu of a nebuliser.

Home nebulisers
Home nebulisers is incorrect. This lady has an acute exacerbation and may benefit from an acute prescription of nebulisers in adition to oral steroids. Home nebulisers are a chronic therapy that would not be appropriate to treat an acute exacerbation with.

Monteleukast
Monteleukast is incorrect. Monteleukast is an option if she fails to gain control over the longer term, but should not be used for short-term relief of symptoms related to an exacerbation.

Stop naproxen
Stop naproxen is incorrect. Only a small percentage of patients have NSAID hypersensitivity.

Oral theophylline
Oral theophylline is incorrect. Oral theophylline tablets are not an appropriate acute therapy for an exacerbation and have limited proven benefit in the chronic treatment of asthma.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents to his GP with symptoms of lower respiratory tract infection. This fails to clear after 2 weeks of oral antibiotics and his chest X-ray reveals a suspicious mass in the central region of the right lung. At bronchoscopy the tumour is noted to be particularly vascular. Histology reveals small polygonal cells with a finely granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and the nuclei are small and round. There is no evidence of tumour metastasis. Which of the following represents the most likely diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
Carcinoid tumour of the bronchus
The histological picture seen here, particularly with respect to the granular eosinophilic staining of the cytoplasm, is highly suggestive of a carcinoid tumour. Bronchial carcinoid is thought to derive from stem cells of the bronchial epithelium known as Kulchitsky cells. Around 80–90% of bronchial carcinoid tumours develop in a bronchus of subsegmental size or greater, and so patients often present with bronchial obstruction that has led to a lower respiratory tract infection. Bronchoscopic tumour resection is not recommended, and total surgical resection should be attempted if there is no evidence of metastases. Trials of laser resection have been mooted for palliation where there are metastases.

stem: A 37-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Department with a 2-week history of haemoptysis and a 3- day history of red-coloured urine. She had a similar problem 2 years ago but recovered fully, and has suffered from intermittent episodes of sinusitis and collapse of her nasal bridge. She looked pale and was tachycardic, her pulse was 128 bpm and regular and her BP was 150/96 mmHg. Bilateral crackles were present on auscultation. Investigation: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 75 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 13 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 480 × 10 9/l (Clotting: normal) 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 6.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 46 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 650 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urine analysis showed blood and protein. The chest X-ray showed patchy interstitial shadowing in both lung fields. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is associated with midline sinusitis, pulmonary haemorrhage and renal vasculitis, making it the most likely diagnosis.

Goodpasture syndrome
This recurs less than microscopic polyangiitis making it a less likely diagnosis here, and is not associated with sinusitis.

Microscopic polyangiitis
Microscopic polyangiitis is more rarely associated with pulmonary haemorrhage and isn’t associated with midline sinusitis. More common features include gastrointestinal vasculitis leading to abdominal pain and GI haemorrhage, and mononeuritis.

Polyarteritis nodosa
Polyarteritis nodosa is a necrotizing vasculitis that affects medium sized vessels. It is associated with microaneurysms that can rupture causing haemorrhage and also with thrombosis which can lead to ischaemia and infarctions. It most commonly affects the skin, gut, joints, peripheral nerves and the kidney. Lungs are usually spared. Therefore, this is not a typical presentation of polyarteriti nodosa.

Tuberculosis
This case clearly describes pulmonary haemorrhage with nephritis. This is consistent with vasculitis. Tuberculosis does not fit with this presentation.

stem: A 30-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner for breathlessness, a persistent cough, and painful swelling of both ankles. She feels short of breath on exertion and this has worsened over the last six months. She is originally from Nigeria and has recently moved to the United Kingdom for work. She has history of type II diabetes mellitus which is well controlled with metformin. Her mother died of chronic lung disease at the age of 50. She is married and lives with her husband and two children. She has smoked one packet of cigarettes daily for the last ten years. She drinks 1–2 glasses of wine daily. She denies using any illicit drugs. She denies any exposure to pets or birds. Her ophthalmological examination shows left anterior uveitis and photophobia. Laboratory studies, including serum calcium, was within normal limits. Her electrocardiogram (ECG) shows sinus rhythm. A tuberculin skin test is negative. Her chest X-ray showed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sarcoidosis
Pulmonary symptoms are the most common finding in acute sarcoidosis, and usually include shortness of breath and a non-productive or dry cough, as seen in this patient. She also has iridocyclitis, which occurs in around 25% of sarcoidosis patients. Hypercalcaemia occurs in only 1 in 10 patients with sarcoidosis. It is also important to note that she is of African descent, as sarcoidosis is more frequent in this group. Löfgren syndrome, which is observed in < 5–10% of patients with sarcoidosis, is the combination of erythema nodosum (EN), hilar adenopathy, migratory polyarthralgia and fever, seen primarily in women. This patient does not have EN, which is an important feature of Löfgren syndrome.

stem: A 60-year-old man, who is a 40-per-day smoker, presents to his General Practitioner with shortness of breath. He suffers with a cough productive of scanty white sputum on most mornings. On examination, there is wheeze throughout his chest and bilateral diminished breath sounds. His oxygen saturation (SpO 2) is 94% in room air. Pulmonary functions test reveals a forced expiratory volume 1 (FEV 1) : forced volume capacity (FVC) ratio = 0.68. There is little response to salbutamol which is his only regular medication. A chest X-ray reveals increased pulmonary vasculature and hyperinflation. What is the most important management option to improve the chance of survival in this patient?
explanation:
Smoking cessation
This patient has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in view of his chronic symptoms of breathlessness and productive cough, significant smoking history and spirometry results. The FEV 1 : FVC ratio is less than 0.7, suggesting an obstructive pattern in the spirometry. Smoking cessation has been clearly proven to improve the survival of COPD patients.

Pulmonary rehabilitation
Patients with COPD often decrease their physical activity as exercise can induce or worsen dyspnoea. The progressive deconditioning associated with inactivity initiates a vicious cycle, with dyspnoea becoming problematic at even lower physical demands. Pulmonary rehabilitation aims to break the cycle. Patient-related

stem: Which of the following is the best agent for treating chlamydial pneumonia in a woman who is 25-weeks pregnant?
explanation:
Erythromycin
Macrolide antibiotics (eg erythromycin) are the treatment of choice for Chlamydia pneumonia and other atypical pneumonias. The most frequent side-effects are nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Treatment is likely to be most effective when it is given over a longer time, when suboptimal doses are avoided and if compliance is strict. In this case macrolides would have the best evidence of safety in pregnancy and efficacy, although most evidence to support safe use is in the third trimester. The other choices are incorrect – All of these antibiotics are less effective than macrolides in treating Chlamydial pneumonia therefore erythromycin is the most appropriate treatment of the options given. Piperacillin, clindamycin and ampicillin can be safely used in pregnancy. Imipenem should be avoided in pregnancy given evidence of toxicity in animal studies.

Piperacillin
Piperacillin is incorrect. As described, this would be less effective than erythromycin.

stem: A 29-year-old intravenous heroin abuser is admitted to the Emergency Department with a severe cough, fever and rigors. He says that he has suffered progressively increasing shortness of breath on exertion over the past few days. On examination he has a pyrexia of 37.9 °C, his blood pressure is 122/75 mmHg and his body mass index (BMI) is 17 kg/m2. You hear mild crackles and wheeze on auscultation of his chest. Investigation: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 245 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 90 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 420 IU/l 100–190 IU/l Oxygen saturations 92% on air, 89% after a walk test The chest X-ray shows diffuse bilateral infiltrates. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
The clinical picture seen here, with relatively little to find on auscultation, but with chest X-ray changes and desaturation on exercise, is very typical of Pneumocystis jirovecii infection. This can be diagnosed on the basis of a sputum sample, although bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) might be required to obtain a suitable sample (the yield for BAL samples is over 90%). Co-trimoxazole or pentamidine are both effective treatments for the condition. Given the possible diagnosis, he should be screened for HIV.

Endocarditis
Endocarditis is incorrect. Intravenous drug users are at risk of right-sided endocarditis. However, the history given here is more in keeping with a primary respiratory infection.

Klebsiella pneumoniae pneumonia
Klebsiella pneumoniae pneumonia is incorrect. Intravenous drug users are at risk of Klebsiella and Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia. However, these typically cause a cavitating pneumonia and one would expect to find more on clinical examination given the degree of hypoxia.

Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia
Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia is incorrect. Intravenous drug users are at risk of Klebsiella and S. aureus pneumonia. However, these typically cause a cavitating pneumonia and one would expect to find more on clinical examination given the degree of hypoxia.

Tuberculosis
Tuberculosis is incorrect. Intravenous drug users are at risk of tuberculosis but the history would normally be longer than a few days, as is mentioned here. The relatively normal auscultation findings and desaturation on exercise are more in keeping with Pneumocystis pneumonia.

stem: A 25-year-old smoker of five cigarettes per day for the last two years comes to the clinic complaining of recurrent haemoptysis that he has had for the past two years. He has been treated for intermittent cough and respiratory infections over the past few years. On examination, he looks a little thin but is otherwise well and has not noted any significant weight loss. Respiratory examination raises the suggestion of left upper-lobe collapse. There are no other abnormal findings. Investigation: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 119 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 5.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 187 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l The chest X-ray shows left upper-lobe collapse. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bronchial carcinoid
Recurrent haemoptysis with segmental collapse is a typical presentation of bronchial carcinoid. The prolonged clinical course, without features of carcinoid syndrome, is typical of a bronchial carcinoid tumour.

Bronchial carcinoma
Because this patient is relatively well and has limited chest disease, bronchial carcinoid is much more likely than a carcinoma.

Bronchiectasis
No features suggest that there is active infection, which makes both left upper-lobe pneumonia and bronchiectasis unlikely. Bronchiectasis tends to take a course similar to COPD, where patients will present acutely with infective or non-infective flares. The two-year history here of ongoing haemoptysis is more suggestive of bronchial carcinoid.

Inhaled foreign body
An inhaled foreign body would be more likely to lie in the right main bronchus and so does not fit with the clinical scenario here.

Left upper-lobe pneumonia
No features suggest that there is active infection, which makes both left upper-lobe pneumonia and bronchiectasis unlikely.

stem: A 62-year-old patient has been admitted with a large, left-sided pneumothorax. He has a past history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), for which he has a home nebuliser and takes a high-dose Seretide inhaler. A chest drain was inserted some 60 h earlier, yet when you review it, the drain is still swinging and producing bubbles. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Change the drain for a larger bore one
explanation:
Cardiothoracic surgical review
In this situation suction may cause further damage, therefore surgical review is preferred with consideration for thoracoscopy and surgical pleurodesis. In patients who are unfit for surgery, either medical pleurodesis or a Heimlich valve could be considered. Suction is not routinely recommended and in this situation may cause further damage. When used in primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) suction must be used with caution. Pressures should be in the range of -10– 20 cm H 20. Caution is advised in PSP because of the risk of pulmonary oedema developing, which appears to be a more common problem in younger patients and in those with larger PSPs.

Remove the drain anyway
Remove the drain anyway is incorrect. This would be dangerous as the continued bubbling suggests an ongoing air leak.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of cough and breathlessness. He has also noticed haemoptysis, which he says has worsened gradually. On examination he has bilateral basal crepitations. His chest X-ray shows diffuse shadowing. He has moderate kidney disease. He is previously well and holds down a job as a solicitor. Which investigation would be most useful in obtaining a diagnosis?
explanation:
Renal biopsy
Goodpasture syndrome consists of diffuse pulmonary haemorrhage and glomerulonephritis with linear deposition of antibodies (90% of which are directed against the α3 chain of type IV collagen) along the glomerular basement membrane (GBM). Serological testing for anti-GBM antibodies and ANCA (anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody) is crucial for confirming the diagnosis, and a renal biopsy is almost always warranted. Some healthy individuals exposed to inhaled oils, hydrocarbons or solvents can have borderline raised anti-GBM antibody levels. Anti-GBM antibodies have also been detected in HIV-negative patients with Pneumocystis pneumonia.

Bronchoscopy
Bronchoscopy is incorrect. Bronchosopy may show evidence of pulmonary haemorrhage in Goodpasture syndrome but is not definitively diagnostic.

stem: A 64-year-old woman is referred to the Medical team from the Orthopaedic Ward. She underwent a right total hip replacement four days ago. She is known to suffer from mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and is on regular inhaled steroids and a short-acting beta-2-agonist. The patient complains of pleuritic left-sided chest pain and dyspnoea. The right lower surgical limb has been swollen since surgery. Given the likely diagnosis, what finding is suggestive of right heart strain?
options: Retrograde flow of contrast into the inferior vena cava
ST-segment elevation in electrocardiogram leads V1–V4
explanation:
Retrograde flow of contrast into the inferior vena cava
Retrograde flow of contrast during computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is suggestive of raised right ventricular pressure due to obstructive shock secondary to a pulmonary embolus. In normal CTPA, there should be no contrast in the inferior vena cava (unless the contrast is delivered by a venous catheter in the lower limb) as it is delivered to the functioning right ventricle by the superior vena cava. Clinical features of pulmonary embolism are: dyspnoea tachypnoea (respiratory rate > 20 breaths per minute): the most common feature, occurring in 85% of patients tachycardia: occurs in 30% of patients atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation and premature beats can also occur fever: a frequent finding; occurs in 34–50% of patients.

stem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the clinic for asthma review. She has brittle asthma, is currently taking oral corticosteroids, and requires up to four courses per year. She requires advice on travel vaccination/making sure her vaccinations are up to date as she plans an extensive 3-month tour. Which of the following is contraindicated while on high-dose oral steroids?
explanation:
Yellow fever
Yellow fever vaccination is a live attenuated vaccine, and as such is contraindicated in patients taking high-dose oral steroids. She should be advised not to travel to a yellow fever endemic area. Examples of other live attenuated vaccines include influenza vaccine and the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella).

Hepatitis A
Hepatitis A is incorrect. Hepatitis A is an antigen based vaccine, and as such may be given in patients taking steroids, although the immune response to vaccine may be blunted so they are not as effective as in other individuals.

stem: A 19-year-old man is seen in the Emergency Department with a 1-week history of cough productive of purulent sputum. He has a history of cystic fibrosis. A chest X-ray reveals left-sided upper lobe pneumonia. Which of the following is the most likely organism to cause the diagnosis?
explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common respiratory pathogen in the early years in cystic fibrosis. The proportion of infections with S. aureus diminishes (in favour of Pseudomonas) with increasing age past late teens. In the age group described, however in the vignette, S. aureus is more common.

Burkholderia cepacia
B. cepacia is a well-recognised pathogen in cystic fibrosis: however, it is not as common as Pseudomonas at any age and certainly not as common as S. aureus.

Haemophilus pneumoniae
H. influenzae is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia. In cystic fibrosis, however, at this age, Staphylococcus is more common. H. influenzae colonisation in cystic fibrosis diminishes in the late teens.

stem: A 49-year-old accountant came to the clinic with increased breathlessness. He had begun to become wheezy after a tooth extraction procedure 5 months ago and also had an associated troublesome cough. He used to smoke 15 cigarettes per day but gave up smoking about 2 months ago. Salbutamol and beclometasone inhalers only poorly controlled his symptoms. Recently he had been unwell: he had had a fever and had lost about 3.2 kg (7 lb.) in weight. There was no history of recent foreign travel and no significant past illness. On examination, he had a temperature of 37.2 °C and occasional rhonchi on both sides. Tests showed: haemoglobin 146 g/l, white cell count 10.2 × 109/l (neutrophils 53%, lymphocytes 30%, raised esoinophils noted), ESR 110 mm in 1st hour; normal U&Es; normal urine dipstick. A chest X-ray showed extensive symmetrical, homogenous shadowing affecting all the peripheral lung field. A skin test for inhaled antigens, including Aspergillus fumigatus, was negative. His serum IgE was normal. A serological screen for parasitic infection was negative. Pulmonary function was within normal limits. Oxygen saturations were 97% and there was no desaturation on exercise. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Cryptogenic pulmonary eosinophilia
This patient has eosinophilia and associated pulmonary signs, but no indications of drug involvement or malignancy. He has cryptogenic pulmonary eosinophilia. Systemic features can occur in this condition, including: malaise weight loss

stem: A 58-year-old smoker with chronic bronchitis was treated with antibiotics for a right upper-lobe bronchopneumonia by his GP. After 6 weeks he was readmitted to hospital. The chest X-ray shows signs of a pneumonia in the same place. What is the most likely reason?
explanation:
Bronchial carcinoma with post-stenotic pneumonia
Non-resolving pneumonia is an indication of bronchogenic carcinoma. An ill-defined homogeneous or patchy consolidation in a segmental or non-segmental distribution might be an indication of bronchogenic carcinoma. Patients with these findings are often initially treated for pneumonia; the lack of response to antibiotic therapy suggests the diagnosis of a malignancy. Radiological signs: An endobronchial lesion commonly leads to partial or complete atelectasis and this is the most common sign of bronchogenic carcinoma Bronchial stenosis and post-stenotic changes are commonly seen because most non-small-cell carcinomas demonstrate intraluminal growth. Narrowing of the main bronchi or a complete cut-off can be identified on chest X-rays Complete endobronchial obstruction can sometimes produce distal mucoid impaction, which can be visible on plain chest X-rays as a tubular or branching opacity

stem: Which of the following investigations is most specific to allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA)?
options: An early positive skinprick test for Aspergillus fumigatus
Computed tomographic (CT) evidence of proximal bronchiectasis
Positive history of exposure to Aspergillus
explanation:
An early positive skinprick test for Aspergillus fumigatus
Positive skinprick tests reflect antigen-specific IgE.

Computed tomographic (CT) evidence of proximal bronchiectasis
Computed tomographic (CT) evidence of proximal bronchiectasis is incorrect. Proximal bronchiectasis is a feature of classical ABPA but it is not pathognomic and other causes of bronchiectasis should be considered.

Positive history of exposure to Aspergillus
Positive history of exposure to Aspergillus is incorrect. A specific exposure history is very difficult to elicit. Most people are exposed to small amounts of Aspergillus regularly and inhale spores in the air. However, only a minority become sensitised to Aspergillus and develop ABPA.

stem: A 55-year-old patient has presented with a 4-week history of shortness of breath and cough with occasional bloody phlegm. He has been smoking 10 cigarettes per day for 25 years. The clinical examination, chest X-ray is reported as unremarkable. Laboratory work up reveals mild CO 2 retention consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 91 mm/h. Which of the following investigations is most likely to give the correct diagnosis?
explanation:
Computed tomography thorax
The finding of a normal chest X-ray does not exclude bronchial carcinoma, as patients presenting with haemoptysis and a normal chest X-ray are sometimes found to have a central tumour on bronchoscopy. A computed tomographic scan is usually done first in case the invasive investigation can be avoided.

Follow-up chest X-ray in 6 weeks
Follow-up chest X-ray in 6 weeks is incorrect. The next step in radiological imaging in this case should be a CT thorax. 6-week follow-up chest radiographs are appropriate in patients with pneumonia to ensure Tutor of resolution consolidation. Persistence of consolidation on a radiograph after 6 weeks may indicate endobronchial

Spirometry
Spirometry is incorrect. Spirometry has no diagnostic value in this situation.

stem: A 30-year-old man from Somalia attends your clinic with a productive cough. Sputum is smear-positive for tuberculosis. What does this mean?
options: He needs treatment for tuberculosis and his close contacts need screening, but he is not infectious to
He needs treatment for tuberculosis, but he is not infectious to close or casual contacts
He needs treatment for tuberculosis, his close contacts need screening and he needs to be isolated
explanation:
He needs treatment for tuberculosis, his close contacts need screening and he needs to be isolated
from casual contacts This gentleman has smear-positive tuberculosis. As such he is highly contagious and requires treatment with antituberculous chemotherapy and his close contacts need screening.

He needs treatment for tuberculosis, but he is not infectious to close or casual contacts
He needs treatment for tuberculosis, but he is not infectious to close or casual contacts is incorrect. Smear- positive tuberculosis means the patient is highly infectious to both close contacts (more than 8 hours spent together per day) and casual contacts, such as other patients on the ward and healthcare workers. He therefore needs to be isolated in a negative-pressure room and contacts should wear particulate masks until he has received anti-tuberculous therapy for 2 weeks. The sputum might remain positive after this time, but the organisms will be dead.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with recurrent chest infections. For some time she has noticed that her nails are yellow and misshapen and that she often has oedematous legs after standing all day in the shop where she works. Examination reveals evidence of lower-lobe consolidation and a possible pleural effusion. This is confirmed on chest X-ray. Her nails are very abnormal, thickened and yellow and she has bilateral lymphoedema affecting her legs. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Yellow nail syndrome
Yellow nail syndrome is an abnormality of lymphatic drainage associated with: Recurrent bronchiectasis Small bilateral pleural effusions Lymphoedema Grossly thickened, yellow nails. Her X-ray changes are chronic and associated with bronchiectasis. Management is with antibiotics to treat episodes of acute infection, and regular follow-up.

stem: A 41-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease presents to the Respiratory Clinic for review. She has been referred with increased shortness of breath and decreased exercise tolerance over the past 6 months accompanied by an intermittent dry cough. Her Crohn’s is currently controlled on long-term azathioprine, although she has had extensive surgery in the past. Her BP is 135/70 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. There are fine crackles throughout both lung fields on auscultation. Pulmonary function testing reveals a restrictive defect. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Interstitial lung disease
The diffuse nature of the clinical signs and the restrictive defect on pulmonary function testing fits best with a diagnosis of alveolitis. A clinical picture similar to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, albeit responsive to steroids, is well described in patients with inflammatory bowel disease, seen more often in patients with Crohn’s, rather than ulcerative colitis.

Asthma
Asthma is incorrect. An obstructive pattern of spirometry would be seen in asthma and wheeze, rather than crackles being heard on auscultation.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with inspiratory stridor. His chest X-ray reveals compression of the trachea by a retrosternal goitre. Which of the following investigations is the most useful to assess the severity of his airway obstruction?
explanation:
Flow–volume loop
Flow–volume loop examination is the best way to ascertain the effects of extrathoracic tracheal compression. Patients with retrosternal goitre show proportionally more reduction in the inspiratory flow rate than in the expiratory flow rate. The test is useful to differentiate these patients from patients who have severe airflow limitation or intrathoracic large-airway obstruction. Partial thyroidectomy might be considered where there is considerable inspiratory airflow restriction.

Forced expiratory volume
Chat Forced expiratory volume is incorrect. Flow–volume loop would be a more useful measure to with AI assess theTutor severity of his airway obstruction.

Forced vital capacity
Forced vital capacity is incorrect. Flow–volume loop would be a more useful measure to assess the severity of his airway obstruction.

stem: A 75-year-old man with a body mass index (BMI) of 31 kg/m 2 presents with a history of worsening breathlessness and cough of about 1 week’s duration. He is normally short of breath and has had to give up walking to the shops, which are only 300 m away. He has a chronic cough that is worse in the morning. He is a smoker and smoked 20 cigarettes per day until he became ill this time. His arterial blood gases in room air are as follows: pH 7.24, Pao 2 6.2 kPa, Paco 2 9.8 kPa, bicarbonate 33 mmol/l. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
explanation:
Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
His blood gas results are most compatible with a patient who has severe COPD with an acute exacerbation.

Obstructive sleep apnoea
Obstructive sleep apnoea is incorrect. Although obstructive sleep apnoea can cause chronic respiratory failure, it is unusual to suffer chronic type II respiratory failure except in combination with some other illness like COPD. If the history gave a higher BMI then obstructive sleep apnoea/obesity hypoventilation syndrome may be considered here. However, the smoking history along with chronic cough makes COPD the most likely cause of his type II respiratory failure.

stem: A 61-year-old woman with nephrotic syndrome comes to the Respiratory Clinic with increased shortness of breath over the past 2 months. A large, left-sided pleural effusion was first diagnosed by her GP at the time of onset of symptoms, and he prescribed an increased dose of diuretics. Despite increased furosemide, peripheral oedema having resolved and her symptoms controlled, the effusion is unchanged on chest X-ray. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Diagnostic pleural aspiration
In this situation, where peripheral oedema has resolved in response to increased diuretic therapy, although the effusion is unchanged, diagnostic pleural aspiration for cytology, protein, LDH, pH, gram stain, culture and sensitivity is most appropriate.

Blind pleural biopsy
Blind pleural biopsy is incorrect. Pleural biopsy could be considered, although this is usual post the aspiration results, and is undertaken under radiological guidance.

CT thorax
CT thorax is incorrect. A CT thorax may be appropriate here and should be considered particularly if diagnostic aspiration reveals the effusion is an exudate.

stem: Which one of the following clinical findings is most suggestive of pulmonary embolism?
options: Chest pain worse on deep breathing and a respiratory rate of 26/min
Haemoptysis of more than 5 ml with a negative chest X-ray
Recurrent chest pain in the same location
Spiking temperatures of 39 °C lasting more than 1 week
explanation:
Chest pain worse on deep breathing and a respiratory rate of 26/min
The clinical features of pulmonary embolism (PE) can be diverse and confusing, and range from no symptoms to sudden death. Sudden shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain with haemoptysis and tachypnoea are the commonest features. However, a diagnosis that rests on clinical grounds alone is often incorrect.

Chest pain on lying flat
Chest pain on lying flat is incorrect. Chest pain on lying flat is characteristic of pericarditis. It is not a classical symptom of PE.

Recurrent chest pain in the same location
Recurrent chest pain in the same location is incorrect. Recurrent chest pain in the same location is unusual for PE and it usually indicates an underlying diseased lung (eg bronchiectasis with recurrent chest infection).

stem: A 62-year-old man with a heavy smoking history is referred to the Chest Clinic after a mass is seen on his chest X-ray. Which of the following clinical features might indicate a possibility of curative surgical resection for bronchial carcinoma?
explanation:
Hypercalcaemia
Hypercalcaemia can be due to bony secondaries or to production of parathyroid hormone- (PTH)-like peptide by the tumour. If the hypercalcaemia is due to PTH-like peptide production, then the tumour might be operable.

Forced vital capacity (FVC) < 1.5 pre-operatively
Forced vital capacity (FVC) < 1.5 pre-operatively is incorrect. FVC of less than 1.5 essentially means there is unlikely to be sufficient reserve after pneumonectomy.

Invasive superior vena cava (SVC) obstruction
Invasive superior vena cava (SVC) obstruction is incorrect. The tumour is inoperable if there is invasive SVC obstruction, which occurs in 4% of cases, usually with small-cell carcinoma.

stem: A 32-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department for review, with progressively increasing shortness of breath and a dry cough over the past few days. His exercise tolerance is significantly reduced and he is only able to walk a few metres around his house before he gets short of breath. He has a past history of haemophilia A and grew up in southern Italy before moving to the UK some 4 years ago. On examination, his BP is 132/74 mmHg, pulse is 85/min and regular. He has some white plaques on his tongue and inside his mouth. There are scattered crackles and wheeze on auscultation of the chest. O 2 saturation measured by pulse oximeter falls from 95% to 92% when you get him to walk up and down the corridor outside the consulting room. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 114 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 191 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 134 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) 710 IU/l 100–190 IU/l Chest X-Ray Perihilar fluffy opacities Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
The diagnosis of haemophilia A raises the possibility that this patient has been previously exposed to inadequately screened factor 8, leading to HIV infection. The white oral plaques suggest candida infection due to immunocompromise. In turn the desaturation on minimal exercise, dry cough, elevated LDH and perihilar changes on chest X-Ray (CXR) fit with a diagnosis of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. The organism is confirmed by detection via PCR of sputum samples. Co-trimoxazole is the treatment of choice, given IV in patients with severe disease.

Invasive aspergillosis
Invasive aspergillosis is incorrect. The diagnosis of haemophilia A raises the possibility that this patient has been previously exposed to inadequately screened factor 8, leading to HIV infection. Immunocompromise is a risk factor for invasive aspergillosis, but this condition has a more rapid onset and progression with a very high risk of mortality within days if untreated.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is incorrect. The history suggesting an underlying diagnosis of HIV implies that the correct answer here will be a condition seen more commonly in immunocompromised individuals. The normal creatinine and CXR findings are not in keeping with a likely diagnosis of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

Haemophilus influenzae pneumonia
Haemophilus influenzae pneumonia is incorrect. Haemophilus influenzae pneumonia will usually present as a lobar pneumonia with a raised WCC. The CXR findings, raised LDH and exertional desaturation are more suggestive of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.

stem: A 60-year-old hairdresser complains that, after an attack of flu last year, she has been more breathless than usual when taking her evening walk. She has also felt short of breath when climbing the stairs. She has become concerned that she has a cardiac problem. She has lost about 6.4 kg (14 lbs) in weight during the last year. She has smoked 20 cigarettes per day for 45 years but does not drink alcohol. Other than an occasional paracetamol for headache, she is on no regular medication. On examination she was apyrexic and had bilateral clubbing. No lymphadenopathy was seen. Her jugular venous pressure was not raised and heart sounds were normal. Bibasal inspiratory crepitations were audible. No pedal oedema was seen. Bilateral reticular shadowing, mostly on the bases, was seen on the chest X-ray. Routine bloods were normal, except for an ESR of 35 mm in the 1st hour. Her high-resolution computed tomography scan showed probable fibrosis, most marked in the basal region. Respiratory function tests showed a restrictive ventilatory defect. Bronchoalveolar lavage showed an increased number of cells – neutrophils and macrophages – but no malignant cells. An open-lung biopsy showed an exudate of intra-alveolar macrophages with patchy interstitial fibrosis. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), synonymous with cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis (CFA), is a progressive and usually fatal disease of unknown cause characterised by sequential acute lung injury with subsequent scarring and end-stage lung disease. It may occur in any decade of life but is most commonly seen between the ages of 50 and 60 years; it is slightly more frequent in males than females. A history of progressive breathlessness on exertion in the absence of wheeze is typical. A dry cough may be present, but sputum production is unusual

stem: A 42-year-old woman has had Raynaud’s phenomenon for many years, but now presents to her general practitioner (GP) with non-specific symptoms of shortness of breath and a dry, non-productive cough, as well as heartburn and a flitting arthralgia affecting a number of small joints. On examination, the GP notices that her face appears a little waxy and expressionless and that her hands are cold, with nodular thickening of the skin over the fingers. There is telangiectasia. The most striking abnormality on respiratory examination is fine end-expiratory crackles on chest auscultation. Chest X-ray reveals a fibrotic lung picture. Antinuclear antibodies are positive. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Progressive systemic sclerosis
The picture of Raynaud’s disease, peripheral calcinosis, oesophageal symptoms, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia and evidence of pulmonary fibrosis is highly suggestive of progressive systemic sclerosis. Positive antinuclear antibodies support the diagnosis. Some 30% of patients are also rheumatoid factor-positive. At present, there are no proven disease-modifying agents and patients suffer from progressive symptoms, including worsening pulmonary hypertension. Antifibrotic agents that have been investigated include D- penicillamine, interferon alpha, interferon gamma and immunomodulatory drugs, eg steroids, methotrexate, cyclosporin. Prostacyclin may be used to treat pulmonary hypertension. Calcium antagonists can prove useful in the treatment of Raynaud’s, and there are a number of therapies that can be used for symptomatic reflux disease.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the Respiratory Clinic two weeks after a curative left upper lobectomy for a T2bN0M0 45-mm adenocarcinoma of the lung. The resection margins were clear. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Follow-up computed tomography thorax in two years
Positron emission tomography-computed tomography scan in one year
explanation:
Adjuvant chemotherapy
Adjuvant chemotherapy is the standard therapy for patients with stage II and III non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) after radical surgery, with improvement in 5-year survival of approximately 5%.

Discharge
Follow-up with a patient is required, even though surgery is considered ‘curative’. Although follow-up regimens vary across the country, reasonable and average protocols is to conduct one or two computed tomography (CT) scans in the first two years and then yearly CT scans for three years.

Follow-up computed tomography thorax in two years
At least two computed tomography scans should be conducted in the first two years of recovery from a T2bN0M0 adenocarcinoma of the lung. Then yearly scans should be performed for three years after.

stem: A 28-year-old Afro-Caribbean nurse develops painful nodules on the shins of her legs. She has a low-grade fever and has lost 5 kg in weight over the past 2 months. Her chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. The most likely outcome of this patient’s illness is?
options: Complete initial remission but soon interrupted by increasingly frequent relapses
Complete remission after appropriate course of steroid and cytotoxic drugs
Complete remission without any specific treatment
Diffuse reticulonodular changes in the lung and progressive shortness of breath
Generalised lymphadenopathy and progressive wasting in 5–10 years
explanation:
Complete remission without any specific treatment
This lady has acute sarcoidosis. Spontaneous remission occurs in nearly two-thirds of patients with acute sarcoidosis.

Complete initial remission but soon interrupted by increasingly frequent relapses
Complete initial remission but soon interrupted by increasingly frequent relapses is incorrect. Stage 1 sarcoidosis (ie bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest radiograph) is not usually associated with frequent relapses. At 5 years following initial diagnosis, 95% of patients previously diagnosed with stage 1 sarcoidosis will be asymptomatic.

Complete remission after appropriate course of steroid and cytotoxic drugs
Complete remission after appropriate course of steroid and cytotoxic drugs is incorrect. Spontaneous remission of acute sarcoidosis occurs in nearly two-thirds of patients.

stem: A 58-year-old memorial stonemason presents to the Chest Clinic. Over the past few years he has noted a gradual increase in shortness of breath, with cough and occasional wheeze. He is a non-smoker and has no other past history of note. His chest X-ray is abnormal, with small, rounded opacities and irregular upper-zone fibrosis. There is hilar lymphadenopathy with ‘eggshell’ calcification. Pulmonary function testing reveals a restrictive picture and there is mild hypoxia. Which diagnosis best fits with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Silicosis
This man’s job is likely to have exposed him to silica dust and he seems to have developed silicosis. Silicosis is characterised by shortness of breath, wheeze and cough, with lung function tests and chest X-ray findings consistent with irregular fibrosis. The pathogenesis involves the activation of alveolar macrophages as a result of the ingestion of silica dust, which leads to the release of a number of proteolytic enzymes and inflammatory cytokines. Chronic silicosis might not progress, but accelerated forms and continued exposure are associated with respiratory failure developing over a period of a few years. Management involves removal of exposure, screening for and treatment of any tuberculosis, and supportive measures such as bronchodilators and oxygen therapy.

Byssinosis
Byssinosis is incorrect. There is a clear aetiology of this man’s pulmonary fibrosis given his occupation and the calcification pattern on his chest radiograph is classical for silicosis.

stem: A 35-year-old woman who has been treated for asthma presents for review. She helps with mucking out at a horse-riding stable over the weekends. She had been well until the past year or so, but since then has been suffering from recurrent chest infections, a dry cough and shortness of breath. There is no haemoptysis. Her full blood count reveals a raised eosinophil count. Chest X-ray reveals evidence of pulmonary infiltration and some lobar consolidation. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
This woman helps out at a stable and is likely to have been exposed to Aspergillus fumigatus. Diffuse X-ray changes, an asthmatic-type presentation originally, now bordering on bronchiectasis, with frequent infections and peripheral blood eosinophilia, all point towards a diagnosis of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). Management involves oral prednisolone initially with the addition of an azole in some cases, and then, later on, bronchodilators. The X-ray changes that appear long-term are a response to a type II hypersensitivity reaction.

Asthma
Asthma is incorrect. There is more going on here than pure asthma. The pulmonary infiltrates on chest imaging are not consistent with asthma alone. The likely exposure to Aspergillus fumigatus that the history suggests makes ABPA most likely.

stem: A 19-year-old woman has recently started work as an apprentice in a carpentry factory. She reports cough and wheeze which worsens as the working week progresses. Unusually, however, she seemed free of symptoms when she joined some friends on a week’s holiday to Spain, and certainly she is better at weekends. Her peak flow in the GP surgery is 450 l/min (predicted 510 l/min). You suspect that she might have occupational asthma. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to diagnose this?
options: Trial of 30 mg prednisolone orally for 1 week
explanation:
Peak-flow diary
This woman should measure morning and evening peak flows for a few weeks, ideally two-hourly, taking note of which days she is at work and which are weekends. It is likely that her peak flows will be significantly better during the weekend period and that she would show a degree of airway obstruction first seen in her peak flow measurement on a Monday evening if she works from Monday to Friday. Exposure to wood dust, flux, plastics, solvents, animal allergens and fungi can all contribute to occupational asthma. The best treatment is to remove the patient from the allergen, so it is crucial to make a diagnosis.

Outpatient spirometry
Outpatient spirometry is incorrect. Given the likely diagnosis here is occupational asthma, the most appropriate method of diagnosis is serial peak-flow monitoring both in and out of the patient’s place of work.

stem: A 45-year-old man, presenting with weight loss and cough, is found to have small-cell lung cancer. Which of the following best describes the additional biochemical and clinical features that can occur in this condition?
options: Cushing syndrome, if present, is characterised by buffalo hump, striae and central obesity
Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy is a rare feature
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) occurs in > 60% of cases
explanation:
Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy is a rare feature
Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy is rare in small-cell carcinoma of the lung.

Acidosis is commonly seen
Acidosis is commonly seen is incorrect. Acidosis is rarely seen.

Hypercalcaemia is commonly seen
Hypercalcaemia is commonly seen is incorrect. Small-cell carcinoma is rarely associated with hypercalcaemia despite the high incidence of lytic bone metastases.

stem: A 69-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is referred with a history of recurrent chest infections, intermittent wheeze and production of half an eggcup of phlegm daily, on occasions with a streak of blood. She is a retired secretary and has never smoked. On examination she had coarse crepitations at both the bases. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bronchiectasis
Bronchiectasis is associated with rheumatoid arthritis, occurring in 3–4% of patients with this condition. As with all other causes of bronchiectasis, it presents with recurrent chest infections and excessive phlegm. Recurrent haemoptysis is a common feature. This woman should undergo pulmonary function tests to assess the presence of airway obstruction, which is associated with bronchiectasis. A high-resolution computed tomography scan of the lungs is the investigation of choice to confirm the presence of bronchiectasis.

Carcinoma of the lung
Carcinoma of the lung is incorrect. There is no history of weight loss, she is a non smoker and the haemptysis here is related to airway inflammation from suppurative lung disease. Lung cancer is unlikely here.

stem: A 45-year-old man is referred to you by a contact tracing programme as he was sitting next to a man later found to have active pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) on a flight from Pakistan. The man identified through contact tracing has no history of TB and has not been vaccinated with the BCG. Clinical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the next step?
explanation:
Mantoux testing
In a patient without previous history of BCG vaccination, the Mantoux test is a very useful initial screening tool. A skin reaction of >15 mm in diameter is strongly suggestive of active TB, a diameter between 6 and 15 mm raises the possibility of infection and warrants referral for further investigation.

Prophylactic triple anti-tuberculous therapy
Prophylactic triple anti-tuberculous therapy is incorrect. Prophylactic triple anti-tuberculous therapy is not an appropriate treatment regime for latent TB. Latent infection (ie a positive Mantoux test with unremarkable chest X-ray and no clinical signs of infection) is treated with either 6 months of isoniazid alone, or 3 months of isoniazid in combination with rifampicin.

stem: A 40-year-old farmer’s wife presents to the GP complaining of increasing shortness of breath, worsening cough with mucus plugs and wheeze. She was diagnosed with asthma some years ago and is managed with combination steroid and long-acting ß-agonist (LABA) therapy. She has had two courses of oral corticosteroids in the past 3 months. On examination there is wheeze on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 130 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.0 × 10 9/l (increased eosinophils) 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 235 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l IgE increased Skin-prick test Aspergillus Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l The chest X-ray is reported as showing scattered pulmonary infiltrates but no focal lesion. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) often presents in patients with asthma who have great difficulty controlling their disease, manifesting with mucus plugs or even haemoptysis. It is defined by a number of criteria, including: Clinical deterioration in asthma symptoms Raised IgE levels Positive Aspergillus serology Pulmonary infiltrates on chest X-ray Corticosteroids are the primary therapeutic agent for ABPA, although the addition of itraconazole may improve the resolution of symptoms.

Aspergilloma
Aspergilloma is incorrect. An aspergilloma is a fungal ball that develops within a lung cavity and would usually be visible as such on a chest radiograph. Aspergillus precipitins are usually positive, but skin testing results are variable.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is incorrect. Expectoration of mucus plugs and eosinophilia are not features of IPF. IPF usually presents with progressive dyspnoea and dry cough. Finger clubbing would be likely to be noted and chest radiograph would typically show basal fibrosis.

Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis
Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis is incorrect. Invasive aspergillosis is rapidly fatal if untreated and mortality remains high even if treated with antifungals. Immune suppressed individuals are most at risk of being affected. The insidious nature of this lady’s symptoms rules out invasive aspergillosis as a cause of her symptoms.

Uncomplicated asthma
Uncomplicated asthma is incorrect. The expectoration of mucus plugs and pulmonary infiltrates noted on chest radiograph indicate that this is unlikely to be uncomplicated asthma. These are features of ABPA.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presented with increasing shortness of breath. She also reported that her abdominal girth had increased over the past few months but had put this down to ‘good living’. On examination her GP noticed a right-sided pleural effusion and a very large mass in her right pelvis. Signs of ascites were also present. CA-125, human chorionich gonadotropin (hCG), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and α-fetoprotein (AFP) levels were all unremarkable. A few weeks later a large ovarian fibroma was removed. Some 6 months later she remains well. Which diagnosis best fits with this picture?
explanation:
Meigs syndrome
This syndrome is characterised by the presence of a benign ovarian fibroma, associated with ascites and a right- sided pleural effusion. The average age at presentation is 48 years. Meigs syndrome is associated in 0.004% of ovarian tumours. The aetiology of the pleural effusion is thought to be related to the size of fibroma, leading to accumulated peritoneal ascites that flows into the pleural cavity via the lymphatics or via abdominal–pleural communications (via the foramen of Bochdalek). Removal of the ovarian mass is associated with resolution of the ascites and pleural effusion and patients have an excellent prognosis.

Cirrhosis
Cirrhosis is incorrect. Liver cirrhosis can result in ascites and a unilateral pleural effusion (usually on the right) and with the mention of ‘good living’ one may suspect alcohol excess, which is a risk factor for cirrhosis. However, the mention of a large ovarian fibroma and the fact that her symptoms resolve on removal of this

stem: A 64-year-old retired plumber who is a 20-per-day cigarette smoker presents with increasing breathlessness. Auscultation of the chest reveals bibasal crackles and you note finger clubbing. His chest X-ray shows widespread pleural plaques with additional reticular shadowing at the bases. Lung function tests confirm mild restriction, with a low Tlco. Which of the following is likely to be true?
options: Inhaled steroids can prevent disease progression
Open lung biopsy is mandatory to establish a histological diagnosis
Oral corticosteroids should lead to a significant improvement in lung function
The most likely diagnosis is extrinsic allergic alveolitis
explanation:
The condition is slowly progressive
Pulmonary asbestosis usually affects patients with a history of heavy asbestos exposure. It presents with progressive breathlessness; clubbing occurs in 43% of affected individuals. The changes typically affect the lower lobes and computed tomography can be useful in detecting the disease. The only management advice is to avoid further exposure to asbestos and to stop smoking. The risk of lung cancer is raised more than 50-fold in smokers with asbestos exposure compared with non-smokers who have not been exposed to asbestos.

Inhaled steroids can prevent disease progression
Inhaled steroids can prevent disease progression is incorrect. Inhaled steroids will have no impact on disease progression in asbestosis.

stem: A 78-year-old woman with a previous history of tuberculosis presents to her GP. She has had three episodes of haemoptysis in the past few months. As an ex-smoker she is worried that she might have lung cancer. Chest X- ray reveals an old tuberculosis cavity containing a mass surrounded by a crescent of air. What is the diagnosis that fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Aspergilloma
This scenario fits the clinical picture of an aspergilloma developing in a pre-existing lung cavity due to old tuberculosis. Diagnosis can be confirmed by sputum culture or by serum precipitating antibody. Treatment of aspergilloma is problematic. Up to 10% of aspergillomas resolve spontaneously but, if treatment is required, possibilities are surgical excision or long-term treatment with oral itraconazole. Surgery should be considered as a first-line option where erosion into a major vessel and massive haemoptysis is a possibility.

Bronchial carcinoma
Bronchial carcinoma is incorrect. Smoking is undoubtedly a risk factor for cancer and haemoptysis can be a feature of lung malignancy; however, the mass seen on this radiograph is within a cavity rather than within the lung parenchyma or bronchi and thus aspergilloma is most likely.

stem: Which one of the following features is encountered least frequently in patients with sleep apnoea syndrome?
explanation:
Female gender
Typically patients are male, middle aged and obese.

Daytime sleepiness
Daytime sleepiness is incorrect. Daytime sleepiness is a cardinal feature of obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome (OSAS). Other symptoms include night sweats, personality change, morning confusion and headache.

Hypertension
Hypertension is incorrect. Hypertension is commonly associated with OSAS. There might be an associated increased risk of pulmonary hypertension and cardiac arrhythmias.

Large neck size
Large neck size is incorrect. Large neck size (typically collar size > 17 inches) is classically associated with OSAS.

stem: A 58-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with suspected community-acquired pneumonia. She has a progressively worsening cough, productive of rusty sputum and shortness of breath over the past three days. She smokes five cigarettes per day, has hypertension treated with lisinopril, but no other significant past medical history. On examination her BP is 105/60 mmHg; pulse is 85/min and regular. There are signs of right lower lobe consolidation on auscultation. Respiratory rate is raised at 32, O 2 sats on 40% O 2 are 96%. Investigations: Hb 131 g/l WCC 15.8 × 10 9/l PLT 203 × 10 9/l CRP 230 mg/l Na + 138 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l Creatinine 122 μmol/l Urea 6.9 mmol/l According to CURB-65 criteria, which of the following is a measure of increased severity?
explanation:
Respiratory rate 32/min
CURB-65 criteria were drawn up to provide standardised assessment of the severity of pneumonia. They are listed below confusion at onset (defined as an AMT of 8 or less) urea greater than 7 mmol/l (19 mg/dl) respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute or greater blood pressure less than 90 mmHg systolic or diastolic blood pressure 60 mmHg or less age 65 or older. The number of criteria correlate well with mortality at 30 days: 0 – 0.7% 1 – 3.2% 2 – 13.0% 3 – 17.0% 4 – 41.5% 5 – 57.0% Any score of 2 or greater usually requires hospitalisation.

Age 58
Age 58 is incorrect. Age ≥ 65 is a measure of increased severity.

CRP 230 mg/l
CRP 230 mg/l is incorrect. CRP is not classed as a measure of increased severity.

Urea 6.9 mmol/l
Urea 6.9 mmol/l is incorrect. Urea greater than 7 mmol/l is a measure of increased severity.

WCC 15.8 × 109/l
WCC 15.8 × 10 9/l is incorrect. WCC is not part of the CURB-65 score, which is the severity scoring system used in the UK. The pneumonia severity index, used in the USA, does include WCC with a WCC < 4 × 10 9/l or > 20 × 10 9/l indicating increased severity of pneumonia.

stem: A 20-year-old woman complains of a sudden onset of dyspnoea associated with pleuritic chest pain. She attends the Emergency Unit in the evening. She takes the oral contraceptive pill and has a BMI of 31 kg/m 2. Her O 2 saturation is 92% on air. Chest X-ray is reported as normal, pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following methods of assessment is the most appropriate to confirm your diagnosis of pulmonary embolism?
explanation:
CTPA
CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA), widely available in most Emergency units, is now seen as the diagnostic test of choice for for pulmonary embolus. In this case, with significant symptoms and hypoxia, it is important to confirm the diagnosis.

d-Dimer
d-Dimer is incorrect. A negative d-dimer test is useful for excluding pulmonary embolism (PE) in patients who are clinically thought to be at low risk, but a ‘positive’ result does not establish the diagnosis. We do not have full clinical information here to calculate this lady’s Well’s score, but it is likely she would be classed as high risk and therefore d-dimer testing would be inappropriate.

stem: A 37-year-old woman comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. She has a history of increased wheeze and shortness of breath over the past 6 months, two episodes of pneumonia, and small amounts of fresh haemoptysis over the course of the past 3 weeks. Her weight has remained stable and she is otherwise well. Past history of note includes mild asthma for which she uses a salbutamol inhaler and she takes the combined oral contraceptive pill. She is a non-smoker. Examination is unremarkable, apart from some scattered wheeze on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count 8.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 x 10 9/l (WCC) Platelets 198 × 10 9/l 150–400 x 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 87 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Round, well demarcated 3-cm diameter opacification right Chest X-Ray lower lobe Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bronchial carcinoid
The gradual development of symptoms of wheeze, haemoptysis and a well-demarcated lesion on chest X-ray, in the absence of a smoking history and no worrying signs of weight loss, raises the possibility of bronchial carcinoid. Around 75% of carcinoid tumours can be visualised on bronchoscopy. Care is exercised when taking biopsies as these are vascular lesions which can bleed significantly. Surgical resection is the treatment of choice, with similar operative approaches to those used for bronchial carcinoma. Response to chemotherapy is poor. These are rare, gradually growing, malignant neoplasms with a low rate of malignancy comprising 1–2% of all primary lung cancers. They commonly arise from bronchial epithelium after repetitive exposure to carcinogens. Histological features of bronchial carcinoids can range from low-grade typical to high-grade aggressive atypical carcinoids.

Adenocarcinoma bronchus
Adenocarcinoma bronchus is incorrect. Carcinomas are more likely to be spiculated rather than well demarcated, and have a shorter duration of symptoms prior to presentation. In addition, the relatively young age and lack of weight loss is more suggestive of a non-malignant cause.

Lung metastases
Lung metastases is incorrect. There are no other symptoms to suggest underlying extrapulmonary malignancy.

Small-cell carcinoma
Small-cell carcinoma is incorrect. Carcinomas are more likely to be spiculated rather than well demarcated, and have a shorter duration of symptoms prior to presentation. In addition, the relatively young age and lack of weight loss is more suggestive of a non-malignant cause.

Tuberculosis
Tuberculosis is incorrect. There is no suggestion of an underlying infection, and the chest X-ray appearance is not typical for tuberculosis.

stem: A 25-year-old patient with epilepsy aspirated gastric juice after a seizure (Mendelson syndrome). What is the most likely clinical symptom or sign?
explanation:
Bronchospasm
Mendelson syndrome is an acute pneumonia caused by regurgitation of stomach contents and aspiration of chemical material, usually gastric juices. It can cause severe bronchospasm. The pneumonia develops rapidly, and within hours the patient can become tachypnoeic, hypoxic and febrile. There is minimal sputum. The condition often follows anaesthesia, when the gag reflex is depressed.

Bradypnoea
Bradypnoea is incorrect. Bradypnoea would not be the most likely result of aspiration of gastric juice.

Laryngospasm
Laryngospasm is incorrect. Laryngospasm would not be the most likely result of aspiration of gastric juice.

stem: A woman who is a known alcoholic was rescued from a burning house. She has no burns and appears clinically well, although she has suffered some smoke inhalation. On examination, her temperature is 34°C and she is haemodynamically stable, with a blood pressure of 122/72 mmHg; she is being treated with high-flow oxygen. Arterial blood gas results show: Pao 2 12 kPa, Paco 2 2.6 kPa, pH normal, bicarbonate normal, O 2 saturation 92% on arterial blood gas vs SpO 2 96% on pulse oximetry. What is the cause for the apparent hypoxia seen on the blood gas sample result vs SpO 2?
explanation:
Carbon monoxide poisoning
Data suggest that around one out of eight episodes of carbon monoxide poisoning are related to domestic fires. It is likely that if this woman had consumed alcohol on the night of the fire then she could have been exposed to smoke for a significant period of time before she realised what was happening. Pao 2 levels remain normal (or are elevated when patients are receiving inhaled oxygen, as here). Oxygen saturation on blood gas measurement might be reduced, however, due to preferential binding of haemoglobin to carbon monoxide. With respect to pulse oximetry, most machines cannot differentiate between carbon monoxide and oxygen binding, so do not be lulled into a false sense of security by a normal pulse oximetry result.

stem: A 65-year-old retired ornamental stone mason comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. He has suffered progressively increasing shortness of breath and a dry cough productive of only small amounts of sputum, despite being prescribed salbutamol and Seretide inhalers. He has also lost weight and muscle strength, and now finds it difficult to walk around 500 m on the flat to the local shop. He smokes five cigarettes per day. His BP is 155/82; pulse is 85 and regular. There are wheeze and scattered coarse crackles on auscultation of the chest. He has mild bilateral ankle swelling. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 132 g/l 135 - 175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.1 × 10 9/l 4 - 11 x 10 9/l Platelets 199 × 10 9/l 150 - 400 x 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 μmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Respiratory function tests Mixed obstructive/restrictive picture Chest X-Ray Multiple small opacities, patchy interstitial infiltrates Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Silicosis
The clue in the history is his work as a stonemason, which over a number of years equates to significant exposure to silica dust. The mixed obstructive/restrictive picture coupled with the chest X-Ray (CXR) appearance here support the diagnosis. Smoking is recognised to accelerate deterioriation in silicosis, and he should therefore be strongly encouraged to stop. Signs of right heart failure are present, which should trigger an assessment of suitability for long-term oxygen therapy. Given that the CXR does not indicate progressive massive fibrosis, there is no value in instituting aggressive immunotherapy.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is incorrect. COPD would show an obstructive pattern on spirometry, hyperinflated lungs on chest radiograph and most likely a heavier smoking history.

Extrinsic allergic alveolitis
Extrinsic allergic alveolitis (EAA) is incorrect. There is no allergen exposure in the history suggestive of EAA. CXR in EAA typically shows changes in the upper lobes.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is incorrect. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis would show a restrictive pattern on spirometry, and CXR, if abnormal, would show basal fibrosis +/- honeycombing if disease was advanced.

Pulmonary siderosis
