Pulmonary siderosis is incorrect. Pulmonary siderosis is an occupational lung disease secondary to exposure to iron and its oxides causing deposits within the lungs. It is seen in workers in steel and iron industries. CXR is similar to that seen in pneumoconiosis. Patients are usually asymptomatic. It does not lead to abnormal lung function tests or fibrosis.

stem: What is the most common cause of haemoptysis in UK patients?
explanation:
Respiratory tract infection
The most common cause of haemoptysis is acute infection, in exacerbation of COPD in particular. But other causes should be excluded while investigating. Bronchial carcinoma, pulmonary infarction and tuberculosis are common causes. Pulmonary haemosiderosis, Goodpasture’s syndrome, microscopic polyangiitis, and trauma are some of the rarer causes worth remembering. The question asks for the commonest cause of haemoptysis in the UK, therefore, respiratory tract infection is the correct answer.

Bronchial carcinoma
Bronchial carcinoma is incorrect. This is not the “most” common cause of those given.

Goodpasture’s syndrome
Goodpasture’s syndrome is incorrect. This is not the “most” common cause of those given.

Pulmonary infarction
Pulmonary infarction is incorrect. This is not the “most” common cause of those given.

stem: A 56-year-old man with suspected squamous-cell carcinoma of the right upper lobe of the lung has a normal FEV1 and normal serum biochemistry. Which one of the following investigations is most appropriate to assess operability?
explanation:
Chest computed tomography
Chest computed tomography is the best method for staging squamous-cell carcinoma of the lung. This would indicate the extent of involvement and would inform the surgical approach. Five-year survival rates are > 75% in stage I disease (no nodes, tumour confined within the visceral pleura) and 55% in stage II disease, which includes resection in patients with ipsilateral peribronchial or hilar node involvement. Abdomen and pelvis CT would also be considered to rule out distant metastases.

Bone scan
Bone scan is incorrect. A bone scan is not required as there is no clinical, haematological or biochemical evidence of tumour spread to bony sites.

Sputum cytology
Sputum cytology is incorrect. Sputum cytology is irrelevant, as the diagnosis has already been established.

stem: A 62-year-old ceramics worker comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. He has suffered from progressively increasing shortness of breath and a dry cough over the past year, yet has failed to respond to salbutamol and low-dose beclomethasone inhalers prescribed by his GP. He smokes five cigarettes per day, but has no other significant past medical history. His BP is 149/89 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. O 2 saturation on air is 92% and there are coarse end expiratory crackles and scattered wheeze on auscultation. Spirometry shows a mixed obstructive/restrictive picture, and chest X-ray shows evidence of mediastinal lymph node calcification. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Silicosis
This man’s job as a ceramics worker means that he will have had significant exposure to silica dust over the past few years. The slowly progressive shortness of breath, coupled with a mixed obstructive/restrictive picture not responding to asthma therapies, and the changes seen on chest X-ray, fit with this underlying diagnosis. There is no specific therapy for silicosis, apart from access to oxygen support where required. A number of large-scale trials have shown no impact at all of corticosteroids. Efforts of employers should be to reduce exposure to silica dust where at all possible, with use of adequate dust extraction equipment and breathing apparatus.

COPD
COPD is incorrect. His minimal smoking history and mixed spirometry make chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) unlikely.

stem: A 38-year-old man presents to the Respiratory Clinic with breathlessness on exertion and has inspiratory crackles in the upper zones bilaterally. He has no other medical conditions. He works as an accountant, which he has done since leaving school. He is an ex-smoker, with a ten pack-year history. A chest X-ray reveals upper zone reticulonodular opacifications, more evident in the lateral view. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation:
Langerhans cell histiocytosis
Pulmonary Langerhans histiocytosis can have a varying presentation on radiography, including a bilateral symmetrical reticulonodular pattern, commonly affecting the upper and middle lung zones. Later disease stages may lead to cyst formation. It is more commonly seen in young patients with a history of current or previous smoking. Pulmonary Langerhans histiocytosis is due to proliferation of Langerhans cells in the bronchiolar and bronchial epithelium, forming granulomas.

Asbestosis
Asbestosis would usually result in lower zone fibrosis and therefore, Langerhans cell histiocytosis is more likely. Many of these diseases, however, can affect both the upper and lower zones as they progress. The patient does not have any asbestosis plaques on his X-ray suggesting exposure.

stem: An arterial blood sample from a 48-year-old male patient with progressive dyspnoea over the past few months has an oxygen tension of 8.5 kPa (normal range is 9.3–13.3 kPa) and a carbon dioxide tension of 8.5 kPa (normal range is 4.7–6.0 kPa). Given these blood gas results, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Ankylosing spondylitis
This is type II respiratory failure. The PaCO 2 rises due to hypoventilation and this can occur acutely due to drug overdose or more chronically with gross obesity, kyphoscoliosis (and similar musculoskeletal disorders such as ankylosing spondylitis) and end-stage muscle, neurological and airway disorders. Apical fibrosis can also occur in ankylosing spondylitis, contributing to respiratory failure.

Lobar pneumonia
Lobar pneumonia is incorrect. Lobar pneumonia can cause hypoxia but a normal or low PaCO 2 (type I respiratory failure) unless exhaustion supervenes, when the patient can start to retain carbon dioxide. They would also present more acutely.

stem: A 36-year-old man is referred to the Respiratory Clinic for review. His wife is concerned about his loud snoring and the fact that he stops breathing during the night for periods of up to 8–10 seconds. On occasion, his wife has found that he is unable to recall his days’ activities at work. He has a past medical history of hypertension and borderline type II diabetes mellitus. On examination, he has a heart rate of 80 bpm and regular and a blood pressure of 145/80 mmHg. His chest is clear on auscultation and his oxygen saturation is 94% on air. He has a normal cardiovascular examination. His body mass index is 39 kg/m 2. Which of the following is the next most appropriate investigation to confirm the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polysomnography
This patient has obstructive sleep apnoea. Symptoms include: daytime somnolence grossly disrupted sleep pattern decreased libido systemic hypertension episodic memory impairment. Further investigation should involve thyroid function testing to rule out hypothyroidism and assessment of the uvula and tonsils to rule out mechanical obstruction that might be amenable to surgery.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with brittle asthma is admitted to the Emergency Department with a viral exacerbation of her asthma. Her usual peak flow is around 490 l/min and she is managed with a high-dose Seretide® (salmeterol) inhaler. On examination her blood pressure is 145/80 mmHg, pulse 105 bpm and regular. She has a respiratory rate of 40/min and looks exhausted. On auscultation you can hear wheeze and decreased air entry. Her peak flow is measured at 180 l/min. Investigation: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 249 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l paO 2 10.5 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa paCO 2 6.4 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa Her peak flow has not improved 30 min after admission despite salbutamol and Atrovent® nebulisers and intravenous hydrocortisone. You arrange review by the Intensive Therapy Unit registrar. While you are waiting for her visit, which of the following is the most appropriate next management step?
explanation:
Intravenous magnesium
A Cochrane meta-analysis showed some benefit from intravenous magnesium in acute asthma, and for this reason it is recommended in acute severe asthma that has not responded to inhaled bronchodilator therapy. Her Pco 2 is just outside the upper limit of normal, so she requires urgent admission to the Intensive Therapy Unit.

Inhaled helium/oxygen mixture
Inhaled helium oxygen mixture is incorrect. Helium-oxygen (heliox) mixtures (eg, helium 70 to 80 percent mixed with oxygen 30 to 20 percent, respectively) are used at some centers for severe asthma exacerbations that are unresponsive to standard therapy or appear to have a component of upper airway obstruction (eg vocal cord dysfunction). Routine use of heliox mixtures for asthma exacerbations alone cannot be recommended due to conflicting data about efficacy.

Intravenous aminophylline
Intravenous aminophylline is incorrect. In acute asthma, IV aminophylline is not likely to result in any additional bronchodilation compared to standard care with inhaled bronchodilators and steroids. Side effects such as stomach pain/cramping and vomiting are increased if IV aminophylline is used. Therefore, it is not recommended routinely and should only be used in specific patients after consultation with senior staff.

Intravenous salbutamol
Intravenous salbutamol is incorrect. Intravenous salbutamol should be reserved for individuals in whom inhaled salbutamol cannot be used reliably.

stem: Which one of the following conditions is most likely to be associated with obstructive spirometry and a normal Tlco (transfer factor for carbon monoxide)?
explanation:
Stable asthma
Asthma is associated with airflow obstruction. Transfer factor is usually unaffected. The Tlco is sometimes increased in patients with bronchial asthma during an attack, but the cause of this change is not known. The other options are all incorrect. These conditions are all associated with a reduced transfer factor. The diffusion of carbon monoxide (CO) from the alveoli to the pulmonary blood is governed by the integrity of the alveolar membrane, the capillary blood volume, or both (the air–blood barrier). A reduction in the diffusion capacity of CO is encountered in conditions affecting the capillary bed size (eg pulmonary emboli, pulmonary vasculitis) or conditions that cause changes in the characteristics of the alveolar membrane, such as diseases in which some form of intra-alveolar filling process has occurred and the air–blood diffusion pathway is actually lengthened (eg pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, alveolar proteinosis). Similarly, the transfer factor for carbon monoxide (Tlco) is reduced in patients with infiltrative disorders of the lung that affect both the capillary bed size and the alveolar membrane integrity (eg sarcoidosis, interstitial lung diseases, collagen vascular diseases). Removal or destruction of lung tissue (eg post-surgery, emphysema) decreases both membrane and blood volume components and produces a low Tlco. An increase in Tlco results occasionally from an increase in capillary blood volume secondary to haemodynamic changes in the pulmonary circulation, an increase in pulmonary artrial or left atrial pressuresChat (eg with in congestive heart failure) or an increase in pulmonary blood flow (eg in artrial septal defect). Alveolar haemorrhage from

stem: A 45-year-old man who races pigeons becomes breathless. Which of the following features is suggestive of extrinsic allergic alveolitis (EAA)?
options: Almost immediate onset of symptoms after exposure
explanation:
Circulating IgG precipitins
Circulating IgG precipitins are suggestive of EAA.

Almost immediate onset of symptoms after exposure
Almost immediate onset of symptoms after exposure is incorrect. EAA can be classified according to how acutely it presents. In the acute form, fever, cough and marked shortness of breath occur 4–6 h after exposure In the subacute form there is weight loss and fatigue

Positive skinprick testing
Positive skinprick testing is incorrect. Despite its name, EAA is not allergic and therefore features associated with allergy and type I reactions do not tend to occur in EAA (ie wheeze, immediate symptoms, raised IgE, positive skinprick test, eosinophilia of blood or sputum).

stem: A 32-year-old man presents to the clinic with weight loss, a dry cough and intermittent, dull, right-sided chest pain. He admits to use of intravenous heroin. On examination, his BP is 110/70 mmHg, his pulse is 75 bpm and regular, and his temperature is 37.9 °C. There is decreased air entry at the right base and his abdomen is soft and non-tender. His body mass index (BMI) is 19 kg/m 2. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.0 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 201 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 123 μmol/l 50–120µmol/l C-reactive Protein (CRP) 187 mg/l 0–10 mg/l PA chest X-ray Right-sided effusion Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation:
Aspirate under ultrasound guidance
In this situation, bedside pleural fluid aspiration under ultrasound guidance is most likely to deliver an underlying diagnosis. It should then be assessed with respect to differential cell count, pH and amylase.

Bronchosopy
Given the presence of a pleural effusion and history suggestive of infection, aspiration of the effusion would be more helpful than bronchoscopy.

CT chest
Prior to attempted complete drainage of the effusion, CT thorax would be indicated. Here, moving to diagnostic aspiration, ultrasound guidance is adequate.

Lateral chest X-ray
A lateral chest X-ray is unlikely to give any additional helpful information in this case.

Thoracoscopy and biopsy
Thoracosopy and biopsy is usually considered when malignant pleural disease is a possibility.

stem: An overweight 54-year-old man landed at Heathrow Airport after a long-haul flight from Australia and collapsed while waiting for his luggage. After fluid resuscitation his systolic blood pressure is only 80 mmHg on arrival at the Emergency Department. His Po2 is 6.3 kPa on a re-breather mask and his Pco2 is 3.1 kPa. His chest X-ray reveals possible slight elevation of the right diaphragm. Electrocardiography reveals tachycardia. Apparently he had had a cough and was laid up for a few days before travelling. Which diagnosis best fits this clinical picture?
explanation:
Pulmonary embolism
This man has circulatory decompensation and profound hypoxia, suggestive of a massive pulmonary embolus. Although not mentioned in the scenario, the electrocardiogram might show the S1Q3T3 pattern in this case, although more commonly sinus tachycardia +/- right heart strain is seen. He has almost certainly acquired his pulmonary embolus secondary to a deep vein thrombosis as a result of his inactivity during the flight. Management in the acute phase includes heparin by continuous infusion, with consideration of thrombolysis using streptokinase if he fails to stabilise with fluid replacement. For a first pulmonary embolus where there is a clear precipitating factor (as in this case), treatment with warfarin or a novel oral anticoagulant (NOAC) would usually be continued for 3 months.

stem: A 26-year-old man presents with fever, headache and a non-productive cough. The chest X-ray shows increased interstitial markings. The laboratory examination shows an elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and anaemia and he is positive for cold agglutinins. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Erythromycin
This patient presents with Mycoplasma pneumonia. The typical patient is usually a young adult who experiences a respiratory tract infection accompanied by headache, myalgia, cough and fever, and with a chest X-ray that shows bronchopneumonia. The cough is often non-productive, but when sputum is obtained it is mucoid, shows predominantly mononuclear cells and no dominant organism. The diagnosis should be suspected in those patients with a relatively mild form of pneumonia, particularly in previously healthy young adults. The pathogen does not have a cell wall and so is not susceptible to penicillin, cephalosporins or other antibiotics that are active against the bacterial cell wall. Macrolide antibiotics (eg erythromycin or clarithromycin) are the treatment of choice for mycoplasmal and other atypical pneumonias. The most frequent side-effects are nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Treatment is likely to be most effective when given over a long period rather than for a short time, when suboptimal doses are avoided and when compliance is strict. A characteristic feature of mycoplasmal pneumonia is the relatively high frequency of extrapulmonary complications, including:

stem: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department with thorax injuries after a road traffic accident. Her chest X-ray shows multiple rib fractures and a right-sided shadow suggestive of a haemothorax. Her O 2 saturation is compromised at 91% on 10 litres of oxygen. What is the next step in her management?
explanation:
Intercostal drain insertion
A haemothorax is the result of bleeding into the pleural space, and is arbitrarily diagnosed on the basis of having a haematocrit that is more than half that of peripheral blood. This distinguishes it from a blood-stained effusion, which can be associated with a number of different pathological processes. The vast majority of haemothoraces are associated with penetrating or non-penetrating trauma, including iatrogenic procedures such as central venous catheterisation. Bleeding usually results from parenchymal laceration or damage to intercostal vessels. A pneumothorax is present in a high proportion of patients. The treatment of choice is to insert a large intercostal drain (28–32 F), allowing evacuation of blood and reducing the incidence of a subsequent fibrothorax. If this reveals continued bleeding, a thoracotomy might be required. Surgery is not indicated simply to remove any residual blood clots because there is spontaneous lysis with no residual damage in the majority of patients.

stem: A 72-year-old man is admitted via the on-call team with an acute respiratory tract infection. He has a 40 pack- year smoking history and continues to smoke 15 cigarettes per day. After recovery from his initial infection, lung function testing indicates that his FEV 1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 s) is less than 50% of predicted, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is diagnosed. This is his third exacerbation this year so far that has necessitated hospital admission. What is the best long-term pharmacological intervention for him?
options: Combination therapy with a long acting anti-muscarinic and a long-acting ß 2-agonist
High-dose inhaled steroid therapy as prophylaxis
Inhaled short-acting anticholinergics for symptom relief
Low-dose beclometasone inhaled-steroid therapy as prophylaxis
Salbutamol as required for symptom relief
explanation:
Combination therapy with a long acting anti-muscarinic and a long-acting ß 2-agonist
NICE guidelines recommend the initial pharmacological therapy is combination therapy with a long acting anti- muscarinic antagonists and a long-acting β 2-agonist. Of course, this combination should be used in conjunction with smoking cessation where possible, and long-term home oxygen therapy if the criteria for its prescription are met.

Inhaled short-acting anticholinergics for symptom relief
Inhaled short-acting anticholinergics for symptom relief is incorrect. Although short-acting anticholinergics and salbutamol may provide temporary symptom relief, they do not have the benefits of long-acting cholinergics or combination therapy in terms of exacerbation frequency reduction and for patients with asthmatic features.

stem: A 25-year-old man is admitted with dyspnoea. Pulmonary function tests reveal a reduced peak expiratory flow rate that is 55% below the normal range for his height and age. He has no past medical history of note, smokes five cigarettes per day and keeps a pet cat. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Asthma
The peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) is an indicator of large-airways disease. It is a measurement of a maximal forced expiration through a peak-flow meter. It correlates well with the forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) and is used as an estimate of airway calibre. The PEFR can be monitored by patients at home to assess asthma control and is of value in both the diagnosis and the management of asthma.

Bronchial carcinoma
Bronchial carcinoma is incorrect. Reduced PEFR is not a classical presenting sign of bronchial carcinoma and the young age and lack of significant smoking history make carcinoma unlikely.

Kyphoscoliosis
Kyphoscoliosis is incorrect. PEFR would not be significantly reduced in kyphoscoliosis.

stem: A 60-year-old previously fit and well man develops a small pneumothorax (<1cm) after a computed tomography- (CT-) guided biopsy of a left upper-lobe mass. He is asymptomatic. The most appropriate management of his pneumothorax should be:
options: Intercostal tube drainage and high-pressure suction
explanation:
Conservative management only
Treatment of pneumothorax remains a difficult area. In this case the patient has a small pneumothorax and is asymptomatic. It is likely this pneumothorax will resolve without invasive intervention. If the patient deteriorates, then aspiration with or without intercostal tube drainage would be the next step.

Aspiration
Aspiration is incorrect. Aspiration is only recommended in patients over 50 with significant smoking history and underlying lung disease if they are breathless.

Intercostal tube drainage and high-pressure suction
Intercostal tube drainage and high-pressure suction is incorrect. Intercostal drain insertion for pneumothoraces is reserved for tension pneumothoraces, large (>2 cm rim) pneumothoraces in breathless patients with underlying lung disease or when aspiration is indicated but is unsuccessful.

stem: Antituberculous treatment for 12 months is recommended for which of the following?
explanation:
TB meningitis
For TB meningitis, a 12-month course of rifampicin and isoniazid should be given with pyrazinamide and another drug for the first 2 months.

Genitourinary TB
Genitourinary TB is incorrect. A 6-month course of treatment is adequate for all non-CNS disease.

Miliary TB
Miliary TB is incorrect. A 6-month course of treatment is adequate for all non-CNS disease.

TB of the spine
TB of the spine is incorrect. A 6-month course of treatment is adequate for all non-CNS disease. This includes TB of the spine, where it is the vertebrae that are affected and not the spinal cord. Surgery may be necessary in addition if there are any features of instability.

stem: A 40-year-old Afro-Caribbean woman who has lived almost all her life in the UK presents to clinic following an insurance medical examination, where she was found to have bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on her chest X- ray. Her computed tomographic (CT) scan confirms hilar lymphadenopathy and reports nodularity in the lung fields. Routine blood tests are unremarkable. What would you do next?
options: Arrange a transbronchial needle aspiration of a lymph node
Observe and repeat her chest X-ray in 3 months
explanation:
Observe and repeat her chest X-ray in 3 months
She can be followed up and observed radiologically at regular intervals. Some 50% of patients with stage 2 sarcoidosis (ie hilar lymphadenopathy and parenchymal infiltrate) recover spontaneously in 2 years.

Arrange a lung biopsy
Arrange a lung biopsy is incorrect. This woman has typical features of pulmonary and lymph-node sarcoid. If the history and radiology is typical, the diagnosis of sarcoidosis can be confidently made and there may not be a need to proceed to tissue biopsy. If there were atypical features and tissue biopsy was required, either transbronchial or open lung biopsy would be preferable.

Commence oral prednisolone
Commence oral prednisolone is incorrect. In the absence of symptoms, she does not need steroid treatment.

stem: A 50-year-old sales representative with a body mass index (BMI) of 34 kg/m 2 is referred to the Sleep Clinic because he keeps falling asleep at the wheel. His wife complains that he keeps her awake all night with his snoring. A sleep study confirms moderate sleep apnoea. He has been warned not to return to driving until he has been treated and his symptoms are under control. Which one of the treatments below would be the most appropriate management in this case?
explanation:
Continuous positive airway pressure
Obstructive sleep apnoea is caused by loss of upper airway pharyngeal muscle tone during rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, which leads to airway obstruction and consequent apnoeic episodes. It affects 1–2% of middle-aged men. CPAP is an effective treatment for sleep apnoea and should be offered (alongside weight loss and alcohol reduction) to this patient.

Mandibular advancement splinting
Mandibular advancement splinting is incorrect. Many trials have looked at the effectiveness of mandibular advancement splints (a tailor-made mouthpiece which helps to keep the jaw forward and aids upper airway muscle tone when asleep). Mandibular advancement splints are recommended as second-line therapy where patients tolerate them or can be used as a first-line treatment in mild sleep apnoea.

stem: A 48-year-old man with hepatitis B is admitted via his GP with a history of breathlessness. He has signs of chronic liver disease and does not want to stay in hospital. His international normalised ratio (INR) is 2.8 and his chest X-ray appears normal. The nurses comment that his oxygen saturation drops from 98% to 91% on room air every time he gets up to leave. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hepatopulmonary syndrome
This gentleman has hepatopulmonary syndrome: Hepatic disease can result in right-to-left shunting, secondary to intrapulmonary vasodilatation mainly in the lower lobes. This is similar to pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (PAVMs) in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, where the PAVMs are located mostly in the lower lobes As a result, there is increased blood flow through the lower lobes when the patient moves from the supine to the erect position. This results in blood from the lower lobes, which is more poorly oxygenated, entering the left side of the heart, this leads to oxygen desaturation in the erect position. This phenomenon is called ‘orthodeoxia’.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with a history of proximal muscle weakness. He has had a cough for eight weeks. He also has pain in the small joints of the hands, and has small haemorrhages in the nail folds. He is apyrexial and there is no lymphadenopathy or clubbing. Bibasal crackles can be heard on auscultation and his chest X-ray reveals diffuse reticular infiltrates. Lung function tests show a restrictive pattern. Abnormal bloods of note include an elevated CK of 890 U/l, and an ESR of 75 mm/1 st hour. What of the following is the most likely underlying cause of his interstitial lung disease?
explanation:
Polymyositis
Polymyositis and dermatomyositis are inflammatory conditions involving the muscle and skin, respectively. Patients often complain of proximal muscle weakness. Pain in the small joints of the fingers is associated with the condition. Patients might present with ragged cuticles and haemorrhages at the finger nail folds. Interstitial lung disease can occur in these patients. Underlying malignancy of the lung, ovary, breast or stomach is present in 5–8% of cases.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. Rheumatoid arthritis is not associated with raised creatine kinase. Proximal muscle weakness with raised CK is more in keeping with polymyositis.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with severe asthma. She is visiting the area on holiday, but her partner informs you that she has had three admissions to the Intensive Therapy Unit at home and has brittle asthma that is poorly controlled with maximum-dose Seretide®, theophylline and intermittent oral corticosteroids. On examination she looks tired and has a respiratory rate of 21/min. There is marked wheeze and poor air entry on auscultation of the chest. Investigation: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 245 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l An electrocardiogram (ECG) shows sinus tachycardia (104 bpm). Saturations are 94% on oxygen on admission with a peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) of 160 l/min. You arrange back-to-back nebulisers and ask the FY2 doctor to repeat some arterial blood gases afterwards. Which of the following would be most worrying when you review the results?
explanation:
Normal carbon dioxide
A normal carbon dioxide in the face of inadequate respiratory effort can indicate increasing fatigue. A normal carbon dioxide in the presence of a slightly reduced oxygen might therefore be an indication for mechanical ventilation. Patients can deteriorate rapidly, so frequent reassessment and early involvement of an intensive- care physician in the management of acute severe asthma is strongly recommended.

Normal bicarbonate
Normal bicarbonate is incorrect. A normal bicarbonate is not an adverse sign in an acute exacerbation of asthma.

Normal pH
Normal pH is incorrect. A normal pH is not an adverse sign in an acute exacerbation of asthma, a low pH is.

Raised lactate
Raised lactate is incorrect. Raised lactate is worrying and implies tissue hypoxia; it can also be a side-effect of salbutamol. However, normal carbon dioxide levels are the most worrying of the options listed and suggests that this patient may deteriorate further and require invasive ventilation.

Slightly low oxygen
Slightly low oxygen is incorrect. Markedly low oxygen would be a worrying sign. Slighty reduced oxygen levels are not of immediate concern, but clearly indicate that the individual needs prompt treatment and continuous reassessment in case of deterioration.

stem: A 21-year-old male smoker presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset of left-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. He takes no regular medication and has not received a diagnosis of significant chest disease. A chest X-ray confirms the clinical suspicion of a left sided pneumothorax with a 2.5cm rim of air. What should the management of his pneumothorax be?
explanation:
Aspiration
The immediate management of a spontaneous primary pneumothorax >2cm is air aspiration.

100% inspired oxygen for 24hrs
100% inspired oxygen is incorrect. High-flow oxygen is helpful regardless of a patient’s oxygen saturations in pneumothorax as it aids resolution of the pneumothorax; however, 100% oxygen is not required. The correct initial management is aspiration.

Conservative treatment
Conservative treatment is incorrect. In a young, stable patient conservative management can be considered if the pneumothorax is small (rim of air is < 2 cm at level of hilum).

stem: A 17-year-old man has been complaining of shortness of breath for the last 2 days. On examination, bronchial breathing is heard over the right lower lobe. What is the most likely diagnosis for this clinical finding?
explanation:
Pneumonia
The classic presentation of pneumonia is of a cough and fever with the variable presence of sputum production, dyspnoea and pleurisy. Most patients have constitutional symptoms such as malaise, fatigue and asthenia, and many also have gastrointestinal symptoms. Although patients with pneumonia usually present with these characteristic clinical features, there can be major differences in presentation, depending on host factors and the aetiological agent. Bronchial breathing is heard over an airless lung, such as in consolidation, atelectasis or dense fibrosis. There is some resemblance to the sounds heard over the normal trachea, but, by comparison with normal breath sounds, bronchial breathing is higher in pitch and more blowing in quality. It does not have to be loud. Bronchial breath sounds are classically heard throughout both inspiration and expiration. Very quiet breath sounds are heard over hyperinflated lungs, as in emphysema, or when breath sounds are prevented from reaching the chest wall by a layer of air, fluid or fibrosis.

stem: A 72-year-old farmer presented with a history of massive haemoptysis. He has a 50-year smoking history and takes inhaled long-acting ß 2-agonists and steroids. His chest X-ray showed a smooth left upper-lobe mass. Investigations showed positive Aspergillus fumigatus precipitins. He was transfused and resuscitated. In the meantime, he had another massive haemoptysis but was maintaining a systolic blood pressure of 145 mmHg and a pulse of 85 bpm. What is the next appropriate management?
options: Nebulised ß-agonist therapy to reduce bronchospasm
explanation:
Angiography and embolisation
With such a long smoking history, this patient is likely to have significant chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. In this respect, although he has a large aspergilloma, it is probably worth first trying angiography and embolisation, with lobar resection as the intervention of next resort. Case series from tertiary referral centres suggest that the bleeding site can be identified and bleeding controlled in up to 90% of cases. Poor prognostic factors for haemoptysis include: Increasing age Pre-existing lung or cardiac disease Respiratory compromise Hypoxia Ongoing haemoptysis

stem: A 72-year-old woman who smokes 5–10 cigarettes per day and has a past history of whooping cough presents with chronic cough and recurrent chest infections for review. She admits to producing frequent amounts of purulent sputum and of intermittently suffering night sweats for a number of months. There have also been occasional episodes of haemoptysis. Chest X-ray reveals hyperinflation, crowded lung markings and small, cyst-like spaces at the lung bases. What is the most likely underlying pathology?
explanation:
Bronchiectasis
The past history of whooping cough and smoking, coupled with the X-ray changes, are very suggestive of bronchiectasis. Non-pharmacological management involves self-physiotherapy and adequate hydration. Chronic intermittent oral antibiotic therapy is used by some physicians, although it might encourage the development of multi-drug resistance and its use is not universally endorsed. Influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations are strongly recommended. Surgical referral might be recommended for patients with chronic severe localised infection that fails to resolve after intravenous antibiotic therapy.

Bronchial carcinoma
Bronchial carcinoma is incorrect. Bronchial carcinoma causing a lobar airway obstruction and subsequent recurrent infectons is a reasonable differential here. However, the history of whooping cough and the chest radiograph appearances point more towards a diagnosis of bronchiectasis.

stem: A 47-year-old man has been admitted to hospital with increasing shortness of breath, sweats and purulent sputum. He is known to the team to be homeless and has a history of alcohol misuse. His Emergency Department records indicate that he was admitted in an unconscious state a few days ago but self-discharged when he woke up. On examination there is pyrexia and dullness at the apex associated with bronchial breathing. His chest X-ray shows right middle-lobe consolidation. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Aspiration
The typical patient with aspiration pneumonia has gingival crevice disease combined with a predisposition for aspiration that is usually due to a suppressed level of consciousness or dysphagia. The clinical presentation is usually more subtle than that for pneumococcal pneumonia, in that the infection evolves over a period of many days, weeks, or even months. Chest X-rays usually show infection in a dependent segment (usually the superior segments of the lower lobes or posterior segments of the upper lobes as these are dependent in the recumbent position), fever and sputum that is often putrid; evidence of chronic disease with weight loss or anaemia is also frequently found.

Mycoplasma infection
Mycoplasma infection is incorrect. Mycoplasma causes an atypical pneumonia and features in the history may include atypical symptoms of pneumonia, such as headache, dry cough, or gastrointestinal upset. The history given in this case is classical for an aspiration pneumonia rather than a pneumona caused by an atypical

stem: A 60-year-old man presents to the Respiratory Clinic. He has a 2-week history of haemoptysis and right-sided hip pain. A chest X-ray shows a mass in the left lower zone. A CT scan of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis shows an irregular left lower lobe 1.3-cm mass in the cardiophrenic angle adjacent to the left hemidiaphragm. A 2 cm mediastinal adenopathy is at the left hilum and subcarinal area. There is an expansive lytic lesion in the right superior iliac crest and pedicle of the T12 vertebra, along with a 1-cm hypoattenuating liver mass.’ Which of the following is the most appropriate cause of action?
options: Computed tomography-guided biopsy of left lower lobe mass
Ultrasound scan-guided biopsy of iliac crest lesion
explanation:
Endobronchial ultrasound biopsy
Endobronchial ultrasound biopsy is most likely to be diagnostic here. This patient has stage IV lung cancer (ie spread to lymph nodes or distant metastasis is present) and the most appropriate course of action is rapid determination of the pathology.

Positron emission tomography
This patient already has stage IV disease. Occasionally, a PET scan is useful if there is oligometastatic disease as a target for high-grade palliative therapy. In this case, however, there is no role.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with a pleural effusion. You perform a diagnostic pleural aspiration. Which of the following is true regarding the results that you might receive from the laboratory?
options: An eosinophilia makes malignancy less likely
Heavy bloodstaining effectively excludes pulmonary embolic disease
High glucose levels occur in rheumatoid arthritis
Low levels of salivary amylase suggest oesophageal rupture
The presence of antinuclear factor is virtually diagnostic of scleroderma
explanation:
An eosinophilia makes malignancy less likely
Pleural fluid eosinophilia makes malignancy and tuberculosis (TB) less likely, and suggests air in the pleural cavity.

Heavy bloodstaining effectively excludes pulmonary embolic disease
Heavy bloodstaining effectively excludes pulmonary embolic disease is incorrect. Heavily bloodstained fluid in the absence of trauma suggests pulmonary infarction or malignancy.

Low levels of salivary amylase suggest oesophageal rupture
Low levels of salivary amylase suggest oesophageal rupture is incorrect. High levels of salivary amylase suggest oesophageal rupture.

stem: A 34-year-old woman is admitted with left-sided pleuritic chest pain and signs consistent with a left leg deep venous thrombosis. D-dimers are elevated and you arrange for her to have a chest X-ray. Which of the following is the most common initial chest X-ray finding in a patient with pulmonary embolism?
explanation:
Normal
All of the other options may be seen in conjunction with a pulmonary embolus, but images are most commonly normal, at least in the initial stages after pulmonary embolism. For this reason when index of suspicion is high, either a CT pulmonary angiogram or a ventilation perfusion scan is required to confirm or refute the diagnosis. The major role of the chest X-ray is in establishing an alternative diagnosis.

Basal atelectasis
Basal atelectasis is incorrect. Basal atelectasis may be seen in conjunction with a pulmonary but embolus, Tutormost commonly images are normal, at least in the initial stages after pulmonary embolus.

Lobar infarct
Lobar infarct is incorrect. Lobar infarct may be seen in conjunction with a pulmonary embolus, but most commonly images are normal, at least in the initial stages after pulmonary embolus.

stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with chronic progressive shortness of breath and bibasal crepitations. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is characterised by an inflammatory cell infiltrate. The main symptoms are dry cough, exertional dyspnoea and malaise. Signs include cyanosis, finger clubbing and fine end-inspiratory crepitation at the bases and in the axillae. Bilateral lower-zone reticulonodular shadows are seen on chest X- ray. Lung damage is often irreversible but pirfenidone is recommended between 50% and 80% predicted. Lung transplantation may be considered. Overall, the median survival is 2–3 years following diagnosis.

Extrinsic allergic alveolitis
Extrinsic allergic alveolitis is incorrect. Extrinsic allergic alveolitis shows a predilection for the upper zones, although, when severe, can affect all zones.

Progressive massive fibrosis
Progressive massive fibrosis is incorrect. Progressive massive fibrosis describes a stage of a number of occupational lung diseases which are caused by mineral dusts – silicosis and coal-worker’s pneumoconiosis. When the irregular or linear opacities become large shadows late in the course of these diseases this is then

stem: Carcinoma of the lung is diagnosed in a 66-year-old smoker. Which of the following techniques would be most reliable in staging of the intrathoracic lymph node involvement?
explanation:
Computed tomographic scanning
Computed tomographic (CT) scanning is recommended as a staging procedure for patients who are candidates for potentially curative surgery. This investigation would identify enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes in order to determine the best approach for biopsy or aspiration cytology of the appropriate lymph node. Where available, positron emission tomography (PET) scanning may be superior, but there are a limited number of scanners in the UK. CT scanning can be performed with or without contrast enhancement, depending on local protocols and the ability to see the relevant mediastinal structures without the need for contrast. Contrast enhancement makes it easier for inexperienced observers to interpret the CT findings. Overall, preoperative CT staging has been shown to overstage or understage when compared with operative findings in 40% of patients. This means that patients should not be denied surgery on the basis of equivocal CT findings, and histological or cytological confirmation of intrathoracic lymph node involvement is required for patients in whom the only contraindication to potentially curative surgery is lymph node enlargement.

stem: A 42-year-old patient was diagnosed with mediastinal tuberculosis 3 weeks ago and commenced on treatment. He presents with worsening breathlessness and stridor. His chest X-ray shows mediastinal lymph nodes that are compressing the carina; although he is distressed, he is alert and orientated and maintaining his oxygenation. You give him an injection of hydrocortisone. What is the next step in the investigation and/or management?
explanation:
Urgent computed tomography (CT) scan
The computed tomographic (CT) scan is the most appropriate investigation. On enhanced CT scans, nodes larger than 2 cm in diameter invariably show central areas of low attenuation and peripheral rim enhancement. Enhanced walls are usually irregular in thickness. CT scan is useful prior to commencing steroid therapy, first to confirm the degree of airway compression and second to assess the response to anti-tuberculous therapy. A number of commentators recommend rapid initiation of steroid therapy, and this would seem sensible prior to progression to CT scanning.

Heparin
Heparin is incorrect. Heparin would be an appropriate therapy for a pulmonary embolus. This gentleman’s dyspnoea has a clear explanation (extrinsic compression of carina) and so treatment for pulmonary embolus would be inappropriate.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department with symptoms of a respiratory tract infection. According to her relatives she has had a cough for the past week, has become progressively more short of breath, and is now confused, convinced that her husband is trying to poison her. On examination she is pyrexial 38.2 °C, pulse is 95/min, her BP is 100/60 mmHg. There are clear signs of a right lower lobe pneumonia and her respiratory rate is 27/min. She tries to hit you during the consultation. Her urea is 5.2 mmol/l on arterial blood gas. Which of the following according to CURB 65 criteria is associated with a worse prognosis?
explanation:
Confusion
The CURB-65 criteria include age > 65, BP < 90 mmHg systolic or 60 mmHg diastolic, respiratory rate > 30/min, urea >7 mmol/l. Patients with 3 or more features are at high risk of death, and thus require urgent hospital admission with IV antibiotic therapy the preferred option. Scores of 1 or 2 are associated with increased risk of death and therefore expert assessment with respect to management is recommended.

Respiratory rate 27/min
Respiratory rate 27/min is incorrect. Respiratory rate > 30/min is associated with a worse prognosis in line with the CURB-65 criteria.

stem: A 38-year-old woman comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. She has had three episodes of lower respiratory tract infection over the past 5 months, and continues to cough up significant amounts of purulent sputum every morning and has night sweats on 2–3 occasions each week. She smokes five cigarettes per day, drinks 10 units of alcohol per week and works as a cleaner at a local school. Examination reveals evidence of right lower lobe consolidation. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 12.2 × 10 9/l (increased neutrophils) 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 201 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 95 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 85 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Chest X-Ray Patchy right lower lobe consolidation Bronchial wall dilatation and thickening CT chest affecting the right lower lobe Which of the following is the mainstay of therapy?
explanation:
Airway clearance physiotherapy
The cornerstone of therapy for bronchiectasis is teaching physiotherapy techniques to allow adequate clearance of mucopurulent sputum each morning.

Inhaled β-2 agonists
Inhaled β-2 agonists is incorrect. Inhaled β-2 agonists only have a role if there is a degree of reversible airways obstruction.

Inhaled corticosteroids
Inhaled corticosteroids is incorrect. Inhaled corticosteroids only have a role if there is a degree of reversible airways obstruction.

Partial lung resection
Partial lung resection is incorrect. Partial lung resection is an option for patients who do not achieve clearance of chronic infection, who otherwise have a good functional status.

stem: A 52-year-old woman who is a non-smoker presents to the Respiratory Outpatients Department with increasing breathlessness. She has a history of rheumatoid arthritis. Lung function confirms: forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1) 1.5 l, forced vital capacity (FVC) 4.4 l, gas transfer factor (Tlco) 70% of predicted and transfer coefficient (Kco) 95% of predicted. What is the likely explanation for her breathlessness?
explanation:
Bronchiolitis obliterans
Bronchiolitis obliterans is characterised by the development of granulation tissue in small airways. It presents with breathlessness and is rapidly progressive in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. Lung function usually shows severe irreversible airway obstruction. The transfer factor may be low but the transfer coefficient (Kco) is often normal.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is incorrect. Both the transfer factor and Kco are either normal or both reduced in COPD.

Emphysema
Emphysema is incorrect. Both the transfer factor and Kco are reduced in emphysema.

stem: An anxious, 25-year-old saleswoman presented with mild shortness of breath on exertion, which had come on gradually over several months. The symptom was intermittent and seemed to get worse in the evening. She had also been on treatment for depression over the previous 2 months. On examination, she has minimal weakness of shoulder abductors and slight weakness of eye opening bilaterally. Deep tendon reflexes are present and symmetrical throughout and plantars responses are flexor. You now have the results of the investigations – FBC, U&E, LFT, electrocardiography, chest X-ray and lung function tests were all normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Myasthenia gravis
This young woman has myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune condition. Muscle weakness might not be apparent on a single examination, so the examination should be repeated – most affected are the ocular and shoulder- girdle muscles Clinical features Respiratory and proximal lower limb muscles can be involved early in the disease. Breathlessness can develop early and cause sudden death. Swallowing problems, slurred speech and difficulty in chewing can be caused by bulbar involvement. Asymmetrical involvement of an external ocular muscle can mimic cranial nerve palsy but pupillary reflexes are normal.

stem: A 72-year-old man comes to the Respiratory Clinic with increased shortness of breath and wheeze. His GP has tried him on a regular salbutamol inhaler, but this has had little effect on his symptoms. Unfortunately he continues to smoke 30 cigarettes per day and has done for the past 50 years. On examination, his blood pressure is 155/85 mmHg and his body mass index (BMI) is 21 kg/m 2. He has respiratory changes consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), including coarse wheeze throughout both lung fields and crackles. Investigation: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 123 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.7 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 201 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 130 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l FEV 1 50% of predicted Transfer factor reduced Which of the following most closely correlates with mortality in COPD?
explanation:
FEV1
The FEV 1 is the factor that correlates most closely with mortality in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Other factors have been built in to the BODE index, an index of mortality in COPD developed by the Medical Research Council (MRC). This index also incorporates the body mass index, dyspnoea and exercise capacity (as evidenced by a 6-min walk test). The BODE index can also be used to estimate the risk of hospitalisation. Stopping smoking will have the biggest impact on this man’s prognosis, with regular short- acting anticholinergics and ß-agonists useful for symptomatic relief. Given that he has severe COPD, as evidenced by his FEV 1, a trial of high-dose inhaled corticosteroid and ß-agonist therapy might be appropriate.

Functional residual capacity
Functional residual capacity is incorrect. This lung function index is not a good predictor of mortality in COPD.

Peak expiratory flow rate
Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) is incorrect. FEV1 rather than PEFR value correlates most closely as a predictor of mortality in COPD.

Residual volume
Residual volume is incorrect. This lung function index is not a good predictor of mortality in COPD.

Total lung capacity
Total lung capacity is incorrect. This lung function index is not a good predictor of mortality in COPD.

stem: A 74-year-old man, who is a retired builder of railway carriages, presents to his General Practitioner (GP). Over the past year or so, he has noticed gradually increasing shortness of breath on exertion. He has a frequent dry and non-productive cough. On examination, the GP notices that he has digital clubbing, peripheral oedema and a raised jugulare venous pressure, with fine end-inspiratory crackles heard at the bases on auscultation. Chest X-ray reveals irregular shadows in the lower lung zones and thickened pleural plaques affecting the lower zones. What diagnosis would fit best with this clinical history and these findings on examination and investigation?
explanation:
Asbestosis
The clue lies in this man’s occupation – asbestos fibres were often used in the building of railway carriages. There is a long gap between exposure to the fibres and asbestosis of some 20–30 years, so many cases are still coming to light, and quite some time after the exposure to asbestos was curtailed. Currently, around 5–10 new cases per 100 000 of the population occur per year. Diagnosis of asbestosis is confirmed on the basis of exposure history, typical imaging studies and isolation of fibres. Arterial blood gas measurement in these patients usually demonstrates hypoxia, while pulmonary function tests demonstrate decreased vital capacity, decreased total lung capacity and decreased gas transfer. Death can occur due to cor pulmonale or asbestos- exposure-related cancer (mesothelioma or bronchial carcinoma). Therapy is with oxygen by prescription and effective management of acute infections, butChat decline with is usually inexorable.

stem: A 66-year-old retired boilermaker presents to the Respiratory Clinic with shortness of breath. He has smoked ten cigarettes per day for the past 30 years. He is fighting for breath on minimal exercise and has shortness of breath at rest. Obstructive lung disease is suspected and spirometry results show: forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1) 1.74 l (predicted 3.0 l), forced vital capacity (FVC) 2.5 l (predicted 2.8 l); post-salbutamol FEV 1 1.81 l, post-salbutamol FVC 2.7 l; transfer factor 55%. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
The forced vital capacity (FVC) is only slightly reduced, but the ratio of the forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1) to the FVC (FEV 1/FVC) is more significantly reduced. Transfer factor is also reduced at 55%. With reversibility of less than 10% post-salbutamol, the most likely diagnosis here is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Stopping smoking is the key initial measure, with trials also indicating that high-dose inhaled steroids combined with long-acting ß2-agonists might reduce exacerbation rates and improve quality of life in comparison with other options.

Asbestos-related pleural plaque disease
Asbestos-related pleural plaque disease is incorrect. Asbestos-related pleural plaque disease is not associated with abnormal lung function.

stem: A 71-year-old man is admitted with an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history. He is usually independent at home and manages with no intervention or social support. He has been unwell for the past three days with an increasing cough that is productive of purulent sputum. On admission, he appears to be significantly hypoxic and hypercapnic, with a p(O 2) of 7.1 kPa and a p(CO 2) of 5.9 kPa. He is very short of breath and appears confused with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13/15. He does not want to be ventilated and wishes to die. He becomes increasingly tired and becomes unresponsive 30 minutes later. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan with respect to management?
options: Ask the family to consent for him to be intubated
Contact hospital legal team to proceed to intubate
Continue on supplemental oxygen and antibiotics only
Intubate, act in the patient's best interest and inform the relatives
explanation:
Intubate, act in the patient's best interest and inform the relatives
Given the confusion, reduced Glasgow Coma Scale score and hypoxia, it is important to act in the patient’s best interests, particularly given his reasonable baseline before his presentation.

Ask the family to consent for him to be intubated
The family should not have the final decision with respect to intubation. The decision on management is the doctor's, but the family should be closely informed with respect to the patient's treatment.

stem: A 38-year-old man presents to the GP complaining of shortness of breath. He has a history of smoking 10 cigarettes per day and is obese. Other history of note includes hypertension, for which he is treated with atenolol 50 mg daily. Pulmonary function shows: Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) 540 l/min (predicted is 600 l/min) Ratio of the forced expiratory volume in 1 s to the forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC) is 90% predicted The FVC falls when measured supine versus standing up Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Obesity-related changes in pulmonary function tests
explanation:
Obesity-related changes in pulmonary function tests
This man has small reductions in the peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) and in the ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 s to the forced vital capacity (FEV 1/FVC), and the FVC falls when measured in the supine position. The most likely explanation here is increased abdominal fat, leading to a functional reduction in FVC. Treatment of choice is aggressive weight reduction, and he should also be encouraged to stop smoking. Finally, atenolol might not be the most appropriate choice of antihypertensive treatment in a young man. If there is a suggestion of erectile dysfunction, a switch to an alternative agent such as an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor should be considered.

stem: A 56-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis complains that she has had recurrent haemoptysis for over 5 years. She has never smoked and her only medication is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agent. She tells you that she coughs up phlegm every day and at times this contains streaks of fresh blood. She has no known respiratory disease, but tends to get frequent chest infections that are relieved by a course of antibiotics. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bronchiectasis
Some 3–4% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis develop clinical symptoms of bronchiectasis, although typical bronchiectasis changes may be seen on up to 30% of CTs of the thorax in patients with rheumatoid. This is characterised by recurrent haemoptysis. The history of expectorating phlegm on most days and frequent chest infections is suggestive of the diagnosis. A high-resolution computed tomography scan of her lungs will establish the diagnosis.

Lung cancer
Lung cancer is incorrect. Her lack of smoking history coupled with a history of rheumatoid arthritis and long (5- year) history of chronic productive cough with recurrent respiratory infections is more in keeping with bronchiectasis than malignancy.

stem: A 50-year-old woman comes to the clinic complaining of breathlessness on exertion, which has been worsening for one year. This is accompanied by wheeze which worsens with exercise, and during the course of the summer when she also has severe hayfever. She has never smoked. The chest X-ray shows mild hyperinflation but is otherwise unremarkable. Her lung function test results are shown below: Test Result Predicted FEV 1 (l) 1.1 1.7–3.0 FVC (l) 2.7 2.0–3.5 FRC (l) 4.2 1.7–3.4 TLC (l) 6.5 3.6–5.6 Tlco (mmol/min per kPa) 5.86 5.7–9.5 Kco (mmol/min per kPa per l) 1.63 1.66 What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Asthma
This woman has obstructive spirometry, with raised lung volumes. This is suggestive of asthma or COPD. She has never smoked and has a normal transfer factor and so she is more likely to have asthma.

stem: A 50-year-old patient presents with blood eosinophilia in association with a radiographic pulmonary infiltrate. A bronchoscopy shows an excess of eosinophils in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid in the absence of pathogenic micro-organisms. The diagnosis of eosinophilic pneumonia is made. What is the best treatment apart from removing the causal factors?
explanation:
Systemic steroids
Eosinophilic pneumonia often responds well to corticosteroid medication, although treatment might need to be prolonged (6 months or more) in patients with the chronic forms of the disorder. The importance of identifying whether it is associated with the causal factors listed below lies in the need to manage these. Otherwise, eosinophilic pneumonia may not respond adequately to steroid therapy; the associated diseases can also produce other manifestations. Ask yourself whether there are any causal factors: Is there parasitic infestation? Have any drugs been administered? Is there asthma? Is there evidence of allergy to parasites or drugs? Is there evidence of allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis (particularly aspergillosis)? Is there evidence of vasculitis? Is there evidence of the hypereosinophilic syndrome?

stem: You are asked to review a patient with known asthma on the Haematology Ward. He is neutropenic from chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma. He has a cough and a low-grade fever, sparse crepitations on chest examination and his chest X-ray shows diffuse pulmonary shadowing. He has been on broad-spectrum antibiotics for one week with no improvement. His sputum has shown a few hyphae, but is culture-negative. His blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg, pulse is 95 bpm and regular. His temperature is 37.9 °C. Oxygen saturation is 91% on air. Blood cultures have been negative. Aspergillus precipitins are negative, as is an Aspergillus skinprick test. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Invasive aspergillosis
Aspergillosis has a wide range of clinical manifestations, reflecting variation in the host immune status and responses. The major sub-types of aspergillosis are: aspergilloma – usually asymptomatic, sometimes mild haemoptysis invasive aspergillosis – fever, cough with copious sputum production, and pleuritic chest pain allergic pulmonary aspergillosis – productive cough, wheeze, and shortness of breath chronic pulmonary aspergillosis – chronic productive cough and shortness of breath. Aspergillosis investigations include:

stem: You see a 70-year-old woman in the clinic with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She currently smokes 10 cigarettes per day and is breathless when walking around her house and garden. She has an FEV1 of 1.2 litres (40% predicted) and an FVC of 2.0 litres (50% predicted). She had minimal bronchodilator reversibility following nebulised salbutamol. Her oxygen saturations are 93% on air and she takes salbutamol only as needed. What would be the next treatment option for her?
explanation:
Long-acting anticholinergic inhaler
This woman has severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) on the evidence of her spirometry and is now symptomatic. Clearly she needs to stop smoking, but the next treatment would be a long-acting anticholinergic inhaler or high-dose inhaled corticosteroids combined with a long-acting β-2 agonist

Oral leukotriene-receptor antagonist
Oral leukotriene-receptor antagonist is incorrect. Oral leukotriene-receptor antagonists are not used in the management of COPD.

stem: You are asked to see a 57-year-old smoker, who complains of shortness of breath some 7 days after a total hip replacement. On examination, he is obese and has a swollen left leg. He is also visibly short of breath. There appears to be increased prominence of vascular markings at the right hilum on the chest X-ray. His calculated alveolar–arterial (a–a) gradient is 34 mmHg (10–24 normal range). Which of the following fits best with his diagnosis?
explanation:
Pulmonary embolus
The alveolar–arterial (A–a) gradient is affected primarily by ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch and shunting. This means that changes in alveolar–arterial gradient occur with ventilatory disorders, such as pneumonia, and disorders of the vasculature, such as a pulmonary embolus. Pulmonary embolus is the most likely diagnosis here. The alveolar–arterial (A–a) gradient is calculated using the following equation (where PAo2 is the alveolar oxygen, and Pao2 and Paco2 are the arterial O2 and CO2 levels, respectively): P Ao 2 – (Pao 2 + Paco 2/0.8) The alveolar oxygen level in kPa is calculated by: (100 - 7)/100 × % inspired O 2 eg for 21% O 2, the P Ao 2 would be 20 mmHg. The gradient is then calculated by taking the arterial partial pressure of oxygen from the alveolar one.

stem: A 41-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis is admitted to the Emergency Department with an exacerbation of her asthma. She is normally well controlled with a regular fluticasone/salmeterol 50 inhaler and her peak flow runs at approximately 450 l/min (540 l/min predicted). She takes methotrexate and naproxen for control of her rheumatoid arthritis. On examination her BP is 137/85 mmHg, with pulse 92/min and regular. There is marked wheeze on auscultation of the chest and her peak flow is reduced to 285 l/min. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 120 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.5 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 167 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 112 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 31 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Chest X-Ray No focal changes She is nebulised in the department and her peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) improves to 350 l/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Oral corticosteroids
A short course of oral steroids is likely to help settle her acute exacerbation of asthma, or wheeze, and help reduce the need for further nebulisation.

Home nebuliser
Home nebuliser is incorrect. If the patient is sufficiently unwell to need nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, then she should be in hospital until off nebulisers for 24 h. Home nebulisers are sometimes needed in severe and end-stage asthma when other options are exhausted. A relatively young patient is unlikely to carry nebulisers with them, making home nebulisers unlikely to be helpful in many exacerbations.

Oral clarithromycin and cortiosteroids
Oral clarithromycin and cortiosteroids is incorrect. There is no indication for antibiotics in this situation, bearing in mind that her CRP is only slightly elevated and the CXR is unremarkable.

Stop methotrexate
Stop methotrexate is incorrect. Methotrexate is a drug that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and thereby functions as an anti-metabolite. It is useful in the management of rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn’s disease and psoriasis. It should be stopped in active infection due to its immunosuppressive effects, but this patient has no evidence of acute infection.

Stop naproxen
Stop naproxen is incorrect. Given that this patient is likely to have been taking non-steroidal anti-inflammatories (NSAIDs) for some time, it is extremely unlikely she will suddenly have acquired sensitivity to naproxen. As such, stopping it will have little impact on her asthma symptoms and may have significant negative impact with respect to her joint pain.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset, right-sided, pleuritic chest pain associated with breathlessness while he was playing football. He was previously diagnosed to have benign skin lesions and fibrofolliculomas of the skin. He has smoked ten cigarettes per day for the last six years. His sister developed a pneumothorax two years ago. His mother was diagnosed with kidney cancer. On examination, his respiratory rate is 16 breaths/min, his heart rate is 92 bpm, saturation 96% in room air, and his blood pressure is 128/66 mmHg. On auscultation of the chest, reduced breath sounds are noted on the right side. A chest X-ray reveals a small pneumothorax which has a 1.5-cm rim between the lung margin and the chest wall. His computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest shows a right-sided pneumothorax and multiple lung cysts. Which of the following investigations will be most useful to reach a diagnosis?
options: Repeat CT chest in four weeks
explanation:
Genetic testing
This patient is known to have pneumothorax, lung cysts and fibrofolliculoma of skin. He has a family history of pneumothorax and renal cancer. The most likely diagnosis in this case is Birt–Hogg–Dubé (BHD) syndrome which is an autosomal dominant syndrome characterised by pneumothorax, lung cysts, renal cancer and skin fibrofolliculomas. This is caused by mutation of folliculin gene, which is the hallmark of this syndrome. Genetic testing, therefore, is the correct option.

stem: A 45-year-old businessman returns to the UK from Texas. Shortly after arriving back he develops an acute illness with substernal ache, arthralgia and breathlessness. A chest X-ray shows soft pulmonary infiltrates in the upper lobes and mild mediastinal widening. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Histoplasmosis
Histoplasmosis is the most common systemic mycosis in North America. It presents with symptoms of an acute upper respiratory tract infection, with substernal pain. Typical X-ray changes include patchy pulmonary infiltrates with mediastinal widening. About 5% of patients have pleural effusions. Arthralgia occurs in about 10% of patients. The diagnosis tests on culture of Histoplasma capsulatum from blood, urine, bone marrow and sputum. In pulmonary histoplasmosis treatment with amphotericin B is not required unless patients show signs of respiratory insufficiency.

Histiocytosis X
Histiocytosis X is incorrect. Histiocytosis X (also known as Langerhans cell histiocytosis) is an uncommon interstitial lung disease primarily related to smoking. Chest imaging characteristically reveals an upper-zone predominance of bilateral, symmetric, ill-defined nodules and reticulonodular infiltrates. As the disease progresses, cystic lesions appear.

stem: A 40-year-old single male carpenter presents to casualty with a three-week history of increasing shortness of breath and night sweats. He is a lifelong non-smoker. Temperature on admission is 38.2°C. On auscultation of his chest he has bilateral inspiratory crepitations. There are no signs of peripheral oedema, and he is thin with a BMI of 19.5. You ask him to walk the length of the ward holding a portable pulse oximeter, and note that his oxygen saturation begins to fall rapidly. Arterial blood gases (on air) reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value pH 7.36 7.35–7.45 pO2 8.0 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa pCO2 5.1 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa Bicarbonate (HCO3-) 20.1 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l His chest x-ray is shown below. Which of the following represents the most likely underlying diagnosis in this case?
explanation: C Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) PCP is most commonly seen related to immunodeﬁciency in patients who are HIV-positive. The fact that he desaturates on a walk test is typical of this condition, as are the clinical signs, which are much more prominent than the subtle ground-glass appearance xray changes. Incidence is highest when the CD4 lymphocyte count falls below 100/mm3. Diagnosis is via sputum to look for cysts of PCP or via bronchioalvelolar lavage ﬂuid if sputum is negative. Treatment is with co-trimoxazole given either orally or IV; alternatives include pentamidine. After one episode of infection, patients should be maintained on prophylactic co-trimoxazole to prevent further acute episodes. A Community-acquired pneumonia The subacute course of this patient’s disease, coupled with the patchy bilateral areas of consolidation, is inconsistent with common causes of community-acquired pneumonia such as S. pneumoniae. B Fibrosing alveolitis The time course of this patient’s symptoms would be considered too short for the onset of ﬁbrosing alveolitis, also known as Idiopathic pulmonary ﬁbrosis (IPF). The desaturation on exercise is also characteristic of PCP. D Pulmonary oedema Patchy consolidation and pyrexia are more consistent with infection versus cardiac failure. The lack of signiﬁcant cardiac risk factors also counts against pulmonary oedema as the cause of symptoms seen here. E Pulmonary embolism Acute-onset pleuritic chest pain is absent from the history given here, and the patchy consolidation and pyrexia don’t ﬁt with an acute PE.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with a history of intravenous drug abuse attends for review. She has a history of gradually increasing shortness of breath over the past 18 months to 2 years. There has been associated intermittent fevers and weight loss of some 5 kg. She has tested negative for hepatitis B some 6 months earlier. On examination there are lower zone inspiratory crackles. Investigations reveal Hb of 92 g/l and a diffuse increase in immunoglobulins, renal function testing is normal. Chest X-ray is shown below. Lung biopsy reveals diffuse interstitial lymphoid inﬁltrates and pulmonary function tests suggest a restrictive lung defect. Which of the following diagnoses ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
A Lymphoid interstitial pneumonia Clinical features of lymphoid interstitial pneumonia include gradual-onset breathlessness over a considerable time, intermittent fevers and weight loss, with inspiratory crackles on examination. There is mild anaemia with a diffuse increase in immunoglobulins. The chest x-ray showing a thin walled cystic lesion in the right mid zone and histology revealing lymphoid interstitial inﬁltrates are in keeping with the diagnosis. Steroids may improve symptoms, although around one-third of patients progress to extensive ﬁbrosis. Associations include HIV, connective tissue disease, hepatitis B infection, chronic active hepatitis and Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

E Respiratory bronchiolitis-associated interstitial lung disease RBALD is primarily associated with heavy smoking and presents with pigment-loaded macrophages in the pulmonary inﬁltrates rather than the lymphocytes seen here. B Idiopathic pulmonary ﬁbrosis Idiopathic pulmonary ﬁbrosis implies there is no identiﬁed underlying cause; against a background of IV drug abuse, secondary interstitial lung disease should be excluded before describing the changes seen here as idiopathic. C Viral pneumonia Given the chronic nature of this patient’s symptoms, viral pneumonia is very unlikely to be responsible. D Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Although hypersensitivity pneumonitis may be seen, particularly against a background of cocaine smoking, it is stated that this patient’s mode of drug abuse is primarily intravenous.

stem: A 57-year-old man with a 40 pack per year smoking history presents to his General Practitioner with fatigue and lack of concentration, making it difﬁcult for him to even attend work. His wife tells you that he is frequently sleeping in front of the television. On examination, his heart rate is 88 bpm and his blood pressure is 136/90 mmHg. He has a normal cardiovascular examination and auscultation of the lung ﬁelds demonstrates mild expiratory wheeze, while oxygen saturation is 91%. His height measures 180 cm, weight 120 kg and neck circumference 44 cm. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment option?
explanation:
C Overnight continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) Overnight continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is the treatment of choice as it has been shown in studies to be effective in reducing obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) symptoms and is the ﬁrst line in moderate to severe disease requiring intervention. However, it does not prevent cardiovascular mortality associated with OSA. Hypnotics worsen OSA, as do alcohol, smoking and obesity, and so patients should alter their lifestyle appropriately, with weight loss and alcohol and smoking cessation as ﬁrst-line treatment. Long-term oxygen therapy has not been shown to have any longterm beneﬁt in OSA patients. E Nocturnal lorazepam This is an inappropriate treatment option for this patient as benzodiazepines are contraindicated in the context of OSA and their use can lead to respiratory failure. A Intra-oral device to prevent snoring Long-term oxygen therapy has not been shown to have any longterm beneﬁt in OSA patients. Intra-oral devices may be useful for mild OSA, but not in daytime sleepiness. B Long-term oxygen therapy This can be used as an adjunct to CPAP therapy or in cases where patients are unable to adhere to CPAP. However, it should not be offered as ﬁrst-line in preference to CPAP. Given this patient’s smoking history, it is likely that he is beginning to develop underlying

chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Although further investigation is warranted, including arterial blood gas analysis, oxygen saturations of 91% on air are not an indication for long-term oxygen therapy. D Modaﬁnil Modaﬁnil is a daytime stimulant used in the treatment of narcolepsy. It is not used in the management of OSA. Modaﬁnil has been shown in some small studies to have beneﬁcial effects in use with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), but not as an alternative. Intra-oral devices may be useful for mild OSA, but not in daytime sleepiness.

stem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. She has been suffering from asthma, conﬁrmed by her general practitioner (GP) on peak ﬂow testing, for the past four years. She has progressively increased her therapy to cope with symptoms of wheeze, shortness of breath on exercise and nocturnal coughing, but she is still not controlled. A past history of paroxysmal atrial ﬁbrillation (AF) is noted, although she is currently not using any medication for prophylaxis. Current asthma medication includes inhaled beclometasone 400 mg twice daily and montelukast 10 mg orally (she originally responded well to the introduction of the oral therapy). On examination, her blood pressure is 115/85 mmHg and pulse 75 bpm and regular. There is bilateral wheeze on auscultation. Peak ﬂow is 390 litres/minute (500 litres/minute predicted). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: B Inhaled salmeterol The updated 2024 guidelines from NICE, SIGN, and BTS recommend adding a LABA, such as salmeterol, to the existing inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) therapy for patients aged 12 and over who are not achieving control with medium-dose ICS and a leukotriene receptor antagonist. This approach aims to improve symptom control and reduce exacerbations. E Oral Theophylline Theophylline can be considered in certain cases but is associated with potential side effects and drug interactions. Given the patient's history of paroxysmal atrial ﬁbrillation, theophylline may increase the risk of arrhythmias and is not the preferred next step. A Inhaled Tiotropium Tiotropium is a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) primarily used in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). While it can be considered as an add-on therapy in certain cases of asthma, current guidelines prioritize the addition of a long-acting beta2 agonist (LABA) for patients not controlled on medium-dose ICS and a leukotriene receptor antagonist. C Oral Prednisolone Oral corticosteroids are generally reserved for acute exacerbations or severe asthma due to potential systemic side effects. In this scenario, other treatment options should be optimized before considering oral prednisolone.
