Surgical  For patients with MPM:  potentially curative; however, it is very difficult to guarantee removal of all cancer cells so the cancer can continue to divide and grow  palliative surgery may be offered.  Prognosis  Pleural plaques may cause mild restriction, though the majority of the time they are asymptomatic.

DR. JAMIL  Pleural effusions associated with asbestos exposure often resolve spontaneously, leaving thickening of the visceral pleura.  Asbestosis is untreatable and death is usually due to respiratory failure or malignancy.  In patients with mesothelioma, prognostic scores can provide useful survival information but should not be used in treatment decision-making.  Other  ‘Hard metal lung disease’:  describes lung damage caused by fine cobalt dust particles  patients are typically exposed when making cutting tools or jet engine parts using hard metals  fibrosis develops after prolonged exposure  a lung biopsy will demonstrate multi-nucleated giant cells (hence the disease being called Giant Cell Interstitial Pneumonia) in the alveoli with granulomas present. Aspergillosis Aspergillosis is a fungal infection caused by the Aspergillus species that primarily affects the lungs and can lead to a range of respiratory symptoms.  Overview Key Facts  Aspergillosis is an infection caused by the inhalation of spores from Aspergillus species, which are filamentous fungi.  It is very rare in immunocompetent hosts.  It encompasses a spectrum of disease including isolated infections of individual areas, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), chronic pulmonary aspergillosis and invasive aspergillosis.  Diagnosis is made via a computed tomography (CT) scan and serum aspergillus galactomannan antigen detection.  Treatment is with antifungal agents such as voriconazole.  Prognosis depends upon the disease pattern. Epidemiology  Aspergillosis is seen in all regions because the fungus is ubiquitous in soil throughout the world.  It mostly occurs in immunocompromised hosts, such as recipients of stem cell or solid organ transplants, those with haematological malignancy or acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS), or those receiving immunosuppressive therapy.  Only 2% of invasive aspergillosis occurs in non-compromised hosts.  Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis occurs on a background of other pulmonary diseases such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), tuberculosis and sarcoidosis.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Aetiology  Aspergillus spp. are ubiquitous fungi that grow in soil.  The fungus grows as a filament and produces aerial stalks. Spores (conidia) are produced at the tips of the stalks.  The spores become aerosolised and are inhaled by humans or they settle on surfaces.  Spores are usually eliminated from the respiratory tract; however, in immunocompromised hosts, there may be colonisation and infection.  There are over 200 species of Aspergillus, but Aspergillus fumigatus is responsible for up to 70% of cases of aspergillosis.  Some other species that cause disease in humans include Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus terreus; A. terreus is resistant to amphotericin B and therefore has a poor prognosis. Pathophysiology  There are four types of disease pattern. 1. Invasive aspergillosis (IA)  Following inhalation of spores, immunocompetent hosts are able to clear the organism via ciliary clearance and pulmonary macrophages.  However, in immunocompromised hosts, the spores germinate and form hyphae, which invade the pulmonary parenchyma.  There is an interaction between aspergillus ligands and Toll-like receptors on macrophages that leads to the production of proinflammatory cytokines.  Hyphae locally disseminate via the pulmonary vasculature, causing inflammation, thrombosis and tissue infarction.  This is followed by haematogenous dissemination into the brain, skin, eyes, heart, kidney, liver, spleen, bone and gastrointestinal tract. There may also be a direct invasion from the paranasal sinus into the orbit and brain parenchyma. 2. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA)  A hypersensitivity reaction, usually to antigens from Aspergillus fumigatus.  Typically affects patients with cystic fibrosis or asthma due to increased mucous secretion and impaired mucociliary clearance which results in reduced clearance of spores.  The allergens induce type I and type III hypersensitivity reactions.  The proximal bronchi become dilated and filled with mucous leading to bronchiectasis and airway obstruction. 3. Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis (CPA)  An indolent, destructive infection of the lung which results in fibrosis and gradual loss of lung tissue.  Describes several types of disease pattern, including:  aspergilloma – a fungal ball consisting of fungal proteins, mucus, tissue debris, inflammatory cells and fibrin that

DR. JAMIL forms in pre-existing cavities, commonly resulting from tuberculosis  aspergillus nodule – a small mass of infection that can be single or multiple and may cause cavitation  chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis (CCPA) – formation of one or more pulmonary cavities, usually occurring in immunocompetent hosts  chronic necrotising pulmonary aspergillosis (CNPA) – similar to chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis, but progresses more quickly and is associated with COPD and excess alcohol use. 4. Isolated infection  Can infect several isolated areas, such as the nails, eyes, skin, sinuses and ear canals.  Endocarditis can occur from direct invasion during cardiac surgery.  Endophthalmitis can occur following trauma or surgery to the eye.  Clinical Presentation Disease entity Signs and symptoms Invasive aspergillosis (IA) Lung manifestations: pleuritic chest pain non-productive cough haemoptysis pleural rub dyspnoea Other manifestations: fever weight loss night sweats fatigue nasal ulcer intracranial – headache, seizure, cranial nerve palsy, altered mental status skin – ecthyma gangrenosum (erythematous, tender, lesions with a necrotic or ulcerated centre) sinuses – facial pain, headache, congestion or sinus tenderness orbits/eyes – endophthalmitis, chemosis, reduced visual acuity, photosensitivity heart – endocarditis GI tract – appendicitis, abdominal pain, ulcers, bleeding Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) Asthma-type symptoms, eg wheezing, dyspnoea Haemoptysis or cough productive of brown mucous

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI Pleuritic chest pain Fever Finger clubbing Weight loss Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis (CPA) Nodules – mostly asymptomatic, but rarely cough, pneumonia or exacerbations of existing lung disease Aspergilloma – mostly asymptomatic, but may cause symptoms described below Chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis (CCPA) and chronic necrotising pulmonary aspergillosis (CNPA) present similarly with cough, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, dyspnoea, weight loss, fever, fatigue and night sweats  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses can include:  other pulmonary fungal infections, eg histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, candidiasis, pneumocystis  mycobacterial infection  pulmonary embolism  malignancy  COVID-19.  Diagnosis/Investigation Laboratory  IA:  positive serum aspergillus galactomannan by enzyme immunoassay; galactomannan is a component of the cell wall; this test has high sensitivity and specificity when performed serially  serum (1-3)-β-D-glucan – not specific for aspergillus as βglucan is found in other fungal infections  PCR detection of ribosomal DNA – may allow early detection when combined with the tests described above.  ABPA:  elevated serum total IgE antibodies and aspergillusspecific IgE  elevated aspergillus-specific IgG  positive weal and flare reaction on skin test  a full blood count will show eosinophilia.  CPA:  elevated serum IgG antibodies. Imaging  IA:  chest X-ray may be normal; other findings include nodules, consolidation, pulmonary infiltrates and cavities

DR. JAMIL  high-resolution chest CT scan – multiple nodules, halo sign (ground-glass opacity surrounding a nodule), aircrescent sign (crescent of air surrounding a fungal colony), infiltrates and pleural effusions  high-resolution sinuses CT scan and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sinuses – mass within the sinus cavity and local bone erosion  high-resolution brain CT scan and MRI brain – focal lesions, space-occupying lesions, abscesses and hemorrhagic areas.  ABPA:  chest X-ray – infiltrates (commonly middle-upper lobe), bronchiectasis and mucoid impaction  high-resolution chest CT scan – mucoid plugging and impaction, bronchiectasis and pulmonary infiltrates.  CPA:  chest X-ray and high-resolution chest CT scan – upper lobe mobile mass with an air-crescent (aspergilloma), multiple nodules and cavities (often associated with pleural thickening). Culture/histopathology  IA and CPA:  sputum culture – sputum yield is usually low but may grow Aspergillus spp.  sputum smear – to identify hyphal elements  bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) for galactomannan antigen enzyme immunoassay, fungal culture or fungal stain  tissue biopsy – the most definitive method of diagnosis; samples are sent for culture and pathology; they may be obtained via CT-guided needle aspiration for peripheral lesions, video-assisted thoracoscopy surgery (VATS) biopsy or open lung biopsy; aspergillus stains with Gomori’s methenamine silver (GMS) stain.  ABPA:  sputum culture and microscopy – mucous plugs, fungal elements and eosinophils.  Management IA  Suspected – since the diagnosis is difficult to confirm, high-risk patients should be treated empirically with amphotericin B or an echinocandin (such as caspofungin).  Confirmed – there are two steps of treatment:  reversal of the underlying immune deficiency – colonystimulating factors may be considered and steroids may be given in reduced doses  antifungal therapy – isavuconazole and voriconazole are the first-line options; if there are signs of improvement, therapy should be continued for at least three months; if there is clinical deterioration, voriconazole can be switched to amphotericin B or an echinocandin, or an echinocandin can be given in combination with voriconazole.  Antifungal prophylaxis with posaconazole may be considered in high-risk patients.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Surgical intervention – may be considered if lesions are continuous with the great vessels or pericardium and in severe haemoptysis from a single cavity. ABPA  The mainstay of treatment is systemic corticosteroids to treat acute symptoms.  Once in remission, treatment is aimed at improving the management of underlying asthma or cystic fibrosis.  Courses of systemic corticosteroids can be repeated during exacerbations of symptoms.  Antifungal therapy is an adjunct rather than primary therapy; considered when systemic corticosteroids are having to be used on an ongoing basis. itraconazole is used most commonly. CPA  Treatment depends on the subtype of CPA.  Stable and asymptomatic aspergillomas can be monitored. There is insufficient evidence that aspergilloma responds to antifungal agents.  Antifungals are used as a curative therapy in aspergillus nodules and to improve symptoms in CCPA and CNPA.  Similarly to IA, isavuconazole and voriconazole are the firstline options. If there is clinical deterioration, voriconazole can be switched to amphotericin B or an echinocandin or an echinocandin can be given in combination with voriconazole.  Surgery is a potentially curative option in aspergillus nodules and simple aspergilloma. Lobectomy is the most common procedure.  Bronchial artery embolisation is a minimally invasive procedure used to control massive haemoptysis.  Prognosis  Prognosis is very poor for IA, with a 1-year survival of 59% in solid organ transplant recipients. Complications include lifethreatening haemoptysis, dissemination, severe hypoxia, obstructive pneumonia and adverse effects of antifungal therapy (such as adrenal suppression and hepatotoxicity).  Prognosis is good for ABPA with prompt diagnosis and treatment. Complications include bronchiectasis, pulmonary fibrosis and adverse effects of corticosteroids and antifungal therapy.  There are limited data for CPA given the spectrum of disease. Simple aspergilloma has a good overall prognosis, but there is significant mortality if associated with massive haemoptysis. Severe disease has a 15–30% mortality in the first six months and mortality is primarily from pneumonia and massive haemoptysis. Asthma Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disorder characterised by airway hyper-responsiveness.

DR. JAMIL  Overview Key Facts  Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disorder characterised by airway hyper-responsiveness.  Key symptoms are wheeze, dyspnoea, and feeling tight-chested which is reversible either spontaneously or with treatment.  An acute attack can be life-threatening and, in the most severe cases, patients may require Intensive Care Unit (ICU) admission and ventilation.  Asthma is thought to be caused by a combination of genetic predisposition and environmental factors.  There is a strong association with atopy (hay fever, allergies, and eczema).  Diagnosis is usually clinical, although tests to support the diagnosis include spirometry, peak flow and reversibility measurements.  Treatment occurs stepwise, and depends on condition severity and the patient’s age, this may require specialist input.  All patients should be followed up on at least an annual basis. Epidemiology  The prevalence of asthma has increased in recent years, particularly among children.  Approximately 8 000 000 are diagnosed with the condition in the United Kingdom (UK), with 5.4 000 000 of those receiving treatment.  The incidence is higher in children than in adults.  Two to three percent of consultations in general practice in are regarding asthma.  There were over 1 200 deaths due to asthma in the UK in 2012.  Asthma is more common in boys than in girls during childhood; however, by adulthood, the sex ratio is reversed.  Aetiology  The development of asthma is likely to be due to a combination of genetic predisposition and environmental factors.  Asthma associated with allergy usually starts in children.  Developing asthma as an adult is often not associated with allergic triggers; instead, it may be occupational asthma due to the repeated inhalation of substance.  Factors associated with increased risk of developing the condition include:  exposure to sensitising agents (allergens)  cigarette smoke  fumes  sprays  workplace exposure (dust, flour, isocyanites).  family and personal history of atopy  infection of respiratory system in childhood/infancy  obesity.  While exposure to the above may also trigger symptoms, typically asthma is triggered by:

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  exercise  infection  gastro-oesophageal reflux  drugs, eg:  aspirin  non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)  beta-blockers.  failure to comply with medication  cold weather.  Clinical Presentation  The hallmark of chronic asthma is variable and reversible airflow obstruction, which causes the following:  shortness of breath  chest tightness  wheeze  cough: at times, the cough may be productive of sputum which may be clear, or yellow/green, due to the presence of eosinophils.  Signs of chronic asthma include the following:  tachypnoea  wheezing, most marked in expiration  hyperinflation of the chest  nasal polyps (particularly in people with aspirin-sensitive asthma)  atopic eczema.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnosis includes:  bronchiectasis  chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)  cystic fibrosis  foreign body aspiration  foreign body  gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD)  heart failure  lung cancer  primary ciliary dyskinesia  tuberculosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  There is no one specific test to diagnose asthma.  The diagnosis is based on a combination of:  history  examination findings  objective tests to detect airway obstruction (when the patient is symptomatic)

DR. JAMIL  specific tests such as direct bronchial challenge tests or fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) testing where applicable.  For children under 5, or those who are unable to perform some or all objective tests, (NICE recommends the use of clinical judgment based on signs and symptoms and results of any positive objective tests available to determine the likelihood of an asthma diagnosis.  Clinical features that are helpful in making a diagnosis of asthma include:  a history of asthma in childhood, eczema or hay fever  a family history of asthma  symptoms of perennial rhinitis, nasal polyps or chronic sinusitis  history of wheezing associated with aspirin, NSAIDs or beta-blockers  otherwise unexplained peripheral eosinophilia.  The diagnosis can often be confirmed by diary recordings of the peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR).  The normal diurnal variation in airway calibre is accentuated in people with asthma and symptoms may be worse early in the morning and at night.  Other tests which can be used to help establish diagnosis include:  challenge tests (require specialist referral):  with histamine or methacholine, or with exercise, can be used to assess airway responsiveness  a pC02 value of 8 mg/ml or less is considered a positive result.  lung function tests:  spirometry: increased lung volumes, reduced FEV1, FEV1 : FVC ratio < 70%  variable peak expiratory flow readings: significant (> 20% difference) diurnal PEFR variability after monitoring at least twice daily for 2–4 weeks  bronchodilator reversibility: significant improvement in PEFR (> 15%) and FEV1 (at least 200 ml) after bronchodilator/trial of oral or inhaled steroids. Improvement of > 400 ml is strongly suggestive of asthma.  FeNO testing:  confirms eosinophilic airway inflammation  FeNO level > or = to 40 ppb is considered positive in steroid-naïve adults.  skin-prick tests:  used to assess atopy  many individuals with asthma make IgE in response to common allergens  a tiny quantity of allergen is introduced into the superficial layers of the dermis and tests are read at 20 minutes  the diameter of the weal produced is measured in millimetres, the size of the weal correlating well with bronchial challenge testing

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  serum total IgE is commonly raised in people with asthma. Specific IgE may be measured by radioallergosorbent testing (RAST). FeNO Level Other Tests Result 40 ppb or more And positive bronchodilator reversibility or positive peak flow variability or bronchial hyperactivity Diagnose asthma 25–39 ppb And positive bronchial challenge test Diagnose asthma Irrelevant Positive bronchodilator reversibility and positive peak flow variability Diagnose asthma  Management Chronic asthma  The aim of prophylactic management in asthma patients includes:  minimising symptoms during the day and night  reducing the need for reliever medication  preventing exacerbations  maintaining normal lung function (FEV1 and PEFR > 80%).  The mainstay of treatment is inhaled corticosteroids for prevention, along with short-acting beta2 agonists for symptom relief.  Treatment should be adjusted in a stepwise fashion following the BTS/SIGN national guidelines.  Markers of steroid responsiveness may include sputum eosinophil levels > 4% and exhaled nitric oxide levels > 10 ppb.  Omalizumab can be considered as an add-on therapy for patients with severe persistent allergic asthma. Non-Pharmacological  Provide education on asthma, proper inhaler technique, and the use of spacers if needed.  Advise on avoiding asthma triggers and allergens.  Consider referral for suspected occupational asthma.  Offer weight loss and smoking cessation advice, as smoking can reduce the effectiveness of inhaled steroids.  Use a peak flow meter for regular monitoring.  Conduct follow-up appointments at least annually, with increased frequency for poor lung function or recent asthma exacerbations.  Monitor asthma control using tools like the Asthma Control Test or Asthma Control Questionnaire.  Ensure vaccinations are up to date.

DR. JAMIL Pharmacological  Follow the current BTS/SIGN and NICE guidelines for asthma management.  For adults, consider the stepwise approach recommended by NICE, which includes:  Prescribing short-acting beta2 agonists (SABA) to all individuals with symptomatic asthma for use as needed as a reliever therapy.  Initiating inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) if the individual uses SABA three times or more a week, experiences symptoms three times a week or more, or wakes up at night due to asthma symptoms once weekly or more. The starting dose should be based on symptom severity.  Adding a leukotriene receptor antagonist (LTRA) as an add-on therapy if low-dose ICS alone is insufficient.  Considering long-acting beta2 agonists (LABA) if lowdose ICS and LTRA do not provide adequate control.  Using maintenance and reliever therapy (MART) regimens with low-dose ICS as appropriate.  Adjusting treatment based on response, with a review in 4-8 weeks.  For children, the stepwise progression may include:  Offering SABA as reliever therapy and low-dose ICS initially.  Considering add-on therapies like LTRA for children aged 5-16 years if symptoms are uncontrolled.  Adjusting treatment based on response, with consideration of increasing ICS dose or seeking advice from an asthma specialist if needed. Acute severe asthma:  Acute exacerbations of asthma may require urgent hospital treatment to manage the attack effectively. An immediate assessment is crucial to determine the severity of the exacerbation. Signs of severe asthma exacerbation include:  Inability to complete full sentences due to dyspnea  Respiratory rate > 25 breaths per minute  Heart rate > 110 bpm  Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) 33–50% of predicted or personal best.  Life-threatening asthma is characterised by any of the following features:  Hypoxemia (oxygen saturation < 92%)  PEFR < 33% of predicted or personal best  Exhaustion  Bradycardia (heart rate < 60 bpm) or arrhythmia  Hypotension  Silent chest  Altered consciousness  Poor respiratory effort  Cyanosis

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Normal or elevated partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO2) on blood gas analysis. Acute severe asthma:  Asthma symptoms may worsen acutely, necessitating prompt hospital treatment to relieve the attack.  An immediate assessment is essential, looking for signs of severity, which include the following:  speech impairment  respiratory rate > 25 breaths per minute  tachycardia (pulse > 110 bpm)  PEFR 33–50% of predicted.  Life-threatening asthma is associated with any one of the following:  hypoxaemia (< 92% oxygen saturation)  peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) < 33% of predicted  exhaustion  bradycardia (heart rate < 60 bpm) or arrhythmia  hypotension  a silent chest  altered consciousness  poor respiratory effort  cyanosis  a normal or raised PCO2.  Arterial blood gas analysis should be performed in hypoxemic patients, and a chest X-ray may be necessary to rule out complications such as pneumothorax.  Management of acute severe asthma includes:  High-flow oxygen therapy with the patient sitting upright  Nebulized bronchodilators (short-acting beta2 agonists and ipratropium)  Systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone or intravenous methylprednisolone)  Consider antibiotics if there is suspicion of bacterial infection  Regular monitoring of PEFR to assess treatment response  Intravenous bronchodilators (eg salbutamol) or aminophylline if there is an inadequate response to nebulised therapy  Intravenous magnesium sulfate for patients with severe asthma not responding to initial treatments.  Consider referral to the intensive care unit (ICU) if any of the following are present:  Deteriorating PEFR  Persistent or worsening hypoxemia  Rising PCO2  Decreasing blood pH  Exhaustion  Altered consciousness  Respiratory arrest.

DR. JAMIL  Criteria for discharge of a patient with asthma exacerbation should include:  PEFR ≥ 75% of predicted or personal best  PEFR diurnal variability < 25%  No requirement for nebulized bronchodilators for at least 24 hours  Provision of a written asthma action plan  Follow-up should be arranged in primary or secondary care within 30 days post-discharge.  Prognosis  The earlier the onset of asthma, the better the prognosis seems to be unless there is associated atopy.  Young boys are more likely to grow out of asthma as they transition into adulthood. Benign Neck Lumps And Swellings Benign neck lumps and swelling can be either congenital or acquired, and can arise from a number of anatomical structures in the neck.  Overview Key Facts  Benign neck lumps and swelling can be either congenital or acquired, and can arise from a number of anatomical structures in the neck.  The most common benign soft tissue tumours found in the neck are lipomas, which usually present as asymptomatic, soft, poorly-defined masses deep to the skin.  Other benign neck lumps include:  cystic hygroma  thyroglossal cyst  branchial cyst  ranula  laryngocele  sialadenitis/sialithiasis (covered separately)  pharyngeal pouch (covered separately).  Occasionally what a patient might identify as a lump is actually part of their normal anatomy, eg structures such as:  transverse process of C1 vertebra  hyoid bone  thyroid or cricoid cartilage.  If the diagnosis is uncertain, referral should not be delayed by undertaking investigations in primary care, particularly in highrisk individuals. Epidemiology Cystic hygroma

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Cystic hygromas occur in approximately one per cent of children with no particular gender or ethnic preponderance. Thyroglossal cyst  Occurs in around 7% of the population and most commonly presents in childhood. Branchial cyst  The most common cause of congenital neck masses, the majority present in childhood.  Occasionally they may present later in life, usually by early adulthood. Ranula  Ranulas usually present in childhood or early adulthood. Laryngocele  The condition is rare, and believed to be more frequent in wind instrument players and glassblowers.  Aetiology  Congenital:  thyroglossal cyst  branchial cyst  cystic hygroma.  Most common acquired benign neck masses are:  ranula  laryngocele  pharyngeal pouch. Pathophysiology Thyroglossal cyst  Persistent connection between the caecum of the tongue and the pyramidal lobe of the thyroid gland causing a mass in the midline. Branchial cyst  Congenital epithelial cysts occurring lateral from the midline, thought to be due to failure of obliteration of the second branchial cleft in embryonic development. Cystic hygroma  A cystic lymphatic lesion that occurs in the posterior triangle of the neck.  Most present at birth or before the age of two years. Ranula  A type of mucocele in the floor of the mouth originating from the sublingual glands.  The two principal causes are:  a blocked duct causing a swelling  a ruptured cyst that leads to extravasation of mucin. Laryngocele

DR. JAMIL  An air pocket that arises from the deepest point of the laryngeal ventricle.  Clinical Presentation Thyroglossal cyst  Midline cystic lump that is near the hyoid bone and moves upwards when the individual swallows or protrudes their tongue. Branchial cyst  painless, slow-growing, smooth, fluctuant swellings in the lateral neck. Cystic hygroma  Can be seen on antenatal ultrasound scans in pregnancy, commonly found in neck and axillae, soft painless swellings, sometimes translucent. Ranula  Clear/bluish cysts usually contained within the floor of the mouth (mylohyoid) but can push through. Laryngocele  An air-filled cyst can bulge internally into the larynx, externally into the neck or be combined (where the connection is through the thyrohyoid membrane).  They usually present with an intermittent neck swelling, which becomes palpable when the the valsalva manoeuvre is performed.  Differential Diagnosis  Thyroid lump/swelling – may be nodular or diffuse  Inflammatory lymphadenopathy  Malignant lesions  Normal anatomical structures.  Diagnosis/Investigation General investigations:  bloods (FBC, U+Es, CRP)  plain neck radiograph  ultrasound scan imaging.  Management  NICE guidance of management of a neck lump of unknown cause:  admit the person immediately if there are symptoms such as stridor, or signs of superior vena cava obstruction  consider admission if the person has dysphagia, signs of aspiration, or symptoms or signs of sepsis.  Consider an urgent referral using suspected cancer pathway if:  there is an unexplained neck lump in a person aged 45 years or older

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  there is a persistent and unexplained neck lump in a person younger than 45 years of age.  Consider arranging an ultrasound scan if there is an unexplained lump that is increasing in size:  For adults 25 years of age and older refer for an urgent ultrasound appointment (within two weeks).  Consider a suspected cancer pathway referral if ultrasound scan findings are uncertain or suggestive of soft tissue sarcoma.  For children and young people up to and including 24 years of age, refer for a very urgent ultrasound appointment (within 48 hours).  Consider a very urgent referral if ultrasound findings are uncertain or suggestive of soft tissue sarcoma.  Specific management options Thyroglossal cyst  Referral to ENT to consider a Sistrunk's procedure. Branchial cyst  Referral to ENT, antibiotics to treat infections or abscess, definitive treatment is with excision. Cystic hygroma  Sclerotherapy or surgical removal. Ranula  Treatment is by surgical excision, which must include excision of the sublingual gland. Laryngocele  Treatment is by surgical excision (endoscopic or external approach depending on size and location).  Prognosis  Will be dependent on the extent of swelling, whether it has affected surrounding structures and the underlying pathology. Thyroglossal cyst  Excellent prognosis after Sistrunk's procedure, approximately 10% recur. Branchial cyst  Persistent problems with infection or drainage is usually resolved with surgical excision. Cystic hygroma  Dependent on the size and time of detection. Ranula  some ranulas may spontaneously resolve without treatment; usually excision is required.  Following excision symptoms usually resolve completely.

DR. JAMIL Laryngocele  Enlargement can cause hoarseness and in severe cases can cause airway obstruction.  Laryngoceles can also become infected (laryngopyocele).  Laryngoceles may also be associated with laryngeal malignancy. Berylliosis Berylliosis is a chronic form of occupational lung disease caused by exposure to beryllium.  Overview Key Facts  Berylliosis is a chronic form of occupational lung disease caused by exposure to beryllium.  The inhalation of fumes from molten beryllium causes an acute alveolitis.  However, most cases of berylliosis are due to chronic low-level exposure.  The condition is associated with people who work in beryllium mining, the aerospace industry, and fluorescent light bulb manufacturing.  Exposure leads to subsequent tissue reaction similar to sarcoidosis:  non-caseating granulomas form in the lungs and lymph nodes surrounded by fibrous tissue  chest X-rays show fine nodulation evenly distributed throughout the lung fields and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.  A positive beryllium lymphocyte proliferation assay in blood and on bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) is strongly associated with the presence of chronic beryllium disease.  Interstitial fibrosis develops with shrinking of the lungs.  Patients develop progressive breathlessness with death ultimately occurring due to respiratory and right heart failure. Bronchiectasis Bronchiectasis is a chronic progressive disease that is characterised by inflamed, dilated, and partially or totally obstructed airways.  Overview Key Facts  Bronchiectasis is a chronic progressive disease that is characterised by inflamed, dilated, and partially or totally obstructed airways.  The condition may affect the whole lung (diffuse) or one area (focal).

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  The most common cause is previous severe lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI).  Symptoms can vary, from mild sputum production and intermittent infection, to persistent production of large volumes of purulent sputum.  In the majority of cases it is diagnosed via computed tomography (CT) scan.  Treatment options include:  airway clearance techniques (chest physiotherapy)  managing acute infective exacerbations with antibiotics  lung transplantation in eligible severe cases. Epidemiology  The number of cases of bronchiectasis is rising.  In the United Kingdom, bronchiectasis affects more women than men.  Prevalence increases with age.  Up to a quarter of patients diagnosed with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) may actually have bronchiectasis.  Aetiology  The most common causes of bronchiectasis are previous severe lower respiratory tract infections, such as:  pneumonia  pertussis  pulmonary tuberculosis  mycoplasma  influenza.  Bronchiectasis is idiopathic in up to 40% of cases (no clear underlying cause).  Congenital defects include:  Marfan syndrome  Williams–Campbell syndrome.  Immune deficiencies include:  human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)  haematological malignancy  post transplantation.  Connective tissue disorders (rheumatoid arthritis and Sjögren syndrome).  Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis).  Allergic broncho-pulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA).  Cystic fibrosis.  Obstructed/compressed bronchus (due to malignancy).  Chemical pneumonitis.  Mucociliary clearance defects:  primary ciliary dyskinesis  Kartagener syndrome  Young syndrome.  Antitrypsin deficiency.

DR. JAMIL  Conditions associated with bronchiectasis include:  rheumatoid arthritis (30% of patients have coexisting bronchiectasis)  malignancy (childhood acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, adult chronic lymphocytic leukaemia)  Sjögren syndrome  yellow nail syndrome and primary lymphoedema  inflammatory bowel disease (usually ulcerative colitis)  infertility  ankylosing spondylitis  immunosuppressive treatment associated with higher risk of infection in general. Pathophysiology  Persistent airway inflammation due to the inflammatory response by the host on microorganisms that colonise the airway.  Development of bronchial wall oedema and increased mucus production.  Inflammatory cells (neutrophils, T lymphocytes, and other immune effector cells) are recruited to the airways.  Release of cytokines, proteases, and reactive oxygen mediators leads to progressive destruction of the airways – causing dilatation and thickening of the bronchi.  Clinical Presentation  Bronchiectasis presents as follows:  chronic sputum production – often mucopurulent – and accompanied by episodes of haemoptysis  occasionally, bronchiectasis can be ‘dry’ – with no sputum production but with episodic haemoptysis  exertional dyspnoea and wheeze  malaise and fatigue  one in three cases demonstrate symptoms of chronic sinusitis.  Examination findings:  basal crepitations, wheeze in the chest  finger clubbing may be present  weight loss and cachexia are prominent (advanced disease).  Complications:  infective exacerbations are the principal problem  haemoptysis – usually settles with treatment of the infection and/or tranexamic acid. Occasionally, embolisation of the bleeding vessel is required.  chest pain over areas of bronchiectatic lung  respiratory failure.  Differential Diagnosis  Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.  Asthma.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Pneumonia.  Chronic sinusitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Bronchiectasis should be suspected in those demonstrating persistent production of mucopurulent or purulent sputum, particularly with relevant associated risk factors.  Appropriate investigations include:  chest X-ray:  useful for subsequent monitoring  may be normal or show obscured hemidiaphragm, thin-walled ring shadows with or without fluid levels, tram lines, tubular or ovoid opacities  in the X-ray below (image A), the lungs are hyperinflated (the diaphragm is depressed and the costophrenic angles are obtuse). The arrow in the picture highlights a port-a-cath. These are most commonly found in patients receiving chemotherapy or those with cystic fibrosis. The arrows in image B indicate dilated bronchi:  CT chest:  the diagnostic procedure of choice  performed in all patients  may show thickened, dilated airways with, or without, air fluid levels; varicose constrictions along airways; cysts and/or tree-in-bud pattern  image D from the CT scan below nicely demonstrates the ‘signet ring sign’. The arrow points to a (dilated) bronchus and its accompanying bronchial artery, which would usually be similar in diameter:

DR. JAMIL  Bloods:  white blood cell (WBC) differential may reveal high eosinophil count in bronchopulmonary aspergillosis  neutrophilia suggests superimposed infection or exacerbations  serum immunoglobulins  serum alpha-1 antitrypsin phenotype and level (replacement therapy is suggested if either abnormal)  rheumatoid factor  serum HIV antibody.  Sputum microbiology:  most commonly shows Haemophilus influenzae, S. pneumoniae or Pseudomonas aeruginosa  mycobacteria and fungi may also be seen.  Pulmonary function tests:  usually obstructive picture but may be normal or show a restrictive or mixed pattern  reduction of the FEV1 suggests the presence of infection or worsening bronchiectasis.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Refer for chest physiotherapist input:  offers active cycle of breathing techniques or oscillating positive expiratory pressure to individuals with bronchiectasis  consider gravity assisted positioning (where not contraindicated) to enhance the effectiveness of an airway clearance technique.  Consider the use of humidification with sterile water or normal saline to facilitate airway clearance. Maintain oral hydration.  Nebulised hypertonic saline can increase sputum yield, decrease sputum viscosity and aid expectoration.  Interventions should be tailored to the individual and may alter during periods of exacerbation.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI Pharmacological If there is an underlying immune deficiency state, treatment with immunoglobulin replacement therapy is beneficial as it reduces frequency of infections – thus preventing further damage.  Mucolytic agents:  specifically, rhDNase (not recommended in patients with non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis)  may be beneficial in a subset of patients to use Nacetylcysteine, erdosteine, and bromhexine  consider pre-treatment with a bronchodilator.  Antibiotics:  used to treat acute exacerbations, the choice of antibiotics should be pathogen-guided where possible – check local guidelines  antibiotic prophylaxis should be considered in patients with three or more exacerbations per year. Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis choice should be guided by sputum culture (commonly used is Azithromycin three times a week). Rotating antibiotics are not routinely recommended  nebulised antibiotics can be used to reduce the microbial load and are particularly useful when a patient is colonised with Pseudomonas spp. if they have more than three exacerbations per year.  Inhaled bronchodilators may be used if there is evidence of reversibility and improvement of lung function or symptoms.  Vaccinations: offer annual influenza immunisation and polysaccharide pneumococcal vaccination to all patients with bronchiectasis. Surgical  Consider transplant referral in bronchiectasis patients aged 65 years or less if the FEV1 < 30%, with significant clinical instability or rapid respiratory deterioration despite optimal medical management.  Earlier referral may be indicated if patients have additional factors, such as: severe secondary pulmonary hypertension, Intensive Care Unit admissions, or respiratory failure (especially if requiring Non Invasive Ventilation).

DR. JAMIL  Prognosis  Prognosis varies widely and depends on co-morbidities, underlying cause and individual progression of disease.  Most people will have a normal life expectancy and symptoms may be minimal.  The prognosis for patients with bronchiectasis will be worse if any of the following factors are present:  extensive disease  frequent exacerbations  primary antibody deficiency disorder  colonisation with Pseudomonas  smoking history.  Complications include:  infection  haemoptysis  pneumothorax  respiratory failure  fatigue  anxiety, depression, and social embarrassment.  Two clinical scoring systems, the Bronchiectasis Severity Index (BSI), and FACED has increased the ability to predict future mortality in patients with bronchiectasis. Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease is a chronic, slowly progressive disease characterised by airflow obstruction that does not markedly change over several months.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a chronic, slowly progressive disease characterised by airflow obstruction that does not markedly change over several months.  COPD is now the preferred term for the conditions in patients with airflow obstruction who were previously diagnosed as having chronic bronchitis or emphysema:  chronic bronchitis - chronic cough and sputum production for at least 3 months of 2 consecutive years in the absence of other diseases recognised to cause sputum production  emphysema - abnormal, permanent enlargement of the airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of their walls without obvious fibrosis. It may be centriacinar (predominantly affecting the upper lobes and associated with smoking), panacinar, paraseptal, or predominantly localised around scars (scar emphysema).  Tobacco smoking is the primary risk factor – the condition progresses even if the patient stops smoking; however, smoking cessation is one of the most important steps in reducing the speed of progression.  COPD is treatable but is not curable.  The long-term prognosis is variable, but the condition is associated with a gradual decline in lung function and an increase in symptoms.  COPD causes approximately 25,000 deaths per year in the United Kingdom (UK). Epidemiology  An estimated 3 million people in the UK have COPD, although approximately 2 million people are undiagnosed.  COPD currently accounts for 5% of all deaths worldwide.  COPD has become the third leading cause of death globally, surpassing previous projections. It is the only one of the ‘top 10’ worldwide causes of death that is increasing.  Aetiology COPD is caused by a number of factors, including:  smoking (usually a history of at least 20 pack-years)  air pollution  low birthweight and low socio-economic status  dust exposure  alpha 1-Antitrypsin deficiency. Exacerbations of COPD can be caused by a range of factors, including:  bacterial infections  viral infections  smoking.

DR. JAMIL Pathophysiology An inflammatory reaction to inhaled stimuli leads to:  airway narrowing  an increased number of goblet cells  mucus-secreting gland enlargement  vascular bed changes. NB: the role of eosinophils in COPD is limited to exacerbations only. The end result of these inflammatory-changes differs slightly:  in emphysema, elastin is broken down and alveolar integrity is lost  in bronchitis, there is excessive mucus secretion due to the combination of larger/increased numbers of goblet cells and ciliary dysfunction.  Clinical Presentation Many patients with COPD will have no abnormal physical signs until the disease is advanced. These signs can include:  hyperinflation of the chest  central cyanosis  weight loss  cor pulmonale: raised jugular venous pressure (JVP), right ventricular heave, loud P2, tricuspid regurgitation, peripheral oedema, and hepatomegaly  flapping tremor  pursed-lip breathing  accessory muscle usage  wheeze  reduced breath sounds. Acute exacerbations can be infective or non-ineffective. Features include:  increased breathlessness (both)  increased sputum production and change in colour (infective exacerbation)  increased cough (both)  more chest tightness than usual (both)  wheezing more frequently (both)  reduced exercise tolerance (both)  new confusion (infective exacerbation).  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnosis of COPD include:  asthma

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  heart failure  lung cancer  interstitial lung disease  bronchiectasis.  Diagnosis/Investigation A diagnosis of COPD can be made if the person meets all of the following criteria:  an age > 35 years  the presence of a risk factor, for example: current smoker, history of smoking, or occupational exposure to chemicals or dust  typical symptoms, such as exertional breathlessness, chronic cough, wheeze, regular sputum production, and recurrent chest infection. Pulmonary function tests (PFTs):  Post-bronchodilator spirometry testing must be used to demonstrate airflow obstruction.  Airflow obstruction is defined as a ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC ratio) of less than 0.7.  FEV1 is classically < 80% predicted, but COPD may be diagnosed in patients with an obstructive FEV1:FVC ratio and an FEV1 > 80% if they have typical symptoms of COPD.  Patients have large lung volumes (TLC) and reduced diffusing capacity of the lung for CO (DLCO) in emphysema.  Degrees of airflow obstruction in COPD may be graded by the FEV1:  mild: FEV1 > 80% predicted  moderate: FEV1 50–79% predicted  severe: FEV1 30–49% predicted  very severe: FEV1 < 30% predicted. Imaging:  Chest radiograph: may be normal or show evidence of hyperinflation, bullae, or prominent vasculature due to pulmonary hypertension.  CT Thorax: may be helpful if symptoms are disproportionate to spirometric impairment or to assess suitability of patients for lung volume reduction surgery. The radiograph below demonstrates severe COPD; the lungs are hyper-inflated, causing the heart to be small in comparison:

DR. JAMIL Blood tests:  Arterial blood gases: may indicate type I or II respiratory failure.  Full blood count (FBC): possible polycythaemia.  Alpha 1-antritypsin levels: should be measured in younger patients or patients with a minimal smoking history or a family history of COPD. ECG: may show P-pulmonale, right axis deviation, right bundle-branch block. Sputum culture: Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae or less commonly staphylococci, Moraxella catarrhalis or Gram- negative organisms.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Pulmonary rehabilitation is increasingly recognised as an important part of disease management.  Chest physiotherapy – useful for patients with excessive mucus.  Smoking cessation.  Domiciliary non-invasive ventilation may be considered in patients who have persistent hypercapnic respiratory failure, that has required previous acute invasive or non-invasive ventilation. It may also be considered in patients who become acidotic or significantly hypercapnic on supplemental oxygen.  Vaccinations. Pharmacological  Short acting bronchodilators (SABA)  Short acting antimuscarinics (SAMA)  Long acting bronchodilators (LABA)  Long acting antimuscarinics (LAMA)

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Inhaled Corticosteroid (ICS)  Oral mucolytics  Diuretics  Oxygen therapy:  long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT)  ambulatory oxygen therapy: for patients who desaturate on exercise and who are shown to have an improvement in their exercise capacity and/or dyspnoea with supplemental oxygen therapy  short-burst oxygen therapy.  Several recent clinical trials have shown no impact of inhaled steroids in addition to long-acting bronchodilators on disease progression in COPD.  However, combination therapy with inhaled steroids and longacting Beta agonists do reduce exacerbation frequency and improve quality of life in:  patients with severe or very severe airflow obstruction (ie FEV1 <50% of predicted) who remain breathless when stable  patients who have had at least two exacerbations each year. Stepwise treatment as per NICE recommendations:  Initial therapy: Inhaled short acting bronchodilators (SABA) OR inhaled short acting antimuscarinics (SAMA)  Combined therapy:  (2a) no asthmatic or steroid responsiveness features, offer LABA + LAMA  (2b) OR asthmatic or steroid responsiveness features present, offer LABA + ICS  Triple therapy: Either add ICS to 2a option or LAMA to 2b option. NB: If a patient has day-to-day symptoms that adversely impact quality of life and the inclusion of ICS (to a LABA + LAMA combination therapy) does not improve symptoms, they should revert back to LABA + LAMA. Key management points in an acute exacerbation of COPD:  Oxygen therapy.  Antibiotic (usually amoxicillin/doxycycline/clarithromycin).  Corticosteroids (usually oral prednisolone).  Beta-2 agonists.  Anticholinergics – nebulised.  Physiotherapy.  Treatments only available in hospital.  IV theophylline  doxapram or NIV (only to be used when NIV unavailable/unsuitable) – indicated if patients’ blood gas shows persistent hypercapnic ventilatory failure or acidosis (pH = 7.35)

DR. JAMIL  invasive ventilation. NICE guidance promotes a degree of self-management by encouraging an individualised exacerbation action plan to be created with the patient. This includes when to adjust bronchodilator usage and the provision of a short course of oral corticosteroids and oral antibiotics to have at home if appropriate. Surgical  Lung volume reduction surgery (for patients with severe emphysema) or bullectomy  Transplantation may be considered in patients under 65 years with:  a FEV1 and DLCO < 20% predicted  a history of hospitalisation with an exacerbation associated with acute hypercapnia  pulmonary hypertension, and/or cor pulmonale despite oxygen therapy.  Prognosis FEV1 considered in isolation is a poor guide to a patient’s symptom burden and prognosis. A combination of factors should be considered when assessing the severity of a patient’s COPD and prognosis:  FEV1  exacerbation frequency  need for intubation and/or invasive mechanical ventilation due to acute respiratory failure  body mass index (BMI)  degree of dyspnoea (which can be objectively measured using the Medical Research Council’s dyspnoea scale)  exercise capacity (which can be measured objectively by a 6minute walk test)  degree of hypoxia  degree of hypercapnia  presence of cor pulmonale. The BODE (BMI, airflow obstruction, dyspnoea, exercise) index  objective assessment of COPD prognosis  score is calculated based on the patient’s BMI, degree of airflow obstruction, level of dyspnoea and exercise capacity  a BODE score > 7 predicts a 31% 2–year mortality rate. The CODEX index (co-morbidities, obstruction, dyspnoea, and previous severe exacerbations) is an alternative to the BODE index.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI Decaf score Used as an inpatient risk-stratifying tool for in patient mortality of patients presenting with exacerbations of COPD.  Dyspnoea  too short of breath to leave house (1 point)  too short of breath to get dressed/wash (2 points)  Eosinophils <0.05 (1 point)  Consolidation on chest Xray (1 point)  Acidaemia <7.3 (1 point)  Atrial Fibrillation (1 point) A DECAF score of three or more indicates increased risk of in patient mortality and patients require prompt treatment with antibiotics. Coal Workers’ Pneumoconiosis Coal workers’ pneumoconiosis is a serious condition consisting of lung damage caused by the inhalation of dust particles from various occupations (most commonly occurs in coal workers).  Overview Key Facts  Coal workers’ pneumoconiosis (CWP) is a serious condition consisting of lung damage caused by the inhalation of dust particles from various occupations (most commonly occurs in coal workers).  It forms one of a group of industrial dust diseases.  Two types exist: simple pneumoconiosis and progressive massive fibrosis.  simple coal-workers’ pneumoconiosis (SCWP):  small, asymptomatic, rounded opacities (< 1 cm in diameter)  seen in the upper zones in chest X-ray  associated with focal emphysema.  progressive massive fibrosis (PMF):  aggregation of nodules to form larger opacities (of at least 1 cm in diameter)  usually background of simple CWP  upper zone and possible cavitating lesions.  The condition develops over decades following exposure, due to inhaled dust progressively building up and causing inflammation, fibrosis, and, in severe cases, necrosis.  Cough, sputum production and dyspnoea occur after this latent period.  Pulmonary function tests show a mixed obstructive/restrictive pattern with reduced KCO.  There is no specific treatment; CWP cannot be cured.

DR. JAMIL  Oxygen therapy may be used in some patients and in severe cases lung transplantation may be considered.  CWP is associated with reduced life expectancy.  Death occurs from progressive respiratory failure. Epidemiology  Marked male predominance (due to occupation rather than predisposition).  Both deaths and hospitalisations have been in decline since the 1980s as a result of decreased coal mining activity in the United Kingdom (UK).  The latency period for CWP is approximately 20 years.  Around 120 deaths per year are associated with CWP in the UK, according to Health and Safety Executive (HSE) statistics.  Aetiology  The incidence of CWP is related to total dust exposure.  Coal mining – especially underground pits.  Increased risk of connective-tissue disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Pathophysiology  Dust particles, 2–5 μm in diameter, are retained in the respiratory bronchioles and alveoli.  This triggers an immune response that eventually results in pulmonary fibrosis.  Clinical Presentation  CWP is characterised by the following clinical presentations:  shortness of breath and chronic cough, which can progress to the production of black sputum  chest examination is usually normal  crackles can be present as can prolonged expiration and wheeze.  Caplan syndrome:  the development of multiple round pulmonary nodules in patients with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis and a background of coal workers pneumoconiosis  nodules may develop before the joint disease, and occur in crops in the periphery of the lung  may be associated with pleural effusion and may ultimately calcify.  Differential Diagnosis  Asbestosis.  Silicosis.  Rheumatoid arthritis.  Sarcoidosis.  Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).  Scleroderma.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).  Systemic lupus erythematous (SLE).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Chest X-ray.  reveals progressive upper zone, non-calcified, small rounded opacities.  Spirometry.  can show restrictive or obstructive patterns or may be normal.  Oxygen saturation.  Arterial blood gas (ABG).  can show degree of lung damage.  High resolution chest CT (HRCT).  can show upper zone interstitial fibrosis; progressively involves the entire lung.  Other investigations to rule out differentials:  tuberculin skin test  bronchoscopic biopsy  interferon gamma-release assay  sputum smear and culture.  Management  There is no specific treatment and the condition cannot be cured.  Chest Physician referral is indicated for management advice and support.  Oxygen therapy may be used in some patients to provided symptomatic benefit.  In severe cases, lung transplantation may be considered to prolong life expectancy.  Removal of occupational risk factors and smoking cessation helps to improve prognosis.  Patients should be advised regarding their legal position and potential for compensation and disability benefits (the condition is a prescribed industrial disease).  The condition is a notifiable disease and cases should be reported by the physician to the patients employer, who will in turn notify the Health and Safety Executive (HSE).  Prognosis  Prognosis is related to the extent of fibrosis and the cumulative exposure to coal dust.  Many patients will die with, and not of, the disease.

DR. JAMIL Community-Acquired Pneumonia Pneumonia is an acute infective condition of the lung usually caused by bacteria, viruses or – rarely – fungi.  Overview Key Facts  Pneumonia is an acute infective condition of the lung usually caused by bacteria, viruses or – rarely – fungi.  Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) occurs outside of hospital.  Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common causative pathogen in community-acquired cases of pneumonia.  Presenting signs and symptoms, as well as severity, varies depending on the underlying pathogen, patient age, and comorbidites.  Severity can be graded using the CURB-65 score, which is also a prognostic indicator.  Treatment depends on the severity of the condition; this determines the route and type of antibiotic needed as well as the need for admission (up to 40% of cases).  The United Kingdom (UK) mortality rate for all patients admitted to hospital with CAP ranges from 5.7%–14% and for those patients admitted to intensive care, it is 30%. Epidemiology  There are approximately 220 000 cases of CAP per year in the UK.  This is equivalent to approximately 5–10 cases per 1 000 adults in the UK.  Aetiology  Streptococcus pneumoniae (60–70%).  Haemophilus influenzae.  Staphylococcus aureus.  Gram-negative organisms.  Atypical organisms include:  mycoplasma pneumoniae (5–15%)  legionella pneumophila  chlamydia psittaci  chlamydia pneumoniae  coxiella burnetii (Q fever).  Viral causes include:  influenza  varicella-zoster  cytomegalovirus (CMV).

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI Pathophysiology  Local pathogen multiplication results in an inflammatory response in the lung parenchyma.  White blood cells interact with organisms resulting in cytokine release.  This activates the entire immune system.  Clinical Presentation  Features can differ depending on the type of pneumonia that is occurring.  Streptococcus pneumoniae:  there is an abrupt onset of illness, with high fever and rigors  examination reveals crackles or bronchial breathing, and herpetic cold sores may be present in more than a third of cases  elderly patients may present with general deterioration or confusion.  Mycoplasma pneumoniae:  tends to affect young adults; it occurs in epidemics every 3–4 years. There is typically a longer prodrome, usually of > two weeks  extrapulmonary complications include:  peri-/ myocarditis  erythema multiforme  erythema nodosum  Stevens–Johnson syndrome  haemolytic anaemia  disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)  thrombocytopenia  meningoencephalitis  cranial and peripheral neuropathies  bullous myringitis  hepatitis  pancreatitis.  Legionella pneumophila:  history is important as outbreaks are usually related to contaminated water-cooling systems, showers or airconditioning systems, though sporadic cases do occur. In examinations, commonly from a ‘European resort’  Legionnaires’ disease usually affects middle-aged and elderly patients, often with underlying lung disease  men are affected more than women (3: 1).  Psittacosis - Chlamydophila psittaci.  a rare illness, causing a gradual onset of symptoms following an incubation period of 1-4 weeks  carried by birds, particularly parrots.  there are marked signs of systemic illness with fever and lassitude.

DR. JAMIL  symptoms include a non-productive cough, dyspnoea, sore throat, nosebleeds and occasionally pleuritic chest pain.  severe headache is common as is photophobia, bradycardia and splenomegaly  some gastrointestinal symptoms may occur.  rose spots can appear on the face and these are called Horder's spots. There may be signs of consolidation but the chest x ray looks worse than the clinical signs suggest.  Staphylococcus aureus:  staphylococcus aureus pneumonia may follow a viral illness  the disease is more common in intravenous drug users  specific features include:  toxin production with extensive tissue necrosis  staphylococcal skin lesions  chest X-rays show patchy infiltrates with abscess formation in 25% of cases, and this organism is responsible for around 10% of parapneumonic effusions.  Other signs and symptoms include:  cough  breathlessness  wheeze  pleuritic pain  fever (less common in the elderly)  increased work of breathing.  Differential Diagnosis  Asthma.  Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).  Pulmonary embolism (PE).  Tuberculosis (TB).  Whooping cough.  Post-natal drip.  Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Clinical judgement should be used to diagnose the condition alongside history and examination.  If the patient has signs and symptoms of community acquired pneumonia, assess for severity using the CRB-65 score:  confusion (< 8/10 score on abbreviated mental test (AMT))  respiratory rate > 30 breaths/min  blood pressure (BP) < 90 mmHg and/or diastolic < 60 mmHg  age > 65 years.  Investigations in primary care include:

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  pulse oximetry (urgent admission for saturations less than 90%)  chest X-ray if there is suspected underlying lung pathology, or if the diagnosis is uncertain (not usually initially required in the diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia  sputum culture – in moderate severity, cases managed in the community.  All patients who are admitted to hospital with suspected severe pneumonia should have the following tests performed on admission as per British Thoracic Society (BTS) guidelines:  oxygenation saturations  arterial blood gases if necessary – may show type I respiratory failure  chest X-ray to allow accurate diagnosis  bloods:  c-reactive protein (CRP) to aid diagnosis and as a baseline measure  full blood count (FBC)  liver function tests (LFT) which may demonstrate transient hepatitis  urea and electrolyte (U&Es) tests to inform severity assessment.  Here, the AP chest X-ray shows consolidations in the left lung base, but as it does not fully obscure the heart border it is difficult to tell which lobe it is in.  The lateral X-ray reveals that the consolidation lies posteriorly and therefore has to be in the left lower lobe. Left lower lobe pneumonia – lateral CXR  Specific investigation findings  Streptococcus pneumoniae:  capsular polysaccharide antigen may be detected in serum, sputum, pleural fluid or urine  increasing incidence of penicillin resistance, particularly in countries such as Spain.  Mycoplasma pneumoniae:

DR. JAMIL  normal white cell count (WCC)  cold agglutinins occur in 50%.  Legionella pneumophila:  diagnosis is by direct fluorescent antibody staining or serological tests; antigen may be detected in the urine.  Staphylococcus aureus:  of all patients, > 25% have positive blood cultures.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Smoking cessation should be advised in the long term for patients with pneumonia.  Patients with a score of 3 or above using the CURB-65 score require urgent hospital admission.  Admission should be considered with a score of 1 or 2.  Home treatment should be considered in patients with a score of 0 (take into account co-morbidities, general frailty, pulse oximetry values and if the patient is pregnant).  If hospital admission is not required, advise rest, hydration, and the use of simple analgesia for symptom relief (alongside antibiotic treatment). Pharmacological  For patients who do not require admission:  amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily (TDS) for five days orally (for adults and children over 12 years)  alternatives include:  doxycycline 200 mg on the first day followed by 100 mg a day for four days  oral clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily (BD) for five days  oral erythromycin (during pregnancy) 500 mg four times daily (QDS) for five days.  you should also give clear information about when symptoms should be expected to resolve, and when to seek further help.  For patients who require admission:  oxygen therapy to maintain target oxygen saturation level  intravenous fluid if circulating volume is depleted  antibiotics: refer to local guidelines.  In hospital:  non severe cases: oral amoxicillin and a macrolide (eg clarithromycin)  severe: intravenous (IV) broad-spectrum, beta-lactamase, stable antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav and a macrolide in severe cases.  Newer fluoroquinolones (eg moxifloxacin) provide an alternative for patients who are allergic to penicillin or macrolides.  IV treatment should be stepped down to oral treatment after 48 hours provided that the patient is improving.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  If a specific organism is isolated, the appropriate antibiotic is given.  Treatment should continue for 7–10 days depending on response.  Up to 21 days of treatment is recommended for legionella pneumonia.  Prognosis  Markers of increased pneumonia severity (and therefore poorer prognosis) include:  hypoxaemia (PO , 8 kPa despite oxygen therapy)  multilobar involvement  white cell count < 4.3 x 109/l or > 20.3 x 109/l  hypoalbuminaemia  positive blood cultures.  Other  Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia is a common first manifestation of immunodeficiency:  it presents with type I respiratory failure and exertional dyspnoea  significant findings are present on chest X-ray despite normal physical exam  prescribe co-trimoxazole and/or corticosteroids if severe. Cystic Fibrosis Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive condition associated with recurrent lung infections and pancreatic insufficiency.  Overview Key Facts  Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive condition associated with recurrent lung infections and pancreatic insufficiency.  CF is the most common fatal autosomal recessive condition in the White population.  It affects 1 in 2500 live births with 1 in 25 adults being a carrier of the gene.  Causes abnormal transport of chloride across the cell membrane.  Main systems affected are the respiratory and gastrointestinal system. It also affects the fertility of men.  Diagnosis can be achieved through screening, sweat testing and genetic testing.  Short term management options include antibiotics for chest infection.

DR. JAMIL  Long term management includes chest physiotherapy, prophylactic antibiotics, mucolytics, nutritional support and regular reviews. Lung transplantation is a last resort.  Average life expectancy is improving due to new therapies, currently approximately 40. Epidemiology 1 in 2 500 live births with 1 in 25 adults being a carrier of the gene.  Aetiology The CF gene lies of chromosome 7 and codes for the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator protein (CFTR). The most common mutation is F508del. Pathophysiology The defect results in abnormal transport of chloride across the cell membrane either failing to reabsorb chloride (as in the sweat gland) or failure to secrete chloride (as in the respiratory system). It causes blockage of airway and ducts as mucus is not thinned. Respiratory system  Airway obstruction due to thick mucus causing frequent infections. Infection occurs in an age-related fashion: young children become colonised with S. aureus and subsequently H. influenzae. In the teenage years, infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa usually occurs.  Chronic infection and inflammation leading to lung damage with bronchiectasis which predominantly affects the upper lobes. GI system  Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency as secretions block the pancreatic ducts in 90% of patients. Subsequent malabsorption results in weight loss, steatorrhoea and fat-soluble vitamin (ADEK) deficiency.  Pancreatic endocrine insufficiency occurs in up to 30% of CF patients with the loss of pancreatic isle cells causing frank diabetes.  Bowel obstruction due to the poor digestion of intestinal contents.  Chronic obstruction of the biliary ductules in the liver may lead to the development of cirrhosis and consequent portal vein hypertension, splenomegaly and the formation of varicose veins. Reproductive system  Fertility is slightly affected due to having thicker vaginal mucus, which can make it harder for sperm to reach the egg.  98% of men will suffer from infertility because the vas deferens is either missing or blocked. The sperm itself is healthy, it just can’t get into the semen.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Clinical Presentation  Newborns may present with meconium ileus.  Recurrent bacterial lung infections in early life.  Breathlessness, reduced exercise tolerance and pneumothorax.  pneumothorax occurs in 10% of CF patients, therefore must be considered in the context of acute chest pain.  Cough with chronic purulent sputum production and occasional haemoptysis.  haemoptysis could be due to erosion of vessel walls and rarely due to pulmonary arterial embolism  the formation and expulsion of tubular gelatinous material is known as plastic (or Hoffman’s) bronchitis  it can also be seen in asthma, bronchiectasis and some respiratory infections.  Abdominal pain, distension, vomiting and severe constipation – all these symptoms are in keeping with bowel obstruction.  Chronic sinus disease.  Faltering growth.  Rectal prolapse in children under 12 years of age.  Differential Diagnosis  Primary immunodeficiency  Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD)  Asthma  Chronic aspiration  Coeliac disease.  Diagnosis/Investigation A diagnosis of cystic fibrosis can be made when there is either:  a positive test results in people with no symptoms, for example, infant screening (blood spot immunoreactive trypsin test also known as the Guthrie’s (heel-prick) test) followed by sweat and gene tests for confirmation  clinical manifestations, supported by sweat testing in children or gene testing in adults for confirmation  clinical manifestations alone, in the rare case of people with symptoms who have normal sweat or gene test results  a sweat chloride result of > 60mmol/l is considered to be positive. If sweat test results lie within the intermediate range (30–59mmol/l) then additional tests to consider include a sinus X-ray and deep throat swab.  Imaging:  chest X-rays: may show hyperinflation, increased markings in upper zones bilaterally (due to bronchial wall thickening and bronchiectasis) atelectasis, fibrosis and apical bullae  CT scan: can be useful for monitoring by documenting the progression of the disease. Mucus plugging can be

DR. JAMIL visualised and a transverse view highlights how dilated the bronchi can become. Chest X-ray showing the typical appearance of CF:  Management Non-Pharmacological Offer people with cystic fibrosis a comprehensive annual review that includes the following:  airway clearing techniques  a pulmonary assessment and monitoring  an assessment of nutrition and intestinal absorption  an assessment for liver disease  testing for cystic-fibrosis-related diabetes, from 10 years of age  a psychological assessment  assessments by a specialist nurse, physiotherapist, pharmacist and social worker  a review of their exercise programme  fertility specialist referral. Pharmacological Options include:  inhaled bronchodilator  mucoactive agents – rhDNase (dornase alfa; recombinant human deoxyribonuclease is the first choice mucoactive agent)  tobramycin (only some patients) – chronic pseudomonas infection  anti-inflammatory azithromycin, ibuprofen, prednisolone  flucloxacillin should be offered as antibiotic prophylaxis against respiratory Staphylococcus aureus infection the point of diagnosis up to age 3

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  inhaled corticosteroid fluticasone propionate or budesonide  CFTR modulator eg ivacaftor  consider a long-term antibiotic to suppress chronic methicillinsensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) respiratory infection in people whose pulmonary disease is stable  fertility issues in women with CF are treated in the same way as they are for women without the condition  fat-soluble vitamins  high-calorie drinks  supplementary pancreatic enzymes. Surgical  When all other options have been exhausted, a bilateral lung transplantation may be considered.  The NHS estimates that around nine out of ten people survive a lung transplant. Of these, most survive for at least a year postoperatively, half will survive for at least five years after having a lung transplant, with many people living for at least 10 years.  Absolute contraindications to a lung transplant include:  patients colonised with Burkholderia cepacia (though can depend on antibiotic sensitivity profile)  sepsis  multiple organ dysfunction  history of non-adherence to treatment  morbid obesity  refractory gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.  Prognosis  Up to 90% of deaths are attributable to respiratory failure as a consequence of lung infection.  Currently, about half of people with cystic fibrosis will live past the age of 40.  Children born with the condition nowadays are likely to live longer than this. Cytomegalovirus Cytomegalovirus is a common worldwide infection with high levels of seropositivity.  Overview Key Facts  Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a common worldwide infection with high levels of seropositivity.  It causes severe illness in the immunocompromised and neonates, but mostly asymptomatic or mild ‘infectious mononucleosis’ type illness in the immunocompetent.  May lead to severe illness in most bodily systems.

DR. JAMIL  Congenital infection risks hearing, neurological and cognitive function.  In the immunocompromised, it may lead to morbidity and mortality.  Treatment and prevention are possible with antivirals. Antivirals needed for all those with immunocompromise or severe congenital infection.  CMV infection is self-limiting and mild in the immunocompetent.  Congenital infection can cause sensorineural deafness, learning disability, sight problems and developmental delay. Epidemiology  High rates of seropositivity worldwide.  The most common cause of non-genetic sensorineural hearing loss in children.  Seropositivity common, studies quote 30–98% positive in the worldwide population, with the higher rates in developing countries (eg high figures in Brazil, lower in Germany).  Two peaks of primary infection – under age 3 and in adolescents (the latter peak thought to be due to sexual activity).  Approximately 1% of all neonates in developed countries have CMV infection, with approximately 5–10% of these being symptomatic.  In developing countries, the occurrence of CMV in live births is approximately 6%.  Aetiology  Transmission, via body fluids/tissues:  blood, blood product transfusion  transplantation from CMV-positive to CMV-seronegative recipient  sexual contact  saliva  transplacental (vertical transmission following maternal latent reactivation or primary infection; congenital infection more likely in primary infection).  Vulnerable groups for severe infection – neonates and the immunocompromised.  Transplant recipients are especially at risk as they may contract CMV from the received material and develop a severe infection due to the immunosuppressants needed to counteract rejection.  Those with HIV are most at risk if CD4+ count is less than 50. Pathophysiology  Human CMV is a β-herpes virus (human β-herpes virus type 5).  Following primary infection, the virus develops latency.  Latency sites – endothelial cells of arterial walls, T cells.  Reactivation in the immunocompetent is normally asymptomatic with active viral shedding at this point.  In the immunocompromised, primary infection or reactivation may cause disseminated and thus severe infection.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Due to the variety of CMV strains that exist, someone can be reinfected, producing a secondary primary infection, but these tend to be milder.  Severe infection is mostly associated with immunocompromised states impacting on CD4 count (eg transplant recipients, HIV, older age).  Clinical Presentation In the immunocompetent  Majority asymptomatic:  possible, ‘infectious-mononucleosis type syndrome’ with – tiredness, pyrexia, lymphadenopathy, mild hepatitis, non-typical lymphocytosis  associated with Guillain–Barré syndrome. In the immunocompromised  Many possible presentations and complications:  hepatitis  GI involvement – mainly gastritis, oesophagitis and/or ulceration  renal – cause of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis or cystitis  pancreatitis  chest – pneumonia, pneumonitis  ocular– uveitis/retinitis  CNS – encephalitis, abscess  primary adrenal insufficiency, due to adrenitis and/or adrenal necrosis  cutaneous – pustles/necrotic ulcers.  Note:  might be referred to as an ‘AIDs- defining illness’  onset post-transplant normally weeks–months. Associated symptoms  Symptoms include:  tiredness  fever  loose stools  nausea, vomiting, reflux, dysphagia  eye – floaters, reduced acuity  skin lesions  swelling  jaundice. Severe complications  Neurological – Guillain–Barré syndrome, meningoencephalitis.  Cardiac – pericarditis.  Haem – haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia.

DR. JAMIL  GI ulceration. Congenital infection in neonates  Symptoms:  lethargy  microcephaly  hearing loss  abnormal head lag  poor muscular tone  abnormal motor function  hepatosplenomegaly  skin – petechiae, purpura.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  infective hepatitides, other causes, eg Epstein–Barr virus  infective oesophagitis, other causes, eg herpes simplex virus  other infectious lymphadenopathy, eg toxoplasmosis  infectious mononucleosis  HIV seroconversion illness  other viral illnesses.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis tends to be due to clinical suspicion and CMV detection. Investigative confirmation  CMV DNA isolation from PCR assay of tissue samples (eg possible from blood, serum, plasma, urine, saliva, amniotic fluid).  CMV antibodies – IgM (indicating primary infection), IgG (latent immunity).  Culture – possible from tissue swabs of patients with active infection. Investigation  First-line: Full blood count In the immunocompetent – raised WCC with abnormal differential In the immunocompromised – low Hb, low WCC, low platelets In neonates – low platelets Urea and electrolytes Not typically abnormal, unless causing renal damage

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI Liver function tests Raised transferases Bone profile If GI involvement may cause raised ALP  Further investigation may be based on system-specific enquiries: Chest X-ray Pneumonia Gastroscopy or colonoscopy Inflammation Ulceration CMV isolated from biopsy CT chest If causing pneumonitis: Nodules Alveoli involvement  Serum viral load measurement – used to monitor treatment effectiveness.  Management  In the immunocompetent antivirals are not needed  Antiviral drug resistance does occur and this needs to be monitored for. Non-Pharmacological  Supportive in mild infection in the immunocompetent, eg analgesia, adequate hydration.  When hospitalised, isolation needed from other patients with infection control measures utilised.  In neonates, antiviral therapy tends to be used in severe cases only.
