Prevention  CMV-status assessment in all transplant donors and recipients.  Only giving CMV-negative material to CMV-negative recipients.  Prophylaxis with antivirals if a CMV-positive transplant is given to a CMV-negative recipient.  Barrier contraception.  Handwashing, especially before and after eating and toileting.  Stringent hygiene in the pregnant.  In HIV patients – regular monitoring of immune status (aiming CD4+ > 100), medication selection and adherence. Occasionally antivirals are given to those with CD4+ < 50 to prevent CMV infection. Pharmacological  Antivirals needed for all those with immunocompromise or severe congenital infection.  Antivirals are the standard treatment of choice; this can reduce infection severity, further deterioration of affected sites and viral load.

DR. JAMIL  Common antivirals of choice are valganciclovir PO or ganciclovir IV; these are given for approximately 1 month.  Route of delivery (PO or IV) dependent on clinical status.  Retinitis – intravitreal antivirals if sight-threatening.  In AIDs – maintenance antiviral therapy may be needed.  Immunoglobulins may be used in combination with antivirals.  Prognosis  Infection self-limiting and mild in the immunocompetent.  CMV-induced hepatitis is normally mild with most recovering fully.  Severe infection may lead to mortality; most deaths from CMV pneumonia.  Congenital infection has the possibility of sensorineural deafness, learning disability, sight problems and developmental delay.  Side-effects of long-term antivirals may contribute to morbidity (eg ganciclovir/valganciclovir can cause bone marrow suppression). Empyema Empyema is defined as a collection of pus in the pleural space and can complicate up to 15% of community-acquired pneumonias.  Overview Key Facts  Empyema is defined as a collection of pus in the pleural space and can complicate up to 15% of community-acquired pneumonias.  Requires prolonged course of antibiotics.  Surgery/drainage/fibrinolytics may also need to be considered.  Mortality is approximately 15–20%; however, prognosis is improved with rapid diagnosis and initiation of treatment. Epidemiology  More common when there is a history of:  excess alcohol consumption  poor dental work  aspiration  general anaesthesia.  Aetiology  Streptococcus species, including Streptococcus milleri and Streptococcus pneumonia, account for approximately 50% of community-acquired pleural infections.  Other causative organisms include Staphylococcus aureus, Gram-negative aerobes, and anaerobes.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Hospital acquired pleural infections are most commonly caused by staphylococci, but other organisms such as the Gramnegative aerobes, Escherichia coli, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa are also known causes. Pathophysiology  The formation of empyema is classically divided into three stages:  exudative stage: accumulation of sterile pleural fluid due to inflammation/infection of lung parenchyma  fibrinopurulent stage: bacteria invade the pleural space and forms fibrinous septae, loculations and adhesions  organisational stage: lung expansion is inhibited, causing ‘trapped lung’ as dense fibrous adhesion form.  Clinical Presentation  A diagnosis of empyema is suspected if a patient is slow to recover from lower respiratory tract infection/does not respond to antibiotics.  Symptoms include:  productive cough  dyspnoea  pleuritic chest pain  malaise.  Signs include:  dull percussion note  decreased breath sounds  reduced vocal resonance  fevers and rigors  clubbing.  Differential Diagnosis  Pneumonia.  Lung abscess.  Malignant pleural effusion.  Oesophageal rupture.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Blood:  cultures  C-reactive protein  full blood count.  Imaging:  chest X-ray: blunting of costophrenic angle or effusion on affected side +/- pulmonary infiltrates. Lateral chest Xrays may confirm pleural fluid not suspected on the posteroanterior chest X-ray  ultrasound imaging: may help to identify pleural infection  computed tomographu (CT) may be helpful in: identifying any underlying abnormality that may be associated

DR. JAMIL with/the cause of the empyema, and providing guidance for drain insertion or the need for surgical intervention.  Thoracocentesis:  frank pus  putrid smell in anaerobic infection  pH < 7.2  total protein > 30 g/dl  lactate dehydrogenase 2–3 times above upper serum level limit  glucose < 3.3 mmol/l  white cell differential: lymphocytes > leukocytes suggests tuberculosis or malignancy  microscopy, culture, and sensitivity.  Management  First-line treatment is intravenous (IV) antibiotics and chest tube drain (+/- intrapleural fibrinolytics – can be used in some patients).  Second-line: video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery is indicated:  alternatively, open thoracic drainage or thoracotomy and decortication; depends on patient, surgeon preference, and equipment availability  and, continuing antibiotics.  Third-line: intrapleural fibrinolytics and continuing antibiotics.  Prognosis  Follow up within four weeks of discharge:  repeat chest X-ray  inflammatory markers should be arranged for all patients.  Continued outpatient care, possibly for several months depending on progress.  The long-term survival of patients with pleural infection is good if prompt treatment is initiated. Eosinophilic Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small and medium vessel vasculitis previously known as Churg–Strauss syndrome, which is characterised by eosinophil-rich, necrotising granulomatous in?ammation.  Overview Key Facts  Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is a small and medium vessel vasculitis previously known as Churg–Strauss syndrome, which is characterised by eosinophil-rich, necrotising granulomatous inﬂammation.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  EPGA is very rare with a prevalence of 10–15 per million people.  The condition may involve the respiratory tract, the renal system, the skin and peripheral nerves.  It typically presents with a history of asthma, sometimes with atopy and recurrent nasal polyps, often over a number of years prior to diagnosis.  More than 7/10 patients also have mononeuritis multiplex.  Renal involvement is less frequently seen and the condition is associated with less severe renal disease compared with granulomatosis with polyangiitis.  The most common renal complication in EGPA is necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis, but eosinophilic interstitial nephritis, mesangial glomerulonephritis and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis are also seen.  Renal involvement leads to haematuria and proteinuria, hypertension and raised creatinine levels.  The antibody associated with the condition is pANCA, which is seen in approximately 50% of cases (higher with glomerulonephritis presentations).  A raised eosinophil count (eosinophilia) is seen in over 90% of patients with advanced disease.  Skin biopsy reveals small-vessel arteriopathy with granuloma formation and is the diagnostic investigation of choice.  Treatment consists of corticosteroids, with or without additional therapy with agents such as methotrexate or cyclophosphamide.  Without treatment, the 5-year survival rate for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is around 25%; with appropriate therapy, this rises to over 60%. Epidemiology  The condition is very rare, with a prevalence of 10–15 per million people.  Affects men and women in equal proportions.  Rarely, the condition may present in childhood.  Aetiology  EGPA is a small to medium-sized vessel vasculitis characterised by eosinophilia.  More than 90% of patients have a diagnosis of asthma.  The exact cause is unknown. Pathophysiology  The cardinal feature of EGPA is the necrotising granuloma composed of an eosinophilic core surrounded by macrophages and epithelioid giant cells.  The pathogenesis of EGPA is still not completely understood.  It is most likely the result of a complex process where environmental and genetic factors lead to an inflammatory response involving eosinophils and B and T lymphocytes.  Clinical Presentation  The main presentations are patients with:

DR. JAMIL  asthma (diagnosed or symptoms suggestive of asthma, including wheeze, nocturnal cough)  sensory neuropathy  lung abnormalities  sinus problems such as abnormal growths (polyps).  The disease may follow three defined phases (or may present atypically, which makes diagnosis difficult): Phase Description Prodromal phase Most patients suffer from asthma and may also have allergies and sinus symptoms in their teens and early adulthood Eosinophilic phase Blood tests show eosinophilia Vasculitic phase Small and medium-sized vessels affected by vasculitis. This is often preceded by constitutional symptoms of weight loss, fever and lethargy The constellation of symptoms in individual cases vary depending on which organ systems are involved:  Respiratory  asthma (> 90% of patients), usually precedes symptoms of vasculitis by several years  allergic rhinitis  paranasal sinusitis  nasal polyps  cough  haemoptysis.  Cardiac  pericarditis or myocarditis  myocardial infarction (secondary to coronary vasculitis)  heart failure.  Renal  hypertension  glomerulonephritis  chronic kidney disease.  Gastrointestinal  bowel ischaemia and perforation  PR bleeding  appendicitis  pancreatitis.  Skin  purpura  livedo reticularis  urticaria  necrotic bullae  digital ischaemia.  Neurological  peripheral neuropathy/mononeuritis multiplex  stroke.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Other  fever  myalgia  weight loss.  Differential Diagnosis Differentials include, but are not limited to:  Other vasculitides:  granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)  polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)  microscopic polyangiitis  Goodpasture syndrome.  Other causes of eosinophilia:  parasitic infections  allergy  asthma  malignancy  chronic eosinophilic pneumonia.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The condition is diagnosed on finding four out of the following:  asthma  blood eosinophilia > 10%  vasculitic neuropathy  pulmonary infiltrates  sinus disease  extravascular eosinophils on biopsy findings.  It is diagnosed clinically, although a biopsy should be sought for pathological confirmation.  Over 50% of patients with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis have a positive pANCA (perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody) result. Other investigations:  Chest X-ray: may show patchy peripheral consolidation and pleural effusions  Pulmonary computed tomography:  peripheral opacification (consolidation or ground-glass opacities)  eosinophilic infiltration may cause bronchial wall thickening, bronchiectasis and the appearance of centrilobular nodules  pleural effusions.  Spirometry: 97% of patients have asthma, so will likely present with an obstructive picture on spirometry  Biopsy:  biopsy from an affected organ is the most useful for determining the diagnosis. If this is not possible or if no localised findings are determined, muscle or nerve biopsy may be performed

DR. JAMIL  lung biopsy may show necrotising granulomas with a central eosinophilic core and necrotising vasculitis  if there is renal involvement, renal biopsy may show focal or crescentic glomerulonephritis.  Management  Treatment is with corticosteroids, with or without additional therapy with methotrexate, azathioprine or cyclophosphamide.  Glucocorticoids alone usually are adequate for the treatment of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.  Cytotoxic drugs are necessary for less than 20% of patients.  Major life-threatening organ involvement may require treatment with pulse doses of intravenous (IV) corticosteroids as well as other cytotoxic agents.  Other treatments include intravenous immune globulin, interferon-alpha and plasma exchange.  Prognosis  Complications of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis depend on the specific organ system involvement.  The principal causes of morbidity and mortality are myocarditis and myocardial infarction secondary to coronary arteritis.  With treatment, the 1-year survival rate is 90% and the 5-year survival rate is 62%.  Overall, without treatment, the 5-year survival rate is about 25%. Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is a necrotising granulomatous vasculitis that affects small to medium-sized arteries, capillaries and veins; it was previously known as Wegener’s granulomatosis.  Overview Key Facts  Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is a necrotising granulomatous vasculitis that affects small to medium-sized arteries, capillaries and veins; it was previously known as Wegener’s granulomatosis.  The condition predominantly affects the respiratory tract and kidneys.  Symptoms of lung involvement include cough and haemoptysis.  Symptoms of renal tract involvement include haematuria and proteinuria.  Symptoms of upper respiratory tract involvement include nasal obstruction, epistaxis, rhinitis, ‘saddle nose’ deformity and subglottic stenosis.  Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss and myalgia are common.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  There may also be skin, eye, ear, gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms.  There is no single diagnostic test, but cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c-ANCAs), a biopsy of affected organs showing necrotising granulomas and vasculitis and imaging are used to aid diagnosis.  The mainstay of treatment is with steroids and cyclophosphamide.  Plasma exchange may be required in severe cases.  Once symptoms have improved, cyclophosphamide may be replaced by methotrexate or azathioprine, and treatment with steroids may continue for several years.  With effective treatment, 80% of patients may achieve remission, although relapses are common. Epidemiology  It affects men and women equally.  It is more common in middle-aged and older people but can present in childhood.  Aetiology  The exact cause is unknown, but approximately 90% of patients are positive for c-ANCA. Pathophysiology  GPA is a necrotising granulomatous vasculitis that affects small to medium-sized arteries, capillaries and veins.  The condition predominantly affects the respiratory tract and kidneys.  It is an immune-mediated vasculitis, but the exact pathophysiology is unknown.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms depend on the organs involved; granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is a multisystem disease with a diverse range of clinical features.  The most commonly affected organs are:  lungs (95% of cases) – cough, haemoptysis  kidneys (80%) – haematuria, proteinuria  upper respiratory tract (75–90%) – nasal obstruction, epistaxis, rhinitis, 'saddle nose' deformity, subglottic stenosis.  Many patients have constitutional symptoms, such as:  fever  weight loss  myalgia.  Other symptoms include:  skin involvement – rashes and ulcers  eye involvement – scleritis, episcleritis, conjunctivitis  ear involvement – chronic ear infections, hearing loss  neurological involvement – mononeuritis multiplex  gastrointestinal involvement – GI bleeding, abdominal pain, diarrhoea.

DR. JAMIL  Saddle nose deformity:  Differential Diagnosis  Due to the wide range of symptoms seen in granulomatosis with polyangiitis, it can be mistaken for a wide range of other conditions. This includes but is not limited to the following conditions.  Other vasculitides:  polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)  microscopic polyangiitis  eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.  If there is lung involvement, chest X-ray changes may be mistaken for:  lung cancer  tuberculosis  pneumonia.  Other conditions:  Goodpasture syndrome  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  rheumatoid arthritis with vasculitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  There is no single diagnostic test.  Bloods:  c-ANCA is positive in approximately 90% of cases in patients with renal impairment  however, in patients without renal impairment, c-ANCA may be negative in up to 50% of patients  renal function tests may be deranged if there is renal involvement  ESR – typically elevated, but non-specific finding.  Urine sample:

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  haematuria  proteinuria  casts.  Biopsy of affected organ (not always possible):  necrotising granulomas with associated vasculitis.  Chest X-ray:  the most common findings are nodules and/or cavitation and pulmonary haemorrhage.  CT imaging:  findings are highly variable  may include nodules, consolidation, ground-glass changes, atelectasis and pleural effusions.  Management Stage 1  Once the disease is recognised, it is treated aggressively with:  high-dose steroids  cyclophosphamide –in some cases, cyclophosphamide may be substituted with methotrexate, rituximab or mycophenolate mofetil.  Plasma exchange may be required in severe cases. Stage 2 (may last 2–5 years)  Once the symptoms have improved and the disease is under control, cyclophosphamide is usually stopped and replaced by methotrexate or azathioprine.  Steroids are continued. Stage 3  If the symptoms return, it may be necessary to:  continue steroids longer-term or  start treatment with rituximab or  restart cyclophosphamide or  consider plasma exchange.  Or a combination of the above.  Prognosis  Without treatment, 2-year survival may be as low as 10%.  With effective treatment, 80% of patients may achieve remission although relapses are common.

JAMIL Guillain-Barré Syndrome Guillain-Barré syndrome is an acute, immune polyneuropathy presenting with rapidly evolving weakness and variable sensory loss which is ascending in nature.  Overview Key Facts  Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) is an acute, immune polyneuropathy presenting with rapidly evolving weakness and variable sensory loss which is ascending in nature.  Most patients report preceding upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) or urinary tract infection (UTI).  The most commonly identified organism causing GBS is Campylobacter jejuni.  The cardinal feature is post-infection ascending paralysis.  Clinical symptoms include:  flaccid muscle tone  hyporeflexia/areflexia  autonomic disturbances  neuromuscular ventilatory failure  symptoms include shortness of breath on exertion, early morning headache and low forced vital capacity (FVC).  Investigations include:  cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis: normal white cell count (WCC) and glucose with raised protein  nerve conduction study: delayed conduction velocities indicating demyelination of peripheral nerves  electrocardiogram (ECG): rhythm disturbances  electrolyte study  pulmonary function tests ie spirometry FVC to monitor ventilation.  Treatment includes:  IVIG and plasma exchange  supportive therapy:  feeding care  ventilatory support (the patient may require intubation and ventilation)  pressure care  analgesia.  Prognosis is generally good:  most people make a full recovery, although this may take months  there is a 5% mortality rate, mostly due to the inhibition of ventilation  around 20% of patients go on to experience long-term complications:

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  weakness  paraesthesia  fatigue. High Altitude Medicine Altitude illness describes a number of conditions which can occur if individuals ascend rapidly to a high altitude (usually > 2500 m but susceptible individuals may experience it at lower altitudes),  Overview Key Facts  Altitude illness (AI) describes a number of conditions which can occur if individuals ascend rapidly to a high altitude (usually > 2500 m but susceptible individuals may experience it at lower altitudes),  High altitude is an elevation > 1500 m.  Altitude illness includes:  acute mountain sickness (AMS).  high altitude cerebral oedema (HACE).  high altitude pulmonary oedema (HAPE).  AMS occurs in up to 25% of individuals climbing to altitudes of 2000–3000 m and up to 50% of individuals climbing to altitudes of 3500–4500 m.  AMS is far more common than HACE or HAPE.  Severe altitude illness can be a life-threatening condition and requires urgent treatment.  Risk factors include:  fast rate of ascent  greater altitude reached  history of altitude illness  individuals with a residential altitude < 900 m  pre-existing CVS conditions (eg congenital heart disease, angina).  As altitude increases, air pressure decreases – reduced O2 delivery into and around the body.  Individuals who ascend gradually can usually acclimatise to the reduction in O2 levels.  If the ascent is too fast, the body doesn’t get chance to acclimatise and altitude illness may occur. AMS HACE HAPE headache gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms weakness fatigue altered consciousness ataxia confusion (~2 h post-ascension). breathlessness orthopnoea wet cough haemoptysis wheeze chest tightness (~2 h post ascension).

DR. JAMIL dizziness (6–10 h postascension).  Individuals climbing altitude may commonly get non-altitude illness headache (eg exhaustion, dehydration or hangover).  It is also important to rule out:  hypoglycaemia  hyponatraemia  hypothermia in patients with symptoms of altitude illness.  All three forms of altitude illness are diagnosed based on clinical findings – severity of illness is related to severity of symptoms.  Travelers who exhibit potential symptoms of altitude illness should not be left unsupervised.  AMS treatment includes:  stopping further ascension and resting  simple analgesia and anti-sickness medication  descending if symptoms do not improve or deteriorate over 1–2 days.  HACE/HAPE require urgent medical treatment – descend as soon as possible for further treatment.  Early descent for altitude illness may be aided by:  supplementary O2  portable hyperbaric chambers  medication including dexamethasone or nifedipine.  The main way of preventing altitude illness is through careful planning – advise avoiding large ascensions in altitude and plan sleeping altitudes accordingly.  Acetazolamide may be taken to help prevent altitude illness in individuals with a moderate-to-high risk.  Severe altitude illness or death is very rare and is avoidable in most cases. Epidemiology  An estimated 9–25 % of unacclimatised individuals who ascend to altitudes of 2000–3000 m develop AMS.  This increases to 35–50 % in individuals ascending to heights of 3500–4500 m.  AMS is much more common than HACE or HAPE.  HACE and HAPE are extremely rare in altitudes < 2800 m and incidence is only ~1–2 % in altitudes of 4000–5000 m.  Aetiology  AI occurs when individuals ascend too rapidly and are unable to acclimatise to the changes in O2 levels.  It usually occurs in altitudes > 2500 m but can occur at lower altitudes (especially in individuals who are more susceptible).  The main risk factors can be split into those relating to the trip and those relating to the individual:  Trip – rate of the ascent, the absolute change in altitude, and the altitude at which a person sleeps.  Individual – previous history of AI, normal residence below 900 m, exertion of arrival at altitude, and pre-

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI existing cardiovascular conditions (eg congenital heart disease or angina). Pathophysiology  Altitude illness can be split into:  AMS  HACE  HAPE.  As altitude increases, the barometric (air) pressure decreases.  The fraction of inspired O2 in the air remains the same (FiO2 = 21 %).  As a result, individuals are unable to take in as much O2 at altitude – reduced delivery of O2 around the body and to the tissues.  Individuals who ascend gradually can usually acclimatise to the reduction in O2 levels and do not become sick.  Acclimatisation happens by:  reduced renal bicarbonate excretion to correct respiratory alkalosis (hyperventilation occurs due to hypoxia)  kidneys stimulated to produce erythropoietin – relative polycythaemia increases O2 carriage in the blood  increased 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (DPG) production shifts the O2 dissociation curve to the right to allow increased O2 offloading at tissues.  If the individual’s ascent is too rapid, then the body does not get chance to acclimatise, and AI may occur.  AMS and HACE are both neurological manifestations of altitude illness – it islikely that they are on a spectrum of the same disease, with HACE being a more severe form of AMS.  HACE and HAPE are severe but uncommon and usually occur together.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms of AMS don’t usually occur on immediate ascent, they tend to present 6–10 hours after reaching altitude (> 2500 m). AMS  AMS is defined as new-onset headache in an unacclimatised individual who has recently arrived at altitude, and 1 or more of the following:  GI symtoms (anorexia, nausea and vomiting)  dizziness  fatigue  weakness.  These criteria are a guide and generally any new symptoms which occur after ascending to altitude should be considered altitude illness until proven otherwise.  AMS is usually self-limiting if further ascent is delayed – usually resolves within 1–3 days. HACE  HACE very rarely occurs and is usually only seen when altitudes > 4500 m are reached.  It is characterised by cerebral oedema which can present with:

DR. JAMIL  reduced consciousness or loss of consciousness  new onset of confusion  new onset ataxia.  It is commonly preceded by AMS so it is important to look for these features.  HACE and HAPE usually occur ~2 days after ascent to altitude (> 3000–4000 m). HAPE  HAPE is the respiratory form of altitude illness.  Initially, symptoms include feeling breathless on exertion and a dry cough.  These can progress into:  breathlessness at rest  orthopnoea (breathlessness when lying flat)  wet cough  blood-stained sputum  wheezing  chest tightness.  HAPE may occur in the absence of AMS or HAE.  HACE and HAPE usually occur ~2 days after ascent to altitude (> 3000–4000 m).  Headache at high altitude is very common, although it is used as part of the diagnostic criteria.  Differential Diagnosis  The symptoms of AMS can easily be confused with other conditions, including:  headache – exhaustion, dehydration, hangover, migraine etc  GI symptoms – gastroenteritis, Traveller's diarrhoea, preexisting GI conditions  weakness and/or fatigue – exhaustion, anaemia etc.  It is important to monitor patients displaying any of these symptoms (having recently climbed at altitude), as AMS can develop into a more severe, life-threatening illness.  Other diagnoses to rule out include:  hypoglycaemia  hyponatraemia  hypothermia.  Diagnosis/Investigation  AMS, HACE and HAPE are all clinical diagnoses – severity is usually subjective based on the intensity of symptoms.  Many high altitude settings are in remote locations with minimal access to healthcare facilities – investigations may be difficult to perform.  Simple examination may help in diagnosis:  Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) in patients who may have developed HACE  percussing and auscultating the chest in suspected HAPE.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Management  Many high altitude settings are in remote locations with minimal access to healthcare facilities – treatment options may be limited.  Travelers displaying any signs or symptoms of altitude illness should not be left alone as their symptoms may progress and become life-threatening. AMS  Travellers who have developed AMS should stop further ascent (may take 1–3 days for sickness to resolve).  It is important that they rest and take simple analgesia (paracetamol or ibuprofen) as required.  Anti-sickness medication may also help symptoms.  If symptoms of AMS do not improve or deteriorate over 1–2 days of rest, then individuals should descend. HACE/HAPE  Travellers exhibiting symptoms of HACE and HAPE require urgent medical attention and should descend as soon as it is safe to do so.  Some experienced travellers may carry medical supplies which can aid descent:  oxygen cylinders  portable hyperbaric chamber (increases barometric pressure to allow greater inhalation of O2)  nifedipine or dexamethasone – both have been proven to help in prophylaxis and treatment of altitude illness. Prevention:  The majority of preventative measures focus on ensuring the ascent is gradual and that patients sleep at an appropriate altitude to what they have gained (eg once over 3000 m, sleep elevation should not increase by > 500 m each day).  Preventative medication may be useful in individuals with moderate-to-high risk of developing altitude illness.  Acetazolamide 125 mg twice-daily (BD) is recommended (should start one day before ascent and continue for two days after reaching highest altitude) – contraindicated in pregnant women.  Individuals should undergo a trial period of ~2 days on acetazolamide before climbing as there are numerous side effects:  polyuria  paraesthesia  nausea  vomiting  headache.  Other risks are present when climbing altitude and these should also be accounted for:  blisters  dehydration  sun exposure  Traveller's diarrhoea  hypothermia or cold injury.

DR. JAMIL  Prognosis  Severe altitude illness or death as a result of altitude illness is avoidable in the majority of individuals who are climbing altitude. Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (formerly known as extrinsic allergic alveolitis) is a complex syndrome resulting from an immunological response due to repeated exposure to a sensitising antigen affecting the respiratory system.  Overview Key Facts  Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (formerly known as extrinsic allergic alveolitis) is a complex syndrome resulting from an immunological response due to repeated exposure to a sensitising antigen affecting the respiratory system.  It is usually immunoglobulin G (IgG) mediated.  Occupational history of the patient is very important.  Avoiding the causative antigen is the most important and effective aspect of management.  Corticosteroids may have a role in treating severe or progressive disease.  Recurrent episodes/long-term exposure can cause irreversible lung damage. Epidemiology  It is more common in non-smokers than in smokers.  More common in middle aged men – this may be due to pattern and likelihood of antigen exposure.  Aetiology  Farmer’s lung  inhalation of thermophilic actinomycetes found in mould on vegetable matter (eg hay, straw and grain) in storage.  Bird fancier’s lung  inhalation of avian serum proteins, found in the excrement and bloom from feathers.  Ventilation pneumonitis  thermophilic actinomycetes grow in the humidification system in air-conditioned buildings.  Bagassosis  exposure to thermoactinomyces sacchari in sugar cane processors.  Malt worker's lung  inhalation of aspergillus clavatus.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Mushroom worker's lung  inhalation of thermophilic actinomycetes. Pathophysiology  Delayed immune response to an inhaled antigen.  Mechanism is Th-1 (asthma is Th-2).  Clinical Presentation  Hypersensitivity pneumonitis can present as either an acute or chronic condition.  Symptoms for both include:  breathlessness  myalgia  fatigue  weight loss.  In the acute form, symptoms (that may include fever and headache) appear within several hours of high-level exposure and usually resolve within 48 hours without causing any fibrosis of the lung.  In the chronic form, the symptoms appear gradually as a result of low-level exposure over a prolonged period of time that causes scarring and damage to the lungs.  Signs:  inspiratory crackles (not very frequent)  finger clubbing (in chronic disease).  Differential Diagnosis  Viral pneumonia.  Usual interstitial pneumonia.  Sarcoidosis.  Pneumoconiosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is made by:  establishing a history of exposure to antigen  demonstrating precipitating antibodies in the patient’s serum.  Investigations:  bloods:  neutrophilia  raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate  C-reative protein.  chest X-ray:  acute: non-specific (micro-nodule, ground glass opacification etc.) or normal findings  chronic: progressive upper zone fibrosis and loss of lung volume.  high-resolution computed tomography (CT):

DR. JAMIL  diffuse or patchy ground glass attenuation, midzone.  spirometry:  restrictive pattern.  histology:  lung biopsy tissue shows a mononuclear cell infiltrate with the formation of non-caseating granulomas.  bronchoalveolar lavage:  fluid has a high lymphocyte count, typically > 40%.  precipitins:  specific IgG antibodies in serum against the identified antigen  note: precipitins and bronchoalveolar lavage lymphocytosis can sometimes indicate exposure, but not the disease.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Allergen avoidance is the most effective treatment.  If related to work, involve Occupational Health professionals.  Respiratory protection (this helps, but it is still possible to inhale particles). Pharmacological  Acute disease:  corticosteroid, tapered off over six weeks.  Chronic disease:  corticosteroids  immunosuppressants. Surgical  Lung transplantation is an option in severe disease.  Prognosis  There is possible progression to irreversible lung fibrosis in some patients, while others develop emphysema.  Prompt diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis is important because the disease is reversible when diagnosed early. Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a specific form of chronic, progressive lung fibrosis of unknown origin that is characterised by usual interstitial pneumonia on lung biopsy.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a specific form of chronic, progressive lung fibrosis of unknown origin that is characterised by usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) on lung biopsy.  It is the most common form of interstitial lung disease among the idiopathic interstitial pneumonias.  The condition presents with progressively worsening breathless and a cough, evidence of cyanosis, finger clubbing and fine, late inspiratory crackles.  Diagnosis may require multidisciplinary input:  respiratory  radiology  histopathology etc.  Treatment aims to slow the rate of scarring.  Prognosis is poor with median length of survival being three years from diagnosis. Epidemiology  The condition affects the middle age and elderly with a mean age of diagnosis at 60–70 years old.  More men than women are affected.  Familial pulmonary fibrosis (FPF) is a subset of IPF (the features of which are indistinguishable from IPF) but tends to occur in slightly younger patients.  Aetiology  Although by definition the aetiology is unknown, researchers suggest that fibrosis may occur in response to damage in the lung.  This damage may be due to:  acid reflux  viruses – links between the Epstein–Barr virus, herpes virus and hepatitis C have all been suggested  environmental factors, eg dusts from wood, textiles, metal or stone, or from cattle or farming.  Some people may be genetically predisposed to develop IPF when their lung is damaged. Pathophysiology  The histopathological changes in IPF are associated with honeycombing, minimal cellular inflammation and regions of proliferating myofibroblasts (known as fibroblastic foci) found in usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP).  Clinical Presentation  Shortness of breath on exertion or at rest.  Cough with or without sputum.  Fatigue.  Cyanosis.

DR. JAMIL  Finger clubbing.  Fine end inspiratory crackles.  Differential Diagnosis  Acute interstitial pneumonia.  Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease:  rheumatoid arthritis  inflammatory bowel disease  progressive systemic sclerosis.  Drug related pulmonary fibrosis:  amiodarone (causes an alveolitis this may be reversible on drug cessation, progressing to diffuse fibrosis; more common when higher doses are used  sulfasalazine  methotrexate  busulfan  bleomycin  cyclophosphamide  nitrofurantoin  gold  melphalan  asbestosis  sarcoidosis  langerhan's cell histiocytosis.  Other respiratory causes of finger clubbing:  lung cancer  empyema  lung abscess  bronchiectasis  extrinsic allergic alveolitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Assessment for suspected idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis involves blood tests to help exclude alternative diagnoses, including lung diseases associated with environmental and occupational exposure, connective tissue diseases and medications:  blood gas analysis: typically shows type I respiratory failure with hypoxaemia and a normal or low PCO2  antinuclear antibodies – normal or mildly elevated in 10– 20% of patients with IPF  rheumatoid factor – normal or mildly elevated in 10–20% of patients with IPF  anticyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies (anti-CCP) – normal in patients with IPF  myositosis panel will be normal in patients with IPF.  chest X ray  small lung volumes  interstitial shadowing most marked at the bases and peripheries.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI X-ray of ‘reticular’ pattern seen in pulmonary fibrosis – lung markings are worse at the base: https://radiopaedia.org/cases/unfolded-aorta  Computed tomography (CT) of the thorax (including highresolution images):  useful to determine radiological pattern of disease (typically UIP)  may be enough to diagnose IPF thus avoiding the need for more invasive diagnostic tests.  Further investigations include:  lung function testing, typically showing restrictive changes  surgical lung biopsy is crucial if there is any diagnostic doubt  bronchoalveolar lavage is only considered when a pattern of UIP is not identified on high-resolution CT  transbronchial biopsy should not be routinely performed but is useful for ruling out certain differentials, such as sarcoidosis.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Pulmonary rehabilitation:  if appropriate after assessment, offer pulmonary rehabilitation including exercise and educational components. Pharmacological  There is no conclusive evidence to support the use of any drugs to increase the survival of people with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.  Antifibrotic drugs, such as pirfenidone and nintedanib, are thought to slow the rate of scarring.  Oxygen therapy may be helpful.  Proton pump inhibitor (PPI) as an adjunct.

DR. JAMIL  Oral N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC) can be used, but the benefits are uncertain.  If already using prednisolone or azathioprine, discuss the potential risks and benefits of discontinuing, continuing or altering therapy. Management of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: Surgical: Lung Transplantation  To be discussed with patients who are deteriorating despite optimum medical management and do not have any absolute contraindications.  Many limit the age of transplantations to < 65 years old, though some do offer it to those > 65 years old.  Prognosis  Mean life expectancy from diagnosis is 2–5 years, but the rate of disease progression is very variable.  The initial rate of decline in the person's condition may predict subsequent prognosis. Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome is caused by presynaptic autoantibodies to P/Q type calcium channels.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is caused by presynaptic autoantibodies to P/Q type calcium channels.  The condition is very rare.  LEMS is most commonly associated with small cell carcinoma of the lung.  Autonomic symptoms are commonly seen in LEMS.  Investigations include creatine kinase (CK), electromyogram (EMG) and muscle biopsy.  Treatment is with 3,4-diaminopyridine and/or pyridostigmine. Epidemiology  LEMS is very rare.  Aetiology  LEMS is most commonly associated most with small cell carcinoma of the lung.  Other neoplastic associations include:  ovarian cancer  breast cancer  lymphoproliferative disorders.  Non neoplastic causes of LEMS include:  diabetes mellitus type I  thyroid disorders. Pathophysiology  Lambert Eaton Myasthenic syndrome is caused by presynaptic autoantibodies to P / Q type calcium channels, resulting in impaired neurotransmitter release.  This ultimately leads to debilitating muscle weakness.  Clinical Presentation  Unlike in myasthenia gravis, eye and bulbar muscle involvement are rare.  Features of LEMS include:  proximal weakness of lower limbs  dry mouth  hypo- or areflexia  rapid progression in cases of underlying malignancy  difficulty in micturition  impotence  dysphagia  dizziness, especially on standing up.

DR. JAMIL  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses include:  myasthenia gravis  motor neurone disease  myopathies  polymyositis  cranial nerve palsy  Graves' disease  botulism.  Diagnosis/Investigation Diagnostic investigations include:  computed tomography (CT) scan/positron emission tomography (PET) scan of chest to exclude malignancy  nerve conduction studies  full blood count (FBC).  Management Management of LEMS:  Treat the underlying cause.  Symptomatic treatment is with 3,4-diaminopyridine (a potassium channel blocker) – 10 mg–20 mg four times per day.  Pyridostigmine may or may not be used.  Corticosteroid therapy may be used.  Plasma exchange and IVIG (rarely).  Prognosis  LEMS has a poorer prognosis, given its relationship to underlying malignancy. Lung Cancer Lung cancer is a malignant tumor that originates in the cells of the lungs, often associated with smoking and exposure to carcinogens, and can spread to other parts of the body if not detected and treated early.  Overview Key Facts  Lung cancer is the most prevalent cancer worldwide.  It accounts for 1 in 3 cancer deaths in men and 1 in 6.5 cancer deaths in women.  The condition is rare under the age of 40 years old, with incidence increasing with age.  Approximately 90% of cases are attributed to smoking.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI Small Cell (20%) Non-Small Cell (75–80%) Small cell is the most aggressive Adenocarcinoma Squamous cell is the most associated with smoking Large Cell Undifferentiated  Common presentations include:  breathlessness  cough  haemoptysis  chest pain  weight loss.  Metastases can occur throughout the body, but the most commonly involved sites are:  supraclavicular and anterior cervical lymph nodes  adrenals  bones  liver  brain  skin. Epidemiology  Over 43 000 new cases of lung cancer diagnosed in the United Kingdom every year.  Lung cancer is rare under the age of 40 years old.  Incidence rises steeply with age, peaking in the 80–84 year age group.  Persistently higher lung cancer rates in urban populations – this may be attributed to passive smoking.  Aetiology  Smoking:  those currently smoking are almost 15 times more likely to die from lung cancer than those who have never smoked in their lives.  Nearly 90% of lung cancers occur in current or ex-smokers.  Atmospheric pollution.  Industrial exposures.  Asbestos fibre.  Aluminium industry.  Arsenic compounds.  Benzoyl chloride.  Silica.  Beryllium.  Increased incidence in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and systemic sclerosis. Pathophysiology Histological types of lung cancer:

DR. JAMIL  Squamous cell (35%): usually arises from a central airway. Heavily associated with cigarette smoking. It has a doubling time of 90 days and the best survival of all the different histological types of lung cancer due its potential operability.  Small-cell (20%): arises in central airways and grows rapidly.  It has a doubling time of 29 days. and is usually metastatic at diagnosis, so surgery is usually inappropriate.  This histological subtype is very sensitive to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, and active treatment options are therefore considered in patients with poor performance statuses.  Adenocarcinoma (30%): often peripheral.  It is slow growing with a doubling time of 160 days.  Undifferentiated large cell (10%).  Bronchiolar–alveolar cell carcinoma (5%).  Clinical Presentation  Patients with lung cancer commonly present with:  cough  breathlessness  haemoptysis  chest pain  hoarse voice  weight loss.  Finger clubbing may be present.  Lung cancer should be suspected if pneumonia fails to resolve radiologically.  An occasional incidental finding is an asymptomatic lesion noted on a routine chest X-ray.  May present indirectly with an intrathoracic complication of lung cancer.  collapse of lung distal to obstructing tumour  recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy causing hoarseness  dysphagia due to compression of the oesophagus by enlarged metastatic lymph nodes or tumour invasion  pericarditis with effusion  phrenic nerve palsy with raised hemidiaphragm  pleural effusion  superior vena caval obstruction causing:  headache  distension of the veins in the upper body  fixed elevation of the jugular venous pressure  facial suffusion with conjunctival oedema.  hypercalcaemia either due to bony metastasis or ectopic parathyroid hormone  spontaneous pneumothorax.  Metastases can occur throughout the body but the most commonly involved sites are:  supraclavicular and anterior cervical lymph nodes  adrenals

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  bones  liver  brain  skin.  Differential Diagnosis  Small cell lung cancer.  Non-small cell lung cancer.  Pneumonia.  Bronchitis.  Exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).  Sarcoidosis.  Secondary metastases in the thorax.  Lymphoma.  Pulmonary tuberculosis.  Differential diagnoses of haemoptysis:  common causes:  carcinoma of the bronchus  pneumonia/acute bronchitis  bronchiectasis  pulmonary tuberculosis  pulmonary embolus  mitral valve disease  infective exacerbation of COPD.  rarer causes:  vascular malformations  mycetoma  connective tissue disorders  vasculitis  Goodpasture syndrome  cystic fibrosis  bleeding diathesis  idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis.  Pulmonary causes of clubbing:  carcinoma of the bronchus  asbestosis  lung abscess  cystic fibrosis  tuberculosis  idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis  bronchiectasis  empyema  mesothelioma.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Suspected cancer referral pathway for patients who:

DR. JAMIL  have chest X-ray findings that suggest lung cancer  are aged 40 and over with unexplained haemoptysis.  Urgent X-ray for patients aged 40 and over with two or more of the following unexplained symptoms, or if they have ever smoked and have one or more of the following unexplained symptoms:  cough  fatigue  shortness of breath  chest pain  weight loss  appetite loss.  Consider an urgent chest X-ray (to be performed within two weeks) to assess for lung cancer in people aged 40 and over with any of the following:  persistent or recurrent chest infection  finger clubbing  supraclavicular lymphadenopathy or persistent cervical lymphadenopathy  chest signs consistent with lung cancer  thrombocytosis.  Investigation pathway as per the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines:  urgent chest X-ray and immediate referral computed tomography (CT) of the thorax  information and support – involve lung cancer clinical nurse specialist  advice on smoking cessation  CT scan.  Patients will be discussed and reviewed at a Lung MultiDisciplinary Team meeting to plan next steps.  Further tests depend on the size/site of tumour.  if peripheral lesions < 10 mm nodules are seen, low probability of nodal malignancy ? positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan  if peripheral lesions > 10 mm then biopsy nodules  if central lesions are present on CT scan, offer flexible bronchoscopy if nodal staging does not influence treatment.  All patients with lung cancer who could potentially have treatment with curative intent are offered PET-CT before treatment.  Confirm the presence of isolated distant metastases/synchronous tumours by biopsy or further imaging (for example, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or PET-CT) in people being considered for treatment with curative intent.  Localised signs or symptoms of bone metastasis should prompt an X-ray as the first-line investigation.  CT head and/or MRI if suggestion of intracranial pathology. The chest X-ray shows 3-cm mass with spiculated margins in the right lung that was confirmed as being an adenocarcinoma following biopsy.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  This patient also happens to huge thoracic aortic aneurysm that is displacing the trachea to the right and evidence on hyperinflation. Soft tissue mass with irregular margins:  The typical appearance of a primary lung cancer is a soft tissue mass with irregular margins (as shown above), whereas lung metastases usually appear as smooth and rounded on CT scans.  Management Non-small cell lung cancer:  treatment with curative intent:  surgery  chemoradiotherapy.  consider for people with stage II or III who are not suitable for/decline surgery.  radiotherapy

DR. JAMIL  if surgery declined/contraindicated ⇢ radical radiotherapy  cannot tolerate/decline chemoradiotherapy  multimodality treatment  systemic anti-cancer therapy for advanced disease  treatment dependent on whether tumour is made of squamous or non-squamous cells.  ablation procedures for primary and secondary lung cancers  percutaneous radiofrequency ablation  microwave ablation  irreversible electroporation.  photodynamic therapy for localised inoperable endobronchial cancer.  Small cell lung cancer:  early stage, surgery is definitive management  limited stage ⇢ chemotherapy +/- radiotherapy  extensive stage ⇢ chemotherapy, consider thoracic radiotherapy with prophylactic cranial irradiation if chemotherapy has been caused a partial/complete response  ablation procedures  recurrence treatment options:  repeat chemotherapy  offer radiotherapy for palliation of local symptoms  limited evidence that second-line chemotherapy will be of benefit if no response to first-line chemotherapy. Pharmacological  Chemotherapy.  Emergence of monoclonal antibody use. Non-Pharmacological  Superior vena cava obstruction can also be treated with radiotherapy (although stenting provides more immediate relief of symptoms).  Palliative radiotherapy is very effective in relieving pain from bony metastases, controlling haemoptysis and cough.  Dysphagia due to oesophageal compression by lymph nodes responds well to radiotherapy.  Unresectable tumours that compromise the trachea or large airways may be palliated by local techniques to maintain airway patency.  These include brachytherapy (intraluminal radiotherapy), laser therapy, airway stents and/or photodynamic therapy.  Surgery  Includes lobectomy, pneumonectomy and segmentectomy.  Best chance of long-term, disease-free survival.  Candidacy dependent on clinical staging.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI Chest radiograph showing a patient who has had a right lung pneumonectomy:  Prognosis  The 5-year survival rate of all lung cancers depends on the clinical stage at diagnosis.  small cell lung cancer: 5-year survival rate is approximately 12%–24% for limited stage.  1% to 5% for extensive stage.  Non-small cell lung cancer 5-year survival rates:  stage IA: 61%  stage IB: 38%  stage IIA: 34%  stage IIB: 22%–24%  stage IIIA: 9%–13%  stage IIIB: 3%–7%  stage IV: 1%.  Paraneoplastic syndromes associated with lung cancer:  syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH):  chiefly associated with small-cell lung cancer  hypovolemic hyponatraemia  may resolve with chemotherapy but recurs with tumour progression  treatment involves fluid restriction initially and demeclocycline for resistant cases.  ectopic adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH):  mainly associated with small-cell lung cancer.  hypercalcaemia:  associated with multiple bony metastases from squamous cell carcinoma

DR. JAMIL  ectopic parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion occurs in a few squamous cancers.  gynaecomastia:  associated with large-cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma.  hyperthyroidism:  rare (due to ectopic thyroid- stimulating hormone (TSH)) – squamous cell lung cancer.  Lambert–Eaton syndrome:  almost exclusively associated with small-cell lung cancer  rare  patients have proximal myopathy, reduced tendon reflexes and autonomic features  clinical picture is similar to myasthenia gravis but unlike myasthenia gravis, weakness improves with repeated muscle contraction.  clubbing:  occurs in 10–30% of lung cancers; may resolve after resection.  hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (HPOA):  produces periostitis, arthritis and gross finger clubbing  most commonly associated with adenocarcinoma  least frequently with small-cell carcinoma  It involves the long bones (tibia/fibula, radius/ulna or femur/humerus). It is associated with subperiosteal new bone formation visible on plain radiograph and is often painful.  Other  Pancoast syndrome (type of non-small cell lung cancer):  tumour of the superior sulcus  commonly presents with pain due to involvement of the eighth cervical and first thoracic nerve roots extending down the medial side of the upper arm to the forearm and hand  the small muscles of the hand can atrophy  Horner’s syndrome may develop  chest X-ray demonstrates a shadow at the extreme apex, and there may be destruction of the first and second ribs. Lung Transplantation Lung transplantation is the transplantation of one or both lungs, alone or in combination with the heart (heart–lung transplant).  Overview Key Facts  Lung transplantation is the transplantation of one or both lungs, alone or in combination with the heart (heart–lung transplant).

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  It is a relatively new procedure, with the first heart–lung transplant performed in 1981 and the first single lung transplant in 1983. Indications  Typical indications for lung transplantation are as follows:  chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD): in young patients with alpha 1-antitrypsin deficiency, single lung transplantation may be suitable  cystic fibrosis: more likely to require bilateral lung transplantation in order to avoid spillage from a chronically infected ‘bad’ lung into the transplanted lung  fibrosing lung diseases: may be suitable for single lung transplantation  congenital heart disease leading to pulmonary vasculopathies such as Eisenmenger syndrome; may require heart and lung transplantation, or lung transplantation combined with correction of the cardiac defect. Selection of the recipient  There is a high chance of mortality with lung transplant.  As such, transplantation is generally only offered to patients who have lung disease with a prognosis of < 1 year.  Often, these patients need ambulatory oxygen preoperatively and have a forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) < 15% predicted.  As the risk to the recipient is so great, donor organs must be exceptionally carefully evaluated to ensure that the risk–benefit analysis is favourable.  The criteria for recipient selection are:  medical therapy is ineffective  activities of daily living are substantially limited  life expectancy is limited  cardiac function is adequate (if lung-only transplantation is planned).  The National Health Service (NHS) lists the following as absolute contraindications for lung transplant:  BMI > 35  untreatable other-organ system failure, unless also considered for a combined multi-organ transplant  unstable critical condition (eg septicaemia or shock)  significant chest wall or spinal deformity that will impede surgical implantation  uncontrolled extra-pulmonary symptoms of a systemic illness, eg vasculitis or systemic sclerosis  substance addiction or abuse (including tobacco) active within the past six months  history of poor adherence to medical treatment.  Some relative contraindications are also listed:  patients > 60 years require special consideration  severely limited functional status

DR. JAMIL  chronic infection with resistant bacteria  obesity with a BMI > 30  malnutrition with a BMI < 17. Selection of the donor  Lung transplantation is limited more than other transplantations by a shortage of donor organs, so much so that around a third of patients die on the waiting list. The problem is particularly acute because after brainstem death, ventilated patients are very likely to aspirate, develop hospital-acquired pneumonia or develop neurogenic pulmonary oedema.  There is ongoing research into ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP) to optimise harvested lungs before transplantation. EVLP involves connecting the pulmonary circulation to a machine and perfusing with fluid, with the aim of reducing inflammation. EVLP may allow the use of donors who do not fulfil the traditional criteria:  age ≤ 55 years  ABO-compatible  clear chest X-ray (CXR)  partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) ≥ 300 mmHg (39.9 kPa) on fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) 1.0, 5 cm H2O positive end-expiratory pressure  tobacco history ≤ 20 pack years  absence of chest trauma  no evidence of aspiration or sepsis  no prior cardiopulmonary surgery  sputum Gram stain: absence of organisms  no purulent secretions at bronchoscopy.  Procedure Procedure: Single lung transplantation  a posterolateral thoracotomy is performed  the aorta and right atrium are cannulated for cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB)  the old lung is excised using clamps on the pulmonary artery, left atrium and bronchus  the donor lung is placed in the thoracic cavity  the artery, vein and bronchus are anastomosed  haemostasis is obtained, drains are placed and the chest is closed. Procedure for lung harvest  the donor is opened from the suprasternal notch to the pubis by the abdominal organ retrieval team  the lungs are mobilised and adhesions divided  the vena cavae and aorta are mobilised, taking care not to injure the right pulmonary artery which runs behind  the donor is heparinised

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  cannulas are placed in the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk  pulmonary drugs that vasodilate may be injected into the pulmonary trunk at this stage  an aortic cross-clamp is placed  cardioplegia fluid is run into the aortic root  the cardioplegia fluid is vented into the pericardium via an incision in the inferior vena cava (IVC)  both cavae, the aorta and the pulmonary trunk are divided  the left atrium is incised so as to leave a patch posteriorly joining the pulmonary veins  the heart is explanted  the left and right pulmonary arteries are separated  using scissors divide the posterior pericardium in a vertical direction between the left-sided and right-sided pulmonary veins  the lungs are inflated by the anaesthetist and the two main bronchi are stapled off before division so that the lungs remain inflated in transit  the lungs are placed on ice for rapid transit to the recipient.  Prognosis  There is significant morbidity associated with a lung transplant, including:  bleeding: from anastomotic joins  bronchial stenosis: at the site of anastomosis  early graft dysfunction: from ischaemic reperfusion injury  rejection: acute or chronic  infections: bacterial, fungal or viral, predisposed to by immunosuppression.  There is 20% mortality at one year and 50% mortality at five years. Mesothelioma And Other Asbestos Related Conditions Mesothelioma is a malignancy of the pleura of the lungs.  Overview Key Facts  Mesothelioma is a malignancy of the pleura of the lungs.  It is an aggressive tumour of the mesothelium, which make up the lining of the serous body cavities including the pleura and peritoneum, pericardial and testicular serosa.  Mesothelioma can therefore in theory affect these other sites, but the most common site for mesothelioma is the pleura (80– 90% of cases.)  Asbestos is the main carcinogen associated with the development of mesothelioma.  Presents as chest pain or breathlessness.

DR. JAMIL  Diagnosis is via a combination of computed tomography (CT), chest X-ray and histological analysis.  Cure is possible only in a very small number of early stage illnesses; this is achieved by surgery.  Chemotherapy and radiotherapy have roles, though there is lack of consensus on how they should be employed.  Prognosis is poor, with median survival only reaching one year; the disease is almost invariably fatal. Epidemiology  Malignant mesothelioma has an incidence of 3.4 : 100 000 in UK males.  There are approximately 2 700 new cases diagnosed every year in the UK.  Incidence of mesothelioma is increasing in industrialised countries.  Aetiology  Asbestos is the main carcinogen associated with the development of mesothelioma  crocidolite and amosite are the types most associated with mesothelioma.  The main industries associated with this are:  mining  ship building  building and insulation. Pathophysiology  Histologically, mesothelioma can be divided into epithelial, sarcomatoid and mixed subtypes.  On light microscopy, they can be difficult to distinguish from sarcomas and adenocarcinomas, although immunohistochemistry can make the distinction clearer. Staging of malignant mesothelioma Tumour (T) Node (N) Involvement of any listed node Metastasi s (M) Stage Ia T1a – primary tumour limited to ipsilateral parietal pleura

Stage Ib T1b – T1a plus focal involveme nt of visceral pleura

Stage II As above plus involveme nt of the diaphragm, or lung

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI Stage III, any of the following : T3 - any locally advanced tumour Or any Nodal involvement N1: Ipsilateral, bronchopulmonar y or hilar nodes N2: Subcarinal or ipsilateral mediastinal nodes

Stage IV, any of the following : T4 – locally advanced unresectabl e tumour N3: Contralateral mediastinal nodes, internal mammary nodes or ipsilateral or contralateral supraclavicular lymph nodes M1: Any metastati c spread  Clinical Presentation Clinical presentation is as follows:  shortness of breath: caused by pleural effusion, this is relieved when the effusion is drained  chest discomfort: initially dull, diffuse and progressive, may be pleuritic in nature  severe chest pain: as the tumour invades the chest wall  fatigue, fever, sweating and/or weight loss  finger clubbing  there may also be a palpable chest wall mass  malignant mesothelioma should be considered in any patient with pleural effusion or radiographic evidence of pleural thickening. In particular, this should be the case if there is chest pain or a history of occupational exposure to asbestos.  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses include:  bronchial carcinoma  other pleural diseases  pleural plaques  other causes of pleural effusion  cardiac failure  parapneumonic effusion  renal failure  other causes of chest pain  pneumonia.  other respiratory infections  tuberculosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Radiological investigations

DR. JAMIL  chest X-ray & CT scan: pleural effusions, pleural thickening, pleural mass or invasion of the ribs leading to bony damage. Mesothelioma (circled) on a chest X-ray  Pleural fluid analysis  may be straw coloured or blood stained. A cytology sample may be done and in some cases; this may show the diagnosis.  Pleural biopsy  this is usually done under ultrasound or CT guidance and is the definitive diagnostic test.  often, percutaneous biopsy may not be adequate for diagnosis, so a formal rib resection may be done:  formal rib resection, in which a mini-thoracotomy incision is made and a small section of rib excised to reveal a window of pleura. A 1-cm-square piece of thickened pleura is taken.  Staging  may be aided by mediastinoscopy and video thoracoscopy.  Management  Curative surgery is only possible in patients with very limited mesothelioma ie stage I. Non-Pharmacological  Radiotherapy may be given after thoracoscopy or drainage to reduce the chance of seeding metastatic disease. However, this is currently debated.  Adjuvant radiotherapy may help to reduce the recurrence after surgery, though this currently has little evidence.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI Pharmacological  Chemotherapy with platinum-based agents is the main chemotherapy drug used.  Chemotherapy improves survival in patients with disease not amenable to surgery. Surgical  Extrapleural pneumonectomy and lung-sparing debulking are the treatments of choice when attempting cure.  Palliative pleurodesis can be done to help with shortness of breath causes by recurrent pleural effusions.  Prognosis  Average survival is poor and current median survival is one year.  Currently, malignant mesothelioma is almost always fatal.  Note that the disease is highly related to occupational exposure to asbestos; upon death, a coroner’s referral should be made which can assist families in seeking compensation.  Other Other asbestos related conditions:  benign pleural disease: pleural plaques and pleural thickening  interstitial lung disease: asbestosis. Pleural plaques  Affect the parietal pleura, occur in 20-60% of patients who have been exposed to asbestos.  These plaques may be asymptomatic or may cause chest pain.  They do not undergo malignant transition.  Diagnosis is possible on CT scan. Diffuse pleural thickening  Not limited to asbestos related disease, and may occur after TB, chest surgery or after a haemothorax.  On chest X-rays, there will be a smooth pleural density; this may blunt the costophrenic angle and affect the lateral wall.  CT scan and pleural biopsy may be required to fully differentiate from malignant lung disease. Asbestosis  This is a typical interstitial lung disease (ILD) that is caused by the inhalation of inorganic particulate matter  this type of interstitial lung disease (ILD) is known as pneumoconiosis.  There is a typical latent period of between 20–30 years.  Presents as slow onset breathlessness, cough and wheeze.

DR. JAMIL  Examination may reveal inspiratory crackles and finger clubbing in advanced disease.  Diagnosis is via a combination of pulmonary function testing, chest X-rays and high-resolution CT  lung function testing shows reduced gas transfer, reduced lung volume with a restrictive spirometry picture  chest X-rays may be normal, or pleural plaques and thickening may be seen.  There is no specific management, but treatment concerns managing other factors that may affect lung function, eg smoking and vaccinations for influenza and pneumococcus. Obstructive Sleep Apnoea Obstructive sleep apnoea is defined as excessive daytime sleepiness along with irregular breathing at night.  Overview Key Facts  Obstructive sleep apnoea is defined as excessive daytime sleepiness along with irregular breathing at night.  Symptoms include:  poor concentration  irritability and personality changes  tiredness  sleeping during the day.  Diagnosed using sleep studies.  Treated using lifestyle modifications and continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), underlying causes should be identified and managed as appropriate.  The condition is linked to poor cardiovascular outcomes in adults.  The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) should be notified of the diagnosis in patients who hold a driving licence. Epidemiology  Approximately 4% of middle-aged men and 2% of middle-aged women are affected in the United Kingdom.  Estimated that 85% are undiagnosed and therefore untreated.  1–2 % of children are also affected by the condition.  an increase of incidence in this age group may be attributed to increasing levels of obesity in children.  Higher prevalence in children with congenital conditions such as Down syndrome or craniofacial abnormalities.  More common in obese individuals.  Aetiology  Both genetic and environmental factors can contribute to the development of sleep apnoea.  Risk factors include:

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  male sex (male : female ratio is 2–3 : 1)  obesity  neck circumference > 43 cm  family history of obstructive sleep apnoea  middle and older age  smoking  alcohol and sedating drugs before bed  acromegaly  hypothyroidism. Pathophysiology  A reduction in the muscle tone of the airway during sleep causes a narrowing that results in an obstruction of the airflow between the soft palate and the base of the tongue.  Results in a partial awakening (which they may or may not realise) and ventilation resumes.  The cycle is repeated several hundred times throughout the night.  Clinical Presentation  Family history of loud snoring interrupted by episodes of apnoea.  Sensation of waking up due to choking.  Sleep feels unrefreshing.  Daytime somnolence.  Poor concentration.  Differential Diagnosis  Other causes of daytime sleepiness to consider include:  narcolepsy  depression  restless legs syndrome  hypoactive delirium in older patients  drugs, for example:  sedatives  beta-blockers  selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.  neurological disorders, eg motor neuron disease or Parkinson’s disease.  Causes of nocturnal choking or gasping:  gastro-oesophageal reflux disease  nocturnal asthma  heart failure (orthopnoea/paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND))  panic attacks and night terrors.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Assess for:

DR. JAMIL  enlarged tonsils  small jaw  nasal blockage (polyps or deviated septum)  features of head or neck cancer, eg:  change in voice character  unilateral epistaxis  dysphagia  rapid onset of symptoms.  blood pressure  body mass index  neck circumference  Epworth Sleepiness Questionnaire; a total score > 10 indicates abnormal daytime sleepiness:  mild (11–14)  moderate (15–18)  severe (> 18).  Refer to a sleep centre for sleep studies to confirm the diagnosis via polysomnography (or limited sleep study).  Refer urgently if:  patient’s livelihood involves them driving  there is co-existent chronic obstructive pulmonary disease  respiratory/heart failure is present.  Obstructive sleep apnoea can be diagnosed if five or more episodes of apnoea, hypopnoea, or both events occur per hour of sleep.  Severity is based on the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI), which refers to number of episodes per hour.  mild: AHI 5–14 per hour  moderate: AHI 15–30 per hour  severe: AHI more than 30 per hour.  Management Non-Pharmacological  CPAP is recommended for adults with mild obstructive sleep apnoea if:  they have symptoms that affect their quality of life and ability to go about their daily activities  lifestyle advice and any other relevant treatment options have been unsuccessful or are considered inappropriate.  Life style advice includes:  weight loss  sleep routine  avoiding substances such as alcohol and nicotine  intra oral devices, eg mandibular advancement device. Surgical  An adenotonsillectomy in children can be considered if there is evidence of adenotonsillar hypertrophy.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  if surgery contraindicated/unlikely to help then consider CPAP.  Surgery is not routinely recommended in adults and would only be considered when the patients and quality of life is severely effected despite trying all other options.  Prognosis  CPAP treatment reduces daytime and nocturnal blood pressure.  Untreated obstructive sleep apnoea is associated with a risk of arrhythmias, stroke and coronary heart disease.  Obstructive sleep apnoea is an independent risk factor for type II diabetes.  Other  Important to identify and treat as consequential effects of obstructive sleep apnoea include:  hypertension  stroke  type II respiratory failure  cardiovascular disease  cor pulmonale  traffic accidents. Occupational Asthma Occupational asthma is the most common industrial lung disease in developed countries.  Overview Key Facts  Occupational asthma (OA) is the most common industrial lung disease in developed countries.  It is caused by irritants in the workplace.  The condition may result from immunological or nonimmunological stimuli.  The mainstay of treatment is to identify and minimise exposure to stimuli. Epidemiology  In Europe, there has been a noted decline in the incidence of OA since 2000.  16.3% of all adult-onset asthma is caused by occupational exposures.  Aetiology  Sensitiser-induced OA (accounting for the majority OA cases) is caused by immunological stimuli.  Irritant-induced OA (including reactive airways dysfunction syndrome) is caused by non-immunological stimuli.

DR. JAMIL Pathophysiology  Once occupational asthma has developed, bronchospasm may be precipitated by other non-specific triggers such as cold air and exercise.  Lung function changes are also similar to those with other forms of asthma.  Immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated response with eosinophilic airway inflammation.  Clinical Presentation  Occupational asthma develops after a period of asymptomatic exposure to the allergen, usually within two years of first exposure.  Asthma symptoms may persist despite termination of exposure.  Risk factors include:  a history of allergies  occupational rhinitis as an warning sign that you may develop occupational asthma  smoking.  Workplaces with high rates of occupational allergens include:  bakeries – flour dust and additives in the flour  hospitals – natural rubber latex proteins in latex gloves, and vapours from surgical techniques  pet shops/zoos/animal laboratories – fur, dander, saliva, and dusts from animal enclosures  farms and agricultural workplaces – grain dust, poultry dust, or other dusts that are a mix of materials from fungal spores, bacteria, endotoxins, mites, animal dander, and faeces.  Workplaces with high rates of occupational irritants include:  car manufacture/repair workshops – isocyanate exposure  woodwork and carpentry workshops – dusts  electronics and assembly industries – fumes from resinbased solder flux  engineering and metalwork workplaces – metal working fluids (MWFs)  hairdressing – bleach containing persulphate and henna  indoor swimming pools – airborne chloramines.  Differential Diagnosis  Occupational eosinophilic bronchitis.  Hypersensitivity pneumonitis.  Chronic bronchitis.  Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Detection depends on a careful history, and 2-hourly peak expiratory flow rate monitoring – both at work and at home.  To identify the substance involved, specific serum IgE levels can be measured.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Non-specific bronchial provocation testing may be performed instead of demonstrating a bronchodilator response:  a PC02 ≤ 8 mg/ml is usually taken as supportive of asthma.  Spirometry pre- and post-bronchodilator.  Chest X-ray – usually normal or signs of hyperinflation.  Skin-prick testing – atopy suggest by immediate appearance of wheal and flare.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Early diagnosis and removal of the individual from exposure to the allergen/irritant are essential if the person is to make a full recovery.  Patient education and environmental control. Pharmacological  Inhaled corticosteroids and bronchodilators.  Prognosis  Prognosis for sensitiser-induced occupational asthma is best with early accurate diagnosis and complete avoidance of further exposure to the sensitiser.  Irritant-induced occupational asthma may clear after months but can persist for several years.  It is possible to get subsequent work-exacerbated asthma, so monitoring may be necessary.  Other  Reactive airway dysfunction syndrome  reactive airway dysfunction syndrome (RADS) refers to bronchial hyper-responsiveness following the inhalation of high concentrations of irritant gas, aerosols or particles  asthma-like symptoms usually develop within minutes to hours after exposure  airway hyper-reactivity persists over a prolonged period of time  ‘irritant asthma’ occurs after multiple exposures to lower concentrations of irritants.  Byssinosis  byssinosis is a form of occupational lung disease caused by exposure to cotton dust, flax and hemp  acute exposure causes airways narrowing in a third of affected individuals  chronic byssinosis develops after years of heavy exposure to cotton dust; symptoms are worse on the first day back after a break from work, and include chest tightness, cough, dyspnoea, and wheeze  there is often a progressive decline in forced expiratory volume during the working shift  prevention is by reducing exposure  bronchodilators may provide some relief of symptoms.

DR. JAMIL Pleural Effusion A pleural effusion is a collection of fluid within the pleural space and can result from pleural, pulmonary and extra-pulmonary diseases.  Overview Key Facts  A pleural effusion (PE) is a collection of fluid within the pleural space and can result from pleural, pulmonary, and extrapulmonary diseases.  PEs can be grouped into two main categories:  transudate (mainly ‘failures’)  exudates (infective and malignancy).  Diagnostic pleural aspiration of effusions will determine the underlying cause.  Tube drainage may be indicated.  Treatment of PEs includes determining and then treating the underlying cause. Epidemiology  As PEs are the result of an underlying pathology, calculating incidence is difficult.  Most causes are secondary to pneumonia, cardiac failure, and malignancy.  Massive PEs are most commonly due to malignancy  Aetiology  Transudate:  low in protein  usually as a result of increased hydrostatic pressure or decreased oncotic pressure  common causes include:  ‘failures’  left ventricular failure (LVF)  cirrhosis of the liver  nephrotic syndrome  other causes of hypoproteinaemia.  uncommon causes include:  myxoedema  pulmonary emboli  sarcoidosis  peritoneal dialysis.  Exudates:  high in protein  usually caused by inflammation and leakage of extravascular fluid  common causes include:  infections: bacterial pneumonia tuberculosis

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  malignancy: primary carcinoma of bronchus, metastatic carcinoma  pulmonary embolism  connective tissue disorders: rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  subdiaphragmatic: pancreatitis, subphrenic abscess  trauma: haemothorax, chylothorax.  uncommon causes include:  infections: fungal, viral, and parasitic  malignancy: lymphoma, pleural tumours  connective tissue disorders: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Sjögren syndrome, immunoblastic lymphadenopathy  subdiaphragmatic: hepatic abscesses  trauma: ruptured oesophagus. Pathophysiology  Imbalance between fluid production and removal within the pleural space is observed.  exudates tend to be caused by changes in local factors  transudate tend to be the result of changes in systemic factors.  Clinical Presentation  The symptoms of PE are:  progressive breathlessness  pleuritic pain  symptoms of the underlying condition.  The majority of malignant effusions are symptomatic.  The signs of PE are:  reduced chest wall movements on the affected side  stony, dull percussion note  diminished or absent breath sounds  decreased tactile vocal fremitus/vocal resonance  bronchial breathing just above the effusion.  There may be signs of the underlying condition.  Differential Diagnosis  Elevated hemi diaphragm.  Pleural tumour.  Chylothorax – usually iatrogenic following surgery above the diaphragm, the cysterna chyli (thoracic duct).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Imaging:  chest x-ray  ultrasound – more sensitive than computed tomography (CT) in detecting pleural fluid septation

DR.
