JAMIL  CT scan – can help differentiate between benign and malignant cause.  Bloods:  full blood count  clotting screen  arterial blood gas  liver function tests  urea and electrolyte tests  C-reative protein.  Sputum:  microscopy, culture and sensitivity.  Diagnostic pleural aspiration of effusions (preferably ultrasound-guided):  do not perform in bilateral effusions in which the clinical setting is strongly in keeping with a transudate cause unless atypical/fail to respond to treatment  assess for:  colour and odour  pH  protein levels: < 25 g/l are consistent with a transudate, while protein levels > 35 g/l are consistent with an exudate  for protein levels between 25–35 g/l, use Light’s criteria  lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) concentration  cytological examination – malignant effusions diagnosed pleural fluid cytology in 60% of cases  gram stain  acid alcohol fast bacilli stain  microbiological culture: the diagnostic yield from microbiological culture is higher if some of the fluid sampled is sent for analysis in blood culture bottles. Paired peripheral blood samples for serum protein and LDH concentrations should be sent  triglyceride count – if significantly raised, strongly suggestive of chylothorax  amylase: in pancreatitis, the amylase level may be higher in pleural fluid than in blood  glucose: particularly low glucose levels (< 1.6 mmol/l) are seen in effusions due to rheumatoid arthritis.  invasive investigations:  percutaneous pleural biopsy  thoracoscopy – used when pleural aspiration inconclusive and malignancy suspected  bronchoscopy – not routine, consider in presence of haemoptysis. The X-ray below shows a ‘white out’ of the right hemithorax. Other differentials for a whiteout include a pneumonectomy, complete collapse of the lung, or a massive lung mass.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  The position of the trachea can help to identify what the cause of the whiteout is:  trachea pulled towards opacity – pneumonectomy or complete collapse of the lung  trachea pushed away from opacity – pleural effusion or huge lung mass.  Management Management is highly dependent on the underlying cause. Pharmacological  Congestive heart failure:  diuretic and physiotherapy  will require an echocardiogram  if symptomatic, requires therapeutic thoracocentesis and oxygen.  Infective:  intravenous (IV) antibiotics, therapeutic thoracocentesis. Surgical  Tube drainage is indicated if:  the pleural fluid pH is < 7.2 (suggesting a developing empyema)  pleural fluid Gram stain and/or culture is positive  frank pus is aspirated.  Malignancy in patients with:  bad performance status: therapeutic thoracocentesis  good performance status: pleurodesis or pleural catheter drainage.  Prognosis  Depends on underlying cause.

DR. JAMIL  Most patients with a pleural effusion will not be affected in the future.  Malignant effusions may change the cancer staging and the prognosis of the cancer.  LENT score is a prognostic score form malignant effusions.  Other  For fluid that has a protein concentration between 25–35, Light’s criteria should be applied.  Light’s criteria state that pleural fluid is exudative if one of the following applies:  pleural fluid : serum protein ratio is 0.5  pleural fluid : serum LDH ratio is 0.6  pleural fluid LDH is more than two-thirds limit of normal serum  a pH < 7.1 also suggests an exudate.  Other rare causes of PE include:  Meigs syndrome  asbestos exposure  familial mediterranean fever  yellow nail syndrome  post-thoracotomy syndrome  Dressler syndrome. Pneumonia Pneumonia is an acute infective condition of the lung usually caused by bacteria, viruses or – rarely – fungi.  Overview Key Facts  Pneumonia is an acute infective condition of the lung usually caused by bacteria, viruses or – rarely – fungi.  Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) occurs outside of hospital (or within two days of hospital admission):  Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common causative pathogen in community-acquired cases of pneumonia.  presenting signs and symptoms, as well as severity, vary depending on the underlying pathogen, patient age and comorbidities.  severity can be graded using the CURB-65 score, which is also a prognostic indicator.  treatment depends on the severity of the condition; this determines the route and type of antibiotic needed, as well as the need for admission (up to 40% of cases).  the United Kingdom (UK) mortality rate of all patients admitted to hospital with CAP ranges from 5.7% to 14%; for those patients admitted to intensive care, it is 30%.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) is defined as pneumonia that develops two days or more after admission to hospital:  it occurs in up to 5% of hospitalised patients, increasing hospital stay by up to eight days.  it confers a worse prognosis than that of CAP, with mortality rates estimated to range from 30% to 70%.  treatment is antibiotic therapy to be started within four hours of establishing the diagnosis.  the choice of antibiotic will vary according to Trust guidelines. Epidemiology  There are approximately 220 000 cases of CAP per year in the UK.  This is equivalent to approximately 5–10 cases per 1000 adults in the UK.  HAP occurs in 0.5–5% of hospitalised patients.  Aetiology Community-acquired pneumonia  Streptococcus pneumoniae (60–70%).  Haemophilus influenzae.  Staphylococcus aureus.  Gram-negative organisms.  Atypical organisms include:  Mycoplasma pneumoniae (5–15%)  Legionella pneumophila  Chlamydia psittaci  Chlamydia pneumoniae  Coxiella burnetii (Q fever).  Virus causes include:  influenza  varicella-zoster  cytomegalovirus (CMV). Hospital-acquired pneumonia  S. aureus.  Gram-negative bacteria:  Klebsiella spp.  Pseudomonas spp.  Escherichia coli  Proteus spp.  Serratia spp.  Acinetobacter spp.  Anaerobes.  Fungi.  S. pneumoniae (and other streptococci) are less common.

DR. JAMIL Pathophysiology  Local pathogen multiplication results in an inflammatory response in the lung parenchyma.  White blood cells interact with organisms resulting in cytokine release.  This activates the entire immune system.  HAP is most commonly the result of introducing oropharyngeal pathogens into the alveoli by micro-aspiration, or leakage of secretions around endotracheal tube:  pathogens may also be introduced via inhalation, macroaspiration, infected intravenous (IV) cannulae and thoracocentesis.  Clinical Presentation  Features can differ depending on the type of pneumonia.  Streptococcus pneumoniae:  there is an abrupt onset of illness, with high fever and rigours  examination reveals crackles or bronchial breathing and herpetic cold sores may be present in more than a third of cases  older patients may present with general deterioration or confusion.  Mycoplasma pneumoniae:  tends to affect young adults; it occurs in epidemics every 3–4 years; there is typically a longer prodrome, usually > 2 weeks  extrapulmonary complications include:  peri-/myocarditis  erythema multiforme  erythema nodosum  Stevens–Johnson syndrome  haemolytic anaemia  disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)  thrombocytopenia  meningoencephalitis  cranial and peripheral neuropathies  bullous myringitis  hepatitis  pancreatitis.  Legionella pneumophila:  history is important as outbreaks are usually related to contaminated water-cooling systems, showers or airconditioning systems, though sporadic cases do occur; in examinations, commonly from a ‘European resort’  Legionnaires’ disease usually affects middle-aged and older patients, often with underlying lung disease  men are affected more than women (3 : 1).  Staphylococcus aureus:  S. aureus pneumonia may follow a viral illness

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  the disease is more common in intravenous drug users  specific features include:  toxin production with extensive tissue necrosis  staphylococcal skin lesions  chest X-rays show patchy infiltrates with abscess formation in 25% of cases and the organism is responsible for around 10% of parapneumonic effusions.  Other signs and symptoms include:  cough  breathlessness  wheeze  pleuritic pain  fever (less common in older patients)  increased work of breathing.  HAP should be suspected in in-patients (admitted for at least two days) with new signs or symptoms including:  breathlessness  reduced oxygen saturations  tachycardia  cough (productive or not)  poor appetite  raised temperature  chest pain  crackles on auscultation of the chest  decreased air entry.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  asthma  acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)  pulmonary embolism (PE)  tuberculosis (TB)  whooping cough  post-natal drip  gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD).  For in-patients, it is also important to consider:  heart failure  acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Clinical judgement should be used to diagnose the condition alongside history and examination.  If the patient has signs and symptoms of CAP, assess for severity using the CRB-65 score:

DR. JAMIL  confusion (< 8/10 score on the abbreviated mental test (AMT))  respiratory rate > 30 breaths per minute  blood pressure (BP) < 90 mmHg and/or diastolic < 60 mmHg  age > 65 years.  Investigations in primary care include:  pulse oximetry (urgent admission for saturations less than 90%)  chest X-ray if there is suspected underlying lung pathology, or if the diagnosis is uncertain (not usually initially required in the diagnosis of CAP)  sputum culture  if moderate severity, cases are managed in the community.  All patients who are admitted to hospital with suspected severe pneumonia should have the following tests performed on admission (or as soon as the diagnosis is suspected in inpatients) as per British Thoracic Society (BTS) guidelines:  oxygen saturations  arterial blood gases if necessary – may show type 1 respiratory failure  chest X-ray to allow accurate diagnosis  bloods:  C-reactive protein (CRP) to aid diagnosis and as a baseline measure  full blood count (FBC)  liver function tests (LFTs) which may demonstrate transient hepatitis  urea and electrolyte (U&E) tests to inform severity assessment.  The anterior-posterior chest X-ray shows consolidations in the left lung base, but as it does not fully obscure the heart border it is difficult to tell which lobe it is in.  The lateral X-ray reveals that the consolidation lies posteriorly and therefore has to be in the left lower lobe. Left lower lobe pneumonia – lateral chest X-ray:

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Specific investigation findings:  Streptococcus pneumoniae:  capsular polysaccharide antigen may be detected in serum, sputum, pleural fluid or urine  increasing incidence of penicillin resistance, particularly in countries such as Spain.  Mycoplasma pneumoniae:  normal white cell count (WCC)  cold agglutinins occur in 50%.  Legionella pneumophila:  diagnosis is by direct fluorescent antibody staining or serological tests; antigen may be detected in the urine.  Staphylococcus aureus:  of all patients, > 25% have positive blood cultures.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Smoking cessation should be advised in the long term for patients with pneumonia.  Patients with a score of 3 or above using the CURB-65 score require urgent hospital admission.  Admission should be considered with a score of 1 or 2.  Home treatment should be considered in patients with a score of 0 (taking into account co-morbidities, general frailty, pulse oximetry values and if the patient is pregnant).  If hospital admission is not required, advise rest, hydration and the use of simple analgesia for symptom relief (alongside antibiotic treatment). Pharmacological  For patients who do not require admission:  amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily (TDS) for 5 days orally (for adults and children over 12 years)

DR. JAMIL  alternatives include:  doxycycline 200 mg on the first day, followed by 100 mg a day for four days  oral clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily (BD) for five days  oral erythromycin (during pregnancy) 500 mg four times daily (QDS) for five days.  also give the patient clear information about when symptoms should be expected to resolve and when to seek further help.  For patients who require admission (or are in-patients up to 48 hours post-admission):  oxygen therapy to maintain target oxygen saturation level  intravenous (IV) fluid if circulating volume is depleted  antibiotics – refer to local guidelines.  In hospital:  non-severe cases – oral amoxicillin and a macrolide (eg clarithromycin)  severe – IV broad-spectrum, beta-lactamase, stable antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav and a macrolide in severe cases.  Newer fluoroquinolones (eg moxifloxacin) provide an alternative for patients who are allergic to penicillin or macrolides.  IV treatment should be stepped down to oral treatment after 48 hours provided that the patient is improving.  If a specific organism is isolated, the appropriate antibiotic is given.  Treatment should continue for 7–10 days depending on response.  Up to 21 days of treatment is recommended for legionella pneumonia. For patients who are in-patients (at least 48 hours post-admission)  Start antibiotic(s) within four hours of establishing a diagnosis.  Check local guidelines on HAP as often the treatment will differ from CAP.  When considering antibiotic regime, the following should be taken into account as per the National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidance:  severity of symptoms or signs (based on clinical judgement as no validated severity assessment tools are available for HAP at present (September 2019))  length of hospital stay before the onset of symptoms  risk of developing complications  recent antibiotic use and microbiological results  the risk of adverse effects with broad-spectrum antibiotics, including Clostridium difficile infection  hospital guidelines/protocols for antibiotics.  Prognosis  Markers of increased pneumonia severity (and therefore poorer prognosis) include:

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  hypoxaemia (PO, 8 kPa despite oxygen therapy)  multi-lobar involvement  white cell count < 4.3 × 109/l or > 20.3 × 109/l  hypoalbuminaemia  positive blood cultures.  HAP can increase hospital stay by an average duration of eight days.  HAP has a higher mortality rate than CAP at > 30% and up to 70%.  Other Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia  This is a common first manifestation of immunodeficiency:  it presents with type 1 respiratory failure and exertional dyspnoea  significant findings are present on chest X-ray despite normal physical exam  prescribe co-trimoxazole and/or corticosteroids if severe. Aspiration pneumonia  Aspiration pneumonia often occurs in patients with very poor health.  Patients who are unlikely to improve their swallow will be at increased risk of aspiration pneumonia.  Nasogastric tubes also increase the risk of aspiration.  Anaerobes are the principal pathogens, arising from the oropharynx.  Gram-negative enteric bacilli may be more common.  There are typically 2–3 separate isolates in each case. These chest X-rays were taken one day apart during the admission of an older patient for a stroke. New dense consolidation in the right lung is clearly visible. The right lung is most commonly involved.

DR. JAMIL  Aspiration occurring in the supine position tends to lead to posterior segment involvement of the upper lobe and the apical segment of the lower lobe, whereas aspirating while sitting upright tends to affect the right middle and lower lobes.  Aspiration pneumonia is treated with metronidazole in combination with a broad-spectrum agent (eg third-generation cephalosporin).  Cavitation/lung abscesses may develop in certain lung infections.  The frequency of occurrences of aspiration pneumonia and the effects on the patient’s quality of life should guide discussions with the patient or family about the overall goals of care.  Some patients may decide to continue to eat and acknowledge the risks associated with this instead of having interventions such as gastrotomy or endotracheal tubes. Pneumothorax A pneumothorax describes air in the pleural cavity.  Overview Key Facts  A pneumothorax describes air in the pleural cavity.  It can be classified as either primary or secondary.  Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP).  usually occurs at rest.  men > women.  commonly present in 20s.  Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP) is associated with underlying lung condition.  Symptoms in PSP can be minimal or absent.  Even a relatively small SSP can demonstrate severe symptoms.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  A tension pneumothorax is a medical emergency and need rapid needle decompression.  There is a higher morbidity and mortality rate with SSP than PSP.  Smoking cessation can reduce rate of recurrence.  Pneumothorax is not usually associated with physical exertion.  While spontaneous pneumothoraces are still described as 'primary' or 'secondary', the 2023 BTS guidelines emphasise clinical status and the presence of high-risk features over strict categorisation or pneumothorax size. Management decisions should prioritise symptom severity, physiological compromise and patient risk factors. Epidemiology  PSP presentation is early 20s.  Pneumothorax is much more common in people who smoke.  Aetiology  Anatomical abnormalities, such as subpleural plebs.  Smoking increases the risk of developing pneumothorax.  PSP patients are, on average, taller and may be of a slim build.  Tension pneumothorax can occur in the following groups of patients:  those ventilated on ICU  trauma patients  following CPR.  Lung disease, especially acute presentations of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).  Chest drains that have become blocked, clamped, or displaced.  Patients receiving non-invasive ventilation (NIV). Pathophysiology  The pressure in the alveoli is normally greater than the intrapleural pressure, and the intrapleural pressure is less than atmospheric pressure.  Gases follow a pressure gradient; therefore, if a communication develops between either the alveolus and the pleural space, or the atmosphere and the pleural space, air will flow into the pleural space.  This will only stop once the pressure gradient no longer exists or the communication is sealed.  The result is an increase in the thorax cavity, and a decrease in the lung volume.  In a pneumothorax, there is an inspiratory accumulation of pleural gases, which will eventual compress the lung and cause respiratory failure.  Clinical Presentation  Shortness of breath.  Chest pain.  Diminished breath sounds.  Reduced lung expansion.  Hyperresonance of percussion note.

DR. JAMIL  Auscultatory ‘clicks’ at cardiac apex.  Trachea shift (rare) in tension pneumothorax. Pulmonary Embolism A Pulmonary Embolism occurs when one or more emboli (most commonly a blood clot in the a deep vein – deep vein thrombosis) become lodged in the pulmonary arterial system.  Overview Key Facts  A Pulmonary Embolism (PE) occurs when one or more emboli (most commonly a blood clot in the a deep vein – deep vein thrombosis) become lodged in the pulmonary arterial system.  This causes obstruction of the artery, leading to respiratory dysfunction.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Can be either provoked (transient risk factors such as immobilisation, oral contraceptives, pregnancy) or unprovoked (no clear identifiable risk factor or permanent risk factors, such as malignancy or clotting disorder).  The condition can range from being asymptomatic to severe respiratory distress and shock leading to death.  Any signs of haemodynamic instability warrant urgent admission and management.  WELLS score is used to determine investigation method in suspected cases. Epidemiology  Can be difficult to determine as can be asymptomatic.  Estimated rate of 60-70 per 100 000.  Aetiology  Thrombotic source (most common):  deep vein thrombosis (DVT).  Non-thrombotic source:  tumours, fat, amniotic fluid, sepsis, air.  Provoked (transient risk factors present):  trauma, surgery, combined oral contraceptive pill, hormone replacement therapy, pregnancy, period of immobilisation.  Unprovoked  either unidentifiable risk factor or persistent risk factor that isn’t easily correctable  eg V Leiden mutation, coagulopathy, malignancy. Pathophysiology  Embolus travels to the arterial system and becomes lodged in the pulmonary artery.  Perfusion of the lung tissue is therefore prevented.  This area become dead space as it is still being ventilated.  Pulmonary arterial pressure increases and cardiac output decreases.  Alveoli can collapse and worsen hypoxemia.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms:  chest pain  cough  haemoptysis  dizziness.  Signs:  tachycardia  hypoxia  pyrexia  raised jugular venous pressure  pleural rub

S1Q3T3 not often seen (in 5-10% of PEs).  Calculate two-level PE Wells’ score (as per NICE):

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  If score > 4 points, PE likely. Next offer:  immediate CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) or  if CTPA cannot be performed, immediate interim parenteral anticoagulant therapy followed by CTPA.  If score < or = 4, then PE unlikely. Next offer:  a D-dimer test. If D-dimer test is positive, offer:  immediate CTPA or  if CTPA cannot be performed, immediate interim parenteral anticoagulant therapy followed by CTPA.  A ventilation/perfusion single photon emission computed tomography (V/Q SPECT) can be considered for patients with renal failure/allergic to contrast/pregnant.  Once PE has been managed adequately, potential underlying causes should be investigated as required in patients with unprovoked PE.  Management NICE recommends immediate admission in patients with signs of haemodynamic instability/ those who pregnant or post-partum, or 2-level Wells score of above 4 points. Initial management includes:  Oxygen via mask  Sit patient upright.  Analgesia  Urgent CTPA. Pharmacological: Treatment for confirmed PE or whist awaiting CTPA if not immediately available (interim anticoagulation): No renal impairment, active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome or haemodynamic instability:  Oral anticoagulant treatment (apixaban, or rivaroxaban).  If not suitable then:  Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) for at least 5 days, followed by dabigatran or edoxaban, or LMWH concurrently with a vitamin K antagonist for at least 5 days or until INR is at least 2.0 on two separate readings, then a vitamin K antagonist alone  Fondaparinux.  Unfractionated heparin may be used instead of apixaban or rivaroxaban in cases of renal impairment (determined by creatinine clearence levels) Patients with active cancer  consider a direct acting oral anticoagulant (DOAC), or LMWH/or LMWH concurrently with a vitamin K antagonist for at least 5 days or until INR is at least 2.0 on two separate readings and then a vitamin K antagonist alone.

Surgical:  Embolectomy (not offered by many centres).  Inferior vena cava filter can be considered if:  patient can’t receive anti-coagulants (remove filter when they can receive anticoagulants)  recurrent PEs despite adequate anticoagulation (permanent filter). Follow up  The choice of treatment will depend on factors such as:  the licensed indication of the treatment  the presence of co-morbidities  contraindication to treatment  patient preference and the preference of the person.  Specialists will usually make clinical decisions on the duration of treatment, which dependent on if the PE is classed as provoked or unprovoked:  provoked PE – treatment is usually continued for 3 months, and then re-reviewed (3 - 6 months for those with active cancer)  unprovoked PE - usually treated for beyond 3 months (often 6 months), duration determined by the patient's risk of further thromboembolism versus the risk of bleeding.  Early mobilisation is recommended.  Provide information on anticoagulation treatment and PE, and provide anticoagulation card and information regarding monitoring.  Discuss possible adverse effects.  Give advice regarding activity, modifications for dental treatment and surgery and implications if trying to become pregnant.  Smoking cessation advice should be offered.  Prognosis  If left untreated there is a high mortality and morbidity rate.  Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) is a rare complication of PE to be aware of.  over the course of months or years, emboli are replaced by fibrous tissue

Pulmonary Hypertension  Overview Key Facts  Pulmonary hypertension describes an increase in pulmonary artery pressure.  Presents with dyspnoea on exertion, fatigue, added heart sound.  Underlying causes include respiratory disease, cardiac disease, systemic sclerosis, thromboembolic disease or may be idiopathic.  The condition can lead to cor pulmonale (right heart failure due to chronic pulmonary arterial hypertension.  Treatments are aimed at managing symptoms as well as resolving the underlying condition. Epidemiology  More common in patients with heart or lung conditions.  High risk patient groups include those with systemic sclerosis, portal hypertension, congenital heart disease and previous pulmonary embolisms.  Incidence in approximately 1 per million people.  Aetiology  Group 1: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), which can be idiopathic (IPAH) or associated with other conditions, notably systemic sclerosis and congenital heart disease.  Group 2: Pulmonary hypertension associated with left heart disease.  Group 3: Pulmonary hypertension associated with lung disease/hypoxia.  Group 4: Pulmonary hypertension due to chronic thromboembolic disease (CTEPH).  Group 5: Unclear or multifactorial mechanisms. Pathophysiology  Pulmonary artery walls become thicker and stiffer.  Reduced expandability restricts the blood flow.  Right side of the heart has to work hard against increased resistance.  Having to work progressively harder causes the right side of the heat to become weaker leading to heart failure (cor pulmonale).

DR. JAMIL  Clinical Presentation  Most commonly progressively worsening breathlessness with no other evidence of respiratory disease.  Dizziness, syncope, oedema and ascites – right heart dysfunction.  Anginal chest pain – exertional myocardial hypoperfusion.  Atrial arrhythmias – atrial flutter and fibrillation, often lead to decompensation and deterioration.  Chest signs:  left parasternal lift  heart sounds  accentuated pulmonary component of the second heart sound  right ventricular third heart sound  murmurs  pansystolic murmur of tricuspid regurgitation  diastolic murmur of pulmonary regurgitation.  wheeze and crackles usually absent.  Differential Diagnosis  Pulmonary embolism.  Congestive heart failure.  Coronary artery disease.  Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Rule out other causes of breathlessness.  ECG – abnormal ECG more likely in severe disease but a normal ECG does not rule out PAH.  May show P pulmonale, right axis deviation, RV hypertrophy, RV strain, right bundle branch block, and QTc prolongation.  Spirometry:  identify any underlying respiratory disease.  Chest radiograph:  prominent vasculature - central pulmonary arterial dilatation  enlarged right atrium and ventricle  normal CXR doesn’t exclude PAH.  Echocardiogram should always be performed when PAH is suspected.  Peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity key finding.  Further imaging:  ventilation perfusion scan – to look for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension or  high resolution CT – for diagnosis/prognosis  CT pulmonary angiogram.  Other tests to consider:

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  bloods: BNP, HIV testing, immunological testing, FBC, LFTs, U+Es, clotting  pulmonary angiogram  exercise test: gives functional and prognostic information  right heart catheterisation: directly measure pulmonary pressure to confirm diagnosis  MRI  overnight oximetry: used when considering sleep disordered breathing. Panels A and C represent anterior-posterior projections, panels B and D represent lateral projections.  Management  Can be split into supportive and specific medical treatment.  The majority of treatments focus on the underlying cause of pulmonary artery hypertension.  Treatment regime is dependent on risk, calculated using the WHO function class. WHO function class criteria Class I: Symptom-free when physically active or resting. Class II: No symptoms at rest but normal activities cause some discomfort and shortness of breath. Class III: Resting may be symptom-free, but normal chores are greatly limited due to shortness of breath or feeling tired. Class IV: Symptoms at rest and severe symptoms with any activity. Pharmacological:  Anticoagulation – recommended in chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension and IPAH.

JAMIL  Diuretics – for heart failure.  Digoxin.  Oxygen therapy.  Calcium channel blockers – in idiopathic pulmonary artery hypertension and only if there is a positive response to an acute vaso-reactive test.  Prostanoids – vasodilator with anti-proliferative effects.  Endothelin receptor antagonist – inhibits vasoconstriction of vascular smooth muscle.  Phophodiesterase-5 inhibitors - vasodilator and antiproliferative effects. Surgical:  Pulmonary endarterectomy.  Balloon pulmonary angioplasty – for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension who cannot undergo endarterectomy surgery.  Atrial septostomy.  Heart-lung transplantation.  Prognosis  Estimated median survival in idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension without specific therapies is 2.8 years.  The condition is associated with high maternal mortality rate in pregnancy – pregnancy should therefore be avoided and termination of pregnancy is recommended in patients with the condition who become pregnant. Pulmonary Hypertension Pulmonary hypertension is characterised by a progressive increase in resistance in the pulmonary circulation, eventually leading to right heart failure (cor pulmonale).  Overview Key Facts  Pulmonary hypertension is characterised by a progressive increase in resistance in the pulmonary circulation, eventually leading to right heart failure (cor pulmonale).  It is important to determine whether pulmonary hypertension is secondary to an underlying condition that may be treatable.  The most common cause of secondary pulmonary hypertension is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Airway rigidity leads to increased circulatory pressures to maintain blood flow.  Diagnosis is made by catheterisation to measure the pulmonary pressure.  Treatment is dependent on the underlying cause, but includes:  symptom management  supportive therapy, and

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  pulmonary vasodilators.  Definitive treatment is transplantation.  Prognosis for untreated primary pulmonary hypertension is poor with the average survival being three years.  With new therapy options, survival rates in treated patients are improving. Epidemiology  Primary pulmonary hypertension (PPH) is a rare disease with an incidence of 2 000 000 per year.  Prevalence is estimated to be between 10–50 cases per million population.  It is a disease of children and young adults.  Women : men ratio is 2 : 1.  Aetiology World Health Organisation (WHO) Venice Classification of Pulmonary Hypertension  WHO Group 1: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension  idiopathic/sporadic  familial – associated with a specific gene mutation – bone morphogenetic protein receptor type 2 (BMPR2)  associated with pulmonary venous or capillary disease  associated with systemic diseases, including:  collagen vascular disease (eg scleroderma)  human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  cirrhosis.  drugs/toxins (eg anorexigens)  portal hypertension  congenital heart disease with shunting left to right (atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect)  persistent pulmonary hypertension of newborn babies.  WHO Group 2: Pulmonary Hypertension Associated with Left Heart Disease  atrial or ventricular disease (dilated cardiomyopathy, ischaemic heard disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)  valvular disease (eg mitral stenosis or aortic stenosis)  extrinsic compression of the central pulmonary veins.  WHO Group 3: Pulmonary Hypertension Associated with Lung Diseases and/or Hypoxemia  COPD  interstitial/fibrotic lung disease  obstructive sleep apnoea  alveolar hypoventilation disorders  chronic high altitude  chronic hypoxia (polio, myasthenia).  WHO Group 4: Pulmonary Hypertension due to Chronic Thrombotic and/or Embolic Disease

JAMIL  pulmonary emboli of proximal arteries  obstruction of distal pulmonary arteries  embolisation of thrombus, tumour, ova, parasites or foreign material  in-situ thrombosis  sickle cell disease.  WHO Group 5: Pulmonary Hypertension caused by Disorders Directly Affecting the Pulmonary Vasculature  inflammatory – schistosomiasis, sarcoidoisis  pulmonary capillary haemangiomatosis  glycogen storage disease. Pathophysiology  Primary Pulmonary Hypertension (PPH)  PPH constitutes < 1% of all cases of pulmonary hypertension and is characterised by a mean pulmonary artery pressure > 25 mmHg at rest, in the absence of another demonstrable cause.  One in ten cases is familial.  PPH is associated with connective tissue disease, vasculitis and HIV infection, and also the use of appetite suppressants (eg fenfluramine).  The pulmonary arteries become dilated and abnormally thickened; there is dilatation of the proximal pulmonary vessels with thick-walled, obstructed, ‘pruned’ peripheral vessels.  As a consequence of the high pulmonary pressure, the right ventricle undergoes marked hypertrophy.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentations for pulmonary hypertension are as follows:  patients present with gradually worsening exertional dyspnoea  in the later stages, angina of effort and syncope occur  fatigue is common and disproportionate to exertion  dry cough  haemoptysis  cyanosis – central  right ventricular heave  loud P2  tricuspid regurgitation  peripheral oedema/ascites  chest pain/angina.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses for pulmonary hypertension include:  cardiomyopathies  pulmonary stenosis  congestive cardiac failure  portal hypertension

Respiratory Disease In HIV And AIDS Advanced HIV infection is associated with various respiratory disorders.  Overview Key Facts  Advanced HIV infection is associated with various respiratory disorders.  The most important are bacterial pneumonia, tuberculosis, and pneumocystic jirovecii (PJP/PCP) pneumonia.  Tuberculosis is very common in endemic settings:  notably sub-Saharan Africa and Eastern Europe  extra-pulmonary and multi-drug resistant forms of TB more common in this group.  Maintain a high index of suspicion for viral, fungal, and protozoal infections.  Useful investigations include induced sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage, X-ray, and CT imaging. Epidemiology  Pneumonia is the commonest opportunistic infection and clinical presentation of AIDS.  PCP pneumonia accounts for 40% of all AIDS-defining illness worldwide.  Aetiology  Bacterial infection – Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis and atypical Mycobacterial infection.  Fungal infection – invasive Aspergillosis, Candida, Histoplasmosis, Cryptococcus, Nocardia.  Viral infection – CMV pneumonitis.

DR. JAMIL  Malignancy – Kaposi’s sarcoma and non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma:  the presence of mucosal Kaposi’s sarcoma within the mouth is an important clinical sign which signals very high likelihood of lung involvement. Pathophysiology  The low CD4 count characteristic of AIDS leads to defective T cell responses and broader immune dysregulation. This places patients at risk of opportunistic infection.  Clinical Presentation  Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is characterised by sub-acute (1-2 weeks) fever, malaise, dry cough, and dyspnoea.  Focal signs are often absent on chest examination.  Tuberculosis infection is more likely to present in an atypical fashion and can occur in patients with any CD4 count:  extra-pulmonary involvement:  TB lymphadenitis – painless lymph node swelling, usually cervical chains  TB spondylitis – back pain and distal focal neurology  TB meningitis – subacute presentation with headache, fevers, vomiting.  fevers, night sweats, and cavitation are less common in people living with HIV.  Acute bacterial pneumonia usually presents with rapid onset (13 days) of fever, cough productive of mucopurulent sputum, chest pain, and malaise.  Differential Diagnosis  Cavitating lung lesions – Mycobacterium tuberculosis (cavitation is seen less frequently in HIV positive patients – other presentations include miliary TB, effusions, consolidation), Nocardia, Staphylococcus aureus.  Consolidation – Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Toxoplasma.  Pleural effusions - Tuberculosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Useful tests in all HIV+ patients presenting with respiratory disease include:  pulse oximetry  chest X-ray  sputum culture, or where appropriate, bronchoalveolar lavage  CD4 count and viral load.  Pneumocystis pneumonia:  pulse oximetry – hypoxia (SpO2 < 94%) is commonly seen in patients with moderate-to-severe disease. However, in those with normal oxygen saturations, an exercise-induced reduction of 5% or absolute fall to < 90% are suggestive of PCP

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  chest X-ray – bilateral interstitial shadowing in mid and low zones is typical. Atypical changes – such as cavitation, upper load opacification and pneumothorax – are seen in 10% patients. X-ray can also be normal in PCP  induced sputum or BAL for PCP cysts – useful test, particularly in the ITU setting.  Tuberculosis:  chest X-ray – cavitation is less common (due to inadequate immune response); may be normal or show miliary picture, consolidation, or effusions  induced sputum/BAL for acid-and-alcohol fast bacillin on ZN stain. Typical appearance of PCP on X-ray with bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates:  Management Pharmacological  The treatment of choice for PCP pneumonia is co-trimoxazole (high dose, 14 days):  side effects of co-trimoxazole are common and often debilitating – these include nausea, vomiting, rash, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia and bleeding  steroids are indicated in severe hypoxia (PaO2 < 9.3 kPa (or 70 mmHg) or SpO2 < 92%)  alternative treatments (second-line or useful in patients with co-trimoxazole intolerance or allergy) include IV pentamidine, clindamycin/primaquine and dapsone/trimethoprim.  Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is indicated in patients who have previously required treatment and in patients with no history of infection with a CD4 count < 200.  Prophylaxis should be continued until CD4 count has increased above 200 with HAART.  Pulmonary tuberculosis treatment does not differ significantly from that in HIV negative patients – combination therapy with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for patients with drug-sensitive TB.

JAMIL  Prognosis  Poor prognostic indicators for PCP infection include:  co-infection  pneumothorax  poor response to treatment  the need for mechanical ventilation.  Recurrent PCP infection is common – 50% of patients will experience a second episode within the next 12 months. Respiratory Failure Respiratory failure is an inability to maintain adequate oxygenation and carbon dioxide excretion.  Overview Key Facts  Respiratory failure is an inability to maintain adequate oxygenation and carbon dioxide excretion.  There are two recognised types of respiratory failure:  Type I respiratory failure  hypoxaemia (< 8 kPa or < 60 mmHg on room air at sea level) with normal or low levels of carbon dioxide (ie one gas is abnormal)  Type II respiratory failure  hypoxaemia with high PCO2 (> 6.5 kPa or > 50mmHG on room air at sea level) (ie two gases are abnormal).  Causes included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), alveolar disease, myopathies, mechanical difficulties, and neurological conditions.  Symptoms can include breathlessness, cardiac dysfunction, confusion, and cardiac arrest.  Treatment options include oxygen therapy, non-invasive ventilation, invasive ventilation, and continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP).  The main diagnostics tests include chest X-ray, blood gas analysis, pulse oximetry, and capnometry. Epidemiology  Prevalence varies widely across the world.  Aetiology  Reduced ventilatory drive  sedatives including opiates and alcohol.  Brainstem disorders such as encephalitis, tumour, or cerebrovascular accident.  Metabolic alkalosis.  Mechanical problems:

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  chest trauma causing flail chest  severe kyphoscoliosis  obesity.  Neurological conditions (affecting chest wall muscles):  Guillain–Barré syndrome  polio  motor neuron disease  spinal muscular atrophy.  Myopathies  muscular dystrophy  myotonic dystrophy  acid maltase deficiency (Pompe’s disease)  hypothyroidism.  Alveolar problems causing barriers to diffusion:  pulmonary oedema  pulmonary fibrosis.  V = Q mismatch  pulmonary embolus  shunt (cardiac or pulmonary).  Reduced inspired partial pressure of oxygen  high altitude.  Upper airway obstruction  laryngeal tumour  obstructive sleep apnoea.  Lower airway obstruction  bronchospasm  sputum retention. Pathophysiology  The lungs cannot maintain the exchange of O2 and CO2 to adequate levels resulting in a performance mismatch.  Decreased oxygen exchange results in cell anoxia.  Decreased carbon dioxide exchange results in accumulation of CO2 in the blood thus increasing the levels of carbonic acid in tissue.  Clinical Presentation  Breathlessness.  Confusion.  Accessory muscles use (sternocleidomastoid, tripod stance).  Tachypnoea.  Stridor.  Difficulty speaking.  Differential Diagnosis  N/A - the key thing is working out what type of respiratory failure is occurring and how it can be corrected.

DR. JAMIL  Diagnosis/Investigation  Bloods: arterial blood gases (ABG) in particular to determine the type of respiratory failure.  Chest X-ray to identify possible underlying causes.  Management Pharmacological  Type I respiratory failure may be corrected by increasing the inspired oxygen concentration.  Type II respiratory failure may require mechanical ventilatory support. Respiratory stimulants such as doxapram may be useful for those with reduced respiratory drive when non-invasive ventilation is either unavailable or considered inappropriate.  Ventilation should be considered when there is failure to maintain oxygenation (PO.8 kPa [60 mmHg]) despite highinspired oxygen concentrations (usually associated with hypercapnia and acidosis). It is often necessary in patients with multiple organ dysfunction associated with sepsis or trauma. Non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation - use of a securely fitting nasal or full facemask. Provides long-term respiratory support in the community:  It is used increasingly to manage episodes of acute respiratory failure due, for example, to exacerbations of COPD  Carried out on general wards using portable bi-level pressure support ventilators.  supplementary oxygen can be given via the port on the facemask  regular monitoring of blood gases is necessary and the ventilator settings are altered in response  as the patient improves, time spent off the ventilator is lengthened until the patient has been weaned.  When noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation (NIPPV) treatment is instituted, a decision as to whether ICU referral would be appropriate if the patient were to deteriorate should be clearly stated in the case notes.  Invasive positive-pressure ventilation - requires access to the airway via either an endotracheal tube or a tracheostomy. Indications for invasive positive-pressure ventilation are:  type II respiratory failure from any cause  paralysis of respiratory muscles (eg Guillain-Barre ´syndrome)  multiple organ failure  trauma cases, including injury to the chest or cervical spine  inability to maintain a clear airway  reduced conscious level – Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score < 5  during and after certain surgical procedures.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Continuous positive airway pressure - delivered through a tightly fitting facemask, or it may be used together with conventional ventilation.  provides a pneumatic splint to the airway and is the treatment of choice for obstructive sleep apnoea  improves oxygenation through the recruitment of collapsed airways  ensures airways remain open even in expiration  high oxygenation levels may cause hypotension as the rise in mean intrathoracic pressure inhibits venous return and reduces cardiac output.  Prognosis  Significant risk of mortality associated with acute respiratory failure.  Those at risk of recurrence of respiratory failure include people with long term conditions such as COPD and asthma. Respiratory Physiology Respiratory physiology is the branch of physiology that focuses on the study of the function and processes of the respiratory system, including the lungs, airways, and breathing mechanisms, to understand how oxygen is taken in and carbon dioxide is eliminated from the body.  Overview Key Facts Lung anatomy overview  The human lung is composed of approximately 300 million alveoli, each around 0.3 mm in diameter.  Gas exchange takes place in the alveoli; the air is transported to these via a series of conducting airways.  Air is warmed and humidified in the upper airways and transported through the trachea, main bronchi and lobar and segmental bronchi to the terminal bronchioles, the smallest of the conducting tubes.  These airways take no part in gas exchange and constitute the anatomical dead space (approximately 150 ml).  The terminal bronchioles lead to the respiratory bronchioles, which have alveoli budding from their walls.  Lung tissue distal to the terminal bronchiole forms the primary lobule. Ventilation  The most important muscle of inspiration is the diaphragm, a muscular dome that moves downwards on inspiration.  The external intercostal muscles assist inspiration by moving the ribs upwards and forwards in a 'bucket-handle' movement.  The accessory muscles of respiration include the scalene muscles, which elevate the ﬁrst two ribs, and sternocleidomastoids, which elevate the sternum; these are not used during quiet breathing.

DR. JAMIL  Expiration is passive during quiet breathing.  During exercise, expiration becomes active and the internal intercostal muscles and the muscles of the anterior abdominal wall are utilised.  The greatest ventilation is achieved at the lung bases and this is matched by increased perfusion in these areas.  The normal lung is very compliant.  Compliance is reduced by pulmonary venous engorgement and alveolar oedema and in areas of atelectasis.  Surfactant, secreted by type II alveolar epithelial cells, substantially lowers the surface tension of the alveolar lining ﬂuid, increasing lung compliance and promoting alveolar stability.  Lack of surfactant leads to respiratory distress syndrome.  Resistance to airﬂow is related to the radius of the airway, but the greatest overall resistance to ﬂow occurs in medium-sized bronchi.  Airway calibre is influenced by lung volume; at low lung volumes, small airways may close completely, leading to areas of atelectasis, particularly at the lung bases. Perfusion  The pulmonary vessels form a low-pressure system conducting deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary arteries to the alveoli where they form a dense capillary network.  The pulmonary arteries have thin walls with very little smooth muscle; the mean pulmonary artery pressure is 15 mmHg and the upper limit of normal pressure is 30 mmHg.  Pulmonary vascular resistance is one-tenth systemic vascular resistance.  Hypoxic vasoconstriction refers to the contraction of smooth muscle in the walls of the small arterioles in a hypoxic region of the lung.  This helps to divert blood away from areas with poor ventilation, so maintaining ventilation and perfusion matching. Control of respiration  The respiratory centre comprises a poorly deﬁned collection of neurones in the pons and medulla.  To a certain extent, the cortex can override the function of the respiratory centre.  Chemoreceptors are crucial to the control of respiration, these may be central or peripheral:  central chemoreceptors are located on the ventral surface of the medulla:  they respond to increased hydrogen ion concentration in the cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF), generated by increased carbon dioxide partial pressure (PCO2) in the blood.  peripheral chemoreceptors are located in the carotid bodies (at the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries) and the aortic bodies (near the aortic arch):  they respond to hypoxaemia, hypercapnia and pH changes.  In people with normal respiratory function, the most important factor for control of ventilation is the PCO2, which is

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI maintained to within 0.4 kPa of baseline (the normal range is 4.7–6.0 kPa).  However, in patients with severe lung disease, chronic CO2 retention develops and the hypoxic drive to ventilation becomes very important.  Ventilation may increase by 15 times the resting level during extreme exercise.  Cheyne–Stokes respiration is characterised by periods of apnoea separated by periods of hyperventilation:  it occurs in severe heart failure or brain damage and at altitude. Oxygen and carbon dioxide transport  Transfer of carbon monoxide is solely limited by diffusion and is used to measure gas transfer:  either a single breath-hold or a steady-state method can be used  results are expressed both as total gas transfer (DLCO) or as gas transfer corrected for lung volume (KCO, ie KCO 1/4 DLCO/VA, where VA is alveolar volume).  Oxygen is transported in the blood by combination with the haemoglobin (Hb) in red cells:  a tiny amount is dissolved (0.3 ml/100 ml blood, assuming PO2 100 mmHg)  the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid in shape  once oxygen saturation falls below 90%, the amount of oxygen carried to the tissues falls rapidly  the partial pressure at which haemoglobin is 50% saturated, is 26 mmHg. JAMIL Decreased levels of 2,3bisphosphoglyceric acid (2,3-DPG) Increased level of 2,3-DGP (encourages offloading of O2 to tissues) Low temperature High temperature Fetal haemoglobin Carboxyhaemoglobin  CO2 is transported in the blood as bicarbonate, in combination with proteins as carbamino compounds and it is also dissolved in plasma.  CO2 is 20 times more soluble than O2 and about 10% of all CO2 is dissolved.  CO2 diffuses into red blood cells where carbonic anhydrase facilitates the formation of carbonic acid, which dissociates into bicarbonate and hydrogen ions.  Bicarbonate diffuses out of the cell and chloride moves in to maintain electrical neutrality.  This can be summarised by the equation (note arrow should be equilibrium arrow as the body is in a constant state of equilibrium in adequate conditions):  H2O + CO2 ⇢ HCO3–+ H+  Acid–base control:  the normal pH of arterial blood is 7.35–7.45  blood pH is closely regulated and variation outside this pH range results in compensation by either the lung or the kidney to return the pH to normal  failure to excrete CO2 normally results in a respiratory acidosis; this is usually due to hypoventilation; hyperventilation causes lowering of the PCO2 and alkalosis  the pH can also be altered by metabolic disturbance  mixed respiratory and metabolic acid–base disturbances are common.  Arterial blood gases:  when recording blood gases, the percentage of inspired O2 should always be stated  the value in kilopascals (kPa) should be multiplied by 7.6 to convert to millimetres of mercury (mmHg). Sarcoidosis Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disorder, primarily affecting young adults, the cause of which is unknown.  Overview Key Facts  Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disorder, primarily affecting young adults, the cause of which is unknown.  90% of patients have intrathoracic involvement, known as pulmonary sarcoidosis.  Chest examination is frequently normal and finger clubbing is rare.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Incidence in the UK is 7 per 100 000 a year.  The skin is the second most commonly affected organ. Other organs such as the eyes, brain, nervous system, liver, and heart may also be affected.  Patients may have no respiratory symptoms or complain of dyspnoea, dry cough, fever, malaise, and weight loss.  Diffuse parenchymal lung involvement may progress to irreversible fibrosis; the mid- and upper zones of the lungs are most frequently affected.  In chronic disease, the lung parenchyma and hilar nodes can calcify.  The characteristic histological lesion is the granuloma composed of macrophages, lymphocytes, and epithelioid histiocytes, which fuse to form multinucleate giant cells.  The disease may present acutely with respiratory difficulty or insidiously with multi-organ involvement.  Treatment, when necessary, involves the use of corticosteroids. Epidemiology  Though sarcoidosis can occur at any age, it commonly affects adults in their 30s or 40s and uncommon in childhood.  The incidence of sarcoidosis is 7 cases per 100 000 in the UK, with both men and women affected equally.  Aetiology  Mechanism not fully understood: it is thought that in sarcoidosis the immune system in impaired, and so attacks health tissue unnecessarily.  There may be a genetic component, though this has yet to be fully discovered.  There is no evidence that is it infectious. Pathophysiology  Granulomas composed of macrophages, lymphocytes, and epithelioid histiocytes, which fuse to form multinucleate giant cells develop.  Most commonly found in the lungs and the lymph glands which drain the lungs. However, they can develop anywhere including: the skin, heart, nervous system, liver, spleen, muscles, nose, sinuses, and eyes.  An abundance of granulomas in one area will result in the progression of symptoms as it hampers the organs ability to work effectively.  Clinical Presentation  Lymphadenopathy:  painless, rubbery lymph node enlargement is more common in Black patients;  cervical and scalene lymph nodes are most frequently affected.  Splenomegaly (25%).  Liver involvement:  common but often subclinical (ie derangement of liver function tests) unless an enlarged liver can be felt

DR. JAMIL  liver biopsy is of diagnostic value in 90% (typical sarcoid granulomas).  Skin:  erythema nodosum (most commonly in White females) in disease with BHL;  skin plaques  subcutaneous nodules  lupus pernio (violaceous lesions on the nose, cheeks, and ears) seen in chronic disease.  Acute anterior uveitis (25%).  Heerfordt–Waldenstrom syndrome:  parotid gland enlargement, uveitis, fever, and cranial nerve palsies.  Neurological manifestations:  cranial nerve palsies (usually facial nerve), meningitis, hydrocephalus, space-occupying lesions, and spinal cord involvement;  granulomas infiltrating the posterior pituitary may produce diabetes insipidus, hypothalamic hypothyroidism, or hypopituitarism.  Cardiac sarcoid:  cardiac muscle/conducting system dysfunction, resulting in arrhythmias, bundle-branch block, or complete heart block.  Renal involvement:  hypercalcaemia  granulomatous interstitial nephritis.  Bone cysts:  with overlying soft-tissue swelling, bone cysts occur most often in the phalanges, metacarpals, metatarsals, and nasal bones;  arthritis is common.  Hypercalcaemia: due to excess production of vitamin D and gut activity causing calcium reabsorption, a lower proportion will develop renal calculi.  Eyes: dry itchy eyes - keratoconjunctivitis sicca.  Differential Diagnosis  Tuberculosis.  Lymphoma. Also consider:  Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)  Histoplasmosis.  Berryliosis.  Hypersensitivity pneumonitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The combination of bi-hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) with erythema nodosum (EN) in a young adult is highly suggestive of sarcoidosis.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  When bi-hilar lymphadenopathy and erythema nodosum are in association with fever and arthralgia, it is known as Lofgren syndrome. Imaging:  CT appearances are often characteristic, showing hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, nodules along bronchi, vessels and, in subpleural regions, ground-glass shadowing, parenchymal bands, cysts, and fibrosis.  Chest X-ray - changes are graded:  stage 0: clear chest radiograph  stage 1: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL)  stage 2: BHL and pulmonary infiltration  stage 3: diffuse pulmonary infiltration  stage 4: pulmonary fibrosis. DR. JAMIL  Tissue biopsies (transbronchial and endobronchial biopsy) can demonstrate non-caseating granulomas in 85–90% of cases with respiratory involvement. Bloods:  Elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) and calcium are consistent with the diagnosis, but are non-specific. May show anaemia and leukopenia due to splenic/bone marrow involvement.  Raised serum urea and creatinine due to kidney involvement.  Deranged LFTs may be present.  The 24-hour urinary calcium excretion is often raised.  Pulmonary function tests – pattern may be restrictive, obstructive, or mixed. Used for disease monitoring as the transfer factor (usually reduced in patients with sarcoidosis) is sensitive to disease exacerbations and treatment.  ECG – may show conduction/rhythm defects.  Bronchoalveolar lavage – CD4 : CD8 ratio is typically raised.  Management Pharmacological:  The recommended first-line treatment is usually corticosteroids. They are indicated in:  patients with persistent hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria despite dietary calcium restriction  ophthalmological complications  neurological complications.  Methotrexate or azathioprine may be used as an adjunct or alone if steroid-sparing agents are required.  If prednisolone is prescribed, the dose should be gradually reduced after four weeks of treatment to the lowest maintenance dose possible for disease control.  Immunosuppressive or anti-inflammatory treatments have only a limited role:

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  can consider if corticosteroids do not provide adequate control/have intolerable side effects.  use of infliximab for treating sarcoidosis is off-label.  Prognosis  The prognosis is generally good, with the resolution in most people within 2 to 5 years.  25% of people will develop residual fibrosis in the lungs or elsewhere.  Common causes of disease-related mortality are lung, cardiac, and neurological disease that is non-responsive to therapy. Silicosis Silicosis is a form of occupational lung disease that is caused by chronic inhalation silicon dioxide – a highly fibrogenic dust.  Overview Key Facts  Silicosis is a form of occupational lung disease that is caused by chronic inhalation silicon dioxide – a highly fibrogenic dust.  The condition is most commonly found in quarry workers, hardrock miners, and ceramic manufacturers; it is also known as Potter’s Rot.  Inhalation of the fine fibres lead to inflammation and eventually fibrosis .  There is usually a latent period of many years, often even if exposure has ended years previously.  It is incurable and often progressive.  Treatment aims to manage symptoms and improve quality of life. Epidemiology  Any worker involved with the breaking, crushing, drilling, grinding, cutting, or blasting of sandstone, marble, flint, slate, soil, mortar, plaster, and sand is at risk of exposure to silica.  Silicosis is associated with an increased incidence of tuberculosis.  Incidence appears to be falling with an incidence of 30 cases in 2018.  Aetiology  Crystalline silica (quartz) is fibrogenic.  Heating silica produces tridymite and cristobalite, forms of silica that have been shown to be fibrogenic in animal models.  Amorphous silica (diatomaceous earth) is a non-crystalline form and is generally thought to be less fibrogenic if is converted to crystalline silica when heated and processed.

DR. JAMIL Pathophysiology  Silica particles enter the alveoli.  Macrophages ingest the particles resulting in cytolysis.  An inflammatory response occurs at the sites of silica deposition.  Macrophages generate fibrogenic proteins and growth factors that stimulate collagen elaboration (IL-1, platelet-derived growth factor, and fibronectin).  A large proportion of patients with silicosis have polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, and immune complexes.  Gradually worsening breathlessness is associated with restrictive lung physiology and a fall in gas transfer.  Clinical Presentation  Acute silicosis:  dry cough, severe breathlessness, weakness, weight loss, pleuritic pain  symptoms develop several weeks and up to five years from the time of exposure  involves very high levels of dust, eg from sandblasting.  Accelerated silicosis:  exposure to higher volumes of silica over a shorter period of time  5–15 year latency period  associated with a variety of immune disorders  the disease can progress even after removal from source of silica exposure.  Simple chronic exposure:  most common  low-level exposure  latency period of about 20 years  risk of developing progressive massive fibrosis, which can cause an area of dullness of chest percussion.  There is an increased risk of connective-tissue disease, vasculitides, lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), active tuberculosis, and chronic renal failure among patients with silicosis.  Joint tenderness and swelling, skin changes, and sclerodactyly may be signs of rheumatoid arthritis and scleroderma.  Differential Diagnosis  Asbestosis.  COPD.  Sarcoidosis.  Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.  Scleroderma.  Rheumatoid arthritis.  Drug-induced pulmonary fibrosis.  Lung cancer.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Diagnosis/Investigation  Chest X-ray:  more specific than lung function tests  non-calcified, rounded opacities in the upper zones (similar to coal workers' pneumoconiosis)  eggshell calcification occurs around enlarged hilar glands.  Computed tomography (CT) chest.  Bloods to look for alternative causes:  full blood count  urea and electrolytes  C-reactive protein  liver function tests.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Smoking cessation.  Removal of exposure.  Pulmonary rehabilitation may be helpful if getting dyspnoea on exertion. Pharmacological  Bronchodilator therapy – if COPD also present.  Oxygen (long-term oxygen therapy) if hypoxic.  Antibiotics may be indicated for episodes of bacterial exacerbations. Surgical  Lung lavage (only in acute silicosis).  Lung transplant – end-stage respiratory failure.  Prognosis  Prognosis is dependent on the extent of fibrosis present at diagnosis and the total amount of exposure.  Patients with the condition are entitled to industrial injuries disablement benefit and may be entitled to compensation. Thyroid Cancer Thyroid cancer is a type of cancer that affects the thyroid gland, leading to abnormal growths or nodules in the neck.  Overview Key Facts  Thyroid cancer accounts for roughly 1% of all cancers.

DR. JAMIL  Main types – differentiated, undifferentiated and primary thyroid lymphoma.  The differentiated papillary type is the most common, with a good prognosis.  More common in women than men with two age incidence peaks – 30s and over 70s.  Risk factors – radiation and type 2 multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN2).  Most patients are asymptomatic, presenting with a nodule and normal TFTs.  Most nodules are referred for an ultrasound scan (USS) and fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) to look for cancer.  Treatment may involve surgery, TSH suppression, radioiodine ablation and radiochemotherapy.  The worst prognosis is for anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Epidemiology  Most common endocrinological cancer, but only approximately 1% of all cancers. Incidence  Big gender split – women approximately 5 per 100 000 and men approximately 2 per 100 000. Age  Rarely seen in children.  Risk increases with age – two peaks, in the mid-late 30s and in the over 70s.  approximately half of the cases are in under 50s. Specific types  Follicular carcinoma is more common in areas with low iodine.  Thyroid lymphoma is common in areas with higher rates of thyroiditis.  Aetiology  It is mostly thought that thyroid cancers are due to genetic alterations.  The commonest thyroid cancer, papillary, is linked to a BRAF (B-type of proto-oncogene mutation). Familial medullary cell carcinoma  Roughly a quarter of medullary carcinomas are hereditary, part of the familial cancer syndrome type 2 multiple endocrine neoplasias. (MEN2).  MEN2 is due to proto-oncogene tyrosine-protein kinase receptor mutations (RET).  This is via autosomal dominant inheritance. Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI Risk factors for thyroid cancer  Ionising radiation exposure (especially in childhood).  Previous goitre.  Previous thyroid nodule.  Having MEN2.  Family history thyroid disease.  Female sex. Pathophysiology  Thyroid carcinomas coming from thyroid epithelium are papillary or follicular (called differentiated) and anaplastic (aka undifferentiated/poorly differentiated).  Differentiated carcinoma types develop from thyroid hormoneproducing cells. They normally do not increase hormone production, instead sometimes thyroglobulin (Tg). This is used in post-follow-up as a marker.  Medullary carcinoma originates from parafollicular thyroid C cells (that produce calcitonin).  Malignant C cells increase calcitonin levels a lot and this can be used to detect disease in medullary cancer post-surgery.  Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma normally occurs due to mutation in a well-differentiated thyroid tumour.  Possible spread of the tumour itself (aka extrathyroid’ spread) can be described as:  minimal, eg to sternothyroid muscle or perithyroid soft tissues  beyond thyroid capsule, eg to subcutaneous tissues, the larynx, trachea, oesophagus or recurrent laryngeal nerve:  more concerning is possible further spread to prevertebral fascia, or if it encases the carotid artery or mediastinal vessels. Tumour staging and grading (one example from many styles, these are the current UK guidelines)  Grading is via U1–U5 system where U1 is normal tissue and U5 is malignant.  TNM’R’ staging is carried out:  T (primary tumour) – T1-4a/b (based on size, limited to the thyroid, the capsule or beyond)  N (regional lymph nodes: cervical or upper mediastinum) – eg those associated with the trachea, larynx, retropharyngeal, cervical or superior mediastinum  M (distant metastases), ie present or not; or even that it cannot be assessed  R (residual disease), ie present or not; or even that it cannot be assessed. RED flags → urgent referral  Thyroid mass with no pain, growing over weeks.  Thyroid pain waxing and waning or persisting over weeks.  Cervical lymphadenopathy is palpable on examination.  Goitre + stridor/hoarseness.  Family history of thyroid cancer.  History radiotherapy/radiation exposure.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI 60 years 50–60 years Familial: 20s–30s 55–65 years Approximately 65 years men > men Women ≥ men Women > men Common and fast Bone, liver, lung Common and fast 25% of these ‘familial’ Worst of thyroid; one of worst of all cancers Mostly nonHodgkin’s type (NHL)  Thyroid nodules in children.  Vocal cord palsy.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  infectious lymphadenopathy  goitre  lymphoma (non-thyroid primary)  benign thyroid nodule (FNAC needed for this diagnosis – only 5–10% of all thyroid nodules are malignant, the rest are adenomas).  Diagnosis/Investigation Diagnosis  Based on clinical history (including risk factor presence), examination and confirmation usually by ultrasound scan (USS) combined with fine needle aspirate with cytology (FNAC).  Specific type diagnosis is based on cytology of the aspirate, or analysis following biopsy or diagnostic hemithyroidectomy. Investigations (listed in roughly the order performed)  Bloods:  TFTs and thyroglobulin (Tg) are often normal  calcitonin – often high in medullary carcinoma.  USS (of thyroid and neck nodes):  sensitive to thyroid nodules and first-line diagnostic test  suspicious features include > 1 cm, non-uniform appearance, associated cervical lymph nodes, microcalcifications.  USS-guided FNAC:  not normally performed unless > 10 mm size or has associated lymphadenopathy or other red flags.

DR. JAMIL  Imaging:  radionucleotide (with iodine uptake, cold spots seen more in cancer than hot spots)  CT/MRI (ie of tumour and all nearby structures/nodes which can help determine surgery type/management).  Laryngoscopy:  might show a paralysed vocal cord.  Possible surgical confirmation:  biopsy – open or via ‘core’ sampling  diagnostic hemithyroidectomy. Some specific investigations  Possible family history – RET proto-oncogene analysis  Possible medullary thyroid cancer (including phaeochromocytoma screening):  bloods – calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels, calcium and PTH  24-hour urine catecholamines  normetanephrine levels (via 24-hour urine or bloods). Post-surgery follow-up  Bloods:  Tg but > 6 weeks post-surgery  thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)  RET analysis for all post-surgery  proven medullary – genetic screening and calcitonin.  Imaging:  USS  possible further imaging (in recurrence, PET is recommended).  Management  Typically – surgery and/or radioiodine and/or chemoradiotherapy are the main options.  If the above is not possible, supportive palliation is the last resort. Referral  Same-day for suspected thyroid cancer + stridor.  Urgent for red flags (ie 2-week wait).  Follow-up post-surgery recommended – ≤ 2 monthly in the first two years and 3–6 monthly thereafter. Non-Pharmacological  Multidisciplinary team (MDT) support essential for all stages, especially following treatment (eg ENT, oncology, pathology, radiology, physio, anaesthetic, nurses, Macmillan nurses, nutrition, speech and language).  Psychological therapies for cancer impact.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Prognosis  As with all cancers, age and health of the patient, specific cancer cell type and staging of the disease (ie degree of local or metastatic spread) are good prognostic indicators.  Lifelong levothyroxine is needed, not only for treatment but also post-thyroidectomy and ablation therapy.  TSH suppression has been linked to bone loss and atrial fibrillation.  Generally, better outcomes if cancer takes up radioactive iodine and thus is detected in radionucleotide scanning.  Most local recurrence is detected before five years. \\\\ \\\\\\\\\\\\ Medullary Anaplastic Lymphoma Indicators: age, how long takes calcitonin to double, 5-year survival approximately 80% < 6 months, even with treatment! 5-year survival: approximately 90% in early disease and approximately 5% in advanced. Average 50% survive to 5 years  post-primary TB  miliary TB.  The most commonly involved site is the lung – but TB also affect lymph nodes, bones, the renal tract, and the gastrointestinal (GI) tract.  Tuberculous meningitis is the most serious complication.  Treatment combination of antibiotic therapy: Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol. Epidemiology Groups most at risk include:  Those on low incomes.  Homeless people.  People with alcohol problems.  HIV-positive individuals.  Immigrants from countries with a high incidence of TB.  Patients with diabetes.  Aetiology  Primary TB: primary infection occurs in those without immunity.  Post-primary TB: organisms disseminated by the blood at the time of primary infection may reactivate many years later.  Miliary TB: widespread dissemination of infection via the bloodstream.

DR. JAMIL  Commonest causative organism is mycobacterium tuberculosis. Pathophysiology Primary TB:  A small lung lesion known as the Ghon focus develops in the mid or lower zones of the lung, and is composed of tubercleladen macrophages.  Bacilli are transported through the lymphatics to the draining lymph nodes, which enlarge considerably and undergo caseation.  Infection is often arrested at this stage and the bacteria may remain dormant for many years.  The peripheral lung lesion and the nodes heal and may calcify. The entire process is often asymptomatic. However, specific immunity begins to develop and tuberculin skin tests become positive. Post-primary TB:  The most common site is the lungs, with bone and lymph node sites being less common.  Reactivation may be precipitated by a waning of host immunity, eg due to malignancy, or immunosuppressive drugs (including steroids). Milliary TB:  The infection is spread via the bloodstream.  Clinical Presentation  Primary infection is often asymptomatic, but may cause mild cough and wheeze or erythema nodosum.  Features of reactivation/reinfection:  persistent cough  haemoptysis  pneumonia  weight loss  night sweats  lymphadenopathy  meningitis  ‘cold’ abscess – anterior triangle, tense, not hot erythematous, slow growing.  In miliary TB, hepatosplenomegaly eventually develops and choroidal tubercles may be visible on fundoscopy.  Children can present with non-specific symptoms and signs such as fatigue, poor weight gain, and persistently raised temperature.  Differential Diagnosis  Upper respiratory tract infection (URTI).  Asthma.  Lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI).  Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI Screening People who are eligible for screening include:  those who are/have been in contact with active laryngeal/pulmonary TB need to be screened for latent TB  people who are immunocompromised  new entrants to the UK from high-risk countries who have not had pre-entry screening  new NHS employees working with patients or clinical specimens  people who have not completed treatment with evidence of TB scarring or untreated fibrotic changes on chest x-ray. Screening tests  Mantoux testing (first line) involves injecting tuberculin intradermally and inspecting the skin for signs of a local skin reaction (induration) after 2–3 days, test is considered positive at an induration of 5 mm or more, regardless of previous BCG vaccination history:  May be offered to children and young people aged 2–17 years who have been in close contact with people with pulmonary or laryngeal TB; and to new entrants to the UK from high TB prevalence countries.  Interferon gamma release assay (IGRA) is a blood test that detects the response of white blood cells to TB antigens.  Both a Mantoux test and IGRA may be offered to people who are severely immunocompromised at risk of TB:  People younger than 65 years of age from under-served groups (such as the homeless or substance misusers) may be offered a single IGRA test.  The use of anti-tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) therapy can be associated with reactivation of latent TB. Patients due to start such treatment should be screened for active/latent/past TB. Those who have had adequately treated past TB should be monitored closely. Where past TB has not been treated fully or latent TB is identified, a course of chemoprophylaxis is given.

DR. JAMIL  Management Non-Pharmacological:  Physiotherapy may be of benefit when there is joint involvement. Pharmacological:  Management of active TB is delivered in a combination of four drugs:  Rifampicin  Isoniazid  Pyrazinamide  Ethambutol.  Short courses of treatment for 6 months are now standard. All drugs are given for 2 months, and isoniazid and rifampicin are continued for a further 4 months.  For patient with active TB of the CNS, continue isoniazid (with pyridoxine) and rifampicin for a further 10 months.  Steroids are also indicated in meningeal TB for at least 3 weeks before being weaned down gradually.  All four drugs are continued until sensitivities are known.  If pyrazinamide has to be discontinued due to side-effects, a 9month regimen is necessary.  Second-line agents (eg ethionamide, propionamide, streptomycin, cycloserine) may be needed.  Compliance can pose major problems and directly observed therapy (D.OT – larger doses of drugs administered three times per week) is used when poor compliance is anticipated. Ongoing investigations and results:  Once 2 weeks of anti-tuberculous chemotherapy has been completed, a smear-positive patient is considered to be noninfectious.  Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) signifies resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid, and currently accounts for 1.8% of tuberculous infections.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Extremely drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) signifies resistance to rifampicin, isoniazid, a quinolone, and a second-line injectable agent (eg amikacin, capreomycin, kanamycin). There were 3 cases of XDR-TB in 2017. Side-effects from these drugs are common. They include:  Hepatitis due to rifampicin, isoniazid, and pyrazinamide. There is an increased risk of hepatotoxicity from anti-tuberculous chemotherapy with age.  Optic neuritis: may be caused by ethambutol; visual acuity should be checked before treatment is initiated. May also cause yellowing of vision.  Peripheral neuropathy: may be due to isoniazid; 10 mg pyridoxine daily is given in those at particular risk of this complication (eg people with alcohol problems, diabetes, and patients with renal failure).  Urinary discolouration (red/orange colour) – Rifampicin. Bacile Calmette-Guerin (BCG) Vaccination:  The school BCG programme has now been withdrawn.  Neonatal BCG immunisation is recommended for babies at high risk of tuberculosis infection.  Unimmunised children between 4 weeks and 16 years of age with an increased risk should be offered BCG immunisation.  The efficacy of BCG varies in different communities but usually helps prevent severe, disseminated disease. If a latent TB infection test is positive, then an assessment for active TB should be performed. If there is no evidence of active infection on the basis of symptoms and chest Xray, the person should be treated for latent TB infection. Chemoprophylaxis is usually either:  three months of isoniazid (with pyridoxine) and rifampicin  six months of isoniazid (with pyridoxine). Surgical:  In Pott’s disease (crush fracture of thoracic spine due to tuberculous osteomyelitis), surgery may be necessary to correct the deformity and prevent spinal complications. May require drainage of abscess and evacuation of infected material.  Prognosis  Milliary TB is universally fatal if left untreated.  Other relevant information:  Tuberculosis (TB) is a notifiable disease. A clinician (usually a TB specialist) should notify a new culture-confirmed case of TB, or where TB is suspected and a decision has been made to treat the person, within 3 working days.  Opportunistic mycobacterial infections.  These account for 10% of all mycobacterial infections. Causative organisms include the following:  Mycobacterium kansasii (most common)  M. xenopi
