JAMIL  M. malmoense  M. avium intracellulare.  These organisms cause disease that is clinically and radiologically identical to TB, and indistinguishable from TB on sputum smear.  pulmonary disease, lymphadenitis (in children), and disseminated infection are the most common clinical problems.  most patients are middle-aged/elderly with significant underlying COPD, bronchiectasis or previous TB.  a minimum of two positive cultures taken a week apart in a patient with an appropriate clinical picture is necessary to make the diagnosis.  The organisms are ubiquitous in the environment and are lowgrade pathogens. Opportunistic mycobacterial infections constitute a relatively higher proportion of mycobacterial infections in patients with acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS).  The onset of symptoms is usually gradual.  Treatment programmes are generally longer than for TB, and are continued for at least 9 months and often for 2 years.  Rifampicin and ethambutol are the mainstay of treatment; clarithromycin or ciprofloxacin may be added.  Opportunistic infections do not need to be notified.  Contact tracing is unnecessary as person-to-person infection is very rare. Ventilatory Support Mechanical ventilation, ventilatory support or assisted ventilation is artificial ventilation or breathing where mechanical or artificial means are used to assist or replace spontaneous breathing.  Overview Key Facts  Mechanical ventilation, ventilatory support or assisted ventilation is artificial ventilation or breathing where mechanical or artificial means are used to assist or replace spontaneous breathing.  Ventilatory support is one of the core components in the management of critically ill patients.  It is the treatment of choice for patients who are having respiratory failure.  Application of ventilatory support and operating a mechanical ventilator requires a lot of expertise and is done by an authorised person in a tertiary care set-up.  Its application may lead to ventilator-associated lung injuries and ventilator-associated pneumonias. Sound knowledge of mechanical ventilation and adequate monitoring during the ventilation enables the physicians and ICU staff to maximise the benefits of mechanical ventilation.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI Epidemiology  Epidemiology of ventilator-associated lung injuries and pneumonia:  24% of the patients will develop ventilator-associated lung injury (VALI) after receiving positive pressure mechanical ventilation  the primary cause of VALI is alveolar overdistension by positive pressure ventilation  alveolar overdistension can be prevented by using small tidal volumes  ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is defined as the infection acquired by a patient after 24 hours of intubation; it occurs in 5–65% of the patients mechanically ventilated (depending upon the diagnosis)  the highest rate of incidence of VAP is in older and immunocompromised patients  improvement of overall sterilisation measures of ICUs and training of nursing staff can reduce the incidence of VAP  a major proportion of neonates who suffer from neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), premature birth and early pneumonia require mechanical ventilation; the survival rate of neonates who require early ventilator support in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) is 64% in the United Kingdom (UK).  Ventilatory support in COVID-19:  approximately 2.5% of COVID-19 patients have needed mechanical ventilation as they fought the infection, during the ongoing pandemic  more than 3300 ventilators were used during the pandemic  survival rates for patients with COVID-19 in intensive care settings remained at 92% in the UK.  Aetiology  It is a life-saving support in all the emergency conditions in which the patient is having respiratory failure:  acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)  head injury  stroke  acute exacerbation of asthma  chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)  severe chest trauma  respiratory failure due to pneumothorax and haemothorax  severe chest infections (pneumonia, bronchitis viral infections).  Ventilatory support has been the mainstay of treatment in critically ill patients worldwide during the COVID-19 pandemic, as it gives time to fight the infection.  Respiratory failure can be divided into type I and type II. Type 1 respiratory failure (hypoxaemic)  Causes:

Type 2 respiratory failure (hypercapnic)  Causes:  ARDS  cervical cordotomy  COPD  drug overdose  head and cervical cord injury  myasthenia gravis  myxoedema  poisonings. Pathophysiology  Pathophysiology of respiratory failure:  respiratory failure can be due to abnormality in any part of the respiratory system or in higher brain centres responsible for respiratory control  it results from either a reduction in ventilating capacity of the respiratory system or increased demand for oxygen (ventilation), or both in some cases  V/Q (ventilation-perfusion) mismatch is the most common cause of hypoxaemic respiratory failure  gas exchange is affected at the alveolar level  the cause may be cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic, such as pneumonia or COPD, etc  hypercapnic respiratory failure occurs as a result of increased carbon dioxide retention and increases PaCO2  it is caused by abnormalities in the central nervous system (CNS), neuromuscular transmission, rib cage structure, the fatigue of respiratory muscles or overall drug-induced CNS depression.  Pathophysiology of VALI:

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  VALI occurs as a result of multiple events associated with mechanical ventilation; it starts with the mechanical remoulding of the lung parenchymal tissue because of the continuous uneven stress and strain  the resulting structural modification initiates an inflammatory response which results in structural deformity of the alveoli.  Pathophysiology of VAP:  the incidence of VAP is very high in ICUs and it is the most common nosocomial infection occurring in ICUs  the main source of VAP is oropharyngeal colonisation by endogenic flora, or by micro-organisms acquired from the patient’s surroundings in ICU, specifically the hands and protective equipment of the ICU staff or respiratory equipment or hospital oxygen reservoir  the stomach also represents a potential site for the colonisation of nosocomial bacteria, viruses or fungi.  Clinical Presentation  Respiratory failure is diagnosed on the basis of arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis.  Assessment of the underlying factor must be initiated as early as possible, along with the treatment of acute respiratory failure which is mechanical ventilation in most cases.  The cause of respiratory failure will be evident after thorough history taking and physical examination.  Signs of respiratory failure:  dyspnoea  cyanosis of the skin and mucous membranes (in hypoxaemia)  confusion or somnolence  tachypnoea  oxygen saturation of less than 80% despite high-flow oxygenation  Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 9 or below in a patient with head trauma causing respiratory insufficiency.  Diagnosis/Investigation  A variety of clinical manifestations are associated with respiratory failure.  Signs and symptoms of respiratory failure may or may not be present. This signifies the need for measuring ABGs in all patients who are seriously ill or suspected for respiratory failure.  ABG measurement is the core component that enables the intensivist to put the patient on ventilatory support.  Chest X-ray is important in decision making.  Echocardiography will assess the right heart function and pressure in the pulmonary artery in patients with hypercapnic respiratory failure or suspected hypercapnic respiratory failure.  Electrocardiogram (ECG) should be performed to rule out the possibility of a cardiovascular cause of respiratory failure.

DR. JAMIL  Pulmonary function tests will differentiate hypoxaemic and hypercapnic respiratory failure by measuring lung volume and gas exchange. Laboratory studies  When there is clinical suspicion of respiratory failure, blood gas analysis differentiates between acute and chronic respiratory failure and this differentiation is very important as the management is different for the two conditions.  A full blood count (FBC) may indicate anaemia or polycythaemia (hypoxaemic failure).  Liver function tests and renal function tests may help to indicate the cause of respiratory failure.  Serum creatine kinase (CK) and troponin I help to rule out recent myocardial infarction.  Normal arterial blood gas levels are:  pH (7.35–7.45)  PaCO2 (35–45 mmHg)  bicarbonate (22–26 mEq/l)  PaO2 (75–100 mmHg). Indications  Ventilatory support will be indicated in all those clinical conditions that are life-threatening or in which spontaneous breathing is halted.  Mechanical ventilation will be required when spontaneous ventilation is not being controlled from respiratory centres located in the brain stem (head injuries, cord injuries, overdosage of general anaesthesia and overdosage of sedatives and opioids).  Conditions that cause fatigue to respiratory muscles, ie increased load on respiratory muscles, can cause respiratory muscle failure to the extent that one may need mechanical ventilation (asthma, COPD, obesity, ascites, anasarca or abdominal compartment syndrome).  Alveolar collapse or lung flooding will cause hypoxaemic respiratory failure (infections, inhalational injuries, fluid overload, blunt chest trauma, aspiration, congestive heart failure for sepsis).  Mechanical ventilation will be required in patients who are unable to breathe from their natural airways in conditions such as injuries to the pharynx or larynx or in the presence of a tumour in the airway. For ARDS:  According to NHS UK, indications for mechanical ventilation are:  severe hypoxaemia: PaO2 <60 mmHg (8.3 kPa) despite 0.6 FiO2  PaCO2: >45 mmHg (6 kPa).  Severe chest trauma with multiple rib fractures on both sides:

DR. JAMIL  high-flow oxygen therapy  extracorporeal membrane oxygenation  intravenous (IV) corticosteroids along with nebulisation  assisted ventilation or mechanical ventilation. Principles of mechanical ventilation  It is used to reduce hypoxaemia or hypercapnia, ie increasing PaO2 or decreasing PaCO2 respectively.  Most appropriate therapy for respiratory muscle fatigue as it gives rest to respiratory muscles. Types of mechanical ventilation  Patients can be mechanically ventilated by either invasive or non-invasive ventilation. Invasive ventilation involves the insertion of endotracheal or tracheostomy tube for mechanical ventilation whereas non-invasive (CPAP or BIPAP) type of ventilation uses a tight-fitting face mask.  1. Positive-pressure ventilation (most commonly used):  can be administered invasively, ie by endotracheal or noninvasively (NIV)  increases airway pressure and promotes gas exchange.  2. Negative-pressure ventilation.  3. Patient-initiated ventilation.  4. Controlled ventilation.  5. Pressure-targeted ventilation.  6. Volume-targeted ventilation. Positive-pressure ventilation  Can be administered invasively, ie by endotracheal or noninvasively (NIV).  Increases airway pressure and promotes gas exchange.  Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation is of two types – continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) and bilevel positive airway pressure (BIPAP):  CPAP ventilation provides a single pressure against which the ventilation takes place, whereas in BIPAP there are two pressure gradients – one is for inspiration and a lower pressure for exhalation  CPAP is used in less-severe respiratory failure cases and BIPAP is used in relatively more severe respiratory cases.  It is indicated in acute exacerbation of COPD, shock, respiratory acidosis, respiratory failure due to chest trauma and oxygen support in cancer palliative patients.  Positive pressure ventilation with invasive airway is indicated in hypercapnic and hypoxaemic respiratory failure and in haemodynamic instability. Pharmacological  Management of mechanical ventilation includes appropriate sedation, analgesia and administration of muscle relaxants to decrease patient discomfort and respiratory effort by patients until satisfactory improvement in the underlying cause is achieved.  Sedation is given immediately after endotracheal tube intubation with the help of propofol, midazolam or ketamine.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  Analgesia is provided by morphine or fentanyl, mostly used in palliative care.  Muscle relaxants such as rocuronium and pancuronium at regular intervals to depress respiratory drive.  Other measures include maintenance of bronchopulmonary hygiene by regular suctioning and chest physiotherapy.  Supportive care includes postural changes to prevent pressure ulcers, prophylaxis for venous thromboembolism and prophylaxis for gastric ulcers.  Prognosis  Prognosis depends on the underlying illness precipitating respiratory failure.  Ventilator-associated pneumonia is responsible for high mortality in ICUs.  Hygiene and close monitoring will increase the chances of patient survival.  Different scoring systems are used to assess the outcome of ventilator support in critically ill patients, ie APACHE II score, SOFA7day, MPM score and SAPS II score.  In most cases, survivors' lung function returns to normal but some may have reduced health-related quality of life for up to 2 years, depending upon the duration of ventilator support. Viral Infections And Antivirals A virus is a small intracellular organism comprising nucleic acid and outer protein coat, they cause a wide spectrum of viral illness worldwide from common cold to HIV infection.  Overview Key Facts  A virus is a small intracellular organism comprising nucleic acid and outer protein coat:  they cause a wide spectrum of viral illness worldwide from common cold to HIV infection  viral infection can cause worldwide pandemics eg Spanish flu pandemic 1918, the current coronavirus pandemic (COVID-19).  Influenza is a very common viral disease worldwide, associated with significant mortality in young children, elderly patients, and the immunocompromised.  Viral haemorrhagic fever is a rare clinical presentation endemic in the tropics and associated with very high case fatality. Examples include Ebola; Lassa fever is a rare clinical presentation.  Many viral infections, including measles, mumps and rubella, are prevented by vaccination. Epidemiology  Horizontal transmission is very common, with various different routes eg body fluid exposure (HIV), blood-borne (Hepatitis B

DR. JAMIL and C), aerosol-borne (influenza) and vector-borne eg Dengue fever.  Vertical transmission of infection is seen in some viral infections, notably HIV, Hepatitis B, Rubella and varicella zoster infection.  Aetiology  Classification is based on the underlying genetic structure (RNA vs. DNA), viral structure, and replication cycle. Important groups of viruses include:  herpes viruses eg HSV-1, are associated with a wide range of clinical disease, including peri-oral and genital ulceration, infectious mononucleosis, and chickenpox  pox viruses – double stranded DNA viruses including smallpox virus  retroviruses eg HIV-1 and HTLV-1. These are single stranded RNA viruses which use a reverse transcriptase enzyme to form DNA that is integrated into the host genome  arboviruses (arthropod-borne viruses) are a group of heterogeneous viruses transmitted by animals, including Dengue virus (mosquito-borne). Pathophysiology  As intracellular pathogens, viruses usually cause disease by directly inducing cell death.  Certain viruses eg EBV, Hepatitis C, and HPV are oncogenic.  Clinical Presentation  There is a wide spectrum of clinical disease associated with different virus types.  Clinical features of influenza infection include:  rhinorrhoea  fever  rigors  malaise  myalgia  arthralgia  dry cough  shortness of breath  Viral hepatitis infection may be asymptomatic, or present acutely with fulminant liver failure, and present after slow insidious progression to chronic hepatitis:  acute – right upper quadrant pain, myalgia, fatigue, nausea and vomiting, diarrhoea. This is usually self-limiting, but a proportion of patients may develop fulminant liver failure with jaundice and confusion (hepatic encephalopathy).  chronic infection (hepatitis B and C) – several years after initial infection, patients develop signs of chronic liver disease eg itch, abdominal swelling, spider naevi.  Herpes viruses have several different clinical presentations:

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI  herpes simplex virus-1 – perioral cold sores; confusion, disorientation and fever due to meningoencephalitis; progressive visual deterioration with ophthalmic HSV  herpes simplex virus-2 – painful genital ulceration; meningoencephalitis  varicella zoster virus – widespread erythematous vesicular rash (chickenpox – primary infection) and subsequent unidermatomal blistering rash (shingles)  cytomegalovirus (CMV) – bloody diarrhoea (colitis) and visual blurring (retinitis) in severely immunocompromised patients eg advanced HIV infection, colitis and retinitis in immunosuppressed patients  epstein-Barr virus (EBV) – primary infection in adolescence or adulthood manifests as fever, persistent pharyngitis, malaise, and myalgia (infectious mononucleosis)  human herpes virus-8 infection causes a mild viral illness in most patients. Reactivation in immunocompromised hosts is associated with Kaposi’s sarcoma.  Mumps is a highly contagious disease of childhood which presents with headache, fever, and bilateral parotitis. Important complications of mumps include orchitis (swollen, painful testicles with long-term sub-fertility) and an acute meningitis.  Measles is a highly infectious disease of childhood which presents with fever and a diffuse erythematous maculopapuilar rash. It is associated with rare but important complications:  pneumonia – cough and shortness of breath  encephalitis – drowsiness, weakness and seizures.  Rubella presents with fever, a diffuse erythematous macular rash, and post-auricular lymphadenopathy. It is usually selflimiting but causes serious complications in pregnancy, including miscarriage and congenital rubella (deafness and congenital cataract).  Differential Diagnosis  Influenza infection – infectious mononucleosis, upper respiratory tract infection, bacterial pneumonia, sepsis.  Acute viral hepatitis – hepatitis A, E, B or C infection, EBV infection, CMV infection, HIV infection, paracetamol overdose, drug toxicity.  Encephalitis – HSV-1 encephalitis, VZV encephalitis, enterovirus, autoimmune disease.  Fever and rash – roseola (self-limiting macular viral exanthem), Scarlet fever, measles, rubella, meningococcal sepsis, relapsing fever, typhus, Dengue fever.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Most viral infections can be diagnosed clinically but in cases of diagnostic doubt, viral PCR and serological testing for specific IgM antibodies (indicating acute infection) can be useful.  In unwell patients, blood tests can be performed to exclude organ damage:  full blood count (FBC) – non-specific findings eg neutrophilia, lymphocytosis, lymphopenia  LFTs – transaminitis seen in acute/chronic Hepatitis and EBV infection.

DR. JAMIL  Serological testing is important in patients presenting with acute or chronic liver disease as Hepatitis B and C can progress to chronic infection and cancer, and are widely treatable.  Chest radiograph is useful in breathless patients (typically see diffuse interstitial shadowing in contrast to focal consolidation with bacterial infection).  Management Non-Pharmacological  Many viral infections, including measles, mumps, rubella, Hepatitis A and E, EBV and Dengue fever are self-limiting and managed conservatively with good supportive care.  Non-immune pregnant women exposed to rubella infection should be referred urgently to an obstetrician and paediatric infectious diseases specialist. Unfortunately, IVIG is not widely effective in preventing congenital rubella and termination is often recommended. Pharmacological  Influenza infection - oseltamivir (Tamiflu) is recommended for ‘at risk’ patient groups – adults > 65 years, children under 6 months, pregnant women and patients with diabetes mellitus, chronic respiratory, heart, kidney and liver disease and severe immunosuppression:  shortens the duration of infection by one day (reducing duration of infectivity) and reduces mortality in critically ill patients  hospital in-patients exposed to influenza infection are generally treated with prophylactic oseltamivir.  Pharmacological treatment of Hepatitis B infection depends on clinical presentation:  fulminant liver failure – antiviral therapy with lamivudine or tenofovir  chronic liver failure – prolonged 6-12 month course of antiviral (entecavir or tenofovir) or pegylated interferon. These treatments are reserved for patients with active chronic disease with potential for high infectivity.  Pharmacological treatment of Hepatitis C infection is reserved for patients with chronic infection lasting > 6 months and is managed by specialists. Surgical  Fulminant liver failure due to Hepatitis B, EBV, or CMV infection may necessitate emergency liver transplantation.  Prognosis  Risk factors for severe influenza include extremes of age, pregnancy, and comorbidities.  Most viral infections are self-limiting with low morbidity and mortality.

Respiratory part 2 L ALRAJHI

stem: A 45-year-old non-smoking man remains breathless at night with a polyphonic wheeze, despite already being prescribed a short-acting b2-agonist by his general practitioner (GP). He is concordant with treatment and has a good inhaler technique. His spirometry result is shown below. Which is the next appropriate therapy to offer according to current NICE guidelines?
explanation: B Inhaled corticosteroids This clinical scenario and ﬂow–volume loop are suggestive of asthma. The spirometry suggests an obstructive picture, with a concave curve pattern. Inhaled corticosteroids at a low dose are the ﬁrst-line maintenance therapy for adults with uncontrolled asthma. D No further treatment The patient is experiencing nocturnal breathlessness, which is an indication for increasing maintenance therapy for asthma. A Long-acting β2-agonist (LABA) A LABA should only be offered after inhaled corticosteroids and an LTRA have already been offered. The LTRA should then be reviewed after six to eight weeks after the addition of a LABA to see if it should be continued. C Leukotriene receptor antagonist (LTRA) An LTRA is only recommended as a stage in adult asthma management after low-dose inhaled corticosteroids have been initiated. E Long-acting muscarinic antagonist A long-acting muscarinic antagonist is used as the next stage in the management of COPD. However, the spirometry result is more in keeping with asthma than COPD, making this answer incorrect.

stem: A 74-year-old male smoker with a 30-pack-year smoking history has an FEV1 of 40% predicted. He has successfully reduced his smoking habit to only 3 cigarettes per day with help from smoking cessation services. However, he can only walk 100 m at a time before he becomes out of breath and feels that he needs to stop. His medication includes an inhaled long-acting beta-agonist and tiotropium. On examination, his BP is 155/85 mmHg and he has coarse crackles and wheeze throughout both lung ﬁelds. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.9 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 210 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 139 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bicarbonate 30 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l pH 7.4 7.35–7.45 PaO2 10.1 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa PaCO2 6.4 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa Which would best improve his exercise tolerance?
explanation: D Pulmonary rehabilitation Given his limited smoking habit, it is likely that a pulmonary rehabilitation programme will have more impact. C Portable oxygen His PaO2 is too high for portable oxygen to be of beneﬁt. A Inhaled beclometasone Low-dose inhaled corticosteroids have no impact on disease progression in COPD, although it appears that high-dose inhaled corticosteroids combined with a long-acting beta-2 agonist does reduce exacerbations, at the expense of increased pneumonia. B Inhaled salbutamol Salbutamol is not likely to impact signiﬁcantly as most patients have very poor reversibility. E Smoking cessation Smoking cessation will have some impact on exercise tolerance, but given his limited habit now, it is likely that a pulmonary rehabilitation programme will have more impact.

stem: A 23-year-old African-Caribbean patient develops painful red nodules on both her shins over 2 days and has noticed painful knees, ankles and wrists. She also complains of mild sweats and weight loss over the past 2 months. Her chest x-ray is shown below. Given the likely clinical diagnosis, what is the most likely outcome for her?
options: Complete remission after a course of steroids
Spontaneous resolution with no long-term sequelae
Spontaneous resolution followed by further relapses
Peripheral lung inﬁltrates and shortness of breath
Increasing weight loss and neurological impairment
explanation:
B Spontaneous resolution with no long-term sequelae This patient has acute sarcoidosis with erythema nodosum, polyarthralgia and mild constitutional symptoms. Her chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) but clear lung ﬁelds. Around 90% patients have BHL at presentation. In 10–20% of cases, symptoms progress to shortness of breath, dry cough and chest pain. The majority of patients (80%) either stabilise or regress, so in the ﬁrst instance treatment is not indicated. Non- pulmonary manifestations include neuropathy, Bell’s palsy, hepatosplenomegaly, uveitis, conjunctivitis, lupus pernio, subcutaneous nodules, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, hypercalcaemia and renal stones. Treatment of acute sarcoidosis is usually supportive, including non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for polyarthralgia, because most recover spontaneously. E Increasing weight loss and neurological impairment Neurological involvement does occur with sarcoidosis, but this is rare, occurring in 5-15% of patients. Neurological involvement tends to be present at presentation and often in disease with other signiﬁcant extra- pulmonary features. This option is incorrect because it is an uncommon outcome. A Complete remission after a course of steroids

Sarcoidosis usually resolves spontaneously and steroids at ﬁrst presentation would not be indicated. Steroids should be commenced if: symptoms worsen or cause limitation to daily activities, pulmonary function deteriorates, CXR signs worsen (e.g. development of cavitation or ﬁbrosis) or if other organ system involvement develops. C Spontaneous resolution followed by further relapses Most patients recover spontaneously, and in 90% this is within 2 years. Less than 10% develop relapses after this point. Relapses and chronic disease are more likely if spontaneous remission does not occur within the ﬁrst 2 years. D Peripheral lung inﬁltrates and shortness of breath The extent of inﬁltrates on CXR is used in staging of the disease and is a guide to prognosis, with the likelihood of relapse increasing as the extent of inﬁltrate worsens. This option is incorrect because it is uncommon.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnoea and a dry cough over several months. He denies chest pain, haemoptysis, fever or weight loss. His past medical history is unremarkable, and he does not smoke. Physical examination reveals ﬁne bibasilar crackles but no clubbing. High-resolution CT of the chest shows bilateral ground-glass opacities with interlobular septal thickening, giving a 'crazy paving' appearance. Bronchoalveolar lavage yields a milky ﬂuid, and cytology reveals periodic acid– Schiff-positive material. What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
explanation:
B Whole lung lavage Whole lung lavage is the gold standard and ﬁrst-line treatment for PAP. It involves sequentially washing out proteinaceous material from the alveoli, providing signiﬁcant symptomatic relief. E Lung transplantation Lung transplantation is reserved for end-stage disease unresponsive to other treatments, which is rare in PAP. A Long-term corticosteroid therapy

Corticosteroids are not the treatment of choice for autoimmune PAP and may exacerbate the condition by increasing the risk of infections. C High-dose oxygen therapy While oxygen therapy may be used to manage hypoxaemia, it does not address the underlying accumulation of alveolar material. D Anti-granulocyte–macrophage colony-stimulating factor antibody therapy Recombinant granulocyte–macrophage colony-stimulating factor therapy targets the autoimmune mechanism in pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) and is used for refractory cases or as a second-line therapy.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to the Respiratory Clinic with his wife, who is extremely worried that he snores heavily every night and often seems to stop breathing. He also falls asleep each evening while watching the TV and has had to stop the car on a number of occasions to take a nap. He drinks two pints of beer each day and smokes ﬁve cigarettes per day. On examination, his BP is 152/85 mmHg and his heart rate is 80 bpm and regular; his BMI is elevated at 32 kg/m2, and his collar size is 18. His Epworth score is 15. He plans to lose weight. Which initial intervention is the most appropriate?
explanation:
A Continuous positive airway pressure For patients with mild symptoms that affect their quality of life and usual daytime activities, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend ﬁxed-level continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). Therapy with CPAP is effective in reducing symptoms and is associated with an improvement in cardiovascular morbidity in patients with hypertension and obstructive sleep apnoea. Forty per cent of patients, however, have an elevated Epworth score after CPAP is initiated, and these individuals should, of course, be encouraged to take other measures such as losing weight. E Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty

Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty is considered in patients who are resistant to other interventions or who have signiﬁcant obstructive sleep apnoea despite weight loss. B Gastric banding Gastric banding would not be appropriate here as it would not treat all presentations and should be considered for patients who are unable to achieve signiﬁcant weight loss. C Mandibular advancement device Patients with mild symptoms that affect their quality of life and usual daytime activities and who are unable to tolerate or decline to try CPAP may try a mandibular advancement device (MAD). A MAD may relieve obstruction and give this patient the opportunity to lose weight and improve his symptoms signiﬁcantly. He should, of course, also be referred for a sleep study and advised that until his symptoms signiﬁcantly improve, he is not to drive. In the event that the device is ineffective and/or he fails to lose signiﬁcant weight, he can be referred for an alternative management option. D Modaﬁnil Modaﬁnil would not be appropriate here as it is used to enhance wakefulness in patients with central sleep disorders.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of shortness of breath and a cough productive of green sputum. There are no other symptoms of note and he has no past medical history. He smokes 15–20 cigarettes per day. On examination, his Glasgow Coma Scale score is 15/15. He has a respiratory rate of 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations of 91% on air. His heart sounds are normal, with a heart rate of 120 bpm and a blood pressure of 101/62 mmHg. On chest auscultation, there are coarse crackles at the left lung base. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 126 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 14.5 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 10 × 109/l 1.5 - 7.0 × 109/l Urea 6.5 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 130 μmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Which factor in this patient’s presentation is the biggest prognostic indicator?
explanation: E Respiratory rate of 32 breaths/min This forms part of the CURB-65 criteria, an evidence-based scoring system used to estimate severity and guide management of patients with community-acquired pneumonia. The components of CURB65 are: confusion (not present in this patient); urea concentration > 7 mmol/l (urea concentration here is < 7.0 mmol/l); respiratory rate ≥ 30 breaths/minute (this patient meets the criteria as his respiratory rate is 32 breaths per minute); systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg (not met in this patient who has a systolic blood pressure of 110 mmHg); diastolic blood pressure < 60 mmHg; and age over 65 years (this patient is 62 years old). A CURB-65 score of zero corresponds to a 0.7% risk of mortality, whereas a score of 5 corresponds to a 57% risk. With a score of 1, this patient’s risk is 3.2%. He would be suitable for outpatient management. If he scores 2 or more, he should be managed as an inpatient. A Age Age of ≥ 65 years counts towards the CURB-65 criteria. This patient is 62 years old, which does score a point on this scale. B Blood pressure This question relates to the CURB-65 criteria – these clinical criteria provide evidence-based guidance on the severity of communityacquired pneumonia and can be used to determine the appropriate management of a patient (admission vs outpatient care, and antibiotic therapy). Blood pressure does form part of the CURB-65 criteria; however, patients score a point if their systolic blood pressure is < 90 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure is < 60 mmHg. This patient has a systolic blood pressure of 110 mmHg, and therefore, this is not the correct answer. The only criterion on which this patient scores against the CURB-65 is his respiratory rate which is ≥ 30 breaths/minute. C Neutrophilia Neutrophilia is not one of the features of CURB-65; the only CURB-65 criterion met by this patient is his respiratory rate which is 30 breaths per minute. D Smoking history Although smoking is a risk factor for more severe respiratory disease, it does not form part of the CURB-65 severity criteria for pneumonia.

stem: A 55-year-old asthmatic patient presents to the Emergency Department with increasing cough and wheeze. She describes a cough productive of brown sputum. There is no other past medical history of note. She is taking a steroid inhaler regularly and increasing doses of beta-agonist, with no alleviation of her symptoms. She has worked in a bakery for many years. She is an ex-smoker and stopped smoking 20 years ago; she has a pet dog and one cat. On examination she has a temperature of 38°C and is breathless at rest. Her BP is 122/82 mmHg, with pulse 88/min and regular. There is reduced chest expansion anteriorly on the left side, with corresponding reduced breath sounds. She has a mild expiratory wheeze. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 141 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 12.7 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 7.37 × 109/l 1.5–7.0 × 109/l Lymphocytes 2.55 × 109/l 1.5–4.0 × 109/l Eosinophils 2.1 × 109/l 0.1–0.4 × 109/l Monocytes 0.6 × 109/l 0.0–0.8 × 109/l Basophils 0.05 × 109/l < 0.1 × 109/l MCV 87.3 ﬂ 80–100 ﬂ Platelets (PLT) 314 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l ESR 28 mm/h 1–20 mm/h CRP 16 mg/l < 10 mg/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 4.8 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 95 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bilirubin 12 µmol/l 1–22 µmol/l ALT 49 u/l 7–55 u/l ALP 61 u/l 30–150 u/l Albumin 36 g/l 35–55 g/l X-ray scan: CT scan on presentation: CT scan taken one month later: What investigation would help make a diagnosis?
options: Positive skin test/radioallergosorbent test for Aspergillus fumigatus
explanation:
C Positive skin test/radioallergosorbent test for Aspergillus fumigatus The chest X-ray shows left upper lobe collapse and demonstrates the ‘veil sign’. This patient has allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). Pulmonary inﬁltrates, blood eosinophilia and asthma are usually secondary to Churg–Strauss syndrome, or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. ABPA is suspected in any patient with asthma who has an abnormal chest X-ray and high peripheral blood eosinophilia. The chest X-ray may show diffuse pulmonary inﬁltrates, and pulmonary, lobar or segmental collapse occurs as a transient feature. The most common cause is sensitivity to A. fumigatus spores. The diagnostic criteria include: • Asthma (in most cases) • Peripheral blood and sputum eosinophilia

• Abnormal chest X-ray (inﬁltrates, segmental or lobar collapse) Positive skin tests/RAST to an extract of A. fumigatus • A. fumigatus IgG serum-precipitating antibodies • Raised total IgE >1000 ng/ml • Fungal hyphae of A. fumigatus on microscopy of sputum. D Metacholine challenge test The methacholine challenge test is used to diagnose asthma, usually where there is some doubt as to the status with respect to hyper-reactivity. A p-ANCA This is an appropriate test for vasculitis and is associated with Churg–Strauss syndrome. The absence of other features of vasculitis, such as mononeuritis, counts against this as the underlying diagnosis. B c-ANCA This is an appropriate test for vasculitis. C-ANCA positivity is associated with Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, where features such as sinusitis, haemoptysis and renal vasculitis co-exist. E Lung function tests Lung functions tests would not be sufﬁciently discriminatory to diagnose allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. They would merely demonstrate a mixed obstructive/restrictive picture.

stem: A 64-year-old homeless man is admitted on the routine medical take. He has lost a signiﬁcant amount of weight over the past few months and now presents with increasing shortness of breath. He is a former heavy smoker. On examination: decreased air entry over the right lower chest and dullness to percussion. Chest X-ray reveals a large, right-sided pleural effusion. Pleural aspiration is performed. Which one of the following features, if present, would be the most speciﬁc indicator of probable underlying malignancy?
options: Uniform blood staining throughout pleural ﬂuid samples
explanation:
C Uniform blood staining throughout pleural ﬂuid

samples Uniform blood staining and a protein level of >30 g/l are supportive of a diagnosis of malignancy. pH can also be useful for interpreting pleural ﬂuid results. Low pleural ﬂuid pH is associated with a number of conditions, including pleural infection and empyema, inﬂammatory effusions such as those related to rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis, malignancy and oesophageal rupture. E Abnormal pleural ﬂuid LDH levels LDH is used to differentiate an exudate from a transudate. Raised LDH is suggestive of an exudate and therefore infectious or inﬂammatory cause. It needs to be measured simultaneously with serum LDH as it is the ratio of pleural ﬂuid to serum LDH that is interpreted. A ratio >0.6 indicates an exudate. A Turbid ﬂuid Turbid ﬂuid is suggestive of an infectious cause. B High pleural ﬂuid neutrophil count This is also indicative of an infective cause. D Abnormal liver function tests Although deranged LFTs may suggest malignancy, there are other causes such as infection (particularly atypical organisms such as Legionella) and chronic disease such as liver cirrhosis.

stem: A 62-year-old man attends for a chest X-ray as part of a medical prior to emigrating to Australia. Unfortunately the chest X-ray reveals a number of rounded opacities predominantly in the left lung ﬁeld, all less than 3 cm in diameter. He has had 5 kg of unintentional weight loss over the past year but no other history of note. Which of the following features would be the strongest pointer to malignancy when the chest X-ray is reviewed?
options: Spiculated margin to one of the nodules, with distortion of neighbouring vessels
A rounded appearance to the nodules
No enhancement with contrast on future CT thorax
explanation:
A Spiculated margin to one of the nodules, with distortion of neighbouring vessels A spiculated margin to one of the nodules, particularly when there is

distortion of neighbouring vessels, raises the possibility of malignancy. Associated ground-glass shadowing, or the presence of cavitation or pseudo- cavitation within the lesion, increases the chances of malignant disease. CT thorax to further characterise the lesions is indicated. D No enhancement with contrast on future CT thorax Enhancement of nodules with contrast on CT thorax increases the likelihood that they are malignant in origin. B Smaller lesion size Lesions larger than 3 cm are more likely to be associated with underlying malignancy. C A rounded appearance to the nodules Rounded appearance to the nodules, implying organised growth, is less likely to be associated with an underlying malignancy. E Age 62 at presentation Older age at presentation and history of smoking are associated with increased likelihood of malignancy.

stem: A 71-year-old patient undergoes radical surgery for an oesophageal adenocarcinoma with oesophagectomy, gastrectomy and splenectomy. Initially he makes a good recovery but you are asked to review him a few days later because he is increasingly short of breath. On examination BP is 142/72 mmHg and pulse 79/min and regular. There is reduced expansion of the left side of the chest and dullness to percussion over the left lung ﬁelds. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 7.9 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 172 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 105 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Chest X-ray Large left sided pleural effusion Diagnostic tap milky coloured effusion, protein content 48g/l Which of the following investigations on the pleural ﬂuid is most likely to contribute to conﬁrming the underlying diagnosis?
explanation: A Triglycerides A triglyceride level greater than 1.2 mmol/l indicates a 99% chance that the ﬂuid in the pleural space is chyle. This is likely to be a complication of surgery, with intra-operative damage to the duct or one of its tributaries. This can cause up to 4 l of ﬂuid per day to leak into the pleural space, leading to the classic symptoms of a large pleural effusion. Initial management is conservative as the thoracic duct leak reduces spontaneously over a few days. If the effusion persists, imaging is needed, with referral for surgical ligation as indicated. C Culture and sensitivity This would identify the organism in an infective pleural effusion but would not aid the diagnosis here. B LDH LDH is used to distinguish an exudate from a transudate, and is therefore utilised to elucidate the cause of pleural effusion when heart failure versus inﬂammation or infection needs to be delineated. It is often done as part of the routine tests on pleural ﬂuid, but will not be the most useful in conﬁrming the underlying diagnosis. D pH Testing the acidity of pleural ﬂuid is used as a guide to treatment in para-pneumonic and malignant pleural effusions: a pH of <7.2 in the former indicates the need to drain, and <7.3 in the latter is associated with worse outcome. Neither is relevant in this clinical scenario. E Glucose Glucose levels are of value in para-pneumonic effusions and identify causes such as tuberculosis or malignancy.

stem: A 54-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) attends for smoking cessation advice. Which of the following methods is likely to be associated with the greatest chance of quitting?
explanation: A Bupropion Studies have shown success in smoking cessation in 20–30% of patients involved in bupropion studies at 1 year, with marginally higher quit rates seen when bupropion and nicotine replacement were combined (35%). Studies have shown that varenicline also aids smoking cessation in combination with motivational support, resulting in higher quit rates when higher doses were used (44% success rate). E Hypnosis Hypnosis aims to improve willpower in the subconscious state, and trials have showed no greater abstinence rate. B Nicotine replacement lozenges Nicotine replacement is associated with a quit rate of only around 10% in clinical trials. C Willpower Willpower quit rates are thought to be around only 2–4% at 1 year in reality. D Nicotine replacement gum Like option B, nicotine replacement is associated with a quit rate of only around 10% in clinical trials.

stem: A 42-year-old man with a history of asthma presents to the GP with shortness of breath and a cough productive of green-yellow, blood-stained sputum. On examination he has oxygen saturations of 91% and bronchial breathing at both bases. He also has reactivation of a cold sore on his upper lip. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 15.2 x 10 9/l 4–11 x 10 9/l Platelets 305 x 10 9/l 150–400 x 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 135 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 130 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 55 mm in 1 h 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Chest X-ray shows bilateral lower-lobe pneumonia. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Streptococcal pneumonia is most commonly associated with reactivation of herpes simplex virus. The clinical picture seen here, with evidence of bilateral consolidation, also fits with this diagnosis. Most guidelines for the management of streptococcal pneumonia recommend combination therapy with a penicillin and a macrolide. This patient should be referred for hospital assessment because an oxygen saturation of 91% raises the possibility that he could deteriorate rapidly.

Klebsiella spp
Klebsiella spp is incorrect. Klebsiella pneumonias typically cavitate and are seen in immune compromised individuals, classically those with alcohol dependence. The cold sore mentioned here should trigger you to focus on streptococcal infection causing the pneumonia.

Legionella pneumophila
Legionella pneumophila is incorrect. Legionella pneumonia is classically associated with concurrent gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatraemia and recent contact with water-cooling systems. None of these is mentioned in this case and his mention of a coldsore indicates a likely streptococcal cause for his pneumonia.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Mycoplasma pneumoniae is incorrect. Mycoplasmal pneumonia is classically associated with a dry cough, headache and malaise. The mention of a cold sore is important here and indicates a likely streptococcal cause for his pneumonia.

Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is incorrect. Staphylococcal pneumonia is more common in immunocompromised patents or as an acquired nosocomial infection. It classically causes a cavitating pneumonia.

stem: A 21-year-old woman presents with breathlessness and tingling around her mouth and in hands. She admits she has been anxious about university examinations. There is no past medical history of note and she is a non- smoker. On examination her BP is 122/72 mmHg, pulse is 72/min and regular and her respiratory rate is 32/min. Her chest is clear and peak flow is 540 ml/min. Which of the following would you expect to find on investigation?
explanation:
Elevated pH
The answer is Elevated pH (Option A). The clinical picture seen here is consistent with acute hyperventilation syndrome. It leads to a respiratory alkalosis with elevated pH, decreased PaCO 2 (therefore option D is incorrect) and increased PaO 2 (therefore option E is incorrect). Eventually compensation occurs, with initially low levels of serum H + rising due to retention by the kidney (therefore option B is incorrect). Ionised calcium levels fall in hyperventilation (therefore option C is incorrect), which produces symptoms of numbness and tetany in severe cases.

Elevated serum calcium
Elevated serum calcium (Option C) is incorrect. The clinical picture seen here is consistent with acute hyperventilation syndrome. Ionised calcium levels fall in hyperventilation, which produces symptoms of numbness and tetany in severe cases.

stem: A 45-year-old woman known to have systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is referred to the Chest Clinic with a history of worsening dyspnoea. She is on a maintenance dose of 15 mg of prednisolone. She has never smoked. She developed an unproductive cough and dyspnoea three months ago. There is no history of fever, night sweats or weight loss. Her doctor has tried various types of inhalers with no benefit. A peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) diary shows no nocturnal dips. A chest X-ray shows a reticulonodular pattern. Examination is unremarkable apart from the skin changes of SLE. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bronchiolitis obliterans
‘Bronchiolitis obliterans’ is the term used to describe fibrous scarring of the small airways. It is seen following: inhalation of toxic fumes exposure to mineral dust viral infections mycoplasma infection Legionella infection bone marrow, heart–lung or lung transplantation rheumatoid arthritis or SLE penicillamine treatment.

stem: A 36-year-old lorry driver who smokes heavily presents with a 2-day history of cough associated with fever. He also complains of right-sided chest pain on inspiration. On examination he is slightly cyanosed. His temperature is 38°C, respiratory rate 38/min, BP 100/70 mmHg and pulse 130 bpm. He has basal crepitations and dullness to percussion at the right lung base. What is the most important next step in confirming the diagnosis?
explanation:
Chest X-ray
The classic presentation of pneumonia is with cough and fever, with or without sputum production, dyspnoea and pleurisy. Most patients have constitutional symptoms such as malaise, fatigue and asthenia, and many also have gastrointestinal symptoms. Examination of the lung might reveal decreased vesicular breath sounds, localised foci of crepitations, dullness to percussion and sometimes a bronchial wheeze. The chest X-ray is a pivotal test for the confirmation of pneumonia.

Blood cultures
Blood cultures is incorrect. Blood cultures will identify infection within the blood stream and may be suggestive of pneumonia if pneumococcus is cultured. However, blood cultures are not a diagnostic test for pneumonia.

stem: A 36-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with breathlessness on exertion and a non-productive cough. He is an ex-smoker but was otherwise previously well. On assessment, he has a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute; his oxygen saturations are 94% on air and he has upper zone inspiratory crackles. The chest X-ray reveals upper lobe lung fibrosis. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?
options: Connective tissue disease-related interstitial lung disease
explanation:
Langerhans cell histiocytosis
This patient has evidence of upper zone pulmonary fibrosis on chest X-ray, with compatible symptoms and respiratory examination findings. Langerhans cell histiocytosis presents with cough, shortness of breath on exertion, fever and a predominance of fibrotic disease in the mid to upper zones of the lung. Pneumothoraces can occur in a minority of patients. Diagnosis, however, can be made incidentally when a chest X-ray is performed for other reasons. Lung function testing would demonstrate a restrictive pattern.

Asbestosis
Asbestosis is incorrect. Asbestosis would usually result in lower zone fibrosis, and therefore, Langerhans cell histiocytosis is more likely. However, many of these diseases can affect both the upper and lower zones as they progress. The patient’s age also makes this unlikely, given the significant time lag that occurs between exposure and the onset of disease in asbestos-related lung disease.

stem: A 60-year-old smoker is being evaluated for a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG). Which is the best pre-operative screen of pulmonary function for this patient?
options: Ratio of the forced expiratory volume in 1 second to the forced vital capacity
explanation:
Ratio of the forced expiratory volume in 1 second to the forced vital capacity
Pulmonary function tests provide the best pre-operative screen for patients being assessed for coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) because they reflect dynamic measurements of pulmonary function in the patient. The arterial blood gas measurements reflect acid–base disorders, but they do not predict pulmonary complications in the post-operative period.

Arterial Pco2
Arterial Pco2 is incorrect. As described, arterial Pco2 does not allow for prediction of possible pulmonary complications in the post-operative period.

Arterial Po2
Arterial Po2 is incorrect. As described, arterial Po2 does not allow for prediction of possible pulmonary complications in the post-operative period.

stem: A 71-year-old man presents to his GP along with his wife. He has severe problems with sleeping at night, with episodes where he snores, stops breathing, is restless and often disturbs his wife from sleep. During the day his family complain that he often falls asleep watching the television, after his dinner or even whilst talking to his wife. He is a smoker of 20 cigarettes per day, has hypertension and suffered a TIA 3 years earlier. Medication includes ramipril 10 mg, simvastatin 40 mg and aspirin 75 mg. On examination his BMI is 32, his BP is 150/90 mmHg and he has signs of right heart failure. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 140 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.8 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 x 109/l Platelets (PLT) 220 × 109/l 150–400 x 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 140 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Obstructive sleep apnoea This patient is obese, with hypertension and right heart failure. He has signiﬁcant symptoms of nocturnal airway obstruction and daytime sleepiness, and this constellation of symptoms and signs ﬁts with a diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnoea. Management of the condition involves aggressive weight reduction and the use of nocturnal CPAP to relieve nocturnal airway obstruction. Clearly this gentleman should also receive very strong advice to stop smoking and should be advised not to drive. E Narcolepsy Narcolepsy is associated with excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations and sleep paralysis. The snoring and periods of apnoea are not consistent with a diagnosis of narcolepsy. A Central sleep apnoea Central sleep apnoea is usually seen in patients with signiﬁcant neurological impairment, and the fact this patient is a smoker and obese is a much stronger pointer to obstructive sleep apnoea. B Nocturnal epilepsy Nocturnal epilepsy is more likely to be associated with tonic–clonic movements, automatisms or sleep-walking, rather than the clinical picture seen here. D Multiple TIAs There are no focal features to suggest TIAs; the recurrent snoring and cessation of breathing is much more suggestive of obstructive

sleep apnoea.

stem: A 38-year-old school teacher from an inner city primary school comes for review in the Emergency Department. She has a chronic cough, night sweats and has lost weight over the past few weeks. Over the past few days she has begun to suffer increasing occipital headaches and drowsiness. She smokes 15 cigarettes per day. On examination in the Emergency Department she is pyrexial 37.9 °C, her BP is 122/70 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. There are scattered crackles and wheeze on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 12.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 201 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 133 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 105 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Lymphocytosis, opening pressure 24 cm H 2O, CSF protein 1.5 g/l TB PCR Positive Which of the following is the optimal initial drug regimen?
explanation:
Isoniazid, pyrazinamide, rifampicin, ethambutol, prednisolone
NICE guidelines recommend the following: Patients with active meningeal tuberculosis (TB) should be offered: a treatment regimen, initially lasting for 12 months, comprising isoniazid, pyrazinamide, rifampicin and a fourth drug (for example, ethambutol) for the first 2 months, followed by isoniazid and rifampicin for the rest of the treatment period a glucocorticoid at the normal dose range (in adults equivalent to prednisolone 20–40 mg if on rifampicin, otherwise 10–20 mg) with gradual withdrawal of the glucocorticoid considered, starting within 2–3 weeks of initiation.

Amikacin, isoniazid, levofloxacin, rifampicin
Amikacin, isoniazid, levofloxacin, rifampicin is incorrect. Amikacin and levofloxacin are potential second-line agents used for the treatment of resistant TB. They are not used first line. Additionally, given the evidence of meningeal TB, prednisolone would be indicated.

Isoniazid, pyrazinamide, levofloxacin, ethambutol, prednisolone
Isoniazid, pyrazinamide, levofloxacin, ethambutol, prednisolone is incorrect. Levofloxacin is a second-line agent used for the treatment of resistant TB. It is not used first line.

Isoniazid, rifampicin, azithromycin, ethambutol
Isoniazid, rifampicin, azithromycin, ethambutol is incorrect. Azithromycin is a potential second-line agent used for the treatment of resistant TB. It is not used first line. Additionally, given the evidence of meningeal TB, prednisolone would be indicated.

Isoniazid, rifampicin, azithromycin, ethambutol, prednisolone
Isoniazid, rifampicin, azithromycin, ethambutol, prednisolone is incorrect. Azithromycin is a potential second-line agent used for the treatment of resistant TB. It is not used first line.

stem: A 38-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by her husband as she has taken to her bed over the past 48 h with a worsening cough productive of purulent, blood-stained sputum, fevers and shortness of breath, such that she is unable even to walk a few paces. She has no past medical history of note and her only medication is the oral contraceptive pill. Apparently she has been suffering from influenza for a few days before she took to her bed. On examination she is pyrexial 38.9 °C, her BP is 95/50 mmHg and she is tachycardic with a pulse of 105 bpm. There are signs of bilateral lower lobe consolidation. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 134 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count 17.2 × 109/l 4–11 x 10 9/l (WCC) Platelets 203 × 109/l 150–400 x 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bilateral lower lobe consolidation with evidence of Chest X-Ray cavitation Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus leads to pneumonia with cavitation and is recognised to occur after initial influenza infection. In this case IV flucloxacillin would be an appropriate initial therapeutic option, with clarithromycin an alternative in patients who are penicillin allergic. There is increased risk of empyema formation after Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia, if it occurs then thoracic ultrasound with guided drainage may be required.

Haemophilus influenzae
Haemophilus influenzae is incorrect. The influenza mentioned in this case relates to the influenza virus, not the bacteria Haemophilus influenza. Haemophilus influenzae is a cause of community-acquired pneumonia, but it does not usually cause cavitation. The key clue to the infecting organism here is the history of influenza which is associated with Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia.

Klebsiella pneumoniae
Klebsiella pneumoniae is incorrect. Klebsiella pneumoniae can cause caviating pneumonia but usually affects the upper lobes and occurs in immunosuppressed individuals or, classically, alcoholics.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Mycoplasma pneumoniae is incorrect. Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes an atypical pneumonia, often with predominant symptoms being dry cough, headache and malaise. It does not cause cavitatory pneumonia.

Streptococcus pneumoniae
Streptococcus pneumoniae is incorrect. Streptococcus pneumonia is the most common cause of community- acquired pneumonia. It does not usually cause cavitation. It is not associated with preceding influenza infection. A history of a recent/current cold sore would be suggestive of S. pneumoniae pneumonia.

stem: A 33-year-old, HIV-positive man presents for review. He is poorly compliant with antiretroviral therapy and his recent CD4 count is only 90/mm3 blood. He complains of a gradual-onset headache, fever, malaise, night sweats and a cough associated with haemoptysis. He is emaciated. On examination, there is widespread lymphadenopathy, there are crackles and wheeze on auscultation of his chest, and tenderness over the liver edge. Blood testing reveals a normochromic normocytic anaemia and a low white cell count. The urea and creatinine levels are raised and liver function tests are abnormal. Sputum samples reveal acid- and alcohol-fast bacilli (AAFB). Chest X-ray reveals calcified lymph nodes, cavitation and areas of lung fibrosis and hilar retraction. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Disseminated tuberculosis
There is evidence of severe tuberculosis (TB) with extrapulmonary spread. TB meningitis presents with a gradual-onset headache and malaise. If left unrecognised it can progress to sudden-onset stupor or coma and there can be an associated VIth nerve palsy. The abnormal liver function tests suggest TB infection of the liver; skeletal and genitourinary sites can also be affected. Treatment involves at least 12 months of dualantibiotic therapy with rifampicin and Isoniazid With quadrouple therapy for two months at the beginning.

stem: You are asked to see a newly diagnosed asthmatic woman who is 8 weeks’ pregnant. She is not on any treatment at the moment. Her peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) diary shows wide diurnal variations and she also gives a past history of eczema. Which of the following statements is true?
options: A leukotriene-receptor antagonist is the first-line treatment
Inhaled steroids are associated with major congenital deformities
Low-dose inhaled corticosteroids would be considered acceptable
Short-acting β2-agonists are contraindicated during the first trimester
explanation:
Low-dose inhaled corticosteroids would be considered acceptable
In general, the medicines used for asthma are safe during pregnancy, including inhaled low-dose corticosteroids.

A leukotriene-receptor antagonist is the first-line treatment
A leukotriene-receptor antagonist is the first-line treatment is incorrect. Leukotriene-receptor antagonists are not the first-line treatment during pregnancy. However, they can be continued in women who have demonstrated significant improvement in asthma control with these agents prior to their pregnancy.

Short-acting β2-agonists are contraindicated during the first trimester
Short-acting β2-agonists are contraindicated during the first trimester is incorrect. Short-acting β2-agonists are not contraindicated in any stage of pregnancy.

stem: An obese man with a history of hypertension presented with history of daytime sleepiness that can come on suddenly, disturbed night sleep and associated vivid dreams. His wife says that he is restless at night and snores almost all the time. He is overweight and has a collar size of 18.5. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Obstructive sleep apnoea
Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) occurs most commonly in overweight middle-aged men and is said to affect around 1–2% of the population. Signs of OSA include loud snoring, daytime sleepiness, unrefreshing sleep, restless sleep, morning headaches, nocturnal choking and reduced libido. Predisposing factors include: Pharyngeal encroachment (e.g. due to obesity, acromegaly, enlarged tonsils) Nasal obstruction (due to nasal deformities, rhinitis, polyps, adenoids) The use of respiratory depressant drugs (e.g. alcohol, sedatives, strong analgesics) Chronic OSA eventually leads to pulmonary hypertension and systemic hypertension, and eventually, if untreated, right heart failure. The answer represents a balance; however, given his neck size, OSA is much more likely than narcolepsy.

stem: A 23-year-old woman who is 34 weeks’ pregnant is admitted to the Emergency Department with shortness of breath, cough and wheeze. She is known to have moderate asthma and normally takes fluticasone 750 µg salmeterol twice a day and salbutamol as needed. Her peak flow is usually 450 l/min. She has been deteriorating over the past 3 days despite increasing her fluticasone and starting 40 mg oral prednisolone daily. She is now unable to speak in sentences, her peak flow is less than 150 l/min and her heart rate is 130 bpm. Her oxygen saturations are 96% and you hear a widespread wheeze on examination. Her Po2 is 12 kPa and her Pco2 is 4.5 kPa. She has been given high-flow oxygen, repeated nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium bromide, and IV magnesium is commenced. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: ITU review with reference to possible intubation and ventilation
Liaise with the obstetricians regarding an emergency caesarian section
explanation:
ITU review with reference to possible intubation and ventilation
She has features of acute severe asthma (unable to talk in sentences, PEFR < 33% and normocapnia) and intubation and ventilation should be considered at this point.

Intravenous aminophylline
Intravenous aminophylline is incorrect. Although intravenous aminophylline is still mentioned as part of the BTS asthma guidelines, it is no longer in mainstream use and a critical care review would be a more appropriate next step.

stem: Which of the following is most likely to prevent curative surgery for lung carcinoma?
options: Forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1) of 1.6 L
Local invasion by primary tumour through the chest wall
Mediastinal lymph nodes enlarged on computed tomography (CT)
explanation:
Malignant pleural effusions
A malignant pleural effusion usually implies widely disseminated disease and any treatment is therefore often palliative.

Forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1) of 1.6 L
A forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1) of over 1.6 L suggests that the patient has sufficient lung function to undergo an operation of this nature, but many of these patients will have considerable cardiorespiratory co- morbidity and a rigorous preoperative assessment is always required.

Hypercalcaemia
Hypercalcaemia could be due to invasion of bone by the tumour, but this is not necessarily so; malignant cells in the lung tumour can produce humoral mediators which lead to an increase in the serum calcium level.

stem: A 67-year-old retired man has been complaining of a 6-month history of increasing shortness of breath, dull right-sided chest pain, loss of appetite and night sweats. He worked all his life in the ship-building industry, where he was exposed to asbestos. He has never smoked in his life. On examination he is slightly cyanosed but there is no clubbing. Examination of the lungs reveals dullness to percussion and reduced air entry at the right base. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Malignant mesothelioma
Malignant mesothelioma arising from the pleura was first recognised in the 1950s, and during the 1960s much evidence accumulated indicating a strong link between the condition and exposure to asbestos. The risk is a function of the concentration of fibres and duration of exposure. Exposure is greatest in those involved in mining or quarrying the material, and in people who handle the raw fibres. Many workers engaged in the ship-building industry during the 1940s and 1950s were exposed to asbestos, and more recently it has been in widespread use in the building industry. It is rare for mesotheliomas to develop within 20 years of exposure and most patients were initially exposed 30 or more years before clinical presentation. In the United Kingdom, although the risk was first recognised in the 1960s, it was not until the mid-1970s that there was a significant reduction in exposure to asbestos. The age of presentation is usually between 50 and 70 years, although the incidence is increasing in older patients. There is a male predominance, reflecting the greater likelihood of previous occupational exposure, which should be sought with a careful lifetime occupational history.

stem: A 29-year-old woman noticed shortness of breath and a dry cough while jogging last winter. She now wakes up twice a week at 0400 h with a troublesome cough. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Asthma
The symptoms of asthma are non-specific: shortness of breath, wheezing, chest tightness and cough. These are manifestations of airway narrowing (which is usually variable in severity over short periods, but can be persistent) and of airway hyper-responsiveness. Asthma as the cause of these symptoms is suggested by the variability in their severity and distinguished by their periodicity (such as daily, weekly, monthly or seasonal), their provocation by specific (such as an allergen) and non-specific stimuli and their reversibility with bronchodilators or corticosteroids. Patients with asthma can be categorised, at any one time, by whether their symptoms are intermittent or persistent, and by the severity of their symptoms and underlying airway narrowing measured by lung function tests (even people with normally mild asthma can develop severe asthma). Mild, intermittent asthma – symptoms occur less than weekly, with normal or near-normal lung function between episodes. Mild persistent asthma – symptoms occur more than weekly but less than daily, with normal or near- normal lung function between episodes. Moderate persistent asthma – symptoms occur daily, with mild to moderate variable airflow limitation.

stem: A 30-year-old lorry driver presents to the clinic. He is obese, with a body mass index (BMI) of 40 kg/m 2 and has been having trouble staying awake at the wheel. His wife says that he has always snored and she has often heard him stop breathing. His baseline oxygen saturation in clinic is 97%. His overnight sleep study shows a 4% oxygen dip rate of 20/hour, and his Epworth Sleepiness Score is 19. What would be the most appropriate initial management for him?
options: Start BiPAP (bilevel positive airways pressure ventilation)
Start CPAP (continuous positive airways pressure ventilation)
explanation:
Start CPAP (continuous positive airways pressure ventilation)
This man has moderate obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA), which is making him sleepy (defined by an Epworth Sleepiness Score of 10 or above). As he is a lorry driver, he cannot drive heavy-goods vehicles until this is treated. The quickest and most effective treatment for severe OSA syndrome is CPAP (continuous positive pressure airways ventilation), which acts as a splint to keep the airway open, leading to a normal night’s sleep.

Mandibular advancement device
Mandibular advancement device is incorrect. Mandibular advancement devices are effective for treating milder OSA – they hold the lower jaw in a fixed position during the night.

stem: A 67-year-old retired boilermaker is referred to the Respiratory Clinic complaining of shortness of breath. He also has a persistent dry cough which he tells you is non-productive of sputum. His GP diagnosed him with asthma and prescribed steroid and salbutamol inhalers, but he tells you this seems to have made little difference to his symptoms. On examination, he looks tired, his body mass index (BMI) is 23 kg/m2, his pulse is 85 bpm and his blood pressure is 142/84 mmHg. His heart sounds are normal. Respiratory examination reveals end-expiratory crackles to the mid-zones on both sides. He is also clubbed. Investigation: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 134 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 301 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Forced Expiratory Volume in the 1 st second (FEV 1) 60% predicted Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) 70% predicted The chest X-ray shows calcified pleural plaques and areas of interstitial fibrosis. Which of the following is the next best step to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
High-resolution computed tomography
There is strong evidence from the history, clinical examination and investigations here that this patient could have asbestosis. We are given the history of his previous occupation as a boilermaker, meaning that asbestos exposure is likely to be an important feature. High-resolution computed tomography is the most useful investigation, allowing clear delineation of pleural plaques and demonstration of pulmonary fibrosis.

Bronchoalveolar lavage
Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) is incorrect. Asbestos bodies detected in BAL fluid would point towards the diagnosis of asbestosis. However, asbestos bodies alone are not diagnostic for disease, because occasionally they are found in people without known exposure.

Carbon monoxide transfer factor
Carbon monoxide transfer factor (Tlco) is incorrect. Tlco would be likely to be reduced, but a reduced Tlco is not sufficiently discriminatory to give the exact diagnosis here.

Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme
Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) is incorrect. Serum ACE can be useful if sarcoidosis is suspected but there are no real pointers to this diagnosis here.

stem: A 30-year-old man from Nigeria descent has been complaining of cough, fever and weight loss. The chest X-ray shows a large upper lobe lesion and the sputum shows acid-fast bacilli that are confirmed to be Mycobacterium tuberculosis by polymerase chain reaction. Drug therapy with isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide is initiated. Over the next four weeks the disease is found to be continuing to progress. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Infection with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis
Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) is defined as resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid, with or without resistance to other anti-TB drugs. Higher levels of resistance occur in ethnic minority groups with isoniazid resistance occurring in 4–6% of such patients. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) positivity, independent of ethnic group, is also a marker for increased drug resistance. Treatment is complex and should only be carried out by physicians with substantial experience in managing complex resistant cases and only in hospitals with appropriate isolation facilities. Patients need to be fully compliant with treatment to prevent further drug resistance. Treatment should start with five or more drugs to which the organism is, or is likely to be, susceptible and should continue until sputum cultures become negative. Drug treatment then has to be continued with at least three drugs to which the organism is susceptible on in vitro testing for a minimum of a further nine months and

stem: An 81-year-old woman who had consulted her GP with symptoms of flu 2 weeks earlier now presents to the Emergency Department. For the past few days she has had increasing cough, associated with purulent sputum and haemoptysis. Her daughter visited and noticed that she had become acutely confused and arranged an ambulance. On arrival to the department she is found to be agitated, with a respiratory rate of 35/min. Blood gases reveal that she is hypoxic, her white blood cell count is 20 × 10 9/l, predominantly neutrophils. Her creatinine concentration is 250 µmol/l. Chest X-ray reveals patchy areas of consolidation, with necrosis and empyema formation. What diagnosis best fits this clinical picture?
explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia
In general, staphylococcal pneumonia only occurs after a preceding viral illness. Patchy areas of consolidation occur that eventually break down into abscesses. Pneumothorax, pleural effusion and empyema are common in staphylococcal pneumonia. Clinical features of severe pneumonia include a respiratory rate > 30/min, diastolic blood pressure < 60 mmHg, confusion, involvement of more than one lobe, low albumin concentration, white cell count > 20 × 10 9/l or less than 1 × 10 9/l, and renal dysfunction. Treatment: fulminant staphylococcal pneumonia, as in this case, carries a high mortality. Standard therapy would be intravenous cefuroxime and clarithromycin, with added flucloxacillin for suspected Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia.

stem: A 55-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department. He is known to have advanced small-cell lung cancer, which has proved refractory to chemotherapy. On this occasion he has severe pain in the right upper quadrant of his abdomen. Medication includes codeine phosphate, and paracetamol for pain relief. Examination reveals a BP of 155/84 mmHg; he is in pain. He has an enlarged painful liver on abdominal palpation. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 101 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 143 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 189 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) 380 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Alkaline Phosphatase 720 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 45 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Three large metastases with USS liver surrounding oedema Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Oral dexamethasone
The most likely cause of the pain seen here is liver capsule pain. Liver enzymes are significantly deranged and there is evidence of oedema surrounding large metastases seen on USS. Dexamethasone will reduce oedema and significantly impact on pain, although of course this is a short-term fix. Studies involving targeted radiotherapy suggest pain can be improved in 80% of cases, and this would be the obvious next step.

Oral lorazepam
Oral lorazepam is incorrect. Lorazapam, a benzodiazepine, is not indicated here. Its main uses are in the treatment of anxiety, insomnia and to treat status epilepticus.

Oral morphine
Oral morphine is incorrect. Opioids are excellent analgesics but the best treatment is dexamethasone, which will treat the underlying cause of the pain.

stem: Which one of the following does not increase the risk of death in patients with severe pneumonia?
options: Atrial fibrillation with fast ventricular response
explanation:
Age 49 years
An age of 49 would not be associated with an increased risk of mortality from pneumonia. The risk factors for increased mortality in severe pneumonia are: Age over 60 years Tachypnoea (respiratory rate > 30/min) Underlying disease Confusion Multilobular involvement Serum albumin < 35 g/l Hypoxia (Pao2 < 8 kPa) Leucocytosis > 20 × 10 9/l Bacteraemia Leukopaenia is also associated with a higher rate of mortality in pneumonia. The CURB-65 severity scores for community-acquired pneumonia are:

stem: Which one of the following statements about cystic fibrosis (CF) is true?
options: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a recognised complication, occurring in 15% of adult CF
Heterozygotes generally have clinically significant disease
Neonatal screening for CF results in a better survival rate and reduced decline in lung function
Reduced body mass index is an absolute contraindication for heart-lung transplantation
