The controlled intake of high-calorie food is the first line of management for patients with CF-related
explanation:
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a recognised complication, occurring in 15% of adult CF
patients The increasing incidence of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is a recognised phenomenon. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is encountered in 1 in 6 adult CF patients. Manifestations of ABPA include asthma symptoms, flitting opacities on the chest X-ray, increased eosinophil count, and hyper- reactivity to the skin prick test and increased specific plasma IgE. The main treatment is high-dose corticosteroids initially, with a smaller maintenance dose. The duration of treatment ranges from a few months to few years. Antifungal agents may be used to allow a reduction in corticosteroid dose.

The controlled intake of high-calorie food is the first line of management for patients with CF-related
diabetes The controlled intake of high-calorie food is the first line of management for patients with CF-related diabetes is incorrect. Diabetes is now seen in almost 10% of CF patients over the age of 20 years, the main manifestations being weight loss, repeated respiratory infections and decline in lung function. The treatment of choice is subcutaneous insulin therapy. Calorie intake should not be restricted in CF patients, who areChat prone withto malnutrition due to their pancreatic insufficiency.

stem: A 60-year-old lady is seen every 6 months in the Chest Clinic for follow-up for her idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Despite a trial of immunosuppression, her symptoms continue to deteriorate. You organise a repeat set of pulmonary function tests. Which one of the results below would best fit this patient? (The options expressed as % predicted values.) FEV 1 Volume of gas expired in first second of forced expiration FVC Total volume of gas expired on forced expiration (forced vital capacity) VA Alveolar volume Kco Transfer coefficient
explanation:
FEV1 60, FVC 65 (ratio 90%), Va 60, Kco 60
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) typically shows a restrictive lung function pattern with a reduced gas transfer factor. The underlying parenchymal fibrosis means that these patients’ lungs have very poor compliance, but high elastic recoil. Static lung volumes therefore are very low. Both the forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1) and the forced vital capacity (FVC) are reduced below predicted values, but because of this high elastic recoil most forced expiratory volume will be expelled in the first second compared to full forced expiration – which leads to a relatively high FEV 1/FVC ratio.

stem: A 46-year-old man with a history of asthma, well controlled with regular low-dose Seretide, presents with a cough productive of purulent, blood-stained sputum. On examination his temperature is 38.6 °C, pulse is 90/min and regular; there is a cluster of cold sores on his upper lip. Auscultation reveals left-sided consolidation. Which of the following causes of lower respiratory tract infection is most likely to be associated with herpes labialis?
explanation:
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Streptococcus pneumoniae is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia and is characteristically associated with herpes labialis. In this case the majority of standard hospital protocols recommend dual therapy with a combination of co- amoxiclav and clarithromycin as the intervention of choice.

Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is incorrect. Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia is more likely to follow a viral respiratory tract infection such as influenza, and we are given no history of a prodromal viral illness here.

stem: You review a 67-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). He has smoked 30 cigarettes per day for the past 40 years. Pulmonary function tests indicate that he has a predominantly emphysematous picture. Which of the following is the most important factor in airflow limitation in severe emphysema?
explanation:
Loss of elastic recoil
Emphysema is characterised by focal destruction limited to the air spaces distal to terminal bronchioles. When the disease is severe, it is loss of elastic recoil that drives airflow limitation. Although airflow limitation is virtually irreversible, the small inflammatory component can respond to high-dose inhaled corticosteroids.

Large-airways obstruction
Large-airways obstruction is incorrect. Large-airways obstruction is a feature of both chronic bronchitis and asthma.

Mucus plugging
Mucus plugging is incorrect. Mucus plugging is most associated with acute asthma.

stem: A 61-year-old plumber is referred to the Respiratory Clinic after being reviewed in the Emergency Department following a fall. He had extensive bruising to the left lower chest. Although no fracture was identified on chest X-ray, a number of calcified pleural plaques were identified. He is a non-smoker and has no signicant past medical history. He does report progressive shortness of breath on exercise over the past 6 months. On examination his BP is 144/90 mmHg; pulse is 85/min and regular. There are scattered crackles on auscultation of the chest, more marked at both bases. Lung function testing revealed evidence of a restrictive defect. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
High resolution CT chest
This patient has likely exposure to asbestos because of his job working as a plumber, and pleural plaques seen on CXR are most likely to be the result of asbestos-related lung disease. The signs on clinical examination and lung function testing indicating a restrictive defect are also consistent with the diagnosis. High resolution CT chest is the next logical step; potential changes not including pleural plaques include: subpleural linear densities parallel to the pleura basilar and dorsal lung parenchymal fibrosis coarse parenchymal bands (up to 5 cm in length), often contiguous with the pleura coarse honeycombing in advanced disease.

stem: In which of the following emergency medical presentations is non-invasive ventilation an established therapy in the presence of respiratory acidosis?
options: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with respiratory acidosis
explanation:
Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with respiratory acidosis
Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) is currently being evaluated in a number of emergency situations. The best evidence relates to exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. In particular, this type of therapy is effective in patients with decompensated type II respiratory failure. Physiological responses (heart rate, respiratory rate and arterial blood gases) improve more quickly with NIV in these patients compared with standard treatment. Intubation is also less frequently required.

Acute asthma
Acute asthma is incorrect. The correct management for acute asthma with respiratory acidosis Chatiswith oxygen, steroids, nebulised bronchodilators, intravenous magnesium alongside urgent critical care/anaesthetic for consideration of intubation and invasive ventilation.

Pulmonary oedema with hypertension
Pulmonary oedema with hypertension is incorrect. NIV is part of a range of therapies for pulmonary oedema, but more usually where pulmonary oedema co-exists with hypertension, diuretics and measures to control blood pressure are normally attempted first.

stem: A 64-year-old demolition worker presents to his GP with a severe, dull, right-sided chest pain. He first noticed it some months ago and he is now having particular problems with shortness of breath. Apparently he was given an asthma inhaler for shortness of breath around 2 years earlier. On examination he appears to have a right- sided pleural effusion and has finger clubbing. He admits to having been exposed to asbestos. On further questioning he says that his brother, who worked with him, died of ‘some sort of lung cancer’ around 2 years ago. X-ray confirms a right pleural effusion with evidence of pleural plaques elsewhere. What diagnosis would fit best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Mesothelioma
The clue to the answer here is the occupation, and the fact that a co-worker has already died of a cancer related to the chest. A restrictive lung defect, evidence of asbestosis, and now a painful pleural effusion would fit best with a diagnosis of mesothelioma. Diagnosis is confirmed by pleural biopsy. The median survival after diagnosis ranges from 12 to 21 months depending on staging. The cancer is poorly responsive to any form of intervention, however, and it is notable that a significant number of patients survive far less than 2 years.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. Rheumatoid arthritis can be associated with pleural effusions but there is no mention of any joint symptoms, and the presence of finger clubbing, pleural plaques andChatprevious with asbestos exposure makes mesothelioma the most likely diagnosis.

stem: A 43-year-old woman has a pleural effusion and evidence of fibrosis on her chest X-ray. She has noticed a facial rash on exposure to sun that has worsened over the past few months. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Systemic lupus erythematosus
Direct pulmonary involvement in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) occurs in 30% (pleuropericarditis, atelectasis, pneumonitis, raised hemidiaphragms and pulmonary fibrosis). An autoimmune screen, with antinuclear antibody (ANA) and anti-dsDNA antibodies, might be useful to confirm the diagnosis.

Actinomycosis
Actinomycosis is incorrect. Actinomycosis is a chronic granulomatous disorder caused by a Gram-positive anaerobe. It is associated with the formation of multiple abscesses and sinuses. When the pulmonary tract is Chata with involved, patients will have a dry or productive cough +/- haemoptysis. Chest X-ray may show poorly defined mass lesion +/- pleural involvement.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is incorrect. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotising vasculitis characterised by granulomas in the upper and lower respiratory tracts and a focal glomerulonephritis.

stem: A 69-year-old former coal-miner is referred to you by the on-call team. There is a smoking history and he has been managed by his GP for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). He has been admitted with dyspnoea that is now so bad that he is unable to manage at home and cannot walk from the chair to the bathroom. He has a cough that is productive of black sputum. Lung function tests show a mixed restrictive and obstructive picture. A chest X-ray shows marked changes with massive fibrotic masses, predominantly in the upper lobes. There are also changes consistent with lung destruction and emphysema. His rheumatoid factor is positive. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Progressive massive fibrosis
Progressive massive fibrosis (PMF) is associated with fibrotic masses in the apices, sometimes up to 10 cm in diameter. There are also emphysematous changes. There is a mixed obstructive and restrictive lung defect with reduced transfer factor. Rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody are often positive. There is usually a history of dust inhalation (eg coal dust), and PMF can progress rapidly, even in the absence of further dust exposure, leading to respiratory failure and eventually death. Category 2 pneumoconiosis progresses to PMF in around 7% of cases. The rate of progression of category 3 pneumoconiosis is much higher, at around 30%. The 0–3 classification is defined by the International Labour Organisation and reflects an increasing density of small opacities on the chest radiograph.

stem: A 54-year-old man who has moved to the UK from Romania has lost 4 kg in weight over the past 4 months. He has a chronic cough and smokes 20 cigarettes per day. Examination reveals a BP of 122/72 mmHg, pulse is 80/min and regular; he is apyrexial. There is no significant lymphadenopathy. Auscultation of the chest reveals bilateral wheeze. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 x 10 9/l Platelets 203 × 10 9/l 150–400 x 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 135 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 92 mm/1 st hour 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Chest X-Ray Evidence of right lateral pleural thickening Quantiferon gamma test positive Which of the following is the most appropriate way to confirm a diagnosis of pleural tuberculosis?
explanation:
Pleural biopsy microscopy and culture
Pleural biopsy should take place under thoracoscopic or radiological guidance to ensure that the abnormal area seen on chest X-ray is biopsied, as the yield from blind biopsy is much lower. Microscopy of a smear may yield mycobacteria, or they may only be seen following culture.

Broncho-alveolar lavage
Broncho-alveolar lavage is incorrect. The yields from broncho-alveolar lavage (BAL), pleural aspiration and sputum microscopy are all much lower than guided pleural biopsy.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR
Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR is incorrect. Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR may be positive, although it would not localise the site of tuberculosis infection.

Pleural aspirate microscopy and culture
Pleural aspirate microscopy and culture is incorrect. The yields from broncho-alveolar lavage (BAL), pleural aspiration and sputum microscopy are all much lower than guided pleural biopsy.

Sputum microscopy and culture
Sputum microscopy and culture is incorrect. The yields from broncho-alveolar lavage (BAL), pleural aspiration and sputum microscopy are all much lower than guided pleural biopsy.

stem: A 32-year-old man with a 2-year history of asthma diagnosed and managed by his GP now presents with weight loss, abdominal pain, diarrhoea and petechial skin changes. During the past week he has become increasingly lethargic with associated feelings of nausea. Other past history of note includes an episode of foot drop, which occurred 3 months ago. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 110 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 10.0 × 10 9/l (raised eosinophils) 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 190 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 234 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 71 mm in 1 hour 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Rheumatoid factor Positive The chest X-ray shows bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and urinalysis shows blood ++ and protein ++. Which of the following is the most likely positive antibody finding in this case?
explanation:
Antimyeloperoxidase antibody
The clinical picture seen here is very suggestive of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which is commonly associated with antimyeloperoxidase antibodies. A raised eosinophil count is seen in over 90% of patients with advanced disease. Skin biopsy reveals small-vessel arteriopathy with granuloma formation and is the diagnostic investigation of choice. High-dose methylprednisolone, with or without cyclophosphamide, is the treatment of choice for this condition.

Anticardiolipin antibody
Anticardiolipin antibody is incorrect. Anticardiolipin antibody is associated with antiphospholid syndrome and may be found in patients with systemic lupus erythromatosus.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibody
Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibody is incorrect. Anti-GBM antibody is associated with Goodpasture’s syndrome.

Antimitochondrial antibody
Antimitochondrial antibody is incorrect. Antimitochondrial antibodies are associated with primary biliary cholangitis.

Cytoplasmic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (cANCA)
Cytoplasmic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (cANCA) is incorrect. cANCA is most associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis which given the clinical picture here is unlikely.

stem: You review a 48-year-old man in the Respiratory Clinic. He is diagnosed with tuberculosis and you want to start quadruple anti-tuberculous therapy. He is very concerned about the potential side effects of therapy. Previous history of note includes abnormal liver function tests and a history of alcohol abuse; most recently he has been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. Recent ALT was 65 U/l, creatinine 102 µmol/l and a liver biopsy has shown early hepatic ﬁbrosis. Which of the following is important to bear in mind when managing his anti-tuberculous therapy?
explanation:
C Pyrazinamide should not be given Drug-induced hepatitis associated with anti-tuberculous therapy can be fatal; for this reason pyrazinamide should not be used in patients with known chronic liver disease, even if it is thought to be

stable. Baseline and regular monitoring of liver function should be undertaken in patients on anti-tuberculous therapy, and where there is a history of chronic liver disease it is advised that this is weekly for the ﬁrst two weeks and then two- weekly thereafter. E Rifampicin should not be given Rifampicin should only be avoided where there is decompensated liver disease and in those patients taking sulphonylureas where it may reduce the effectiveness of these agents. A Ethambutol should not be given Ethambutol can accumulate in patients with chronic kidney disease, leading to optic neuropathy, and therefore should be given at a lower dose. The creatinine of 102 µmol/l seen here means that dose adjustment is not required. B Isoniazid should not be given In stable liver disease it is acceptable to give up to two drugs which may have hepatotoxicity, usually isoniazid and rifampicin only. D Pyridoxine should not be given Pyridoxine should be given in addition to isoniazid in those with renal impairment, to prevent peripheral neuropathy.

stem: A 63-year-old woman who is a lifelong smoker is found to have non-small-cell lung cancer. Which of the symptoms below is most likely to be her presenting symptom?
explanation:
Cough
Non-small-cell lung cancer can present in a number of different ways. The most common presentation is cough (45%) followed by breathlessness (37%). Chest pain and haemoptysis occur in about a third of patients; anorexia and weight loss affect about a fifth; and 3% experience dysphagia. About 15% of patients are asymptomatic, their lung cancer being detected on a routine chest X-ray being performed for another reason.

Breathlessness
Breathlessness is incorrect. Cough is the most common presentation affecting 45% of patients compared to 37% of patients for breathlessness.

Chest wall pain
Chest wall pain is incorrect. Cough is the most common presentation affecting 45% of patients compared to 33% of patients for chest pain.

stem: A 48-year-old woman is admitted with a 2-day history of fever with rigors and breathlessness. On examination, she looks extremely unwell and is confused and cyanosed. She has a respiratory rate of 36/min and a systolic blood pressure of 86 mmHg. There is dullness on percussion and bronchial breathing at her right base. The chest X-ray reveals consolidation. Which of the following would be the most appropriate antibiotic regimen to use?
explanation:
Intravenous co-amoxiclav and intravenous clarithromycin
This woman has severe pneumonia as defined by the British Thoracic Society (BTS) guidelines, which requires the presence any two of the following features: Confusion Urea > 7 mmol/l Respiratory rate > 30/min Hypotension (systolic BP < 90 mmHg, diastolic BP < 60 mmHg) Appropriate treatment (as recommended by BTS) is with intravenous antimicrobials: Co-amoxiclav 1.2 g three times daily or cefuroxime 1.5 g three times daily or cefotaxime 1 g three times daily or ceftriaxone 2 g once daily

stem: A 73-year-old man with severe COPD managed with high-dose combination steroid and long-acting beta- agonist (LABA) inhaler is admitted to the Emergency Room. He has suffered increasing shortness of breath and a worsening cough over the past few days and is now completely unable to get his breath. On examination he is pyrexial (38.2 °C) and there are chest signs consistent with both right-sided consolidation and pulmonary oedema. He looks tired and his respiratory rate has fallen to 13/min. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 131 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 10.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 x 109/l Platelets (PLT) 295 × 109/l 150–400 x 109/l Sodium (Na+) 134 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 128 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 52 mg/l < 10 mg/l CXR Right-sided consolidation, with evidence of pulmonary oedema Blood gases on controlled O2 via a 40% venturi reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values pH 7.28 7.35–7.45 pO2 7.8 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa pCO2 7.1 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage his O2 replacement?
options: Decrease inspired pO2 to 28% by mask
Increase inspired O2 to 60% by mask
explanation: D BiPAP This patient has evidence of both LVF and right-sided pneumonia, a long history of COPD and is beginning to tire. The acidosis seen here can drive worsening respiratory muscle weakness, and risks increasing CO2 retention further. BiPAP can reverse acidosis and signiﬁcantly reduces progression to intubation and ventilation. C Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) BiPAP reduces the work of breathing during inspiration more than CPAP, and hence confers a potential advantage in COPD versus CPAP alone. A Continue 40% O2 by mask Acidosis and CO2 retention is potentially progressive, and continuing the status quo here with respect to O2 replacement is considered inadequate. B Decrease inspired pO2 to 28% by mask This will drive hypoxia in addition to CO2 retention, putting the patient at risk of cardiac rhythm disturbance and worsening pulmonary oedema. E Increase inspired O2 to 60% by mask Once acidosis is established, respiratory muscle weakness is progressive; increasing inspired O2 won’t reverse this and will at best lead to a minor, short-term incremental improvement in oxygenation.

stem: A 74-year-old man presents to the clinic complaining of increased shortness of breath. He has smoked 40 cigarettes per day for the past 30 years. Medications include diclofenac and paracetamol for joint pain. He comes to the clinic with a chest X-ray from his GP which shows a spiculated left hilar mass. What would the classical respiratory findings over the abnormal area be?
explanation:
Whispering pectoriloquy
Whispering pectoriloquy is a sign of consolidation. It is likely here because of the tumour and the locally trapped secretions. It is very likely this man has bronchial carcinoma, and an endobronchial biopsy may be the easiest way to obtain a histological diagnosis.

Decreased breath sounds
Decreased breath sounds is incorrect. Decreased breath sounds are associated with conditions such as pneumothorax and pleural effusion.

Hyper-resonance
Hyper-resonance is incorrect. Hyper-resonance is associated with pneumothoraces.

stem: A 39-year-old woman from Zimbabwe presents to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of increasing shortness of breath and dry cough. She has a 1-day history of sudden onset of sharp chest pain which is worse on coughing, movement and deep inspiration. She describes having had night sweats and a poor appetite for 2 months. Her weight has decreased by about 5 kg. She has a past medical history of genital herpes and depression. She is married and has two children who live in Zimbabwe. She moved to England 2 years ago and has not travelled since. She is a smoker of 20/day and drinks little alcohol. On examination, she looked unwell. Observations: temperature 38.3 °C, BP 108/72 mmHg, pulse 120/min, regular, respiratory rate 30/min. Auscultation of her chest revealed inspiratory crackles bibasally. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 102 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 6.4 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Lymphocytes 1.0 × 109/l 1.5 - 4.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 439 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 141 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 75 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l MCV 79 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ CRP 73 mg/l < 10 mg/l Urea 5.0 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Glucose 5.7 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Blood gases on 80% oxygen: pH 7.46 PCO2 3.44 kPa PO2 10.77 kPa Bicarbonate 17.6 mmol/l Base excess –3.5 Her chest X-ray is shown below. What is the most likely underlying cause?
explanation:
B HIV

For the purpose of the exam, people who have lived abroad (especially Africa and South America), businessmen who work abroad, men who have sex with men (MSM) and intravenous drug users, are more likely to have HIV. This lady has HIV – the history of living in Zimbabwe and the low lymphocyte count are the clues. Pneumocystis jirovecii is the most common opportunistic infection to cause pneumonia in AIDS – especially when the CD4 count is <200/mm3. It accounts for about 50% of cases of pneumonia in AIDS and 40% of all AIDS-deﬁning illnesses. Patients usually present with a fever, dry cough and breathlessness. They are usually hypoxic and desaturate on exercise. In P. jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) the chest X-ray usually shows bilateral interstitial shadowing and cysts in the mid and lower zones. However, the CXR may be normal. Pneumothorax (because the cysts rupture) may be present in up to 10%. Diagnosis is now usually made by PCR of sputum or BAL ﬂuid. Other diagnostic methods include staining induced sputum or BAL with indirect immunoﬂuorescence with monoclonal antibodies. Treatment is with high-ﬂow oxygen and high-dose co-trimoxazole. Prednisolone should be added in severe cases (PO2 <9.5 kPa). C Bronchiectasis The patient has a non-productive cough and gives an acute history of pulmonary infection, making bronchiectasis unlikely. A Lymphoma Given the patient is from sub-Saharan Africa and is presenting with a history suggestive of disseminated lung infection HIV is more a likely cause than lymphoma for the night sweats and weight loss. D Sarcoid This patient presents with a history of pulmonary infection with fever, sweats and raised CRP. Sarcoidosis would be expected to present with chronic respiratory symptoms including a dry cough, and other features such as erythema nodosum. E Common variable immune deﬁciency This condition is present from birth and there would be a history of previous recurrent infections since childhood.

stem: You are asked to review a 74-year-old man on the ward who was admitted four days earlier with a right lower- lobe pneumonia. He has a history of smoking ten cigarettes per day, and is treated with ramipril, furosemide and aspirin for a history of ischaemic heart disease with episodes of left ventricular failure. On examination his temperature is 37.4 °C (down from 38.8 °C on admission), his blood pressure is 142/82 mmHg; pulse is 70 bpm and regular. There are residual crackles at the right base, but his fluid balance appears to be correct. He is confused; according to nursing staff they have to provide him with most of his care, and he has been aggressive on occasions. Investigation: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 124 g/l 135–175 g/l 10.9 × 10 9/l (down from 13.1 × 10 9/l White Cell Count (WCC) 4–11 × 10 9/l on admission) Platelets 233 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 129 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urinalysis is negative for blood and protein. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
explanation:
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
This patient has a resolving pneumonia, yet his sodium remains low at 129 mmol/l. Given that he is not in positive fluid balance as judged by clinical examination, syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) is the most likely diagnosis. In the first instance, he should be managed with fluid restriction, at around 1200 ml/ day. If he fails to respond to fluid restriction, demeclocycline induces nephrogenic diabetes and corrects serum sodium over the course of a few days. He will require a 6-week repeat chest film to determine whether any underlying consolidation has resolved.

Cardiac failure
Cardiac failure is incorrect. The history states his fluid balance is correct and that crackles are heard on auscultation; thus cardiac failure is unlikely.

Multi-infarct dementia
Multi-infarct dementia is incorrect. This gentleman’s confusion and aggression is almost certainly related to his acute infection and/or hyopnatraemia. There is no history of previous stroke or transient ischaemic attacks and his blood pressure and pulse are normal, making multi-infarct dementia unlikely.

Normal-pressure hydrocephalus
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus is incorrect. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus occurs as a consequence of a build-up of cerebrospinal fluid. Affected patients classically have an abnormal gait, dementia and urinary incontinence. The confusion and aggression described in this case is likely acute secondary to infection and/or hyopnatraemia and there are no other features in this case to suggest a diagnosis of normal-pressure hydrocephalus.

Undiagnosed cerebral secondary malignancy
Undiagnosed cerebral secondary malignancy is incorrect. There is nothing mentioned in this case alluding to the presence of a malignancy. Brain metastases can certainly cause confusion and aggression, but there is a more likely explanation here, namely acute infection and hyponatraemia.

stem: A 46-year-old man presents with breathlessness, orthopnoea and a dry cough. He has a BMI of 31, and underwent a coronary artery bypass graft 6 months ago. On examination his BP is 145/84 mmHg; pulse is 85/min and regular. There is occasional wheeze on auscultation of his chest, but nil else of note. Lung function tests reveal the following: FEV1 75% predicted FVC standing 80% predicted FVC supine 48% predicted TLCO 85% predicted What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Diaphragmatic palsy
Phrenic nerve injury leading to diaphragmatic palsy is usually temporary in most cases, but may not resolve in others, and given that the supine FVC is significantly reduced, it is the most likely diagnosis here.

COPD
COPD is incorrect. The FEV 1/FVC is essentially normal, ruling out COPD.

stem: A 60-year-old patient was referred with a 1-year history of persistent cough productive of mucopurulent sputum throughout the year. He has been treated by his GP for recurrent chest infections. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bronchiectasis
Bronchiectasis should be suspected when there is a history of persistent cough productive of mucopurulent or purulent sputum throughout the year. Patients have frequently been treated for recurrent chest infections and labelled as ‘bronchitic’, often despite the absence of a history of smoking. Those presenting as adults often recall a ‘chesty cough’ or ‘wheezy bronchitis’ associated with upper respiratory tract infections in childhood, followed by complete resolution of symptoms in their teens and early adult life, before the symptoms return after a viral trigger. Patients might produce mucoid sputum early in their disease, developing purulent sputum when they suffer an exacerbation associated with a viral upper respiratory tract infection. Productive cough Postnasal drip – common (there is a history of chronic sinusitis in around 30%) Tiredness – many patients find this more troublesome than the productive cough Acute exacerbations, with: Purulent sputum

stem: A 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes was admitted from a care home with a cough, fever and chest pain. He has been managed with IV co-amoxiclav for four days but is not improving. Other medication of note includes ramipril, atorvastatin, aspirin and mixed insulin BD. On examination he is pyrexial at 38.5 oC, with BP 100/60 mmHg and pulse 95/min. Auscultation of the chest reveals coarse crackles at the right base consistent with continuing pneumonia. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 13.4 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 231 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 145 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 12.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Sputum culture MRSA sensitive to fusidic acid, gentamycin, vancomycin and rifampicin, resistant to co-amoxiclav Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
D Switch to IV vancomycin This man has nosocomial pneumonia, most likely acquired from his care home. The usual dose for vancomycin is 1 g BD 12-hourly, or 15 mg/kg. Vancomycin is effective as a single agent. It is only effective IV for this indication, due to poor absorption from the GI tract. It is implicated in nephrotoxicity and this patient already has a degree of renal impairment. Along with commencing vancomycin and careful monitoring during its use, other changes should be made to his medications and measures to prevent further decline in his renal function should be taken. A Continue co-amoxiclav The patient has failed to improve on this agent and the sputum culture has proven resistance to it. Persisting with this would be detrimental to the patient and increase the risk of antibiotic resistance. B Add oral fusidic acid Widespread use of topical fusidic acid has encouraged the development of S. aureus resistance and therefore the use of fusidic acid alone as an anti-staphylococcal agent is not recommended. C Switch to oral rifampicin Oral rifampicin is an option for MRSA, but it is associated with rapid development of resistance when used as a single agent. E Add IV gentamicin Although the sputum culture has shown that the MRSA in this case

is sensitive to gentamicin, this patient already has a degree of kidney disease and therefore gentamicin is contraindicated. There would also be no sense in continuing the co-amoxiclav.

stem: A 25-year-old basketball player is brought to the Emergency Department with a history of sudden onset of right-sided chest pain and breathlessness. On examination, tachycardia is noted. Decreased breath sounds are heard on the right side. What is the probable diagnosis?
options: Rupture of a subphrenic abscess through the diaphragm
Rupture of a subpleural tuberculous focus
explanation:
Rupture of apical subpleural blebs
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax is caused by the rupture of apical pleural blebs. The incidence of pneumothorax is highest in young men (aged 15–30 years) and smoking, height and the presence of apical subpleural blebs appear to be the most important aetiological factors. Height might have been a significant factor in this case because the patient is a basketball player.

Lobar pneumonia
Lobar pneumonia is incorrect. Lobar pneumonia usually presents with a history of cough, fever and malaise.

Pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary embolism is incorrect. The majority of patients with pulmonary emboli present with either pleurisy, shortness of breath or haemoptysis. Around 75% of pulmonary emboli arise from deep vein Chatthrombosis with in the lower limb. (There do not appear to be any risk factors for venous thromboembolism in this case.)

stem: Which of the following treatments improves the long-term prognosis in patients with chronic hypoxemia in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)?
explanation:
Long-term domiciliary oxygen therapy
The only treatment that improves the long-term prognosis in (selected) patients with COPD is long-term domiciliary oxygen therapy, given for at least 15 h per day, as shown by two multi-centre trials, one conducted by the Medical Research Council (MRC) in the UK, and the other by the Nocturnal Oxygen Therapy Trial (NOTT). The reasons for the improvement in survival with oxygen therapy in patients with COPD are still uncertain, but are not clearly related to improvements in pulmonary haemodynamics. As usual, survival is related to the level of pulmonary arterial hypertension in patients who receive long-term oxygen therapy. In the MRC trial, there was no significant improvement in pulmonary arterial pressure following oxygen therapy, but the increase of 3 mmHg per year in pulmonary arterial pressure in the control group did not occur in those who were treated. Overnight oxygen therapy, which abolishes nocturnal desaturation, also decreases pulmonary arterial pressure. In addition to the improvement in survival, a number of studies have examined other effects of supplementary oxygen therapy. The effects of oxygen therapy on breathlessness remain unclear. However, several studies have shown that oxygen therapy can lead to an improvement in exercise endurance in patients with COPD, associated with a reduction in ventilation at a given submaximal work rate, and an improvement in walking distance and in the ability to perform daily activities.

stem: A 25-year-old laboratory worker comes to the clinic for review. She complains of shortness of breath and wheeze during the course of the working week, although this improves over the weekends and when she takes an extended break on holiday. She has kept a peak-flow diary and it clearly indicates a reduction in peak flow that is progressive during the course of the working week and improves on a Saturday and Sunday. Which of the following is occupational asthma most commonly triggered by?
explanation:
Isocyanates
Immunologic OA (occupational asthma) are divided into two categories, high-molecular-weight (eg, flour, laboratory animal proteins) and low-molecular-weight (eg, diisocyanates, trimellitic anhydride, formaldehyde). Low-molecular-weight chemicals are incomplete antigens (ie, haptens) that combine with a protein to produce a sensitizing neoantigen. High-molecular-weight organic agents are complete sensitizing antigens. OA should be suspected and evaluated in every patient with adult-onset asthma. It is estimated that 5 to 25 percent of all adult-onset asthma cases are occupationally related. Isocyanates are the most common cause of occupational asthma,( more common in laboratory worker) followed by flour/grain. Toluene diisocyanate, methylene diphenyl diisocyanate, and hexamethylene diisocyanate are used in polyurethane and plastics production, spray painting, foam coating manufacturing, and adhesive/sealant production use. Specific IgE testing is available for the majority of antigens, and may be informative with respect to altering work patterns to avoid triggers. Avoidance of the causative agent is crucial and may result in significant changes in work patterns for many patients.

stem: A 49-year-old Romanian man recently arrived in the UK and attends the Respiratory Clinic. He has been diagnosed with tuberculosis previously and is in his third month of chemotherapy with rifampicin, pyrazinamide and isoniazid started in Romania. Over the past few weeks his cough has worsened again and he is feeling increasingly lethargic, with further weight loss. Investigation: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.3 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 205 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 89 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 104 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l The chest X-ray shows some progression of right upper-lobe consolidation compared with the previous film. Which of the following is the most appropriate next treatment step?
options: Switch to a macrolide and rifampicin-based regime
Switch to a macrolide, rifampicin and linezolid regime
explanation:
Add fourth and fifth drugs
The evidence we are provided with, including worsening symptoms, an elevated C-reactive protein, and some progression of chest X-ray changes during first line anti-tuberculous therapy raises the possibility of multi-drug resistant tuberculosis). Most guidelines recommend progression to five agents, the specific choices of drugs depending on the which drugs the strain is resistant to.

Add a fourth drug
Add a fourth drug is incorrect. A single drug should never be added to a failing regimen in the treatment of tuberculosis.

Continue the three-drug regimen
Continue the three-drug regimen is incorrect. The current drug regimen is not treating his tuberculosis adequately.

Switch to a macrolide and rifampicin-based regime
Switch to a macrolide and rifampicin-based regime is incorrect. Most guidelines recommend progression to five agents – rifampicin, pyrazinamide, isoniazid, ethambutol and streptomycin.

Switch to a macrolide, rifampicin and linezolid regime
Switch to a macrolide, rifampicin and linezolid regime is incorrect. Most guidelines recommend progression to five agents – rifampicin, pyrazinamide, isoniazid, ethambutol and streptomycin.

stem: A 36-year-old lorry driver who smokes heavily has been complaining of a 2-day history of cough associated with fever. He also complains of right-sided chest pain on inspiration. On examination, he is slightly cyanosed, has a temperature of 38 °C, a respiratory rate of 38/min, a BP of 100/70 mm/Hg and a pulse rate of 130 bpm. He has basal crepitations and dullness to percussion at the right lung base. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Atelectasis due to carcinoma of the lung
explanation:
Lobar pneumonia
The classic presentation of pneumonia is of a cough and fever with the variable presence of sputum production, dyspnoea and pleurisy. Most patients have constitutional symptoms such as malaise, fatigue and asthenia, and many also have gastrointestinal symptoms. Examination of the lung might reveal decreased vesicular breath sounds, localised foci of crepitations, dullness to percussion and sometimes bronchial wheeze. The chest X-ray is a pivotal test for the confirmation of pneumonia.

Mesothelioma
Mesothelioma is incorrect. There is no history suggestive of asbestos exposure here. The acute nature of this gentleman’s symptoms combined with evidence of infection make pneumonia a more likely diagnosis. Mesothelioma would typically have a more gradual onset of symptoms and present with progressive dyspnoea and/or chest pain.

stem: You are referred a 68-year-old man who smokes 40 cigarettes per day and has had chronic cough for the past 6 months, increasingly associated with haemoptysis. He also has a dull ache on the left side of his chest, and his chest X-ray reveals a left hilar mass that is suspicious of bronchial carcinoma. You are considering radical radiotherapy in this man. Which of the following is the most significant contraindication to radical radiotherapy?
explanation:
Malignant pleural effusion
Studies have shown that the presence of a malignant pleural effusion is predictive of poor outcome with radical radiotherapy.

Adenocarcinoma
Adenocarcinoma is incorrect. Adenocarcinoma is not a contraindication to radical radiotherapy.

Forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) < 60%
Forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1) < 60% is incorrect. It was previously thought that patients with a forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1) of less than 50% were at particular risk of post-radiotherapy pneumonitis, but it has been shown that some patients enrolled in radical radiotherapy trials with severe disease actually showed a small improvement in lung function.

stem: The nurses on the ward ask you to look at a chest drain that has been inserted in a patient for a pneumothorax. They are concerned about whether it is still working. When the patient coughs, nothing happens. When he breathes in and out, the fluid in the tube moves up and down. What does this mean?
options: Air and fluid are draining from the pleural space
Air is no longer draining from the pleural space as the drain is blocked
Air is no longer draining from the pleural space, but the drain is still working
Fluid alone is draining from the pleural space
He needs to commence suction to the drain
explanation:
Air is no longer draining from the pleural space, but the drain is still working
The fluid level rising and falling in the drain (swinging) shows that it is still in contact with the pleural space and the fluid level is moving with respiration.

Air and fluid are draining from the pleural space
Air and fluid are draining from the pleural space is incorrect. Air is not bubbling out of the drain when the patient coughs because the air has stopped draining from the pleural space and the lung has re-inflated.

Air is no longer draining from the pleural space as the drain is blocked
Air is no longer draining from the pleural space as the drain is blocked is incorrect. If a drain does not bubble or swing, then it is blocked or kinked and is not working.

stem: A 32-year-old contract spray painter presents to the Respiratory Clinic for review. His asthma is becoming increasingly difficult to control and he now requires fluticasone 500 µg/day and salmeterol 100 µg/day just to perform reasonable activities of daily living. He reports that the only time he has felt well in recent months is when he spent 3 weeks on holiday at his mother’s house at the seaside. Chest X-ray reveals mild hyperinflation, and lung function reveals an obstructive defect. What is the diagnosis that best fits with his symptoms?
explanation:
Occupational asthma
This patient works as a paint sprayer, and asthma is known to be associated with isocyanates, which can be a component of industrial paints or lacquers. Other people who can develop occupational asthma include: Welders Laboratory animal workers Farmers Millers and grain handlers Workers manufacturing biological washing powders Workers involved in metal refining Workers involved in the industrial coatings business.

stem: A 63-year-old lifelong smoker, who has worked for many years in a shipyard, presents with a 7-month history of increasing breathlessness. On examination, he has a blood pressure of 145/85 mmHg and a pulse of 75 bpm; his body mass index (BMI) is 31 kg/m2 and he also appears to have finger clubbing. Auscultation of the chest reveals bibasal inspiratory crackles. The chest X-ray is reported as showing evidence of pleural plaques. Pulmonary function testing reveals a mixed obstructive/restrictive picture. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his breathlessness?
explanation:
Asbestosis
Shipbuilding, car manufacture, boiler making and plumbing industries are all associated with a risk of asbestos exposure. Hence this man’s occupation puts him at significant risk. The findings on auscultation of the chest, coupled with the finger clubbing and the restrictive component seen on pulmonary function testing all point towards asbestos-related pulmonary fibrosis (asbestosis).

Asbestos-related pleural plaques
Asbestos-related pleural plaques is incorrect. Although this man does indeed have asbestos-related pleural plaques seen on chest X-ray, plaques themselves are not thought to contribute to breathlessness.

stem: A 44-year-old man is admitted with right-sided pneumonia. He has been unwell for 3–4 days with malaise, fever, cough and muscular pain. He also has a rash on his abdomen and neck pain. He was previously fit and has not travelled abroad. He is a plumber and he keeps pigeons as a hobby. According to his wife, two of his favourite pigeons died 2 weeks ago. Which organism would you be suspicious of as being responsible for his pneumonia?
explanation:
Chlamydia psittaci
Chlamydia psittaci infection (psittacosis) is characterised by malaise, fever, myalgia and pneumonia. Exposure to an ill bird and a rash (Horder’s spots) are pathognomonic. In the context of his history, Chlamydia would be very high on the index of suspicion. Erythromycin or tetracyclines are the drugs of choice.

Legionella pneumophila
Legionella pneumophila is incorrect. Pneumonia secondary to L. pneumophila would usually be associated with features such as exposure to water coolers, air-conditioning units and the presence of gastrointestinal symptoms, deranged liver function tests and hyponatraemia. Given none of these is described, and the history of exposure to birds that died, a diagnosis of psittacosis is more likely.

stem: A 21-year-old woman who is visiting the United Kingdom from East Africa comes to the Emergency Department for review. She has been suffering from chronic cough, fevers and weight loss over the last six months and is worried there may be a serious underlying problem. There is no past medical history of note, apart from an episode of shingles on the chest wall some 12 months earlier. On examination, she is thin, with a body mass index (BMI) of 20 kg/m2, and there is generalised lymphadenopathy. There are coarse breath sounds in the mid and lower zones bilaterally on auscultation. Investigations reveal the following: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 109 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 4.8 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Lymphocytes 1.0 × 109/l 1.5–3.5 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 171 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 95 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Mantoux test: Negative Her chest X-ray is shown below: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Tuberculosis Human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) infection is a recognised cause of negative Mantoux, in the presence of active TB, the most likely clinical picture here. The chest X-ray picture ﬁts with miliary TB, and the symptoms of fevers, cough and weight loss also support the diagnosis. Increased exposure to HIV is seen in patients from the African subcontinent. Initiation of anti-tuberculous therapy, coupled with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) once the diagnosis of HIV is conﬁrmed, are the most appropriate next steps. A Pertussis scarring Scarring over the long term from pertussis leads to symptoms and signs of bronchiectasis. With respect to the chest X-ray ﬁndings, these can include parallel line opacities, known as tram tracks, caused by dilated, thickened bronchi. Ring opacities or cystic spaces may be seen which are large (2 cm in diameter), and these result from cystic bronchiectasis. The signet ring sign, which is said to be characteristic of bronchiectasis, corresponds to a dilated bronchus, immediately adjacent to a smaller pulmonary artery. B Sarcoidosis Sarcoidosis is characteristically associated with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. It does not ﬁt with the multiple peripheral nodules seen here on the chest X-ray. C Scleroderma Scleroderma (systemic sclerosis) does not ﬁt with the picture seen here on chest X-ray. The chest X-ray may be normal in early pulmonary ﬁbrosis related to systemic sclerosis. Over the longer term, generalised patchy opaciﬁcation consistent with pulmonary ﬁbrosis is seen, rather than the nodular changes seen here. E Varicella pneumonia Previous varicella pneumonia does lead to nodular calciﬁcation seen on chest X-ray, but it would not explain the symptoms of active infection reported here.

stem: A 25-year-old man presents with left-sided pleuritic chest pain. It had come on suddenly 3 days previously. Initially he thought it was secondary to his workout in the gym. However, since it did not improve and he noticed that he was slightly more breathless than usual, he went to the Emergency Department. He has no signiﬁcant past medical history. He is a smoker of 20/day. On examination he looked well. He was a tall, thin man and was not short of breath at rest. Examination was unremarkable except for a clicking sound which was synchronous with the heart sounds. CXR was unremarkable. Which of the following investigations may help with the diagnosis?
explanation:
D Lateral decubitus CXR A click synchronous with the heart sounds is a recognised sign of a small left apical pneumothorax. He is a tall, thin man and a smoker, which are both risk factors for developing a pneumothorax. There is a strong association between pneumothoraces and smoking. The most recent British Thoracic Society (BTS) guidelines suggest that if the postero-anterior (PA) chest X-ray is normal and a small pneumothorax is suspected, a lateral decubitus chest X-ray provides added information in up to 14% of cases (see weblink below). For patients in the lateral decubitus position, air rises to the non-dependent lateral location. Only 5 mL of pleural air may be needed to detect pneumothorax in this position. The treatment of a primary pneumothorax in a non-smoker, <50 years old, with no evidence of underlying lung disease, with a rim of air of <2 cm and no breathlessness is to discharge and follow up as an outpatient. Although this patient is a smoker there is nothing to suggest underlying lung disease, and it is likely that his apical pneumothorax is too small to safely aspirate. Patients should be given analgesia if required and clear instructions to return if their symptoms get any worse. E Repeat CXR BTS guidelines recommend the use of lateral decubitus CXR. Repeating a CXR will not help as the CXR may look the same. A ECG BTS guidelines recommend the use of lateral decubitus CXR. ECG may be abnormal in pneumothorax, which may include abnormal left axis deviation and right axis deviation. There may be QRS abnormalities as well. B Echocardiogram

BTS guidelines recommend the use of lateral decubitus CXR. Ultrasound may be useful in diagnosing traumatic pneumothorax, and the cardiac function may be affected by expanding pneumothorax. C Expiratory CXR BTS guidelines recommend the use of lateral decubitus CXR. Whilst there is a thought process that expiration results in the lungs reducing in volume, and theoretically improving visability of pneumothorax, they are not recommended in BTS guidelines.

stem: An 18-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with acute onset of shortness of breath, dizziness, tingling in both hands and chest pain. She has presented with the same symptoms three times in the last month. The clinical examination and chest X-ray are both normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hyperventilation syndrome
Psychogenic breathlessness is a diagnosis of exclusion, although there might be clues in the history and examination. The sighing and irregular breathing will be readily noticeable to a keen observer. Associated complaints directly related to the hyperventilation are paraesthesia in the hands (and perhaps feet), dizziness and collapse. Non-specific features, such as fatigue, insomnia, weakness or chest pains, can all be part of the syndrome. Depression and anxiety can be aspects of the underlying psychiatric state. By definition, in pure psychogenic breathlessness, the chest X-ray and lung function are normal. Some patients develop breathlessness because they have been told that they have a ‘shadow on a lung’ or exhibit a degree of breathlessness disproportionate to a mild functional abnormality due to anxiety. These patients tend to have an obsessional personality or might be looking for compensation for supposed lung damage due to injury or occupation.

stem: A 45-year-old oil executive returns from Indonesia for investigation after an extended period of illness. During his stay he has developed asthma, associated with progressive malaise and weight loss. He is now lethargic and has lost 6.4 kg (1 stone) in weight in the past 3 months. His chest X-ray is abnormal, with basal reticulonodular and alveolar infiltrates. Blood testing reveals a marked peripheral blood eosinophilia. The filarial complement fixation test is positive. What is the most likely cause of this clinical picture?
explanation:
Infection with Wuchereria bancrofti
This is a picture of tropical pulmonary eosinophilia, associated with infection with Wuchereria bancrofti (a condition associated with microfilaria). The treatment of choice is a 10–14-day course of diethylcarbamazine to eradicate the infection. The condition is seen in South Asia and presents with cough, wheeze, fever, lassitude and weight loss with peripheral lower limb swelling due to proximal lymphatic obstruction.

Brucellosis
Brucellosis is incorrect. Brucellosis is a zoonotic bacterial infection. Symptoms are typically fever, anorexia, fatigue and weight loss. It is also associated with bone and joint symptoms, gastrointestinal symptoms and neuropsychiatric symptoms. Active pulmonary disease is relatively rare and it is not associated with eosinophilia or a positive filarial complement fixation test.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents to the Respiratory Clinic for review with increasing shortness of breath over the past 4–6 months. She used to be able to walk her dog, but she now finds her exercise tolerance limited to only a few hundred metres. There is a dry cough but no significant wheezing, and her GP has tried a salbutamol inhaler with no effect. She has a 10-pack-year smoking history, takes medication for hypertension and has complained of symptoms consistent with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) in the past. On examination her BP is 135/85 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. There is early bilateral clubbing. Auscultation reveals bilateral inspiratory crackles, more marked in the mid-zones and at the lung bases. Abdomen is soft and non-tender and her BMI is 22. SpO 2 on air is 91%. Chest X-ray reveals patchy shadowing, which is more marked at the lung bases. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
The slowly progressive shortness of breath, coupled with a lack of response to salbutamol, clubbing and inspiratory crackles on examination, and patchy chest X-ray changes, fits best with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. BNF recommends the use of nintedanib, a tyrosine-protein kinase inhibitor, as a treatment option for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Bronchiectasis
Bronchiectasis is incorrect. A chronically productive cough with history of repeated chest infections would be expected if the underlying diagnosis was bronchiectasis.

stem: What are the NICE indications for home oxygen?
options: Low forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1)
explanation:
Cor pulmonale and low PO2
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) states that the following are indications for considering long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT): Stable patients with a PaO 2 of < 7.3 kPa when stable Patients with a PaO 2 of 7.3–8.0 kPa who are stable but who have an additional risk factor (e.g. secondary polycythaemia, nocturnal hypoxaemia, peripheral oedema, pulmonary hypertension). Oxygen should be used for at least 15 h per day.

Low forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1)
Low forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1) is incorrect. A patient with a low FEV 1 may also have significant chronic hypoxia and therefore would benefit from home oxygen therapy. However, a low FEV 1 without significant chronic hypoxia is not an indication for home oxygen therapy.

stem: A 70-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted to the Pulmonary Department with dyspnoea. He is given 40% oxygen via face mask, nebulised bronchodilators and intravenous steroids. One hour later, he becomes drowsy. Blood gases are taken on arrival and repeat arterial blood gases are taken after treatment. The results show: Investigation Result Repeated result Normal value pH 7.38 7.24 7.35–7.45 PaO 2 5.3 6.6 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa PaCO 2 6.0 8.4 kPa 4.6–6 kPa An electrocardiogram is performed which shows atrial fibrillation with a rate of 138 bpm. Which of the following is the next step in this patient's management?
explanation:
Non-invasive ventilation
This patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is in progressively worsening type II respiratory failure. Respiratory failure can be classed as either: type I respiratory failure

stem: A 58-year-old man with a history of heavy asbestos exposure has smoked 20 cigarettes a day since he was 17. What is his increased risk of developing bronchial carcinoma compared with a lifelong non-smoker who has never been exposed to asbestos?
explanation:
50× increased risk
Asbestos exposure increases the risk of developing bronchial carcinoma by a factor of 5 and smoking increases the risk by a factor of around 10 or 11. If a patient has both risk factors then the risk is cumulative and is approximately 50× greater than the risk in a lifelong non-smoker who has never been exposed to asbestos.

20× increased risk
20× increased risk is incorrect. Asbestos exposure increases the risk of developing bronchial carcinoma by a factor of 5 and smoking increases the risk by a factor of around 10 or 11. If a patient has both risk factors then the risk is cumulative and is approximately 50× greater than the risk in a lifelong non-smoker who has never been exposed to asbestos.

stem: A 46-year-old cardiologist attended a local conference last weekend and fell ill with a fever of up to 40°C that lasted for 2 days. He had associated shortness of breath and a dry cough. In addition, he had loose motions for a day. His blood results showed deranged liver function tests and hyponatraemia. His white cell count was 10.2 × 10 9/l. Bibasal consolidation was seen on his X-ray. What would be the most effective treatment for his condition?
explanation:
Clarithromycin
This is a case of Legionella pneumonia. Legionella outbreaks are seen in previously fit individuals staying in hotels or institutions where the shower facilities and/or the cooling system are contaminated with the organism. The incubation period is 2–10 days.Flu-like symptoms, fever, malaise and myalgia typically precede the development of a dry cough and dyspnoea. Extrapulmonary symptoms include anorexia, diarrhoea and vomiting, hepatitis, kidney disease, confusion and coma. A chest X-ray shows bibasal consolidation, sometimes with a small pleural effusion. Blood results show an elevated white count, hyponatraemia and deranged liver function tests. Urinalysis might show haematuria. Diagnosis is by the urinary antigen test, which is highly specific. It is important to remember that the organism does not show up on Gram-staining.The preferred treatment is with the macrolide, clarithromycin. Ciprofloxacin can also be effective and rifampicin can be used.

Cefuroxime
Cefuroxime is incorrect. Cefuroxime is rarely prescribed now due to risk of Clostridium difficile infection.

stem: A 22-year-old man who has started his first job in a paint spraying shop a few weeks earlier comes to the Respiratory Clinic complaining of increased shortness of breath. He says that his problems progress during the week, and are accompanied by a dry cough. They resolve during the weekend when he is off work. He has tried a salbutamol inhaler, which came from the GP, although he says this only gave him very minor benefit. On examination his BP is 115/82 mmHg, pulse is 65/min and regular. His chest is clear. BMI is 23. Peak flow is 550 (605 predicted). Which of the following is the most useful next step in confirming a diagnosis of occupational asthma?
explanation:
Serial peak flow measurement
The telling features of this case are that symptoms increase during the working week and are relieved at weekends, and that when he visits you in the clinic, on a day off, his chest is clear and peak flow is only slightly reduced. Serial peak flows will confirm a progressively worsening picture consistent with asthma, where peak flows fall from Monday to Friday and improve over the weekend.

RAST testing for paint allergens
RAST testing for paint allergens is incorrect. RAST testing may be positive for allergens, but it would not necessarily indicate exposure or underlying occupational asthma.

stem: A 70-year-old man with moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) attends the Emergency Department with increasing dyspnoea. He has been found to have a 3-cm pneumothorax. What would be the optimal management for this patient?
options: Chest drain insertion if needle aspiration fails
Conservative management, with observation and repeat chest X-ray after 4 hours
Conservative management, with observation and repeat chest X-ray after 12 hours
explanation:
Chest drain insertion initially
This is a man with a pneumothorax secondary to his COPD. He is symptomatic and the British Thoracic Society (BTS) Guidelines suggest he should not undergo needle aspiration but proceed to chest drain insertion initially, given the rim of the pneumothorax is > 2 cm and he is breathless.

Chest drain insertion if needle aspiration fails
Chest drain insertion if needle aspiration fails is incorrect. This is appropriate management of a primary pneumothorax > 2 cm.

Conservative management, with observation and repeat chest X-ray after 4 hours
Conservative management, with observation and repeat chest X-ray after 4 hours is incorrect. Pneumothoraces with a > 2 cm rim should be actively treated with either aspiration (in primary pneumothoraces) or chest drain insertion (secondary pneumothoraces).

stem: A 68-year-old man who has a long history of smoking presents to the Emergency Department with worsening shortness of breath. His general health has deteriorated over the past few months and recently he has been prescribed a salbutamol inhaler by his GP for cough and wheezing, particularly on exercise and at night. On examination he is lip pursing and has considerable wheeze on auscultation of the chest. He is pyrexial at 37.8°C and has purulent sputum. He can only manage a peak flow of 150 l/min. Arterial blood gas sampling reveals a Pao2 of 7.2 kPa. He is allergic to penicillin. Which of the following would be the most appropriate choice for antibiotic therapy in this man?
explanation:
Clarithromycin 500 mg bd orally
This man has an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The most common causative pathogens are Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis. The most appropriate antibiotic of the options listed would be a macrolide such as clarithromycin. It should be noted, however, that in patients taking theophyllines, concomitant use of macrolides can increase serum aminophylline levels. Other important acute treatments in this case would be repeated nebulisation with salbutamol and ipratropium 4- to 6-hourly, oxygen therapy and oral steroids. Non-invasive ventilation might be considered where the pH is 7.3 or less and the patient is not improving after 4 h of medical therapy.

stem: A 17-year-old man with a history of cystic fibrosis comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. Despite pancrelipase tablets and eating a high-calorie, high-carbohydrate diet, he is finding it very difficult to maintain his weight. He asks about using vitamin supplements. Which of the following vitamins is it most important to supplement in cystic fibrosis?
explanation:
Vitamin A
Cystic fibrosis results in malabsorption of fat, therefore vitamin supplements for fat-soluble vitamins are recommended. These include vitamins A, D, E and K. Recommended daily levels for vitamin supplementation are: vitamin A 4000–10 000 IU (1200–3000 mcg), vitamin D 800–2000 IU (20–50 mcg) and vitamin E 150– 300 IU (100–200 mg).

Folate
Folate is incorrect. There is no need to routinely supplement folate in patients with cystic fibrosis.

Vitamin B6
Vitamin B6 is incorrect. Studies of B vitamins in patients with cystic fibrosis do not suggest significant B vitamin deficiency.

stem: A 40-year-old woman comes to clinic with a 1-year history of breathlessness and chest pain on exertion. She has a loud P2 on listening to her heart and her electrocardiogram (ECG) shows right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy. Her pulmonary function tests are normal, although blood gas analysis shows hypoxia. Echocardiogram shows a resting pulmonary artery pressure of 29 mmHg. Computed tomography shows enlarged pulmonary arteries, but no clot. What feature in her history might help with the diagnosis?
explanation:
Previous amphetamine use
This woman has pulmonary hypertension with no obvious cause and certainly no evidence of chronic thromboembolic disease. Primary pulmonary hypertension (PPH) is a rare disease of uncertain aetiology. It has, however, been associated with anorectic drug use (fenfluramine, dexfenfluramine), amphetamine use and possibly cocaine use.

Previous breast cancer
Previous breast cancer is incorrect. Breast cancer is unrelated to pulmonary hypertension.

stem: A 23-year-old woman with known brittle asthma is admitted to the Emergency Department. By the time you see her she has received her second salbutamol nebuliser. She is managed with high-dose Seretide and monteleukast and has had two previous admissions to the ITU in the past 18 months. On examination her BP is 110/70 mmHg, and pulse is 105/min and regular. She has severe wheeze on auscultation and a respiratory rate of 28/min. Arterial blood gas is analysed. Which of the following would be the strongest indication for intubation?
explanation:
PaCO2 6.0 kPa
Clinical signs associated with life-threatening asthma are well described, as presented here. Any one of the following in a patient with severe asthma is considered of particular concern: Clinical signs Measurements Altered conscious level PEF < 33% best or predicted Exhaustion SpO 2 < 92% Arrhythmia PaO 2 < 8 kPa Hypotension ‘Normal’ PaCO 2 (4.6–6.0 kPa) Cyanosis

stem: A 53-year-old parrot expert presents for review. For some months he has suffered increasing tiredness, high fevers at night, cough and muscle ache. Chest X-ray reveals a diffuse pneumonic picture. His white blood cell count is normal and transaminases are just above the normal range. Two sets of blood cultures prove negative. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Chlamydia psittaci pneumonia
Chlamydia psittaci pneumonia was originally described in people who kept the psittacine family of birds (e.g. parrots). The peak age at presentation is 30–60 years and it has an equal sex distribution. Mortality is low (0.7%). The incubation period is 1–2 weeks, but the illness can follow a protracted course over a number of months. Symptoms are as described, and liver function tests might show mild abnormalities in up to 50%. The chest X-ray can show segmental or diffuse consolidation. Diagnosis is confirmed by enzyme immunoassay; treatment is with macrolide or tetracycline antibiotics.

Mycoplasma pneumonia
Mycoplasma pneumonia is incorrect. Mycoplasmal infections occur in epidemics every 4–5 years, more commonly among close-knit populations such as those in schools and colleges. Mycoplasmal infection is not associated with exposure to birds. The peak age of presentation of Mycoplasma pneumonia is 5–20 years, and Mycoplasma pneumonia accounts for about 7% of all community-acquired pneumonias. Cold agglutinins are associated in up to 50% of cases and muscle tenderness is reported to occur in up to 50%. The X-ray

stem: A 72-year-old woman is admitted with sudden-onset, left-sided pleuritic chest pain with shortness of breath. She is being treated for asthma, which has been well controlled on a low dose of inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting ß-agonist. She underwent a left hemiarthroplasty 12 days ago and was discharged because she was doing well. Her chest is clear on auscultation. She is tachycardic (132 bpm) and an electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia. Her peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) is 300 l/min (previous best 400 l/min). Arterial blood gases are as follows: pH 7.34, Pao 2 7.6 kPa, Paco 2 3.5 kPa. She is started on oxygen. A chest X-ray is normal. What would be the most appropriate immediate action you as the medical FY2 should take under supervision?
options: Request a chest X-ray in expiration
Start low-molecular-weight heparin, suspecting pulmonary embolus, and request a
Start low-molecular-weight heparin, suspecting pulmonary embolus, and request computed
Start nebulised bronchodilators and monitor the PEFR
explanation:
Start low-molecular-weight heparin, suspecting pulmonary embolus, and request computed
tomographic pulmonary angiography A CTPA would be the imaging investigation of choice in this case, after starting low-molecular-weight heparin

Start low-molecular-weight heparin, suspecting pulmonary embolus, and request a
ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scan

stem: A 48 year old patient who has had wheezy breathlessness for many years and who has previously been shown to have pulmonary infiltrates on chest X-ray and blood eosinophilia undergoes a high-resolution computed tomographic scan. This shows proximal bronchiectasis. Apart from his lung symptoms he has no other significant medical illnesses. Which of the following tests would be most useful in establishing the cause of her bronchiectasis?
explanation:
Aspergillus skin-prick test
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is characterised by: Asthmatic symptoms Peripheral blood eosinophilia Positive skin tests or circulating precipitins to Aspergillus fumigatus Abnormal chest X-ray Raised total IgE A proportion of patients develop proximal bronchiectasis as a consequence of mucus plugging. Treatment during acute episodes is usually with oral corticosteroids. Of the options listed, aspergillus skin-prick test is the most specific investigation for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.

stem: A 54-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents to the Respiratory Clinic complaining of a chronic cough and haemoptysis. He has lost 4 kg in weight recently. He has an abnormal chest X-ray, consistent with bronchial carcinoma. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 110 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 352 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 65 mm in 1 hour 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Sodium (Na +) 132 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 130 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy reveals adenocarcinoma of the bronchus. You arrange computed tomography of the thorax. Which of the following would tend to rule out the possibility of a surgical cure?
options: Forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) 1.6 l
explanation:
Malignant pleural effusion
Pleural effusion implies pleural involvement and this would preclude a surgical cure.

Forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) 1.6 l
Forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1) 1.6 l is incorrect. A forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1) of less than 1.5 l precludes surgery for bronchial carcinoma because there is not enough lung reserve.

Horner syndrome
Horner syndrome is incorrect. Horner syndrome is attributable to local nerve involvement and therefore does not exclude successful surgical excision of the primary tumour.

Ipsilateral mediastinal lymph node involvement
Ipsilateral mediastinal lymph node involvement is incorrect. Contralateral lymph node involvement implies distant spread and again precludes surgery.

Superior vena caval obstruction
Superior vena caval obstruction is incorrect. Superior vena caval obstruction is not an absolute contraindication to surgery.

stem: A 46-year-old man came to the clinic with his partner. She complained that he has become lethargic, increasingly sleepy in the daytime, has a headache in the morning and has some impairment of intellectual ability. He has a BMI of 34 kg/m 2, smokes 20 cigarettes per day and drinks about 30 units of alcohol per week. There is no significant past history or drug history. Other than a slightly lower air entry in both lungs, there was no other significant finding on examination. Chest X-ray showed emphysema. Arterial blood gas results were: pH 7.41, Pao 2 9.8 kPa, Paco 2 5.8 kPa. Which investigation is most likely to reveal the suspected diagnosis?
explanation:
Polysomnographic studies
This patient has obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome, a condition that most often occurs in overweight middle- aged men and affects 1–2% of the population. Pathophysiology Respiratory muscle activity is reduced during sleep, especially during rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, when the diaphragm is the only active muscle. Apnoea occurs when the sucked-back tongue closes the airway at the back of the throat. When awake, this tendency is overcome by the action of the opening muscles of the higher airway, but these become hypotonic during sleep. Partial narrowing causes snoring, while critical narrowing leads to sleep apnoea. This results in hypoxia and an increased respiratory-effort stimulus to overcome the obstruction. Important contributory factors are:

stem: A 28-year-old woman who is 4 months’ pregnant comes to the clinic for review. She has worsening shortness of breath and wheeze, and is using her salbutamol inhaler up to 6–8 times / day. On examination her BP is 125/75 mmHg; pulse is 68/min and regular. There is scattered wheeze on auscultation of her chest. Which of the following is the optimal next step in management of her asthma?
explanation:
Add beclomethasone 200 mcg BD
NICE guidelines recommend following the same ladder of therapy for chronic asthma in pregnant women as in those who are not pregnant. As such the optimal next step is the addition of inhaled corticosteroids. The next step is then either addition of a leukotriene receptor antagonist (LTRA), or, if an LTRA is not clinically appropriate, the addition of a long-acting inhaled beta-agonist (LABA).

Add montelukast
Add montelukast is incorrect. Montelukast is only considered in those patients who have not achieved control after trial of an inhaled corticosteroid. A leukotriene receptor antagonists and long-acting beta agonist can be added as part of a MART regimen.

stem: A 50-year-old woman with known rheumatoid arthritis who is treated with long-term methotrexate and prednisolone presents to the clinic with increasing shortness of breath and a non-productive dry cough. She is a lifelong non-smoker. On examination her BP is 146/86 mmHg, and pulse is 82/min and regular. There are sparse coarse crackles and wheeze on auscultation of her chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 124 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.8 × 10 9/l 4–11 x 10 9/l Platelets 199 × 10 9/l 150–400 x 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 120 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Forced Expiratory Volume in the 1 st second (FEV 1) 45% of predicted Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) 85% of predicted Not reversible by salbutamol. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bronchiolitis obliterans
Bronchiolitis obliterans is a rare complication of rheumatoid arthritis, associated with irreversible obstructive lung disease. High-resolution computed tomography (CT) reveals bronchial wall thickening and air trapping.

Adult-onset asthma
Adult-onset asthma (Option A) is incorrect. Adult-onset asthma seems unlikely given the clinical scenario as pictured.

Caplan syndrome
Caplan syndrome is the name given to a combination of rheumatoid arthritis and pneumoconiosis.

COPD
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease seems unlikely given the clinical scenario as described.

Methotrexate pneumonitis
Methotrexate pneumonitis would result in a restrictive lung picture.

stem: A 56-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department complaining of left-sided pleuritic chest pain. She has been unwell in bed with flu for the past few days. A past history of ischaemic heart disease and treated NYHA grade II heart failure is noted. On examination her BP is 110/72 mmHg; pulse is 85/min and regular. Heart sounds are normal and her chest is clear. Abdomen is soft and non-tender, her left calf is 2 inches greater in diameter than the right, and is tender to palpation. Her BMI is 23.
