O 2 saturation is reduced at 91%. Her white count is in the normal range; D-dimer is markedly elevated at >1000. Which of the following is the likely finding on chest X-ray?
options: Less prominent pulmonary vasculature on the left
Prominent pulmonary vasculature on the left
explanation:
Normal film
This patient’s history, examination and investigations are suggestive of a pulmonary embolus. In the majority of cases of pulmonary embolism (PE) the chest film is in fact normal.

Less prominent pulmonary vasculature on the left
Less prominent pulmonary vasculature on the left is incorrect. Although in massive proximal PE there may be diminished pulmonary vasculature on one side, this is very rarely seen.

stem: Which one of the following statements about sarcoidosis is true?
options: A positive tuberculin test in a patient with chronic sarcoidosis is suggestive of active tuberculosis
Clubbing of the fingers is an early feature
Jaundice and portal hypertension are the predominant features of hepatic sarcoidosis
Parenchymal lung disease is often accompanied by pleural effusion
When hypercalcaemia manifests, it is usually resistant to steroid therapy
explanation:
A positive tuberculin test in a patient with chronic sarcoidosis is suggestive of active tuberculosis
Sarcoidosis is a systemic disorder of unknown cause. Its pathological hallmark is the non-caseating granuloma, which primarily affects the respiratory tract, skin, eye, heart, kidneys and liver. A tuberculin test is usually negative in chronic sarcoidosis, but most patients with sarcoidosis who develop tuberculosis become tuberculin-positive. This is suggestive but not an absolute indicator of active infection.

Clubbing of the fingers is an early feature
Clubbing of the fingers is an early feature is incorrect. Clubbing of the fingers is not a recognised feature of sarcoidosis.

Parenchymal lung disease is often accompanied by pleural effusion
Parenchymal lung disease is often accompanied by pleural effusion is incorrect. Pleural disease is relatively infrequent, with effusions occurring in fewer than 5% of patients.

stem: A 64-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his wife with drowsiness and confusion. He has a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and attends the Chest Clinic. He had been commenced on antibiotics by his general practitioner (GP) two days earlier for an exacerbation of his COPD. Which of the following blood gases (on 2 l O 2/min) fit best with this man’s condition?
options: pH 7.14, PaCO 2 7.3 kPa, PaO 2 9.1 kPa, bicarbonate 14 mmol/l
pH 7.24, PaCO 2 9.3 kPa, PaO 2 8.1 kPa, bicarbonate 31.2 mmol/l
pH 7.38, PaCO 2 5.3 kPa, PaO 2 8.1 kPa, bicarbonate 30 mmol/l
pH 7.38, PaCO 2 8.3 kPa, PaO 2 8.1 kPa, bicarbonate 38 mmol/l
pH 7.54, PaCO 2 3.3 kPa, PaO 2 9.1 kPa, bicarbonate 24 mmol/l
explanation:
pH 7.24, PaCO 2 9.3 kPa, PaO 2 8.1 kPa, bicarbonate 31.2 mmol/l
This patient has acute on chronic respiratory acidosis. In respiratory acidosis there will be raised PaCO 2 and hydrogen ion concentration. The elevation of the bicarbonate reflects renal buffering from his chronic respiratory failure. In acute respiratory acidosis every 1-kPa rise in CO 2 produces 6 nmol/l of hydrogen ion and a 1-mmol/l increase in bicarbonate. In contrast, in chronic respiratory acidosis, the increase in hydrogen ions per kPa rise in carbon dioxide falls to about 2.5 nmol/l.

pH 7.38, PaCO 2 5.3 kPa, PaO 2 8.1 kPa, bicarbonate 30 mmol/l
pH 7.38, PaCO 2 5.3 kPa, PaO 2 8.1 kPa, bicarbonate 30 mmol/l is incorrect. These results would not be expected with this man’s clinical presentation.

stem: A 26-year-old man presents with fever, headache and a moderately productive cough. The chest X-ray shows increased interstitial markings. Laboratory examinations show an elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), anaemia and cold agglutinins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Mycoplasma pneumonia
Acute, cold, autoimmune, haemolytic anaemia is commonly seen in adolescents and young adults following infection with Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Haemolysis occurs approximately 1–2 weeks following infection and is most commonly associated with a rise in polyclonal anti-I IgM antibodies with mycoplasma pneumonia. The typical patient is usually a young adult who experiences a respiratory tract infection accompanied by headache, myalgia, cough and fever, whose chest X-ray shows bronchopneumonia. The cough is often non- productive, but when sputum is obtained it is mucoid, shows predominantly mononuclear cells and shows no dominant organism. The diagnosis should be suspected in patients with a relatively mild form of pneumonia, particularly in previously healthy young adults. A characteristic feature is the relatively high frequency of extrapulmonary complications, including: Rash Neurological syndromes (aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, neuropathies), Myocarditis Pericarditis

stem: A 21-year-old man with no history of previous chest disease presents to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset pleuritic chest pain. He says he was just working on his car when the worst pain he had ever had began. On examination in the Emergency Department his saturations are measured at 93% on air. He has hyper-resonance and decreased breath sounds over the right lung. A chest X-ray shows almost complete collapse of the right lung. He undergoes an air aspiration and 2.5 l is aspirated. A repeat chest film reveals a 1.5-cm rim of air and he is still short of breath. Which of the following describes the correct management?
explanation:
Chest drain
British Thoracic Society (BTS) guidelines consider that if 2.5 l of air is aspirated, and the chest X-ray appearance has not adequately resolved, then formal chest drain is the next step; also if symptoms still exist after aspiration, a chest drain is required. In patients with previous chest disease a rim of air > 2 cm necessitates formal chest drain insertion as the initial step.

Observation
Observation is incorrect. This gentleman has a large pneumothorax and therefore requires admission and drainage of his pneumothorax.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with increased shortness of breath and left-sided pleuritic chest pain which came on suddenly over the past 90 min. He has a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), for which he takes a high-dose Seretide inhaler. Unfortunately, he continues to smoke 20 cigarettes per day. His BP is 100/60 mmHg with a pulse of 95/min. There are decreased breath sounds on auscultation of the left side of the chest. Chest X-ray reveals a > 2 cm left-sided pneumothorax. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Discharge to return the morning after
explanation:
Insert a chest drain
This patient has a secondary pneumothorax (history of COPD), and it is larger than 2 cm with symptoms, therefore insertion of a chest drain is the only option.

High-flow oxygen therapy for 24 h
High-flow oxygen therapy for 24 h is incorrect. High-flow oxygen can aid resolution of pneumothoraces but definitive management with chest drain is required in a secondary pneumothorax > 2 cm. High-flow oxygen in patients with COPD is not advised as a routine measure in pneumothoraces given the risk of hypercapnoea.

stem: A 72-year-old man with a history of ischaemic heart disease including two previous myocardial infarctions over the past 3 years presents to the Emergency Department with a cough productive of rusty coloured sputum, significantly increased shortness of breath and fevers over the past 3 days. Medication of note includes atorvastatin, amlodipine, furosemide and ramipril. Examination reveals a BP of 88/50 mmHg and he is pyrexial with a temperature of 38.2 °C. There are signs of consolidation at the right base on auscultation. O 2 saturation is 90% on air and respiratory rate is 32/min. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 135 - 175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 15.1 × 10 9/l 4 - 11 x 10 9/l Platelets 203 × 10 9/l 150 - 400 x 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 131 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 165 μmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Urea 17.1 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 285 mg/l 0 - 10 mg/l Chest X-Ray Right lower lobe consolidation Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
options: IV clarithromycin + IV co-amoxiclav, stop statin
Oral clarithromycin and IV co-amoxiclav, stop statin
explanation:
IV clarithromycin + IV co-amoxiclav, stop statin
By CURB criteria this patient has severe pneumonia (urea > 7 mmol/l, respiratory rate > 30/min, BP < 90 mmHg systolic), making a CURB score of 4, including the fact he is 72 years of age. This implies mortality of 15% or greater; as such he should be managed aggressively with dual IV therapy. Milder disease can be managed with oral clarithromycin and IV co-amoxiclav, and younger patients with uncomplicated pneumonia can potentially be managed with a completely oral regimen. Levofloxacin can be added to macrolide and co-amoxiclav when legionella is suspected. His statin may be discontinued while the clarithromycin is given because of the significant CYP3A4 inhibitory effect of the antibiotic.

Oral amoxicillin
Oral amoxicillin is incorrect. Amoxicillin alone fails to cover potential gram negative causes of pneumonia, and causes of pneumonia where penicillins are ineffective such as mycoplasma.

Oral clarithromycin, stop statin
Oral clarithromycin is incorrect. Oral clarithromycin alone is inadequate given the patient has severe pneumonia.

Oral clarithromycin and IV co-amoxiclav, stop statin
Oral clarithromycin and IV co-amoxiclav is incorrect. Although oral bioavailability of clarithromycin is high, guidelines from the BTS recommend IV clarithromycin in severe pneumonia at least initially.

stem: A 17-year-old is admitted to the Respiratory Ward with a third exacerbation of cystic fibrosis in the past year. She is studying for science A levels and asks you about the primary defect which underlies the development of cystic fibrosis. How is the defect best described?
explanation:
Defect in chloride transport
The primary defect in cystic fibrosis is in the protein transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR), which functions as a chloride channel. Six classes of CFTR defects have been described, of which delta-F508 is the most common: A. complete absence of CFTR protein synthesis B. defective protein maturation and early degradation (caused by the delta-F508 mutation) C. disordered regulation (diminished ATP binding and hydrolysis) D. defective chloride conductance E. diminished transcription due to promoter or splicing abnormality F. accelerated channel turnover.

stem: You are asked to see a 63-year-old man who was admitted to the Coronary Care Unit a few hours ago after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for an inferior myocardial infarction. The nurses are concerned because he is hypotensive and relatively bradycardic with a BP of 90/60 mmHg and a pulse of 65/min. His jugular venous pressure (JVP) is elevated. O 2 saturation is 93% and his chest is clear on auscultation. You decide to insert a jugular line to aid with respect to his fluid management. Quite soon after the procedure he deteriorates with increased shortness of breath and decreased right-sided breath sounds on auscultation. His saturation drops to 89% and a portable chest film indicates a right lung collapse. Which of the following is the most likely complication of line insertion to have occurred?
explanation:
Pneumothorax
Pneumothorax is seen in up to 15% of patients who undergo subclavian line insertion, although it is much more rarely seen in conjunction with jugular venous puncture. The lung collapse and drop in saturation raises the possibility of pneumothorax. In this situation chest drain insertion is required.

Air embolism
Air embolism is incorrect. Air embolism would not lead to partial lung collapse but would lead to shortness of breath and cyanosis.

stem: A 62-year-old man has idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). Which of the following lung function abnormalities would be typical of IPF?
options: Decreased ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 s to forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC)
Narrowing of the alveolar–arterial (a–a) gradient on exercise
explanation:
Increased lung elastic recoil
IPF lungs are stiff, ie poorly compliant, and therefore if compliance is low then elastic recoil will be high, as the two are inversely related.

Decreased ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 s to forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC)
Decreased ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 s to forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC) is incorrect. Typical lung function abnormalities in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (known previously as cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis) include a decreased FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 s) and FVC (forced vital capacity) with an increased ratio of FEV1 to FVC, ie a restrictive ratio.

Increased gas transfer factor
Increased gas transfer factor is incorrect. Gas transfer factor (Tlco or Dlco) is reduced, as is gas transfer coefficient (Kco).

stem: An 18-year-old man presents with a gradual onset of pallor, weakness, lethargy, dry cough and occasional haemoptysis. There are no extrapulmonary features. His chest X-ray shows diffuse pulmonary infiltrates. Lung biopsy shows no vasculitic changes and no evidence of immunoglobulin or complement deposition. His gas transfer factor (Tlco) is found to be elevated. Renal function is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis
Idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis tends to occur in younger people and is characterised by pallor, weakness, lethargy, dry cough and occasional haemoptysis. There are no abnormal immunological features. Gas transfer is elevated as blood is already in the alveolar space.

Behçet’s disease
Behçet’s disease is incorrect. We are given no history of orogenital ulceration, which counts a against diagnosis of Behçet’s.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is incorrect. There are no signs of sinusitis or renal disease, making granulomatosis with polyangiitis less likely.

stem: A 46-year-old man who works in a meat factory is found to have Q fever pneumonia. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: He requires high-dose penicillin for his treatment
His occupation is not important for the diagnosis
The organism is usually inhaled from infected particles
The organism responsible is Coxiella pneumoniae
There are never any long-term sequelae of the disease
explanation:
The organism is usually inhaled from infected particles
Coxiella burnetii infection is acquired through contact with animals. The organism is very resistant to drying and is inhaled from infected particles. A chest radiograph might show multilobar consolidation.

He requires high-dose penicillin for his treatment
He requires high-dose penicillin for his treatment is incorrect. Treatment is with prolonged courses of tetracyclines.

The organism responsible is Coxiella pneumoniae
The organism responsible is Coxiella pneumoniae is incorrect. Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents with sudden left-sided pleuritic chest pain while working on a house clearance. He is usually fit and well, has no significant medical problems and takes no medication. On examination his respiratory rate is 16 bpm, his BP is 125/82 mmHg, and pulse is 85 bpm and regular. He is in pain, although breath sounds are normal on auscultation. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 134 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 x 10 9/l Platelets 201 × 10 9/l 150–400 x 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Chest X-Ray 1 cm left-sided pneumothorax O 2 saturation 98% on air Which of the following is the correct way to manage him?
options: Discharge with analgesia and review in clinic in approximately 2 weeks
explanation:
Discharge with analgesia and review in clinic in approximately 2 weeks
This patient has a minimal pneumothorax and his pain should settle with adequate analgesia. As such it is appropriate to discharge him with review in clinic in approximately 2 weeks. Of course he should be warned to return as soon as possible if shortness of breath or pain worsens.

Admit for overnight observation
Admit for overnight observation is incorrect. This patient has a minimal pneumothorax and his pain should settle with adequate analgesia. As such it is appropriate to discharge him with review in clinic in approximately 2 weeks. Of course he should be warned to return as soon as possible if shortness of breath or pain worsens.

Attempt percutaneous aspiration
Attempt percutaneous aspiration is incorrect. In the event the pneumothorax was > 2 cm in size, aspiration would be the initial management of choice.

Discharge with review after 12 h
Discharge with review after 12 h is incorrect. This patient has a minimal pneumothorax and his pain should settle with adequate analgesia. As such it is appropriate to discharge him with review in clinic in approximately 2 weeks. Of course he should be warned to return as soon as possible if shortness of breath or pain worsens.

Insert chest drain
Insert chest drain is incorrect. In the event the pneumothorax was > 2 cm in size, chest drain insertion may be considered following a failed aspiration.

stem: A 59-year-old man with a recent CABG some 3 months earlier presents to the clinic for review. His main complaint is shortness of breath on exercise, and particularly on lying flat in bed. His operation is thought to have gone well and he has no residual angina. Medication includes ramipril 10 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg and atorvastatin 20 mg. On examination he looks well, his BP is 123/72 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular; his BMI is 31. His chest is clear on auscultation. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 5.6 × 10 9/l 4–11 x 10 9/l Platelets 178 × 10 9/l 150–400 x 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Vital capacity 88% of predicted, falls to 55% of predicted on lying down Which of the following is the most likely cause of his shortness of breath?
explanation:
Diaphragmatic palsy
The most striking feature of the scenario is the fall in vital capacity on moving to the supine position. Although some reduction is seen in obese patients because of abdominal pressure, it is nothing like as great as that seen here, meaning that the only possible diagnosis is diaphragmatic palsy, most likely as a result of the recent surgery.

Heart failure
Heart failure is incorrect. Heart failure is unlikely in the presence of normal findings on auscultation, such as those described in the scenario.

Obesity
Obesity is incorrect. The most striking feature of the scenario is the fall in vital capacity on moving to the supine position. Whilst some reduction is seen in obese patients because of abdominal pressure, it is nothing like as great as that seen here, meaning that the only possible diagnosis is diaphragmatic palsy, most likely as a result of the recent surgery.

Pulmonary fibrosis
Pulmonary fibrosis is incorrect. Pulmonary fibrosis is unlikely in the presence of normal findings on auscultation, such as those described in the scenario.

Renal artery stenosis
Renal artery stenosis is incorrect. Renal artery stenosis is unlikely in the presence of a normal creatinine.

stem: A 35-year-old woman visits her GP complaining of a dry, non-productive cough and lethargy. There has been slow weight loss over the past few months and there is a nodular rash on her shins. Blood testing reveals mild hypercalcaemia, a non-specific increase in immunoglobulins, normochromic normocytic anaemia and a raised serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) level. A chest X-ray reveals bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Tuberculin skin testing is negative. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is most common in young women and the UK prevalence is approximately 19 per 100 000 of the population. It is a multisystem granulomatous disorder. 50% present with respiratory symptoms or abnormalities on chest X-ray. 10% of cases are associated with erythema nodosum. 25% of cases are associated with uveitis. 10% of established cases are associated with hypercalcaemia. A definitive diagnosis is usually obtained via transbronchial biopsy in over 90% of cases. The disease severity varies among racial groups, and it is more severe in black populations. Treatment with corticosteroids is usual practice for severe disease or persistent changes on chest X-ray, but mortality in the UK from sarcoidosis is probably less than 5%.

stem: A 22-year-old private from the local army base is brought to the Emergency Department for review. He has suffered from pleuritic chest pain, a dry cough and shortness of breath over the past 2–3 weeks, and is now complaining of persistent tiredness and finds it difficult even to do the simplest tasks because of confusion/mental slowing. He is fit and well with no previous medical history. On examination he is pyrexial 38.4°C, his BP is 122/72 mmHg; pulse is 85/min and regular. There are signs of right-sided consolidation. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 135 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 13.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 203 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 132 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 95 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 180 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Chest X-Ray Right middle lobe consolidation Which of the following is the most likely underlying organism?
explanation:
Mycoplasma
Mycoplasma occurs in epidemics and risk, therefore, is increased among those who live in institutions, such as members of the armed forces who live in barracks. It also occurs more commonly in the 5–20 years population. The gradual onset of symptoms fits best with mycoplasma as the underlying diagnosis. Other associations with mycoplasma potentially include acute hepatitis, idiopathic thrombocytopaenic purpura (ITP), transverse myelitis, arthritis and Stevens–Johnson syndrome. Mycoplasma is sensitive to macrolide antibiotics, so a standard empirical regimen of co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin is appropriate in this situation.

Klebsiella pneumoniae
Klebsiella pneumoniae is incorrect. Klebsiella pneumoniae causes a cavitating pneumonia, which occurs more frequently in patients with a history of alcoholism.

Pneumocystis jirovecii
Pneumocystis jirovecii is incorrect. Pneumocystis jirovecii occurs in immunocompromised patients and we have no evidence this patient is immunocompromised; it is also associated with generalised ‘fluffy’ shadowing rather than the lobar pneumonia seen here.

Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is incorrect. Staphylococcal pneumonia usually occurs post influenza and is, like Klebsiella, associated with cavitation.

Streptococcus pneumoniae
Streptococcus pneumoniae is incorrect. Pneumococcus is a differential here, but the sub-acute onset would be unusual with respect to presentation.

stem: A 62-year-old smoker with a 2-day history of cough and fever is admitted with a diagnosis of left-sided pneumonia and left-sided pleural effusion up to the 6th intercostal space. Pleural fluid is aspirated and sent for tests. Which one of the following is an indication for inserting a chest drain?
explanation:
Pleural fluid pH < 7.2
Pleural effusions should be drained: When the fluid is infected When the pH is < 7.2 When a Gram stain shows the presence of organisms When the fluid is frankly purulent When clinical improvement is slow despite antibiotic therapy

Bloodstained pleural fluid
Bloodstained pleural fluid is incorrect. This is not an indication for insertion of a chest drain.

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents to the Emergency Department with a severe asthma attack. What is the most important therapy to relieve her bronchoconstriction?
explanation:
Salbutamol
The actions of β-agonists in asthma result from the stimulation of β-adrenoreceptors that are located in the airways, on airway epithelium, and in submucosal glands, airway and vascular smooth muscle. Beta-adrenergic receptors in the airways are entirely β 2, with the exception of some ß 1-receptors on submucosal glands. Beta 2-agonists can influence airway function through several mechanisms: Relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle by a direct effect on ß2-receptors Inhibition of mast-cell mediator release Enhanced mucociliary clearance Inhalation of a β 2-agonist by a patient with asthma increases airway calibre and reduces airway hyper- responsiveness. Beta 2-agonists also cause tachycardia and increased cardiac output, systemic vasodilatation and increased muscle blood flow. The tachycardia and increased cardiac output are the results of both stimulation of cardiac β-adrenoreceptors and a reflex response to peripheral vasodilatation. In addition, β 2- agonists cause tremor and have metabolic actions, of which hypokalaemia is probably the only potentially important clinical effect.

stem: A 61-year-old man presents to the Respiratory Clinic with a 6-month history of breathlessness. He has a history of rheumatoid arthritis and is taking methotrexate and prednisolone. He has a smoking history of 80 pack-years. On examination, he has a body mass index of 33 kg/m 2 and rheumatoid changes in his hands and multiple rheumatoid nodules. There are mild basal crepitations on auscultation of the left lung base. Investigations show a haemoglobin 101 g/l (normal value 115–155 g/l). Lung function tests reveal the following: Forced expiratory volume in one second: 78% predicted Forced vital capacity: 79% predicted Transfer capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide: 48% predicted Carbon monoxide transfer coefficient: 92% predicted Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Increased body mass index
This patient has breathlessness secondary to increased BMI. The correction of transfer capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide for lung volumes (the carbon monoxide transfer coefficient) suggest that this restriction is extrathoracic. Causes of this include increased body mass index, chest wall deformity and Chat neuromuscular with dysfunction of the chest wall.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis comes to the clinic for review. Recently she has been suffering from increased shortness of breath. She takes diclofenac and methotrexate for her arthritis. Other history of note includes smoking of ten cigarettes per day. On examination, her blood pressure is 145/82 mmHg and she is mildly clubbed. On auscultation there are inspiratory crackles throughout both lung fields. Investigation: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 122 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 5.6 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 200 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 139 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Anti-GBM antibodies Negative Forced Expiratory Volume in the first second (FEV 1) 84% Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) 81% Gas transfer coefficient (Kco) Reduced pO 2 7.8 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa pCO 2 3.5 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Methotrexate pneumonitis
The lung function picture, coupled with bibasal crackles and the patient taking a medication known to be capable of causing pneumonitis is consistent with methotrexate pneumonitis. Management includes cessation of methotrexate, cessation of smoking and supplemental oxygen therapy. Corticosteroids may also be of value. Other drugs which can lead to pulmonary fibrosis include bleomycin, busulfan, amiodarone, gold, penicillamine, crack cocaine and heroin.

Asthma
Asthma is incorrect. Asthma would be associated with bilateral wheeze rather than crackles and obstructive spirometry with a likely normal Kco.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is incorrect. Although this woman smokes, the forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1) is not disproportionately reduced, so fibrosis rather than obstruction is the more likely cause.

stem: A 68-year-old man with bronchiectasis is found to have acid-fast bacilli in his sputum. The microbiology report suggests that this might be an opportunistic or atypical mycobacterium. Which of the following is the least likely infectious agent?
explanation:
Mycobacterium leprae
Mycobacterium leprae is the causative organism of leprosy so is not the most likely cause of the presentation described. The other choices offered, are incorrect in the context of the question asked - these organisms are all ‘opportunistic’ mycobacteria, ie they can colonise structurally abnormal lung, for example in patients with: Cavitary disease Bronchiectasis Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease Cystic fibrosis Such patients might not always require treatment. However, if treatment is required, then it is usually for longer than the standard 6 months needed to treat pulmonary tuberculosis.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-month history of a cough and breathlessness which he says has progressively worsened with the production of blood-streaked sputum. He also reports feeling lethargic. There is no past medical history of note and he smokes 15 cigarettes per day. On examination, he has a blood pressure of 125/80 mmHg and a heart rate of 101 bpm and regular. There are bilateral crackles on auscultation. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 99 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 12.3 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 156 × 10 9/l 150–450 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5 mmol/l Creatinine 245 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 66 mm/hour 0–22 mm/hour Which of the following investigations will confirm the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies
This patient has anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease. Patients present with pulmonary haemorrhage and a rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, with linear deposition of antibodies along the GBM. Bilateral crackles and reduced haemoglobin levels also raise suspicion of pulmonary haemorrhage and raised creatinine levels indicate renal impairment. Serological testing for anti-GBM antibodies from the kidney should be performed to reach a diagnosis. Steroids, other immunosuppressant drugs and plasmapheresis are all used to control renal disease and are also helpful in treating pulmonary haemorrhage. Patients should not smoke and should avoid hydrocarbon exposure.

Acid-fast bacilli
Miliary tuberculosis could potentially present with the symptoms described in this history. Absence of classical infective symptoms, however, such as fevers, night sweats and purulent sputum, makes vasculitis a more likely diagnosis.

Computed tomography pulmonary angiography
The clinical examination and laboratory investigation findings, along with the presence of kidney disease, are not in keeping with pulmonary embolism. Although haemoptysis is a feature of pulmonary embolism, clinical examination of the chest is usually normal making computed tomography pulmonary angiography inappropriate here.

Spirometry
Spirometry is used in respiratory disease to investigate patients with an obstructive or a restrictive pattern of breathing. It is not, however, used in the diagnosis of vasculitic diseases such as anti-GBM disease.

Urinary legionella antigen
The two-month history of symptoms makes pneumonia an unlikely cause of this patient’s symptoms. Haemoptysis in legionella pneumonia is uncommon and legionella pneumonia is not directly associated with kidney disease.

stem: A 45 year old woman is referred by the GP to the respiratory care clinic with shortness of breath of unknown origin. Spirometry results: KCO 60%, FEV1/FVC 90%. Which of the following is most likely to be the underlying cause of these pulmonary function test results?
explanation:
A Sarcoidosis A FEV1/FVC of 90% indicates a restrictive cause. All the above diseases are evidenced by a restrictive pattern, except bronchiectasis which can result in an obstructive pattern. Only sarcoidosis would reduce the transfer coefﬁcient as there is damage to the alveolar cells themselves. Other conditions where a reduction in KCO is reduced include those such is idiopathic pulmonary ﬁbrosis, where there is also loss of alveolar function. D Pneumonectomy Pneumonectomy is most likely to have been performed for chronic bronchiectasis or lung cancer, both of which would be unusual in a 45-year-old woman and wouldn’t be expected to impact on transfer factor in the remaining lung. B Severe kyphoscoliosis Abnormalities of the thoracic cage lead to a reduction in available lung volume for gas exchange but don’t impact on the transfer coefﬁcient. C Muscular dystrophy Similar to kyphoscoliosis, muscular dystrophy can lead to a restrictive lung pattern but doesn’t impact on gas transfer.

E Bronchiectasis Bronchiectasis produces an obstructive lung pattern on pulmonary function testing.

stem: A 29-year-old breathless Afro-Caribbean woman is referred by the ophthalmologists with anterior uveitis and a suspected diagnosis of sarcoidosis. She admits to suffering increased shortness of breath and a dry cough for up to a year. Which of the following clinical features is most strongly associated with sarcoidosis?
options: A slowly worsening picture of breathlessness with no periods of improvement
Decreased gas-transfer factor (DLCO) with decreased gas-transfer coefficient (KCO)
explanation:
Decreased gas-transfer factor (DLCO) with decreased gas-transfer coefficient (KCO)
Decreased gas-transfer factor (DLCO) with decreased gas-transfer coefficient (KCO) is correct. Decreased gas transfer factor (DLCO) accompanied by elevated gas transfer coefficient (KCO) is characteristic of extrathoracic restriction and not of intrapulmonary restriction which sarcoidosis would be – both are usually decreased in intrapulmonary sarcoidosis.

A slowly worsening picture of breathlessness with no periods of improvement
A slowly worsening picture of breathlessness with no periods of improvement is incorrect. Spontaneous remission of respiratory symptoms is not uncommon and might allow a ‘wait and see’ policy to be adopted at the outset before embarking on immunosuppressive therapy.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with acute asthma. She has had a cough and progressively worsening symptoms over the past 3 days. This will be her fourth hospital admission in recent years and she has had two previous stays on the Intensive Care Unit. On admission to the department you note that she is drowsy and has a pulse of 95/min, poor respiratory effort and bilateral poor air entry. Which of the following biochemical features on 40% oxygen would best fit with a near fatal attack?
explanation:
Paco2 7 kPa, Pao2 7 kPa, pH 7.18
This lady has a life-threatening exacerbation of her asthma. Patients with life-threatening asthma are hypercapnic and hypoxic, with an acidosis, and are at severe risk of death. Continuous nebuliser therapy with salbutamol, intravenous hydrocortisone and urgent ITU assessment are essential. Evidence from a Cochrane analysis also indicates that intravenous magnesium might be of value as acute therapy. It is essential that such patients are kept in hospital for at least 5 days, as sudden death due to asthma in this patient group is documented to occur some 2–5 days after this type of acute admission.

Paco2 4 kPa, Pao2 11 kPa pH 7.37
Paco 2 4 kPa, Pao 2 11 kPa pH 7.37 is incorrect. This lady has life-threatening asthma which is associated with respiratory acidosis, which is not shown by these gas results.

stem: A 19-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of left-sided niggling pleuritic chest pain. She reports that this was not limiting her activity, but that she ‘thought she needed to get it checked out’. She has no previous respiratory history of note and her only medication is the oral contraceptive pill. Her respiratory rate is 12/min, she is not cyanotic and her oxygen saturations are 98% on room air. The chest X-ray shows a 1.2-cm rim of air, reported as being consistent with a pneumothorax abutting the wall of the left lung. Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan?
options: Discharge and review in Medical Outpatients
Insert a formal chest drain with suction
Insert a formal chest drain without suction
explanation:
Discharge and review in Medical Outpatients
This woman should be discharged and reviewed in Medical Outpatients with a repeat chest X-ray. British Thoracic Society (BTS) guidelines on the management of pneumothorax with minimal symptoms indicate that discharge with appropriate follow-up is appropriate. It should be stressed to patients, however, that if they develop any increase in breathlessness at all they should return to the hospital immediately.

Insert a formal chest drain with suction
Insert a formal chest drain with suction is incorrect. Chest drain insertion is only required for primary spontaneous pneumothoraces in patients who are breathless and/or the rim of air is > 2 cm and needle aspiration has failed. Suction should only be instituted after discussion/consultation with the specialist thoracic team.

stem: A 18-year-old boy is brought to the Emergency Department after a fire in his parents’ house. He inhaled a lot of smoke and has a hoarse voice, stridor and burned nasal hairs. Owing to deterioration in his peak flow rate and arterial blood gases, he has been intubated, ventilated and transferred to the intensive care unit where his condition is now stable. In terms of investigation, what is the definitive investigation in assessing this boy’s condition?
explanation:
Bronchoscopy
Inhalation of hot smoke can burn the upper airways and contributes significantly to deaths due to fires. Upper airway obstruction due to heat injury and mucosal swelling usually develops within 24 h of exposure, but stenosis due to scarring can develop later. A hoarse voice, stridor, severe conjunctivitis, burned nasal hairs and falling peak flow values all suggest significant upper airway damage. Bronchoscopy is then the best tool to establish whether there is significant oedema or mucosal ulceration obstructing the airways.

Chest X-ray
Chest X-ray is incorrect. Chest X-ray is not the preferred investigation for a patient who has been exposed to severe smoke inhalation.

stem: Which of the following is the best predictor for obstructive sleep apnoea?
explanation:
Neck size
Neck size is the best predictor of obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA), with a size of more than 43 cm (17 inches) being associated with an increased risk in men (16 inches) in women. The mass loading from the obese or muscular neck overwhelms the residual dilator muscle action of the pharynx when the patient is asleep, causing airway obstruction and subsequent apnoea. Patients might also have a small or set-back mandible, which predisposes them to OSA as well. Typically, patients also have upper body obesity, which is the typical male fat pattern.

Abdominal girth
Abdominal girth is incorrect. Abdominal girth is not as good a predictor of OSA as neck size.

Uvulopalatal distance
Uvulopalatal distance is incorrect. Uuvlopalatal distance is not as good a predictor of OSA as neck size.

stem: A 26-year-old woman arrives in the UK from Australia. A few days later she presents to hospital with pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. She is not on the oral contraceptive pill and has no family or personal history of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE). A pulmonary embolus is confirmed radiologically and she is started on warfarin. How long would you continue warfarin therapy in these circumstances?
explanation:
3 months
This young woman’s only risk factor is the long-haul flight, which is only a temporary risk factor. That being said, this would be considered a provoked PE, as such 3 months’ anti-coagulation is sufficient. Current recommendations updates by NICE (2020) regarding mangmant of provoked PE suggests to consider stopping anticoagulation treatment 3 months (3 to 6 months for people with active cancer) after a provoked DVT or PE ( if the provoking factor is no longer present and the clinical course has been uncomplicated. If anticoagulation treatment is stopped, the patient should be givee advice about the risk of recurrence regarding signs and symptoms to look out for, and who to contact if this occurs (during normal working hours and out of hours services).

stem: A 67-year-old patient with lung cancer complains of a cough and has difficulty breathing. He has swelling of his face, neck, upper body and arms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Superior vena cava syndrome
Superior vena cava syndrome (SVCS) is a collection of symptoms caused by the partial blockage of the vein that carries blood from the head, neck, chest and arms to the heart. Symptoms include difficulty breathing, coughing and swelling of the face, neck, upper body and arms. In rare instances, patients might describe hoarseness, chest pain, difficulty swallowing and coughing up blood. Physical signs of SVCS include swelling of the neck or chest veins, collection of fluid in the face or arms and rapid breathing. The syndrome of superior vena cava obstruction can be relieved in about 80% of cases, but these patients usually require a more conventional course of 5–10 fractions of radiotherapy. Some centres now use SVC stents for symptomatic relief, placed by an interventional radiologist.

stem: A 21-year-old trainee nursery nurse presents to the Emergency Department acutely unwell. She has had a cough and has become progressively worse, now with severe shortness of breath. Her flatmate reports that she has become unsteady on her feet over the past few days. There is no important past history of note. She smokes 20 cigarettes per day. There is a striking rash over her scalp, face and trunk, with a mixed crop of vesicles and pustules that is suggestive of chickenpox. On examination she has bilateral cerebellar ataxia. Which diagnosis best fits with this clinical picture?
options: Acute varicella zoster virus infection with central nervous system and lung involvement
Generalised viral infection of unknown origin
explanation:
Acute varicella zoster virus infection with central nervous system and lung involvement
Although uncommon, lung involvement with acute chickenpox infection can occur. The pneumonitis generally begins around 1–6 days after the appearance of the skin eruption and is more common in young adults, with cigarette smokers being particularly at risk. This woman was not exposed to chickenpox as a child, and exposure has now occurred due to her work as a nursery nurse. The chest X-ray normally shows diffuse lung changes throughout both lung fields, but symptoms are commonly worse than the X-ray picture would suggest. Central nervous system involvement is rarer, occurring in around 1 in 1000 cases, and presenting with acute truncal ataxia. Treatment is with intravenous aciclovir, with support in a high-dependency or intensive-care setting if needed.

Generalised viral infection of unknown origin
Generalised viral infection of unknown origin is incorrect. There is a clear description of chicken pox in this case.

stem: The parents (both cystic fibrosis gene carriers) of a child with cystic fibrosis (CF) come to see you for advice after reading about CF on the internet. Which of the following bits of information from their internet printout is correct?
options: Burkholderia cenocepacia is a significant pathogen
Pneumothorax occurs in approximately 25% of patients
The gene defect is a mutation on chromosome 6
The probability of a further child being affected is 50%
There is evidence of pulmonary disease at birth
explanation:
Burkholderia cenocepacia is a significant pathogen
Burkholderia cenocepacia infection is associated with increased mortality and is a contraindication to lung transplantation.

Pneumothorax occurs in approximately 25% of patients
Pneumothorax occurs in approximately 25% of patients is incorrect. Pneumothorax is seen in up to 5% of patients over 10 years of age and approximately 50% recur.

The probability of a further child being affected is 50%
The probability of a further child being affected is 50% is incorrect. The probability of a child born to two carriers being affected is 25% as CF is an autosomal recessive condition.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents to the Emergency medical take as a GP referral. He has had a non-productive niggling cough over the past few weeks, and most recently severe headaches and swelling of his face and arms. He smokes 20 cigarettes per day and has done so for 40 years. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 155/85 mmHg; you notice dilated veins over his arms and upper chest, his face looks plethoric, and there is evidence of oedema. Auscultation of the chest reveals poor air entry and wheeze consistent with COPD. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 138 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 9.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 188 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 112 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Chest X-Ray Large right hilar mass Right hilar mass suspicious of bronchial CT scan carcinoma,leading to SVC compression Which of the following is the definitive intervention for the SVC compression?
explanation:
Stenting
This patient has Superior Vena Cava (SVC) obstruction as a result of extrinsic compression from an underlying bronchial carcinoma. A NICE review has concluded that stenting offers a greater degree of success in terms of relief of symptomsresolving SVC obstruction than radiotherapy, and is therefore, the intervention of choice here.

Chemotherapy
Chemotherapy is incorrect. Chemotherapy may be a first-line option in cases of histologically proven small-cell cancer.

Corticosteroids
Corticosteroids is incorrect. Corticosteroids are most useful where the cause of compression is an underlying haematological malignancy.

Radiotherapy
Radiotherapy is incorrect. Radiotherapy may be an option later; if radiotherapy is used initially then stenting becomes significantly more difficult due to local fibrosis.

Surgical bypass
Surgical bypass is incorrect. Surgical bypass is only really an option for benign tumours, and there is little evidence to indicate that it confers any better benefit than stenting.

stem: Which one of the following conditions is most likely to be associated with a decreased diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO)?
explanation:
Pulmonary embolism
DLCO, the diffusing capacity in the lung for carbon monoxide, is decreased in any condition that reduces the effective alveolar surface area or affects the alveolar membrane. Examples include pulmonary embolism and emphysema, in which the alveolar surface area is reduced.

Acute poliomyelitis
Acute poliomyelitis is incorrect. This will not affect DLCO.

Dehydration
Dehydration is incorrect. This will not affect DLCO.

Polycythaemia
Polycythaemia is incorrect. This will increase DLCO.

stem: A 48-year-old man is reviewed in the Respiratory Clinic. He complains of increased shortness of breath over the past 6 months, and admits in fact to reduced exercise tolerance for the past 1–2 years. He has a dry cough that is unproductive of sputum and his GP has tried salbutamol and beclomethasone inhalers with little effect. Past history of note is that he keeps two parrots, which he tells you are currently healthy. On examination his temperature is 37.2 °C; pulse is 70/min and regular; BP is 122/72 mmHg. There is wheeze on auscultation. You suspect extrinsic allergic alveolitis (EAA). Which of the following would be most consistent with EAA due to parrot antigen exposure?
explanation:
Bilateral upper lobe fibrosis
Bilateral upper lobe fibrosis is the classical pattern of pulmonary changes seen with EAA.

Chlamydia antibody positivity
Chlamydia antibody positivity is incorrect. Chlamydia antibody positive merely indicates prior exposure, and is not a marker of EAA.

Elevated IgE
Elevated IgE is incorrect. Elevated IgE may be seen for a number of reasons, eg asthma, ABPA and is not necessarily related to EAA.

stem: A 50-year-old lawyer attended a clinic with a 15-day history of dyspnoea and weight loss over the past 6 months. He reports his sputum to be clear. On examination, a diagnosis of pleural effusion was made that was confirmed on chest X-ray. A pleural tap revealed few red cells and lymphocytes and a protein level of 40 g/l. What should be the next investigative step?
explanation:
Computed tomography of the thorax
BTS guidelines from 2010 recommend contrast computed tomography (CT) as the most appropriate next investigation here. A CT is required to demonstrate the architecture of any underlying effusion and contribute both to diagnosing the cause and assist in possible drain placement.

Bronchoscopy
Bronchoscopy is incorrect. Bronchoscopy would only be indicated if investigations such as contrast CT and pleural biopsy were non-diagnostic and a lung mass amenable to bronchoscopic sampling was seen on CT.

Sputum examination for tubercle bacilli
Sputum examination for tubercle bacilli is incorrect. It is justifiable to test sputum for tuberculosis in this case, but this is not a history highly suggestive of TB and the next most appropriate investigation is CT.

stem: A 50-year-old hospital porter is an inpatient on the Surgical Ward after a routine cholecystectomy. He normally smokes 30 cigarettes a day. Four days after the operation he begins to spike fevers and expectorate green phlegm. A chest X-ray shows lobar consolidation in his right lung. He has oxygen saturations of 85% on air. He is started on antibiotics. Which one of the following treatments would you choose?
explanation:
Cephalosporin and an aminoglycoside
This patient has a hospital-acquired pneumonia, the third most common hospital-acquired infection after urinary tract infections and wound infections. As these pneumonias occur in hospital the pathogens involved are very different from those that cause community-acquired pneumonia. Gram-negative organisms are far more common, owing to: Colonisation of the oropharynx by Gram-negative bacilli, which is very common in hospitalised patients, who have often been on broad-spectrum antibiotics already Increased risk of micro-aspiration of nasopharyngeal secretions Increased likelihood of immunodepression. Antibiotics that will cover such organisms should therefore be started, most commonly as combination therapy. A third-generation cephalosporin with an aminoglycoside is the current British Thoracic Society Chat (BTS) with recommendation.

stem: A morbidly obese 36-year-old man presents for review. His main reason for attendance is that his wife is concerned about his loud snoring and the fact that he stops breathing during the night for periods of up to 8–10 s, followed by coughing, snoring or waking. Recently he has become hypertensive and is also on treatment for impotence. His 24-h urinary free cortisol level is normal. Which diagnosis best fits this picture?
explanation:
Obstructive sleep apnoea
Symptoms of sleep apnoea include: Memory impairment Daytime somnolence Grossly disrupted sleep pattern Decreased libido Systemic hypertension Further investigation should involve thyroid function testing to rule out hypothyroidism, and assessment of the uvula and tonsils to rule out mechanical obstruction that might be amenable to surgery. Diagnosis of sleep apnoea is made using overnight oximetry.

stem: A 33-year-old man is found to have strongly positive Aspergillus precipitins in his blood and complains of a cough with intermittent bloody sputum. He has a business working as a builder, particularly involved in renovating farm houses and barns. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Type I hypersensitivity to Aspergillus fumigatus
explanation:
Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis
Aspergillus precipitins (IgG antibodies to Aspergillus) are typically found in chronic pulmonary aspergillosis (which can include the presence of an aspergilloma). The history of potential significant Aspergillus exposure (eg from mouldy hay in barns) alongside cough and haemoptysis with the presence of raised precipitins to Aspergillus make this diagnosis likely.

Invasive aspergillosis
Invasive aspergillosis is incorrect. Invasive aspergillosis occurs in immunocompromised patients and is associated with severe respiratory illness including respiratory failure and severe sepsis. This condition has a high mortality, even with appropriate treatment with antifungals.

stem: A 59-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease is admitted for observation the evening after a house fire. He is thought to have inhaled a significant amount of smoke. The nurses put out a critical care call as he has deteriorated rapidly with increasing shortness of breath and hypoxia. He is intubated and ventilated by the ITU registrar. On examination his BP is 135/72 mmHg, and pulse is 88/min and regular. Which of the following favours a diagnosis of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)?
options: Fluid in the horizontal fissure on chest X-ray
explanation:
Increased elastic recoil
The answer is Increased elastic recoil (Option D). ARDS is associated with increased elastic recoil.

Fluid in the horizontal fissure on chest X-ray
Fluid in the horizontal fissure on chest X-ray (Option A) is incorrect. Fluid in the horizontal fissure on chest X-ray implies fluid overload and an increased pulmonary artery wedge pressure. ARDS is associated with low pulmonary artery wedge pressure.

High pulmonary artery wedge pressure
High pulmonary artery wedge pressure (Option C) is incorrect. ARDS is associated with low pulmonary artery wedge pressure.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with primary pulmonary hypertension (PPH) diagnosed 1 year earlier, currently managed with bosentan and sildenafil, comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. She has had increased shortness of breath over the past few weeks despite dual therapy for pulmonary hypertension. On examination her BP is 142/82 mmHg; pulse is 85/min and regular. Her chest appears clear; there is bilateral pitting oedema of the ankles. O 2 sats at rest are low at 91%. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her shortness of breath?
explanation:
Intra-pulmonary shunting
A number of mechanisms are postulated as contributing to the hypoxia seen in primary pulmonary hypertension (PPH). These include shunting and reduced diffusion capacity due to arterial fibromuscular hyperplasia.

Euvolaemic pulmonary oedema
Euvolaemic pulmonary oedema is incorrect. There are no signs on examination of pulmonary oedema.

Low cardiac output
Low cardiac output is incorrect. Given that this patient’s systemic BP is essentially normal at 142/82 mmHg, low cardiac output is unlikely as a cause of hypoxia here.

stem: At the time of discharge of a 75-year-old non-smoker with known chronic obstructive pulmonary disease it was decided that, according to the criteria, he should be having long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) at home. Which of the following options is not considered as a lone criterion for LTOT (where FVC = forced vital capacity; FEV 1 = forced expiratory volume in 1 second)?
options: Arterial blood gas showing PaO 2 7.2 kPa
Arterial blood gas showing PaO 2 7.8 kPa with pulmonary hypertension
Arterial blood gas showing PaO 2 7.2 kPa with PaCO 2 7.2 kPa
Arterial blood gas showing PaO 2 7.8 kPa PaCO 2 7.5 kPa with pulmonary hypertension
explanation:
Cor pulmonale
Cor pulmonale in the absence of hypoxia may have a primary cardiological underlying cause and therefore may not require home oxygen therapy. An MRC trial showed that if PaO 2 was maintained > 8.0 kPa for > 15 hours a day, the 3-year survival improved by 50%. UK Department of Health guidelines suggest that long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) should be provided for: Patients who are clinically stable and non-smokers with PaO 2 < 7.3 kPa, FEV 1 ≤ 1.5 l and FVC < 2 l despite maximal treatment. These values should be stable on two occasions more than three weeks apart. Patients with a Pao 2 of 7.3–8.0 kPa and pulmonary hypertension showing right ventricular hypertrophy and a loud S2 and features of cor pulmonale.

stem: A 49-year-old man with unexplained cough undergoes bronchoscopy and transbronchial biopsy. Histology shows evidence of neutrophil infiltrate, but there is no evidence of granulomas. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polyarteritis nodosa
Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) affects medium-sized arteries and the infiltrate is composed of neutrophils; granulomas are absent. However, PAN affecting the lungs is rare but histologically is the best answer here as it is the only option that does not give granulomas.

Berylliosis
Berylliosis is incorrect. Berylliosis shows features similar to those of sarcoid. Both are characterised by non- necrotising granulomata distributed in the parenchyma and along the lymphatic routes.

Histoplasmosis
Histoplasmosis is incorrect. Histoplasmosis is the most common fungal infection in North America and has both acute (usually self-limiting) and chronic (affecting people with previous lung disease) forms. Granulomas will be seen on biopsy.

stem: A young adult was referred because of cough and shortness of breath. Extrinsic allergic alveolitis was diagnosed. Apart from reduction of exposure to the allergen, which other therapy is most likely to be successful?
explanation:
Corticosteroids
Once a firm diagnosis has been made, the management centres on reduction of further exposure to the allergen. Ideally, affected individuals change their relevant working, domestic and recreational environment completely, but this can mean a profound loss of income or great expense and is often an unrealistic goal. It also cannot be fully justified on purely medical grounds because continued exposure does not inevitably lead to progressive disease. Affected individuals who continue to work in the occupation responsible for their disease can often reduce their exposure substantially by changing the pattern of their particular duties. An alternative is to use industrial respirators, which filter out 98–99% of respirable dust from the ambient air. These are especially valuable when exposures are intermittent and short, but they can be uncomfortably hot when worn for long periods or when the work is heavy, and so compliance with their use can be poor. When there is progressive disease, exposure should be stopped. This may involve a loss of earnings, and may entitle the affected worker to compensation. Some people with progressive disease refuse to change their occupation or hobby, and their physician must weigh the possible advantages of long-term corticosteroid therapy against the risks.

stem: A 72-year-old man with known severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is brought to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of nausea, vomiting and tremor. His normal therapy consists of nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, and oral theophylline. Which recently prescribed antibiotic could have led to the development of his symptoms?
explanation:
Ciprofloxacin
This is a ‘know it or you don’t’ question. Oral theophyllines can be used in the treatment of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). They have a number of important drug interactions. Commonly prescribed drugs that can increase serum theophylline levels include clarithromycin, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, oral contraceptives and allopurinol. Consideration should be given to reducing theophylline dose when these drugs are prescribed.

Amoxicillin
Amoxicillin is incorrect. Amoxicillin does not affect serum theophylline levels.

Co-amoxiclav
Co-amoxiclav is incorrect. Co-amoxiclav does not affect serum theophylline levels.

stem: You review a 71-year-old former boilermaker. He has had increasing shortness of breath and vague right-sided chest pain over the past few months. He has a history of smoking 30 cigarettes per day for 30 years. On examination, he appears to have a large right-sided pleural effusion. This is confirmed on chest X-ray. Pleural fluid evaluation reveals this to be an exudate and you suspect an underlying mesothelioma. Which of the following fit best with the pathophysiology of mesothelioma?
options: Cigarette smoking is a known primary risk factor
Drainage of pleural effusion is never associated with tumour seeding along the track
Loss of material from chromosome 22 is commonly seen in mesothelioma cell lines
Simian SV40 is the most common primary cause
Surgical cure is possible in 30% of cases
explanation:
Loss of material from chromosome 22 is commonly seen in mesothelioma cell lines
Loss of material from chromosome 22 is an abnormality commonly seen in mesothelioma, and it is thought that this may contain code for tumour suppressor genes.

Cigarette smoking is a known primary risk factor
Cigarette smoking is a known primary risk factor is incorrect. Exposure to asbestos is the primary risk factor associated with the development of mesothelioma. The role of cigarette smoking has been under much debate; a categorical link to increased risk of mesothelioma on top of asbestos exposure has not been proven.

Drainage of pleural effusion is never associated with tumour seeding along the track
Drainage of pleural effusion is never associated with tumour seeding along the track is incorrect. Tutorof Drainage pleural effusion may cause tumour seeding along the track.

stem: A 58-year-old man is referred by his GP with probable obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA). Which of the following features is most strongly associated with OSA?
explanation:
Daytime somnolence
Daytime somnolence is the predominant symptom of OSA.

Body mass index of 26 kg/m2
Body mass index of 26 kg/m 2 is incorrect. Obstructive sleep apnoea is associated with obesity (of which hypothyroidism is a cause) and sedatives such as alcohol.

Epworth sleepiness score of 6
Epworth sleepiness score of 6 is incorrect. The Epworth sleepiness score can be between 0 and 24 (the higher the score, the more sleepy the patient is) and 6/24 is low. A score of 11 or more is suggestive of OSA.

Normal blood pressure
Normal blood pressure is incorrect. OSA is associated with hypertension.

stem: After a tennis match, a thin 20-year-old woman complains of left-sided chest pain that radiates into her abdomen. The physical examination reveals reduced air entry at the left base of the lung with hyper-resonant percussion. The abdominal examination shows generalised tenderness. A few minutes later she develops cyanosis. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Tension pneumothorax
Tension pneumothorax occurs when the intrapleural pressure exceeds the atmospheric pressure throughout inspiration as well as expiration. It is thought to result from the operation of a one-way valve system, drawing air into the pleural space during inspiration and not allowing it out during expiration. The development of tension pneumothorax is often (but not always) heralded by a sudden deterioration in the cardiopulmonary status of the patient, which is related to impaired venous return, reduced cardiac output and hypoxaemia. The development of tension in a pneumothorax is not dependent on the size of the pneumothorax, and the clinical scenario of tension pneumothorax can correlate poorly with chest X-ray findings. The clinical status is striking. The patient rapidly becomes distressed with rapid, laboured respiration, cyanosis, sweating and tachycardia. It should be particularly suspected in people on mechanical ventilators or nasal non- invasive ventilation who suddenly deteriorate or develop EMD arrest, and is frequently missed in the intensive care unit setting.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is admitted with a history of recent upper respiratory tract infection and subsequent progressive lower-limb weakness. Examination confirms loss of her lower-limb reflexes and grade 4/5 power in her arms. Which of the following lung function tests would be most useful for assessing her respiratory muscle reserve?
explanation:
Forced vital capacity (FVC)
The history and examination findings suggest the onset of Guillain–Barré syndrome. The most important and reproducible bedside lung function test to perform in such a patient is the forced vital capacity (FVC). This will detect respiratory muscle involvement earlier than arterial blood gases or the peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR).

Flow–volume curves
Flow–volume curves is incorrect. This would not be as helpful; the most useful test for assessing her respiratory muscle reserve is forced vital capacity.

Forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1)
Forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1) is incorrect. This may well be normal; the most useful test for assessing her respiratory muscle reserve is forced vital capacity.

stem: You review a 26-year-old woman who has been admitted to the neurological ward for treatment. She complained of ascending symmetrical weakness and loss of sensation affecting both lower limbs. This began after a diarrhoeal illness. A diagnosis of Guillain– Barré syndrome was made. She is complaining to the nurses of increasing shortness of breath. You are aware that a deterioration in respiratory function can predict mortality. She is 50 kg in weight. FVC on admission was noted to be 1.5 l. You arrange for it to be checked again. What level of FVC would indicate the threshold for respiratory support?
explanation: D 1.0 l Deterioration in FVC is closely predictive of deterioration with opportunistic respiratory tract infection, and associated increased morbidity and mortality. Patients with Guillain–Barré syndrome should be monitored with regular spirometry. The threshold for increased respiratory intervention is said to be around 20 ml/kg FVC, which would put this at around 1 l in this patient. Minimal sedation and aggressive physiotherapy while on the Intensive Care Unit can serve to reduce the possibility of infection. Overall poor prognosis in Guillain–Barré is associated with rapid progression of symptoms, advanced age, prolonged ventilation (>1 month) and severe action potential reduction on neuromuscular testing. A 1.5 l 1.5 l corresponds to around 30 ml/kg FVC, which is above the recommended threshold for respiratory support. B 1.4 l 1.4 l is above the level where respiratory support is likely to be required, meaning that patients may be inappropriately admitted to the High-dependency Unit, putting pressure on bed space for other patients. C 1.3 l 1.3 l is around 30% above the level where respiratory support is likely to be required. E 0.6 l At 0.6 l FVC, type 2 respiratory failure and pneumonia are possible sequelae. Respiratory support should happen at the higher threshold of 1.0 l for FVC.

stem: A patient with lung cancer underwent radiotherapy 2 weeks ago. He now complains of a severe dry cough, increasing dyspnoea and tachypnoea. On examination there are local crepitations and his chest X-ray shows hazy consolidation that corresponds to the irradiation field. What is the most important therapy to relieve his symptoms?
explanation:
Corticosteroids
This patient presents with radiation pneumonitis. Symptoms begin within a few weeks of radiotherapy and can persist for weeks or months. They occur in 10–30% of patients following radiotherapy for lung cancer. A cough (which can be severe and can produce thick sputum) and breathlessness are the principal symptoms, but may be accompanied by fever of variable degree. In cases where symptoms are slight, no specific treatment is needed. However, in more severe disease, corticosteroids produce relief during the acute phase in most patients. Any response to corticosteroids occurs within 3–4 days, with clinical and radiographic improvement, and treatment should be continued for 3–4 weeks before tapering and stopping. Corticosteroids do not, however, influence the extent of subsequent pulmonary fibrosis. Symptomatic relief of cough and hypoxaemia by an opioid antitussive and oxygen supplementation may also be needed. Prevention offers the best means of control, and further development of methods to detect undue susceptibility and early disease may prove to be valuable in developing safer fractionating protocols.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with her 15-year-old son, who has recently been diagnosed with asthma. She has researched the pathology of asthma and has a number of questions about potential causative factors. Which of the following responses best describes the pathology of asthma?
options: Asthma occurs due to a combination of airway hyper-responsiveness, airflow limitation and airway
Asthma predominantly occurs due to airflow limitation
Asthma predominantly occurs due to airway hyper-responsiveness
Asthma predominantly occurs due to airway hyporesponsiveness
Asthma predominantly occurs due to airway inflammation
explanation:
Asthma occurs due to a combination of airway hyper-responsiveness, airflow limitation and airway
inflammation This is a ‘know it or you don’t’ question. In many Western countries the prevalence of asthma is increasing, particularly during the second decade of life, where it can affect up to 10–15% of the population. The pathogenesis can be described as having three components: Asthma is characterised by airflow limitation that is usually reversible spontaneously or with treatment, although later on in the disease there may be an irreversible component to airflow limitation. There is also airway hyper-responsiveness to a wide range of external stimuli. A predominantly eosinophilic pattern of inflammation occurs, with associated plasma exudates, oedema, mucus-plug formation, bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy and long-term epithelial damage.

stem: A 36-year-old primary schoolteacher who works in a deprived area of London presents with increasing shortness of breath accompanied by sudden-onset, right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She gives a history of influenza for a few days before this acute presentation and also says she suffered a pulmonary embolus 2 years ago while taking the contraceptive pill (and describes her pain as identical to that she experienced on that occasion). On further questioning it transpires that her mother had suffered from recurrent deep vein thrombosis. Arterial blood gases reveal a pO2 of 7.2 kPa on a non re-breather mask, with a pCO2 of 3.2 kPa. Her chest X- ray reveals a wedge-shaped area of consolidation affecting her right middle and lower lobes. The white blood cell count is normal. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Recurrent pulmonary embolism
The suspicion, given that this lady has had a previous pulmonary embolism while taking the oral contraceptive pill, is that she has an inherited disorder of clotting. It is crucial during the initial work-up to take extra samples for clotting studies before commencing heparin treatment. Predisposing factors for recurrent pulmonary embolism include: Antithrombin III deficiency Protein C deficiency Factor V Leiden mutation

stem: A 52-year-old patient presents with cough and is found to have a squamous lung carcinoma. He is quite sure that it is work related, he has worked in a chemical factory since leaving school. He smoked five cigarettes per day until he was aged 34, having started smoking at the age of 16. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Isocyanates
Isocyanates are a recognised risk factor for the development of non-small-cell lung cancer. Other aetiological factors include smoking, asbestos exposure and exposure to polycyclic hydrocarbons or the products of coal burning. Exposure to isocyanate fumes occurs in chemical workers, particularly those who work in the rubber industry, and this exposure is most likely to be associated with squamous-cell carcinoma of the bronchus. Most squamous-cell carcinomas present as obstructive lesions, which can manifest as infection. Around 10% of cases present with cavitating lesions, but widespread metastases occur relatively late.

Aromatic amines
Aromatic amines is incorrect. Aromatic amines are associated with bladder carcinoma.

Coal dust
Coal dust is incorrect. There is nothing in the history to suggest coal dust exposure.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with asthma is seen on the ward round. She was admitted the previous day with anaphylaxis due to latex exposure. She asks you about immunotherapy for anaphylaxis. What do you tell her about immunotherapy for anaphylaxis?
options: It takes 2 months to complete the treatment course
This gives patients protection against anaphylactic episodes for about 15 years
This is a universally safe treatment for anaphylaxis
This is a well-established treatment for all causes of anaphylaxis
This is useful in patients who cannot avoid latex exposure
explanation:
This is useful in patients who cannot avoid latex exposure
This is true and is an indication for immunotherapy.

This is a well-established treatment for all causes of anaphylaxis
This is a well-established treatment for all causes of anaphylaxis is incorrect. Allergen immunotherapy aims to desensitise a person to the allergen they are allergic to. It is useful in people who cannot avoid exposure to the allergen. It is only performed in a few centres but experience is increasing. It is not available for all types of anaphylaxis. Most common indications are severe hayfever and anaphylaxis to wasp stings. It cannot be used in people with chronic asthma because of the risks of bronchoconstriction, which should be explained to her as the reason why it would not be an appropriate measure for her.

stem: You review a 72-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), who asks about the provision of oxygen therapy at home. In which of the following settings have randomised controlled trials shown that long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) reduces mortality?
options: Cor pulmonale caused by chronic airflow obstruction
explanation:
Cor pulmonale caused by chronic airflow obstruction
Two controlled studies (in a mostly male population) indicated that life can be prolonged by the continuous delivery of 2 l/min of oxygen via nasal prongs to achieve saturations of greater than 90% for a large proportion of the day and night. Improvements in pulmonary artery hypertension were obtained in patients who used oxygen for more than 15 h/day, but mortality was only improved in patients who used oxygen for more than 18 h/day. Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) should therefore be considered in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and a forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1) of less than 1.5 l, an arterial partial pressure of oxygen (Pao 2) of less than 7.3 kPa and carboxyhaemoglobin of less than 3%. Although oxygen cylinders can be provided for intermittent use by patients for the relief of symptoms of breathlessness, they have no effect on prognosis.

Cystic fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis is incorrect. Although oxygen cylinders can be provided for intermittent use by patients for the relief of symptoms of breathlessness, they have no effect on prognosis.

stem: A breathless 70-year-old smoker presents with the following lung function tests Forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) 1.5 l (60%) Forced vital capacity (FVC) 1.8 l (55%) FEV1/FVC ratio 84% Total lung capacity (TLC) 66% predicted Residual volume (RV) 57% predicted Carbon monoxide transfer factor (Tlco) 55% predicted Transfer coefficient (Kco) 60% predicted What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
Interstitial lung disease
The lung function tests show a significant restrictive defect. Only interstitial lung disease or obesity can fit this picture. But given the decrease in Kco (ie after correcting for alveolar volumes), the most likely answer is interstitial lung disease.

stem: A 48-year-old builder working in the UK for over 5 years presents to your clinic with a 1-year history of wheeze and cough that is worse in the early hours of the morning. On direct questioning he admits to mild haemoptysis over the past few days with no increase or change in his sputum production, occasional mild night sweats and he has noticed a slight weight loss over the past few months due to decreased appetite. His past medical history includes previous alcohol excess and type 2 diabetes. A chest X-ray taken two years ago showed clear lung ﬁelds and no signs of previous lung pathology. Which of the following pathologies is the most likely cause of his haemoptysis?
explanation: C Semi-invasive aspergillosis This is a chronic indolent disease that affects people with mild immunosuppression, such as those with diabetes or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or those who abuse alcohol, are elderly or on prolonged steroid use. If left untreated there is a signiﬁcant associated mortality; however, it is difﬁcult to diagnose due to its slow progression both radiologically and clinically. Symptoms include cough, wheeze, bronchitis and constitutional symptoms, and about 15% present with haemoptysis. E Asthma exacerbation Night sweats and haemoptysis are not features of asthma exacerbation. A Aspergilloma This is a ball of fungus within a pre-existing cavity such as that caused by tuberculosis (TB). With a recent clear chest X-ray (2 years ago), this patient is unlikely to have any cavities in which an aspergilloma could reside. Furthermore, aspergillomas are usually asymptomatic but can cause weight loss, cough and haemoptysis, which can be massive and require emergency surgical excision. Oral antifungals can be given, but with limited success. B Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) This is an IgE and IgG reaction to Aspergillus sp. in asthmatics. The key criteria for diagnosis include a long history of asthma, skin-prick/IgE, positive/IgG precipitins to Aspergillus fumigates, central bronchiectasis, elevated total serum IgE, blood/sputum eosinophilia and pulmonary inﬁltrates. D Invasive aspergillosis This patient is not acutely unwell. This condition occurs in immunosuppressed individuals and is caused by haematogenous spread of the fungus, so prompt diagnosis and treatment are required to prevent a high mortality rate.

stem: A 35-year-old African female presents with a 6-months history of night sweats, shortness of breath on exertion and dry cough. She also gives a history of weight loss and arthralgia over the same period of time. She had been intermittently unwell for 1 year before the development of these symptoms. She recalls a painful rash on her shins 3 months ago, which resolved spontaneously. She gives no history of eye problems, polyuria or polydipsia. She denies chest pain or tightness. She denies any past medical problems and is not on any medications. On examination she appears well at rest. There is no joint swelling or redness. Cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examinations are normal. A high resolution CT of the thorax has revealed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with evidence of early ﬁbrosis. Which investigation is most likely to help conﬁrm the diagnosis?
explanation:
E Transbronchial lung biopsy
