If his sudden weakness is due to brain metastases then he would be started on urgent dexamethasone and should be assessed for cranial irradiation. If confirmed as SCC, this patient's prognosis would be very poor, with a median survival of only 9 months for patients with extensive disease. Patients with renal impairment who require contrast enhanced imaging should be given the lowest possible dose of isosmolar or low-osmolar nonionic contrast alongside extra hydration (approx 100ml/hour) for at least 4 hours before and after the contrast is injected.

stem: A 37-year-old patient with haemophilia A has been complaining of fever and dry cough. An interstitial pneumonia was diagnosed. He only makes intermittent contact with medical services although he has been made aware that he is HIV positive. After 7 days' treatment with doxycycline 200 mg/day his temperature was still 39 °C and a chest X-ray showed increased interstitial infiltrates. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (formerly called Pneumocystis carinii) typically presents with gradually increasing dyspnoea and cough over weeks, but sometimes as an acute illness with rapid deterioration over a few days. Patients with haemophilia A were more susceptible to HIV due to frequent blood transfusions that were not screened in the past. The chest X-ray usually reveals diffuse ground-glass opacities, which strongly suggests the diagnosis, but it sometimes shows nodular opacities, lobar consolidation, or even a normal film. Cystic abnormalities and spontaneous pneumothoraces in patients with known or suspected HIV infection are usually caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is unlikely in a patient who has had a CD4+ cell count above 200 cells/µl in the preceding 2 months in the absence of other HIV- associated symptoms. Approximately 90% of patients with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia have an elevated serum lactic dehydrogenase, but this may also occur with other pulmonary diseases.

stem: A 35-year-old woman who was previously fit and well presents with breathlessness that has been getting worse over 3–4 months. Her sister died a few years ago of a lung disease. On examination, her jugular venous pressure is raised and she has a palpable heave at the left sternal edge. Her BMI is 23, blood pressure is 135/72 mmHg and her pulse is 80 beats per min and regular. What would your provisional diagnosis be?
explanation:
Familial primary pulmonary hypertension
Primary pulmonary hypertension presents with breathlessness, fatigue, angina (due to right ventricular ischaemia) or presyncope/syncope. About 6% of all patients with primary pulmonary hypertension have a family history of the condition, which exhibits an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance with incomplete penetrance. Physical signs include: Elevated JVP Left parasternal heave Pansystolic murmur (tricuspid regurgitation) Right ventricular S4 Peripheral oedema

stem: A 36-year-old woman presents to the Respiratory Clinic with breathlessness on exertion. Her pulmonary function tests show normal spirometry, but a decreased gas transfer factor and a decreased transfer coefficient. She has known limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Which antibody is most associated with the underlying condition?
options: Anti-RNA polymerase I, II and III
explanation:
Anti-centromere antibodies
Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis is associated with anti-centromere antibodies and is more commonly associated with pulmonary artery hypertension secondary to pulmonary vasculature disease, which is the cause of the decreased gas transfer.

Anti-Scl-70
Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis is associated more with pulmonary artery hypertension secondary to pulmonary vasculature disease, which is the cause of the decreased gas transfer. Anti-Scl-70 is associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

Anti-RNA polymerase I, II and III
Anti-RNA polymerase I, II and III are associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

stem: A 17-year-old man presents to the Respiratory Clinic for review. He has suffered recurrent otitis media, gastrointestinal infections and, most recently, four episodes of pneumonia over the past year. He tells you that he has always been sickly as a child and, as such, is below the 25th centile with respect to height. On examination, his blood pressure is 115/82 mmHg; pulse is 80 bpm and regular. You cannot hear his heart sounds on auscultation and there are coarse bibasal on listening to his chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 131 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.2 × 10 /l 4–11 × 10 /l Platelets (PLT) 203 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l Sodium (Na ) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 95 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ECG Right axis deviation, positive QRS in aVR, poor R wave progression His chest x-ray is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Primary ciliary dyskinesia Classically, patients present with respiratory tract infections including pneumonia, upper respiratory tract infections, otitis and sinusitis. Situs inversus is the reversal of the internal organs which is in keeping with the quiet heart sounds, ECG appearances and chest x-ray making the diagnosis of primary ciliary dyskinesia a strong possibility. The chest x-ray also shows The signs of bronchiectasis including tram lines which is commonly found alongside situs inversus. C IgA deﬁciency IgA deﬁciency is usually associated with increased risk of gastrointestinal infections and immunoglobulin deﬁciencies are not consistent with dextrocardia per se. A Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis Patients with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis usually present with uncontrollable asthma despite treatment. A chest X-ray in these patients would typically show changes in keeping with bronchiectasis, such as ‘tram lines’ and ‘gloved ﬁnger shadows’. B Idiopathic nasal polyposis The recurrent infections and chest X-ray ﬁndings are not consistent with nasal polyposis. Patients with nasal polyposis may complain of nasal fullness or stufﬁness along with difﬁcultly sleeping due to

nasal obstruction. D IgG deﬁciency Isolated IgG deﬁciency rarely causes such recurrent infections and immunoglobulin deﬁciency is not consistent with dextrocardia. Patients with combined IgA and IgG deﬁciency are at much greater risk of recurrent infections.

stem: A 19-year-old woman comes to the Sleep Clinic for review. She complains of excessive daytime sleepiness such that she feels she is unable to keep up with her university course. In addition on two separate occasions over the past few months, she has collapsed, appearing to be unconscious, without warning, on one occasion while in animated debate with friends, on the other occasion while laughing at a movie. She has no past medical history; her only medication is the combined oral contraceptive pill. She drinks 10 pints of beer per week and smokes five cigarettes per day. Examination reveals a BP of 115/80 mmHg, pulse is 65/min and regular. No neurological abnormalities are identified. Her BMI is 23. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 130 g/l 115 - 155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.2 × 10 9/l 4 - 11 × 10 9/l Platelets 212 × 10 9/l 150 - 400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.1 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 89 μmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Glucose 5.1 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.5 mmol/l* 12 lead ECG Normal Given the suspected diagnosis, which of the following is the intervention most likely to relieve day-time sleepiness?
explanation:
Modafinil
The history here fits best with narcolepsy (the excessive day-time sleepiness) and cataplexy (the episodes of collapse), and treatment with the stimulant modafinil is appropriate. Sleep hygiene measures such as avoiding stimulants including caffeine prior to bed, regular exercise and planning for 7–8 h sleep per night may also be of benefit.

Alcohol reduction
Alcohol reduction is incorrect. Reduction of excessive alcohol intake may have an impact on symptoms, although 10 pints of beer per week is unlikely to be a significant contributor to sleepiness.

Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)
Unlike in obstructive sleep apnoea, CPAP is not likely to have any significant impact on symptoms.

Levetiracetam
Levetiracetam is a treatment for epilepsy. The history described here suggests a diagnosis of narcolepsy.

stem: A 78-year-old white woman presents with left upper-lobe cavitating consolidation and sputum samples confirm the presence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which is fully sensitive. There is no previous history of treatment for tuberculosis (TB). The most appropriate antibiotic regimen is?
options: Rifampicin/isoniazid/pyrazinamide/ethambutol for 2 months, then rifampicin/isoniazid for 4 months
Rifampicin/isoniazid/pyrazinamide for 4 months, then rifampicin/isoniazid 8 months
explanation:
Rifampicin/isoniazid/pyrazinamide/ethambutol for 2 months, then rifampicin/isoniazid for 4 months
In a white patient with pulmonary Mycobacterium tuberculosis that is fully sensitive and not previously treated, the use of four drugs for 2 months (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol) and then two drugs (rifampicin and isoniazid) for 4 months is perfectly acceptable.

Rifampicin/ethambutol 12 months
Rifampicin/ethambutol 12 months is incorrect. Until sensitivities are known, empirical treatment for tuberculosis should include four drugs, usually rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. Treatment can be stepped down to two drugs after 2 months if the organism is fully sensitive. Duration of therapy for pulmonary TB is 6 months not 12.

stem: Which of the following relates to an exacerbation of chronic bronchitis in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
options: An elevated white cell count indicates exacerbation
Gram staining is inconclusive and blood cultures are necessary
Moraxella catarrhalis is commonly a cause of COPD exacerbation
Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole combinations are effective in the treatment of M. catarrhalis infection
explanation:
Moraxella catarrhalis is commonly a cause of COPD exacerbation
Along with Haemophilus influenzae and Streptococcus pneumoniae, M. catarrhalis is a common cause of exacerbations of chronic bronchitis and pneumonia in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Symptoms of moraxella infection tend to be mild to moderate in severity and it is quite common for the white cell count not to be raised.

An elevated white cell count indicates exacerbation
An elevated white cell count indicates exacerbation is incorrect. An elevated white cell count may Chat beAIdue with to Tutor another cause, e.g. it may be secondary to oral steroid use. Additionally, white cell count may be normal in an exacerbation of COPD.

Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole combinations are effective in the treatment of M. catarrhalis infection
Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole combinations are effective in the treatment of M. catarrhalis infection is incorrect. Resistance to both trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole combinations and tetracycline has been reported. The most appropriate choice would be a combination of ampicillin and clavulinic acid, which suppresses M. catarrhalis ß-lactamases.

stem: A 49-year-old woman has been admitted with haemoptysis and epistaxis. Her chest X-ray shows multiple rounded lesions with alveolar shadowing. Her serum is positive for cytoplasmic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (c-ANCA). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
Almost all patients will have evidence of granulomatous lung disease at presentation, which is often accompanied by alveolar capillaritis. The bronchi can also be affected and bronchial stenoses occur as late manifestations. Symptoms include: Cough Dyspnoea Haemoptysis Chest pain (which can be pleuritic) Signs on chest examination depend on the nature of the pulmonary lesions and include: Fine crepitations Bronchial breathing

stem: A 26-year-old man presents to the medical assessment unit. The patient has progressively worsening dyspnoea and chest discomfort over the previous 24 hours. He had been given a salbutamol inhaler by his general practitioner (GP) some three months earlier for exercise-induced wheeze and shortness of breath. On examination, he is tachycardic at 120 bpm and tachypnoeic at 30 bpm, with bilateral wheeze on auscultation. On examination of the supraclavicular areas and neck, there is palpable cutaneous emphysema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Asthma Severe asthma exacerbations can lead to pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum, both of which can cause subcutaneous emphysema (cutaneous air tracking from the lungs into the subcutaneous tissues). This is a rare but recognized complication of severe asthma, especially in young patients with a history of wheezing. The patient's wheezing, tachypnoea, and cutaneous emphysema suggest an acute and severe asthma attack with secondary pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum. Early recognition of this complication is important in guiding management. D Pulmonary embolism Pulmonary embolism (PE) is unlikely to cause subcutaneous emphysema. Although PE can cause dyspnoea and tachypnoea, there is no suggestion in the vignette of classic risk factors (eg, deep vein thrombosis, recent surgery) for PE, and subcutaneous emphysema is not a typical ﬁnding. A Oesophageal rupture This is typically caused by trauma or vomiting, and it can lead to the development of mediastinal emphysema and subcutaneous emphysema. However, the patient's history does not suggest vomiting or trauma, and oesophageal rupture is less likely without these triggers. C Gas gangrene Gas gangrene causes subcutaneous emphysema but is usually associated with signiﬁcant systemic illness, including sepsis, shock, and necrotic tissue. This is less likely in this patient, given the absence of visible necrosis or signs of sepsis.

E Lung malignancy While lung malignancy can sometimes cause subcutaneous emphysema, it is a rare complication. This is particularly unlikely in a young patient with no signiﬁcant smoking history or other risk factors for cancer.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to the Respiratory Medicine Clinic due to cough and shortness of breath on exertion for the past six months. He has a past medical history of gastro-oesophageal reﬂux disease, for which he takes omeprazole 10 mg per day, and he smokes ten cigarettes per day. Pulmonary function tests reveal a forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) to FVC ratio of 1, with FEV1 85% of predicted and FVC 84% of predicted. Chest X-ray reveals increased interstitial lung markings, and high- resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest reveals a pattern in keeping with usual interstitial pneumonia. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following intervention options for this patient has been shown to have an impact on survival time?
explanation:
A Administration of proton pump inhibitor (PPI) This patient has idiopathic pulmonary ﬁbrosis (IPF), as evidenced by his restrictive pattern of lung disease on pulmonary function testing and the pattern of usual interstitial pneumonia on high-resolution computed tomography. Minimal treatment options are currently available for IPF. Pulmonary rehabilitation is recommended to improve quality of life; smoking cessation is recommended to prevent the occurrence of co- morbid chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and nintedanib and pirfenidone have been shown to reduce the functional decline in IPF but are currently only recommended, according to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines, to be started in individuals when the person has a FVC of between 50% and 80% predicted, with the caveat that medication is stopped if the disease progresses (a conﬁrmed decline in percentage predicted FVC of 10% or more) in any 12-month period. The only intervention that has been shown to be independently associated with increased survival in patients with IPF and gastro-oesophageal reﬂux disease is PPIs.

E Smoking cessation Smoking cessation is recommended in patients with IPF to reduce the risk of developing concomitant COPD. However, it is not independently associated with improvement in survival time. B Nintedanib Both pirfenidone and nintedanib have been trialled in patients with IPF and have shown beneﬁcial outcomes in reducing the functional decline in IPF. However, there is currently no evidence that these medications are able to improve survival. C Oxygen therapy Currently, there is no evidence that oxygen therapy improves survival in patients with IPF. Its beneﬁcial effects may be an improvement in exercise tolerance and a reduction in the risk of developing pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale. D Pulmonary rehabilitation Pulmonary rehabilitation has been proven to improve quality of life and functional status. It does not show any impact on survival time and the effects seen are reduced six months after the programme. This may be related to the ﬁnding that patients do not keep up with exercises at home following a rehabilitation programme.

stem: A 24-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department having felt unwell for the last couple of days. He tells you that he has had ﬂu for the last four days. He complains of a dry cough, headache, fever, malaise and muscle pains. On examination, he is unwell with a blood pressure of 110/60 mmHg, pulse of 92 beats per minute and a respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute. His oxygen saturation is 95% on air. On auscultation, he has scattered crackles in both lung ﬁelds. His cardiovascular and abdominal examinations are unremarkable. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 98 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 12.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 278 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 130 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 112 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l MCV 89 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ CRP 86 mg/l < 10 mg/l Blood ﬁlm Coombs’ test Fragmented red cells, reticulocytosis + How would you treat this patient?
explanation:
B Clarithromycin This is the typical presentation of Mycoplasma pneumoniae with a few days’ history of dry cough and ﬂu-like symptoms. Cold-agglutinins associated with the infection may also drive an autoimmune haemolytic anaemia with positive Coombs’ test. Infection is seen in epidemics, particularly where young adults live in close proximity, for example in an army barracks. C Flucloxacillin Flucloxacillin is an option for post-inﬂuenza pneumonia, which is considered as a possible diagnosis when patients present with cavitating pneumonia following ﬂu infection. A Ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin could be an option in combination with vancomycin for the treatment of community-acquired pneumonia where patients are penicillin allergic but is not a ﬁrst line choice. D Gentamicin Gentamicin was considered additive to the effects of penicillins in

severe infection – for example in endocarditis, although is now mainly reserved for the treatment of severe Gram-negative infections. E Rifampicin Rifampicin is used as dual therapy in the treatment of severe legionella infection.

stem: A 55-year-old asthmatic patient presented in December with increasing cough and wheeze. She described a cough productive of brown sputum. She had no other past medical history. She was taking a steroid inhaler regularly and increasing doses of beta-agonist with no alleviation of her symptoms. She worked in a bakery for many years. She is an ex-smoker and stopped smoking 20 years ago. She has a dog at home. On examination, she had a temperature of 38 °C. She was breathless at rest. She had reduced expansion anteriorly on the left side, with corresponding reduced breath sounds. She had a mild expiratory wheeze. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 141 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 12.7 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 7.37 × 109/l 1.5 - 7.0 × 109/l Lymphocytes 2.55 × 109/l 1.5 - 4.0 × 109/l Monocytes 0.6 × 109/l 0.0 - 0.8 × 109/l Basophils 0.05 × 109/l < 0.1 × 109/l Eosinophils 1.9 × 109/l < 0.45 × 109/l MCV 87.3 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ Platelets (PLT) 314 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l ESR 28 mm/h 1 - 20 mm/h CRP 16 mg/l < 10 mg/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 4.8 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 95 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Bilirubin 12 µmol/l 1 - 22 µmol/l ALT 49 u/l 7 - 55 u/l ALP 61 u/l 30 - 150 u/l Albumin 36 g/l 35 - 55 g/l Chest X-ray on presentation is shown below: Chest X-ray taken one month earlier: What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
C Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis The chest X-ray shows left upper lobe collapse and also the ‘veil sign’. This patient has allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). Pulmonary inﬁltrates, blood eosinophilia and asthma are usually secondary to Churg–Strauss or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. ABPA is suspected in any patient with asthma who has an abnormal chest X-ray and high peripheral blood eosinophilia.The chest X-ray may show diffuse pulmonary inﬁltrates, and pulmonary, lobar or segmental collapse occur as transient features. The most common cause is sensitivity to Aspergillus fumigatus spores. The lack of other features of vasculitis such as mononeuritis, or markers of elevation such as raised CRP counts against vasculitis as an alternative diagnosis here. The diagnostic criteria include: • Asthma (in most cases) • Peripheral blood and sputum eosinophilia • Abnormal chest X-ray (inﬁltrates, segmental or lobar collapse) • Positive skin tests/RAST to an extract of A. fumigatus • fumigatus IgG serum-precipitating antibodies • Raised total IgE >1000 ng/ml • Fungal hyphae of A. fumigatus on microscopy of sputum. The lung and eosinophils: • Loefﬂer syndrome (eosinophils about 10% of blood WCC), also known as acute eosinophilic pneumonia/simple eosinophilic pneumonia. Mild self-limiting illness with transient migratory pulmonary shadows. Associated with parasitic infections, drug allergies and exposure to inorganic chemicals • Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (eosinophils >20%) – in tropical countries usually due to migrating larvae of the ﬁlarial worms Wucheria bancrofti and Brugia malayi • Chronic/prolonged pulmonary eosinophilia (eosinophils >20%) – eosinophilic pneumonia persisting for more than one month. Chronic debilitating illness characterised by malaise, weight loss, fever and dyspnea • Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (eosinophils 5–20%) as in this case • Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (eosinophils 5– 20%) associated with asthma • Hyper-eosinophilic syndrome (eosinophils >20%: eosinophilic inﬁltrations of various organs – e.g. lungs, heart, bone

marrow. Can be associated with an eosinophilic arteritis • External agents – drugs, toxins, parasitic infection. A Occupational asthma The patient working as a baker is irrelevant – occupational asthma is unlikely to cause a productive cough or these chest X-ray features. It can be screened for using serial peak ﬂow measurements and comparing those at home to those at work. B Exacerbation of asthma The chest radiograph features and clinical examination ﬁndings are not in keeping with an exacerbation of asthma. D Churg-Strauss syndrome This patient does not have the diagnostic criteria for Churg–Strauss syndrome. Although the eosinophil count is elevated there is no other evidence of vasculitis. E Loefﬂer syndrome Loefﬂer syndrome is associated with ﬂeeting pulmonary inﬁltrates but not with intermittent lobar collapse. It is associated with parasitic worm migration to the lungs. We’re given no indication that this is a potential cause here.

stem: A 42-year-old man, who is known to be HIV positive, presents with a cough productive of rusty-coloured sputum. He has been feeling unwell for around a week or so. On examination he is pyrexial (38.2oC) with a BP of 135/70 mmHg. His pulse is 95/min and regular. Auscultation of the chest reveals an area of bronchial breathing over the left lower lung ﬁeld. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 124 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 13.1 × 109/l (Neutrophilia) 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 195 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CXR Left. lower lobe consolidation His chest x-ray is below Which of the following types of pneumonia is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Streptococcus pneumoniae This man has community-acquired pneumonia which is most likely to be S. pneumoniae. The estimated attack rate is higher in HIVinfected patients (5.9/1000 vs 0.31/1000 in non-HIV infected patients). Resistance patterns are similar in HIV and non-HIV infected patients, and invasive disease is rare and tends to occur in patients with a low CD4 count. The chest x-ray showing lobar consolidation (note the absence of the outline of the left hemidiaphragm indicating left lower lobe infection) and neutrophilia ﬁts best with a S. pneumoniae episode rather than another cause for the respiratory tract infection. A Pneumocystis Pneumocystis pneumonia is associated with diffuse patchy consolidation, and the hallmark of the condition is desaturation on exercise (usually measured with a hand-held pulse oximeter). B Staphylococcus aureus Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia, even in the context of underlying HIV infection, normally follows an episode of inﬂuenza. C Mycoplasma Mycoplasma pneumonia often follows a slightly more subacute course than streptococcal pneumonia, with a dry cough, chest pain

and wheeze, that can be present for a few days before patients engage with medical services. E Klebsiella Klebsiella pneumonia is associated with lobar infection with cavitation and is seen most commonly in patients with a history of alcoholism.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with breathlessness. He has a medical history of scoliosis, for which he had previous surgery privately. Examination reveals he is 204 cm in height, with an arm span of 198 cm and a weight of 79 kg. His BP is 122/78 mmHg and his heart rate is 130 bpm. There is reduced air entry on the right. His ECG from triage is below: What complication of his underlying condition is this patient most likely experiencing?
explanation:
C Pneumothorax Patients with Marfan syndrome, indicated by the measurements (tall and thin, with a large arm span), are at risk of emphysematous changes and lung bullae. Such lung changes can predispose patients to spontaneous pneumothoraces. A CXR and management dependent on the size of pneumothorax are indicated. A Pulmonary embolus While the patient does have sinus tachycardia and a pulmonary embolus is possible, there are no obvious underlying risk factors for a pulmonary embolus.

B Tricuspid regurgitation Mitral valve prolapse, rather than tricuspid regurgitation, is common in patients with Marfan syndrome. D Pleural effusion While a pleural effusion does result in reduced air entry, they do not have a higher incidence in patients with Marfan syndrome. E AF Marfan syndrome is most strongly associated with mitral valve prolapse than with other cardiac abnormalities. The ECG here also demonstrates sinus rhythm.

stem: A 35-year-old, HIV-positive, East African patient presents to A&E with shortness of breath and night sweats. On examination he is thin and tachypnoeic, and has a right base that is stony dull to percussion with reduced air entry. On his chest X-ray there is a moderate-sized pleural effusion. His past medical history includes tuberculosis (TB) as a child for which he can’t remember whether he had treatment. His initial three sputum samples do not stain for acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl–Neelsen (ZN) stain. You want to carry out a test with the highest pick-up rate for TB diagnosis. Which of the following would be the most useful?
explanation:
B Pleural biopsy culture Tuberculous effusion occurs in about 30% of patients with TB; this is comparable to HIV-positive and -negative patients. ZN stains are positive in about 75% of cases. Indications for pleural biopsy are exudative recurrent pleural effusion of unknown aetiology and pleural mass or thickening. E Heaf test This test has been discontinued since 2005 and has been replaced by the Mantoux test – a person's medical risk factors determine at which increment (5, 10 or 15 mm) of induration the result is considered positive. Other techniques used include bronchoscopy/endobronchial ultrasound in those who have a non-productive cough/ unhelpful sputum culture and a high index of clinical suspicion.

A Pleural ﬂuid aspirate culture ZN stains of pleural ﬂuid are positive in 10–20% of tuberculous effusions. C Pleural biopsy histology Although it may demonstrate granulomas, it cannot give bacterial sensitivities. D CD4 count A low CD4 count not only predisposes to TB. CD4 cell counts give an indication of the health of the immune system. Monitoring CD4 cell counts is less important while taking HIV treatment than before starting. The count should go up when you take HIV treatment. Patients with higher CD4 counts present similar to those who are HIV-negative with TB. Adenosine deaminase (ADA) levels are useful when TB is suspected in those with negative pleural ﬂuid or biopsy cultures. However, raised ADA levels can be observed in other conditions leading to a false-positive diagnosis of TB, such as in empyema, rheumatoid effusion and malignancy.

stem: A 62-year-old cleaner comes to the Respiratory Clinic complaining of increasing shortness of breath and a persistent cough. She used to work sweeping up for a plumber and boiler maker. She has begun to get tired while walking the dog, which is spoiling the enjoyment of her time off. She smokes ﬁve cigarettes per day. On examination, she is ﬁnger-clubbed and you can hear ﬁne endinspiratory crackles. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 128 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 4.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 210 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 140 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l FEV1 2.7 FVC 3.1 CXR Shown below Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Asbestosis The clue is very clear that, in her work at a plumbers, this woman is likely to have had signiﬁcant exposure to asbestos. The chest Xray ﬁndings of bilateral pleural plaques also point towards asbestos exposure. High- resolution computed tomography (CT) is important to conﬁrm pulmonary ﬁbrosis, and pulse oximetry normally reveals a degree of hypoxaemia. Despite extensive trials, neither corticosteroids nor second-line immunomodulatory agents have any signiﬁcant impact on the course of the disease. A Asthma The chest X-ray ﬁndings here are consistent with early pulmonary ﬁbrosis related to asbestos exposure, and FEV1/FVC is 87%. B Solderer’s lung Solderer’s lung is a cause of occupational asthma but does not result in the pleural plaques seen on chest X-ray here, nor the reticulo-nodular pulmonary shadowing. D Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) COPD leads to obstruction on pulmonary function testing and is not associated with the chest X-ray changes seen here.

E Idiopathic pulmonary ﬁbrosis Idiopathic pulmonary ﬁbrosis is a diagnosis of exclusion, and this patient’s job working with a plumber is associated with a high risk of asbestos exposure. The pleural plaques on chest X-ray do conﬁrm previous exposure to asbestos ﬁbres.

stem: This 72-year-old woman presents with several months’ history of dyspnoea, cough and weight loss. There is a history of COPD for which she takes seretide BD, and coarse crackles and wheeze consistent with the diagnosis are evident on auscultation. Her Postero-anterior (PA) and lateral chest radiographs are shown below: Which of the following investigations is most appropriate to conﬁrm the diagnosis?
explanation:
A Fibre-optic bronchoscopy ± transbronchial biopsy The combination of the history with a solitary lung nodule on chest X-ray is highly suggestive of bronchial carcinoma. Bronchoscopy enables the tumour to be directly visualised and samples taken for cytology and histology. The extent of carinal involvement can also be seen – if the tumour involves the ﬁrst 2 cm of either main bronchus, it is deemed inoperable. B CT guided ﬁne-needle aspiration biopsy The combination of the history with a solitary lung nodule on chest X-ray is highly suggestive of bronchial carcinoma. CT-guided FNA carries more risk than bronchoscopy, and the lesion should be easily accessible via the bronchoscopy route. CT scanning of the thorax is however still useful in assessing involvement of the mediastinum and lymph nodes. If surgery is being considered, it should be

extended to the abdomen and brain to exclude distant metastases. C Respiratory function tests The combination of the history with a solitary lung nodule on chest X-ray is highly suggestive of bronchial carcinoma. Respiratory function tests are not useful in diagnosis, but are essential if pneumonectomy is being considered, as a forced expiratory volume (FEV1) of <2.0 l means that there will in all likelihood be insufﬁcient respiratory reserve post surgery. D Sputum for cytology The combination of the history with a solitary lung nodule on chest X-ray is highly suggestive of bronchial carcinoma. This option is incorrect, because sputum cytology is a low-yield diagnostic tool. It is unlikely to be able to provide enough malignancy cells from a sputum sample in order to make a histological diagnosis. In addition, the patient may not even be producing sputum. If an infective diagnosis is being considered, sputum induction could be carried out in order to obtain a sample. E Mediastinoscopy The combination of the history with a solitary lung nodule on chest X-ray is highly suggestive of bronchial carcinoma. Mediastinoscopy is an invasive procedure that involves making an incision in the anterior chest wall in order to introduce the endoscope. It is used to obtain mediastinal lymph node biopsies, for example, for staging lymph nodes involved in lung cancer or for the diagnosis of sarcoidosis or lymphoma. However, on reviewing the above chest radiographs, the mass should be easily accessible using the less invasive technique of bronchoscopy, so this should preclude mediastinoscopy.

stem: A 44-year-old man presented with a rash on his legs and feeling generally unwell with malaise, weight loss and fevers. He also had recently noticed some loss of sensation over the top of his right foot, with the foot- dragging when he walked. He had been diagnosed with asthma by his general practitioner many years ago and used a salbutamol inhaler as required. He also had a constant watery nasal discharge, but no epistaxis. He was a non-smoker. On examination, he had low-grade pyrexia and scattered wheeze in his chest. Heart sounds were normal. His abdomen was soft and non-tender, with no masses. He had a purpuric rash on his lower limbs and several tender subcutaneous nodules on his forearms. He had a right foot drop but no other neurological abnormalities. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 106 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 10.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 390 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Neutrophils 6.2 × 109/l 1.5–7.0 × 109/l Eosinophils 2.2 × 109/l 0.04–0.4 × 109/l Monocytes 1.6 × 109/l 0.0–0.8 × 109/l Basophils 0.1 × 109/l < 0.1 × 109/l MCV 94 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ ESR 82 mm/h 1–20 mm/hour Sodium (Na+) 120 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l ALP 80 IU/l 30–150 IU/l ALT 30 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Urea 5.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l GGT 42 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Bilirubin 14 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Antinuclear antibody (ANA) Negative pANCA Positive Urinalysis Normal His chest x-ray is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangitis This man presents with the classic triad of asthma, eosinophilia and systemic vasculitis. There is usually a prodromal period for many years consisting of allergic rhinitis and late-onset asthma, which can be difﬁcult to control. The chest X-ray here shows pulmonary inﬁltrates bilaterally. Other ﬁndings occasionally found include nodules, transient hilar lymphadenopathy and pleural or pericardial effusions. Mononeuritis

multiplex can occur. Anti- neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) is positive in approximately 40% of cases. Renal involvement is rare. Treatment is with high-dose corticosteroids, azathioprine or cyclophosphamide. A Systemic lupus erythematosus Although SLE is associated with an erythematous rash on sun-exposed areas, the eosinophilia, negative ANA and positive pANCA would be unusual for a diagnosis of lupus. B Polyarteritis nodosa pANCA is classically not positive in patients with PAN. In addition, the symptoms of signiﬁcant asthma poorly responsive to conventional therapies, and eosinophilia, are inconsistent with a diagnosis of PAN. D Anti-GBM disease This presents with rapidly progressive pulmonary and kidney disease, accompanied by haemoptysis and kidney disease due to glomerulonephritis. Eosinophilia isn’t a feature, nor is mononeuritis multiplex. E Granulomatosis with polyangitis This is associated with pulmonary and renal vasculitis with haemoptysis and a progressive rise in serum creatinine. There is usually sinusitis. cANCA rather than pANCA is more likely to be positive, and eosinophils are not elevated.

stem: A 68-year-old man with a 10-year history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents with a 6- month history of increasing exertional dyspnoea and fatigue. He also has a cough productive of yellow sputum, episodes of chest pain, nausea and anorexia. He stopped smoking 2 years ago. On examination, he had raised jugular venous pressure (JVP), right parasternal heave, a loud second heart sound and an ejection systolic murmur at the left second intercostal space. On chest auscultation, he had scattered expiratory wheeze and bi-basal crepitations. He had pitting leg oedema. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 180 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 8.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 220 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bilirubin 16 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Urea 4.6 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l ALP 50 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Gamma-glutamyltransferase (γGT) 100 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ECG Right ventricular hypertrophy, peaked P waves CXR Shown below Which of the following therapies is most likely to improve longterm prognosis?
explanation:
B Long-term oxygen therapy This man has developed cor pulmonale, which is deﬁned as right heart failure secondary to pulmonary hypertension. Causes include any chronic lung disease, pulmonary vascular disease, hypoventilation neuromuscular disorders and thoracic cage abnormalities. Long-term home oxygen therapy for at least 15 hours per day can reduce hypoxia, which lowers pulmonary resistance and can improve symptoms and increase life expectancy. C Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor In contrast to left ventricular impairment, ACE inhibitors do not have any prognostic beneﬁt and may, in fact, make matters worse. In systolic heart failure, they are of prognostic beneﬁt and very useful. A High-dose furosemide Diuretics can be used for right ventricular failure, but care should be taken to avoid excessive ﬂuid depletion. In heart failure, these do not

improve long-term prognosis. D Regular venesection This patient has polycythaemia secondary to chronic hypoxia as a mechanism of compensation. Venesection improves prognosis in haemochromatosis and can also be used for primary polycythaemia. E Daily amoxicillin There is no role for antibiotic prophylaxis in either cor pulmonale or COPD.

stem: A 56-year-old man is referred to the outpatients department with a 2-year history of increasing breathlessness and deteriorating exercise tolerance. He has a non-productive cough and always feels tired, so much so that he has needed to ask his wife to help him look after his pigeons, which he has been racing for many years. Over the last year he has lost about 1 stone in weight. He has a past medical history of asthma as a child. In his social history, he has had no history of recent foreign travel, except to France. He has always worked in a bank and is an ex-smoker who drinks minimal amounts of alcohol. On examination, he is not clubbed. On auscultation of his chest, he has ﬁne inspiratory crackles. ABGs on air reveal: ABGs on air reveal: pH 7.36 PO 7.4 kPa PCO 4.7 kPa Lung function tests: FEV1 70% predicted FVC 64% predicted KCO 53% predicted TLCO 55% predicted His chest X-ray is shown below: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Extrinsic allergic alveolitis The patient has interstitial lung disease, demonstrated by the slowly progressive shortness of breath, type I hypoxia and restrictive lung function tests with reduced TLCO and KCO. In the chest radiograph there is reticular nodular shadowing. The diagnosis is extrinsic allergic alveolitis secondary to pigeons – bird fancier's lung. This is caused by inhaled avian serum proteins (usually IgA) present in the pigeon's feathers and excreta. It is a hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by a speciﬁc immunological response to inhaled organic dusts. EAA may present either as an acute or a chronic disease. Acute disease develops several hours after exposure to high concentrations of the allergen. Breathlessness and ﬂu-like symptoms occur sometimes with headaches, fever and myalgia. Symptoms usually resolve within 48 h. The patient has chronic disease, as it has progressed to interstitial lung disease with ﬁbrosis. The diagnosis of extrinsic allergic alveolitis is made by: • Identifying a potential source of antigen • Characteristic clinical features: this patient has chronic EAA and presents with similar features to pulmonary ﬁbrosis – clubbing tends to occur later (idiopathic pulmonary ﬁbrosis would typically be associated with clubbing) • Characteristic radiology (usually upper lobe ﬁbrosis) • Lung function tests – showing a restrictive defect with reduced carbon monoxide gas transfer • Demonstrating precipitating antibodies (precipitins) in the patient's serum • Resolution or improvement of symptoms following avoidance of exposure to the cause • Histology of lung tissue biopsy showing a mononuclear cell inﬁltrate with the formation of non- caseating granulomas • Fluid obtained from bronchoalveloar lavage has a high lymphocyte count (typically >40%). Treatment is avoidance of the antigen. Corticosteroids may improve recovery in acute attacks but do not seem to provide long-term beneﬁt. They are not usually helpful once ﬁbrosis has occurred. Other causes of EAA include: • Farmer's lung, due to Micropolyspora faeni and Thermactinomyces in mouldy hay, straw and grain Bagassosis due to Thermactinomyces sacchari in sugar cane processing

• Malt worker's lung due to Aspergillus clavatus Mushroom worker's lung due to thermophilic actinomycetes Ventilation and water-related contamination, e.g. due to thermophilic actinomycetes contaminating air- conditioning systems Veterinary workers and animal handlers Workers in milling and construction, e.g. wood dust pneumonitis due to Alternaria spp. Causes of upper-zone ﬁbrosis: • Progressive massive ﬁbrosis/coal worker's pneumoconiosis Ankylosing spondylitis • Sarcoid/silicosis Tuberculosis • Extrinsic allergic alveolitis Radiation (depending on site). A Bronchopulmonary aspergillosis The chest radiograph shows diffuse inﬁltrates. CXR ﬁndings in ABPA are more likely to include proximal bronchiectasis, lobar collapse or discrete pulmonary inﬁltates. C Idiopathic pulmonary ﬁbrosis There is a clear precipitant to interstitial lung disease here. D Psittacosis Psittacosis is an infection caused by Chlamydia psittaci. It usually presents with a sudden onset of fever, dry cough and headache following a recent exposure to birds. Psittacosis is typically linked to parrots. The duration of symptoms is too long for psittacosis, and the chest X-ray changes are too widespread. E Sarcoidosis Exposure to pigeons and weight loss make EAA more likely than sarcoidosis.

stem: A 23-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department following sudden-onset left-sided pleuritic chest pain. His past medical history includes recurrent shoulder dislocations. He is on no medications. On examination, he is tall with a long arm span. He appears short of breath and clammy. Observations reveal a heart rate of 95 bpm, BP of 110/55 mmHg, respiratory rate of 23 breaths per minute and oxygen saturations of 96% on room air. There is evidence of reduced air entry on the left-hand side and a ‘click’ on auscultation. CXR reveals a 2.5-cm pneumothorax on the left. What is the most appropriate management of this patient?
options: Discharge with outpatient review in 2–4 weeks
explanation: D Needle aspiration with 16– 18–G cannula This patient is tall and thin, with a history of joint dislocation. The suspicion is that he may have Marfan syndrome, which may be associated with a pneumothorax. The pneumothorax is over 2 cm. He is symptomatic, warranting immediate intervention. This should initially be needle aspiration with a cannula to aspirate a maximum of 2.5 litres. If this fails, the insertion of a small-bore chest drain is recommended. E Observation for 24 hours This patient is clinically unwell as a result of his pneumothorax and therefore requires prompt management. Observation would not be appropriate. A 8– to 14–Fr chest drain If this patient shows evidence of haemodynamic instability, the ﬁrst-line treatment would include chest drain insertion due to the risk of this being a tension pneumothorax. Additionally, if this patient does not show clinical improvement after needle aspiration, then a chest drain would be required. B Discharge with outpatient review in 2–4 weeks Guidelines from the British Thoracic Society for the management of pneumothorax indicate that patients with pneumothoraces of below 2 cm who are haemodynamically stable and not symptomatic can be discharged and reviewed in the outpatient setting in 2–4 weeks. C High-ﬂow oxygen therapy High-ﬂow oxygen therapy should be given due to this patient’s breathlessness. In addition, oxygen may promote the resolution of a pneumothorax. However, this patient requires active intervention with needle aspiration due to his breathlessness and the size of the pneumothorax.

stem: A 25-year-old man with a known history of alcohol and drug abuse presents with a 14-day history of fever, dry cough, hypoxia and tiredness. He is emaciated. His temperature is 39.4°C and he has cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. His chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial shadowing. What is the most likely cause for his illness?
explanation:
Pneumocystis pneumonia
The history is suggestive that the patient is immunocompromised. Pneumocystis pneumonia can present with a normal X-ray or bilateral interstitial shadowing, which is often perihilar in distribution. Both tuberculosis and Pneumocystis infection are likely in an immunocompromised patient, but the X-ray findings (i.e. the bilateral nature of the changes) are more suggestive of Pneumocystis rather than tuberculous infection.

Alcoholic cardiomyopathy
Alcoholic cardiomyopathy is incorrect. The clinical picture is one of infective pneumonia rather than of alcoholic cardiomyopathy.

Pneumococcal pneumonia
Pneumococcal pneumonia is incorrect. Pneumococcal pneumonia usually presents with lobar consolidation.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who is breastfeeding presents to the on-call GP with a cough productive of rust- coloured sputum. She has also had increasing fevers over the past few days. On examination, her temperature is 38.6 °C, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg and pulse 90 bpm. She has bronchial breathing at the right base on auscultation of her chest. She is allergic to penicillin. Investigation: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 125 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.5 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 211 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 90 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l A chest X-ray shows a right lower-lobe pneumonia. Which of the following would be the most appropriate antibiotic choice?
explanation:
Clarithromycin
Clarithromycin is an appropriate choice in penicillin-allergic patients for the treatment of community-acquired pneumonia.

Cefalexin
Cefalexin is incorrect. Cefalexin would be a reasonable choice if there were no alternatives, but there is 10% crossover with penicillin allergy.

Ciprofloxacin
Ciprofloxacin is incorrect. Ciprofloxacin is associated with tendon rupture in juvenile animal models and is therefore not recommended during breastfeeding.

Co-amoxiclav
Co-amoxiclav is incorrect. This patient is allergic to penicillins, which immediately rules out co-amoxiclav, which is a combination of amoxicillin and clavulanic acid.

Flucloxacillin
Flucloxacillin is incorrect. This patient is allergic to penicillins, which immediately rules out flucloxacillin.

stem: A 55-year-old dairy farmer attends the Respiratory Clinic with shortness of breath, chronic cough, lethargy and night sweats. He has a history of type II diabetes, for which he takes metformin. Apparently, the farm has had ﬁnancial troubles over the past few months because of the need to cull approximately 50% of the herd due to tuberculosis (TB). On examination, his BP is 135/75 mmHg and his heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. His BMI is 35 kg/m2. He has wheeze on auscultation of the chest, as well as a few scattered coarse crackles. Pulmonary function testing (PFT) reveals a mild restrictive defect. His CXR is shown below: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Miliary TB This patient has symptoms of chronic lung disease, and the CXR shows bilateral interstitial inﬁltrates. Given the fact that the patient has been exposed to TB, this is most likely to indicate miliary TB. The diagnosis should be conﬁrmed with at least three sputum samples, and given the extent of the infection, contact tracing and testing are essential. E Obesity hypoventilation syndrome This is associated with a mild restrictive defect on PFT but not with nodular shadowing on the CXR, nor with the auscultation ﬁndings seen in this patient. A Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis This leads to an obstructive picture on PFT and symptoms consistent with poorly controlled asthma. Patchy shadowing is usually apparent on the CXR rather than the nodular appearance seen in this patient. B Asthma Asthma is more likely to be associated with a normal appearance on the CXR and would not ﬁt with other constitutional symptoms of infection, including lethargy and night sweats seen here. C Idiopathic pulmonary ﬁbrosis This would be associated with a restrictive defect on PFT, although coarse crepitations and nodular appearance on the CXR would not be expected. Patchy shadowing on the chest X-ray and inspiratory crepitations would be expected.

stem: An 18-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department drowsy and confused. He has recently complained of symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection. He has a past medical history of Duchenne’s muscular dystrophy. Over the past few weeks, he noted that he seemed to be suffering intermittent morning headaches and intermittent confusion. On examination, he is drowsy but able to obey simple commands. His respiratory rate is 13 breaths per minute. Air entry is poor on auscultation, with crackles at the left base. Investigation Result Normal value pH 7.3 7.35–7.45 pCO2 7.0 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa pO2 7.0 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa Which of the following would represent the most appropriate management in this case?
explanation: E Non-invasive ventilation This man has evidence of chronic carbon dioxide retention, as evidenced by his morning headaches, intermittent confusion and drowsiness. A further indication of respiratory muscle, particularly diaphragmatic and weakness may be indicated by breathlessness during swimming. Chronic hypoventilation has likely led to an opportunistic respiratory tract infection associated with his cold. At present, he has mild respiratory acidosis, and the situation may be remediable with non-invasive ventilation and antibiotics. Since Duchenne's muscular dystrophy is progressive, intubation and ventilation should be carefully considered. A 60% oxygen therapy Therapy with 60% oxygen will have a very limited impact, if any, on improving this patient’s hypoxia due to his hypoventilation and worsening acidosis. Therefore, this is not an appropriate option for this patient. B 35% oxygen therapy Like higher percentages of oxygen, 35% oxygen will not reverse the impact of hypoventilation with respect to respiratory acidosis. Therefore, it would not be appropriate here. C 28% oxygen therapy Therapy with 28% oxygen will not improve oxygenation and will not reverse the impact of hypoventilation, making it unlikely to be appropriate for this patient. D Intubation and ventilation Intubation and ventilation should be carefully considered in the context of Duchenne’s muscular dystrophy. It is a progressive condition and the risk is that the patient may become un-weanable from the ventilator. As such, non-invasive ventilation is preferred here. Ideally, patients should consider an advanced directive before they become unwell so that their wishes with respect to invasive therapies are already established.

stem: A 20-year-old man with epilepsy presents to the Emergency Department with a three-day history of cough and increasing shortness of breath. He has foul-smelling sputum. He had a generalised tonic–clonic seizure one week ago. On examination his temperature is 40 °C, he has right-sided crepitations and his chest X-ray shows a right middle lobe infiltration. Which one of the following options is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Pneumonia due to anaerobes
Anaerobic pleuropulmonary infections include aspiration pneumonia, necrotising pneumonitis, lung abscess and empyema, as well as infection secondary to bronchiectasis and bronchial carcinoma. The anaerobes involved in these infections are the oropharyngeal commensals. Anaerobic pleuropulmonary infection usually results from oropharyngeal aspiration, but occasionally from haematogenous seeding. Patients with an anaerobic lung abscess will usually admit to the revolting taste (as well as smell) of their sputum. Definitive bacteriological diagnosis of anaerobic pleuropulmonary infection usually requires culture of an invasive specimen, obtained either by bronchoscopy or percutaneous transthoracic aspiration.

Pneumonia due to Gram-positive aerobes
Pneumonia due to Gram-positive aerobes is incorrect. This list includes streptococci, and staphylococci, the history of tonic–clonic seizure followed by probable aspiration counts against these as potential causes.

stem: A 76-year-old woman, who is generally fit and lives independently, is admitted with an acute exacerbation of her chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She has been put on bronchodilator therapy. One hour after admission she remains distressed, with a respiratory rate of 30/min and is peripherally cyanosed. Repeated arterial blood gases show a severe respiratory acidosis. The report of her latest arterial blood gas is: pH 7.25, Pao 2 6.5 kPa, Paco 2 9.8 kPa. She is on 28% oxygen. She is becoming exhausted and her oxygen saturation is 76%. The on-call intensivist says that there are no intensive care beds available for mechanical ventilation. Which of the following management options is correct for a patient in such a situation?
options: Continue with bronchodilator therapy and arrange repeat arterial gases in 1 hour
Give an intravenous infusion of aminophylline
Intubate the patient at the bedside and ventilate manually
Transfer her to another hospital with a mechanical ventilation facility
explanation:
Arrange for non-invasive, positive-pressure ventilation
Enhancing ventilation by unloading fatigued ventilatory muscles is an important goal in treating such acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Non-invasive, positive-pressure ventilation (NIPPV), in the form of BPAP is particularly helpful in patients with acute hypercapnic respiratory failure. It should, therefore, be considered when there is a need for ventilatory assistance in COPD patients. NIPPV has been shown to reduce intubation rates, lower hospital mortality rates and lead to shorter hospital stays.

Transfer her to another hospital with a mechanical ventilation facility
Transfer her to another hospital with a mechanical ventilation facility is incorrect. This lady isChat toowith unwell for ambulance transfer. It is more appropriate to administer immediate treatment with NIPPV.

stem: A 56-year-old retired man who smoked was diagnosed with smear-positive Mycobacterium tuberculosis. He used to work as a stonemason. Which occupational lung disease is most likely to predispose this patient to mycobacterium tuberculosis infection?
explanation:
Silicosis
Stonemasons, fettlers, slate miners and slate workers are at risk of developing silicosis. Silica acts as a toxin to macrophages, so impairing their function. This results in an increased risk of contracting a Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.

Berylliosis
Berylliosis is incorrect. Berylliosis is associated with exposure to beryllium which may occur in professions associated with primary production, metal machining and reclaiming scrap alloys. Uses of beryllium include the manufacture of nuclear reactors and weapons, X-ray tube windows, spark plugs, electrical components, aircraft parts, welding and electronics.

stem: As the medical FY2 on call you are summoned to the Emergency Department to see a 25-year-old man whose condition has suddenly deteriorated. He arrived about 45 minutes earlier with a 2-hour history of central, pleuritic-type chest pain and breathlessness. He collapsed while waiting to go to the Radiology Department. He is now agitated and cyanosed. His pulse is 128 bpm and his BP is 76/40 mmHg. The oxygen saturation reading is 76% with the patient breathing high-flow oxygen via a rebreathing mask. On respiratory examination you hear reduced breath sounds in the right lung field and there is deviation of the trachea towards the left. On percussion it is resonant bilaterally. What immediate course of action should you take?
options: Ask for an urgent portable chest X-ray
Check his arterial blood gases and start nebulisation with salbutamol
Contact the Intensive Care Unit for urgent mechanical ventilation
Insert a large-bore needle into the left 2nd intercostal space
Insert a large-bore needle into the right 2nd intercostal space
explanation:
Insert a large-bore needle into the right 2nd intercostal space
Insertion of a large-bore needle should be attempted to reduce the pressure in the right hemithorax. If the diagnosis is correct, this will be accompanied by a loud ‘hiss’.

Insert a large-bore needle into the left 2nd intercostal space
Insert a large-bore needle into the left 2nd intercostal space is incorrect. The clinical signs are compatible with a right sided tension pneumothorax so needle decompression should be performed on the right chest

stem: A 60-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 6-month history of dyspnoea on exertion and a non-productive cough. On examination, there is clubbing and crepitations are heard at the lung bases. There is no wheeze on lung auscultation. Lung function tests show a reduced vital capacity and an increased ratio of the forced expiratory volume in 1 second to the forced vital capacity (increased FEV 1/FVC). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
This is a classical history of interstitial lung disease. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), previously known as cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis (CFA), is a progressive and usually fatal disease of unknown cause characterised by sequential acute lung injury with subsequent scarring and end-stage lung disease. It may occur in any decade of life but it is most commonly seen between the ages of 50 and 60 years; it is slightly more common in males. Clinical features: A history of progressive breathlessness on exertion in the absence of wheeze is typical A dry cough might be present, but sputum production is unusual until the later stages of the disease Constitutional symptoms such as weight loss and lethargy can occur Haemoptysis is uncommon, but should suggest the development of lung malignancy – people with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis have a seven- to 14-fold increased risk of developing lung cancer Chest pain is uncommon

stem: A 42-year-old man presents to the Respiratory Clinic with very poorly controlled asthma despite therapy with high-dose Seretide and oral monteleukast. He is using a salbutamol inhaler up to once every 10 days, taking multiple puffs per day and waking up to three times per night because of coughing. He also has problems with sinusitis, which has not so far responded to intranasal corticosteroids. On examination his BP is 135/72 mmHg; pulse is 80/min and regular. There is quiet wheeze on auscultation of the chest. You note livedo reticularis on skin examination. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 10.3 × 10 9/l 4–11 x 10 9/l Platelets 191 × 10 9/l 150–400 x 10 9/l Eosinophils 2.1 × 10 9/l 0-0.4 x 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 102 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 67 mm/1 st hour 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Chest X-Ray Patchy pulmonary infiltrates Urine Blood +, protein + Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
The picture of resistant asthma, coupled with peripheral blood eosinophilia >10% and sinusitis is typical of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. 30-60% of patients with Churg Strauss are pANCA positive.

Goodpasture syndrome
Goodpasture syndrome is incorrect. Goodpasture is associated with pulmonary haemorrhage and significant renal disease.

Idiopathic asthma
Idiopathic asthma is incorrect. The information given here suggests there is an underlying multisystem disorder causing this patient’s symptoms. There is respiratory, renal and dermatological involvement, and the degree of eosinophilia is more marked than you would expect to see in a case of idiopathic asthma.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
Systemic lupus erythematosus is incorrect. SLE is associated with joint disease and symptoms of asthma are not a prominent feature.

stem: Which of the following cell types is the most important antigen-presenting cell during sensitisation?
explanation:
Dendritic cells
The dendritic cell is a key antigen-presenting cell. After uptake of antigen, it migrates from the site of antigen uptake to the regional draining lymph node, where it presents processed antigen to T cells, stimulating either proliferation of established memory cells or differentiation of naive T cells reactive to the antigen presented.

Eosinophils
Eosinophils is incorrect. Eosinophils are not antigen-presenting cells. The most important antigen-presenting cell during sensitistation is the dendritic cell.

Neutrophils
Neutrophils is incorrect. Neutrophils are not antigen-presenting cells. The most important antigen-presenting cell during sensitisation is the dendritic cell.

stem: A 56-year-old alcoholic is admitted to the Emergency Department with a pyrexia and cough productive of green sputum. He admits to drinking around 8 pints of cider per day and an unspecified amount of gin. He has been admitted on a number of occasions with decreased consciousness and once previously with aspiration pneumonia. On examination, he is pyrexial (38.2 °C), with a blood pressure of 105/60 mmHg, and has bilateral coarse breath sounds and crackles on auscultation. Investigation: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 12.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 245 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 140 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l The chest X-ray shows cavitating lesions in the upper lobes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Klebsiella
Klebsiella pneumonia is more common in patients with a history of alcoholism and the typical picture is one of cavitating lesions predominantly affecting the upper lobes, as seen here. Third-generation cephalosporins or quinolones are used as standard therapy for Klebsiella infection. Klebsiella pneumonia has a mortality rate of up to 50%, and patients who respond poorly to therapy are at increased risk of lung abscess formation.

Legionella
Legionella is incorrect. Legionella does not usually cause cavitating pneumonia.

Mycoplasma
Mycoplasma is incorrect. Mycoplasma does not usually cause cavitating pneumonia.

Pneumococcus
Pneumococcus is incorrect. Pneumococcus does not usually cause cavitating pneumonia.

Tuberculosis
Tuberculosis is incorrect. Tuberculosis is the main differential diagnosis here but the history described is classical of Klebsiella pneumonia (alcohol dependence, history of decreased consciousness with aspiration and upper lobe cavitation).

stem: A 71-year-old man comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. He has a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) managed with high-dose Seretide and tiotropium, and right heart failure for which he takes ramipril and bumetanide. He has an exercise tolerance of 80 m and has had two COPD exacerbations in the past year. On examination his BP is 135/85 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. Auscultation reveals bilateral poor air entry and wheeze. He has bilateral pitting oedema to just above the ankles. His BMI is 23. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 138 g/l 135 - 175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 9.3 × 10 9/l 4 - 11 x 10 9/l Platelets 189 × 10 9/l 150 - 400 x 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO 3 -) 32 mmol/l 24 - 30 mmol/l Creatinine 122 μmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l pH 7.44 7.35 - 7.45 pO 2 7.8 kPa (7.7 kPa 3 months earlier) 10.5 - 13.5 kPa pCO 2 6.5 kPa 4.6 - 6.0 kPa Which of the following is the most important argumentation justifying prescription of long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) in this patient?
options: pCO2 6.5 kPa and right heart failure
pO2 7.8 kPa and right heart failure
Presence of right heart failure irrespective of pO2
explanation:
pO2 7.8 kPa and right heart failure
O 2 is the main driver for LTOT prescription. Guidelines state that LTOT should be offered to patients with PaO 2 less than 7.3 kPa when stable, or greater than 7.3 kPa and less than 8 kPa when stable, who also have secondary polycythaemia, peripheral oedema, nocturnal hypoxaemia or pulmonary hypertension. CO 2 retention is a driver for pulmonary hypertension, and the presence of right heart failure allows the less stringent threshold for O 2 prescription to be used, as here.

Exercise tolerance 80 m
Exercise tolerance 80 m is incorrect. Although exercise tolerance is associated with poorer prognosis, it is not a driver for oxygen prescription.

pCO2 6.5 kPa and right heart failure
pCO 2 6.5 kPa and right heart failure is incorrect. It is the degree of hypoxia, not hypercapneoa that dictates the need for long-term oxygen therapy.

Presence of right heart failure irrespective of pO2
Presence of right heart failure irrespective of pO 2 is incorrect. LTOT only confers a survival benefit in patients with right heart failure with a pO 2 < 8 kPa when stable. It would therefore be inappropriate to prescribe LTOT in a patient with a pO 2 greater than this, even in the presence of heart failure.

stem: A 19-year-old army cadet is admitted to hospital with cough, headaches and malaise. He has a temperature of 38°C. His blood count and renal and liver function are normal. Cold agglutinins are positive. A chest X-ray shows bibasal shadowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Mycoplasma pneumonia
Mycoplasma pneumonia is a common cause of pneumonia, often occurring in young people. It is characterised by headaches, malaise and cough. The chest X-ray findings might not correlate with the patient’s condition. The white blood count can be normal and cold agglutinins occur in only half of patients. Extrapulmonary complications Pericarditis Myocarditis Erythema multiforme Vomiting Diarrhoea Meningo-encephalitis

stem: A 50-year-old man patient was referred by his GP because of a long-standing history of persistent cough productive of mucopurulent sputum. He also noticed increasing shortness of breath. The patient has been treated several times for recurrent chest infections. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bronchiectasis
Bronchiectasis should be suspected when there is a history of persistent cough productive of mucopurulent or purulent sputum throughout the year. Patients have frequently been treated for recurrent chest infections and labelled as ‘bronchitic’, often despite the absence of a history of smoking. Patients can produce mucoid sputum early in their disease, developing purulent sputum when they suffer an exacerbation associated with a viral upper respiratory tract infection. Such exacerbations can be associated with pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, fever and sometimes wheeze. People who present as adults often recall a chesty cough or wheezy bronchitis associated with upper respiratory tract infections in childhood, followed by complete resolution of symptoms in their teens and early adult life before these return after a viral trigger. Upper respiratory tract symptoms such as nasal drip are common, and in about 30% of cases there is a history of chronic sinusitis. Patients with bronchiectasis also suffer from undue tiredness, which many find more troublesome than the productive cough.

stem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review 4 weeks after discharge from the ward following an asthma attack. She was diagnosed with asthma at the age of 7 years and has been taking inhaled beclometasone 400 μg daily and salbutamol as required since then. She tells you that since discharge she has been using her salbutamol three times a day and has been waking two or three times a night with coughing. On examination, her peak flow is 340 l (predicted is 570 l). She has scattered wheeze throughout both lung fields on examination. She had a good inhaler technique with volumatic as assessed in the clinic. Investigation: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.5 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 231 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 12 mm in 1 hour 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 80 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l The chest X-ray shows no evidence of consolidation. Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan for her according to NICE guidelines?
options: Add low-dose oral theophylline to her regimen
Add oral montelukast to her regimen
Add twice-daily inhaled salmeterol to her regimen
Change her to 800 μg of fluticasone
explanation:
Add oral montelukast to her regimen
Under NICE guidelines, a trial of montelukast, a leukotriene receptor antagonist, is recommended in an attempt to gain control of asthma symptoms. This should be reviewed 1 to 2 months later and, in the event that this trial fails, or a long-acting beta agonist is the next step.

Add low-dose oral theophylline to her regimen
Add low-dose oral theophylline to her regimen is incorrect. Low-dose oral theophylline is a final option in the standard medical management of asthma.

Add omalizumab
Add omalizumab is incorrect. Omalizumab, an anti-IgE antibody, is reserved for patients with severe allergic asthma in whom other treatments have been unsuccessful and require at least four acute courses of corticosteroids per year.

Add twice-daily inhaled salmeterol to her regimen
Add twice-daily inhaled salmeterol to her regimen is incorrect. A LABA is only recommended in the event that a trial of a leukotriene receptor antagonist fails. This is in contrast to previous BTS guidelines.

Change her to 800 μg of fluticasone
Change her to 800 μg of fluticasone is incorrect. Fluticasone is twice as potent as beclomethasone, so this option is doubling the amount of steroid medication. Increasing to a moderate or high dose steroid could be considered after a trial of a leukotriene receptor antagonist and the addition of salmeterol.

stem: A 24-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-week history of worsening shortness of breath and a non-productive cough. He has a past medical history of human immunodeficiency virus and reports reduced compliance with his antiretroviral medication. On examination, he has oxygen saturations of 94% on air. His chest is clear on auscultation and his heart sounds are normal. A chest X-ray shows bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
options: Oral rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol and pyrazinamide
explanation:
Intravenous co-trimoxazole
This patient has Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (previously known as Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia), which typically presents with gradually increasing dyspnoea and cough over several weeks, although sometimes it presents as an acute illness with rapid deterioration over a few days. Chest X-ray usually shows diffuse ground-glass opacities, which strongly suggests the diagnosis. Sometimes, however, it shows nodular opacities or lobar consolidation, or can even be normal. Lactate dehydrogenase is raised in approximately 90% of patients with P. jirovecii pneumonia and it is unlikely for a patient to have CD4 count of above 200 cells/mm3 in the preceding two months in the absence of other HIV-associated symptoms. Recommended treatment is with co-trimoxazole therapy. Intravenous pentamidine can be given in severe cases and steroids may be introduced if the patient is hypoxic.

stem: An obese 40-year-old woman with a history of asthma presents with progressive breathlessness. On examination she has a raised jugular venous pressure, ankle oedema, right parasternal heave and a murmur consistent with tricuspid regurgitation. Chest auscultation is clear. You understand from her husband that she has had progressively worsening symptoms over the past year. He has noticed that she has had particular problems with snoring and stopping breathing at night since he met her. Arterial blood gas results show: pH 7.39, Po 2 7.3 kPa (normal range 11.3–12.6 kPa), Pco 2 4.9 kPa (4.7–6.0 kPa). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Secondary pulmonary hypertension
The history of snoring is suggestive of sleep apnoea. Sleep apnoea is known to result in chronic nocturnal hypoxia, which in turn leads to pulmonary artery vasoconstriction. Eventually cor pulmonale develops, which is seen here.Treatment for this woman is likely to involve aggressive attempts to lose weight and nocturnal ventilatory support, probably using continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) ventilation.

Atrial septal defect
Atrial septal defect is incorrect. Atrial septal defects can cause pulmonary hypertension, but patients would usually have a younger age at presentation. On auscultation split 1st and particularly 2nd heart sounds are often heard and an ejection systolic murmur is heard when moderate to large left to right shunts develop.

stem: A 43-year-old patient with rheumatoid arthritis has been referred to you because of increasing shortness of breath and dry cough. Which medication is most likely to be responsible for her symptoms?
explanation:
Methotrexate
Methotrexate is an effective and moderately toxic disease-modifying anti-rheumatoid drug (DMARD). Pulmonary complications, in the form of pneumonitis (inflammation of the lung), are rare idiosyncratic reactions and are potentially lethal. The classical presentation is with rapid onset dyspnoea (shortness of breath), which may result in death after a few days. Therefore, patients should be advised to stop methotrexate if they experience dyspnoea or cough and to seek immediate medical attention.

Gold
Gold is incorrect. Gold has been superceded by newer and less toxic DMARDs. Side-effects from gold include dermatitis, stomatitis, haematuria, proteinuria including nephrotic syndrome and blood dyscrasias. Cases of pulmonary toxicity have been reported in the literature, but are relatively rare.

Ibuprofen
Ibuprofen is incorrect. Ibuprofen is not associated with pulmonary toxicity.

stem: A 35-year-old woman who has recently started work in a soldering plant where electronic components are assembled comes to the Respiratory Clinic complaining of episodic cough and wheezing, particularly on the days when she is at work. She smokes 5–10 cigarettes /day. She comes to the clinic on her third day off shift. Her BP is 122/72 mmHg; pulse is 70/min and regular. Her chest is clear with no obvious wheeze. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 22 mm/1 st hour 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 92 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR) 510 (590 predicted) Chest X-Ray Normal Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Serial peak flows
The history is consistent with occupational asthma, occurring as a result of exposure to solder flux, which may contain colophony. The optimal investigation is serial peak flows because it is important to demonstrate that airflow obstruction is related to exposure to the allergen, especially given the history of tobacco use. Very strict rules are laid down by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) with respect to colophony exposure, and in parallel to confirmation of the diagnosis by peak flow examination, an evaluation of protection measures for staff at the plant is also advised. If occupational asthma is confirmed, then patch testing to confirm the reaction to solder is advised, and she should ideally be transferred to another area of the plant or provided with measures to minimise exposure to solder fumes.

Bronchoscopy
Bronchoscopy is incorrect. Bronchoscopy is not indicated in the investigation of occupational asthma.

Colophony challenge
Colophony challenge is incorrect. Colophony challenge may be indicated/performed if serial peak flow readings are in keeping with a diagnosis of occupational asthma.

IgE testing for colophony
IgE testing for colophony is incorrect. IgE testing for colophony may be indicated/performed if serial peak flow readings are in keeping with a diagnosis of occupational asthma.

Skin prick testing for colophony
Skin prick testing for colophony is incorrect. Skin prick testing may be indicated/performed if serial peak flow readings are in keeping with a diagnosis of occupational asthma.
